> Magha, Saṃvat 1963, Śaka 1828. All rights, including those concerning further printing and so forth, have been reserved by the author. Introduction: The science of astrology (Jyotiḥśāstra), consisting of the three branches of Siddhānta, Saṃhitā, and Horā, is said to be the eye of the Veda.

Just as the auspicious and inauspicious objects of the world can be seen only with the eyes, so too the adoption and rejection of auspicious and inauspicious actions ordained by the Vedas—such as which action should be performed at what time and when it should not be performed, and in what manner it should be done—is accomplished through the "eye" of the science of astrology (*jyotiṣa*).

Just as a man with eyes, seeing thorns, mud, and other obstacles lying on a path, is able to protect himself from them, so too one who understands astrology, by knowing all auspicious and inauspicious actions, can remain happy through the performance of auspicious deeds.

When a person, having taken birth in this mortal world, accomplishes even those deeds difficult for the gods to achieve by performing the highest actions, what wise man, having come to such an excellent realm, would fail to strive for his own spiritual elevation?

Reflecting thus, the great sage Nārada, who by his very nature is a benefactor to all living beings, composed the three-part treatise on astrology (*jyotiḥśāstra*) for the welfare of mankind; among these, this third part, the *Horāskandha*, is renowned by the name *Nāradasaṃhitā*.

This work contains numerous topics, including: the introduction to the scriptures; the movements of the planets; the protection against the year-long planetary influences (*abdarakṣaṇa*); the results of the year (*saṃvatsaraphala*); lunar days (*tithi*), weekdays (*vāra*), asterisms (*nakṣatra*), planetary conjunctions (*yoga*), and auspicious moments (*muhūrta*); eclipses (*upagraha*); solar transits (*saṅkrānti*); the transit of the planets (*grahagocara*); the chapter on the strength of the moon and stars (*candratārābalādhyāya*); considerations regarding the ascendant (*lagnavicāra*); considerations regarding the first appearance of menses; the sixteen sacraments (*saṃskāra*) from conception (*garbhādhāna*) to marriage; oaths (*pratijñā*); journeys (*yātrā*); house-entry (*gṛhapraveśa*); immediate rain (*sadyovṛṣṭi*); the characteristics of the cosmic tortoise (*kūrmalakṣaṇa*); portents (*utpāta*); propitiatory rites (*śānti*), and so forth. (4) [End of] the Introduction.

The description of useful rites has been composed in thirty-five chapters through simple and grand verses. Who does not know the greatness of the divine sage Nārada? Just as a yogi is a knower of wisdom, so too is he great by virtue of the majesty of his knowledge of reality; he has placed many profound subjects within this *Nāradasaṃhitā* composed by himself. Furthermore, many other excellent works on astrology (*jyotiṣa*) are currently extant.

However, this Nārada Saṃhitā is a work of the Ṛṣis (Ārṣa Grantha). Its status as a Vedāṅga is indeed authentic. Although it is easy to understand, the scripture becomes difficult in certain places due to the profundity of its subject matter. Realizing that the general public might not be able to properly grasp its entire intent, we have had a vernacular commentary composed by Paṇḍita Vasatirāma Jyotirvid, a resident of Berī-Āman, thereby making this Saṃhitā beautiful.

Having had it printed on high-quality paper and bound in an excellent cover, it has been prepared; it is hoped that people, by studying this work, will benefit themselves as well as others. ॥ Śrīḥ ॥ Now begins the Table of Contents for the Bhāṣā-Ṭīkā of the Nārada-saṃhitā. && ihaCC®ī (Note: The provided source text appears to be a mix of Hindi and Devanagari script with some typographical artifacts. Now begins the Nāradasaṃhitā, together with its commentary in the vernacular: Smaller than the smallest, directly the Lord, greater than the greatest, the Self hidden in the cave of the living being—He who transcends the senses is victorious! (1)

The Supreme Self—who is subtler than the subtlest and greater than the greatest, and who is beyond the senses, meaning not perceivable by any sense organ such as the eyes—resides in the inner organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) of the living being in a state of supreme excellence; He is the manifest Supreme Lord. Vasiṣṭha, Atri, Manu, Paulastya, Lomaśa, Marīci, Aṅgiras, Vyāsa, Nārada, Śaunaka, and Bhṛgu were celibate students (*brahmacārins*). 2.

Balājī, Ācārya Vasiṣṭha, Atri, Manu, Pailastya, Lomaśa, Marīci, Aṅgiras, Vedavyāsa, Nārada, Śaunaka, and Bhṛgu. (2) Cyavana, Yavana, Garga, Kaśyapa, and Parāśara—these eighteen profound scholars were the originators of the science of astrology (jyotiḥśāstra). (3) Cyavana, the teacher Yavana, Garga, Kaśyapa, and Parāśara—these eighteen became the profound pioneers of the science of astrology. (3)
The Siddhānta, Saṃhitā, and Horā constitute the three-fold form of this stainless eye of the Veda, the infinite science of light known as Jyotiḥśāstra. (3)
This treatise is said to be the supreme science of astrology (Jyotiḥśāstra), which is like a pure eye and possesses three divisions (skandhas) consisting of Siddhānta, Saṃhitā, and Horā. 4.
The connection of this treatise is stated to be that it is an auxiliary limb (aṅga) of the Veda.
And the subject matter is the determination of the auspicious and inauspicious aspects of the world.
This science of astrology is called a Vedāṅga; it describes the auspicious and inauspicious conditions of the world. (5)
Of sacrifices, Vedic study, the passage of the sun into a new zodiacal sign, and the sixteen sacramental rites;
And the purpose [of this] is to be understood through the determination of each respective time. 6.

The determination of the authentic timing (muhūrta) for sacrifices, Vedic study, auspicious periods such as the *saṃkrānti*, and the sixteen sacraments (*ṣoḍaśakarma*) occurs solely through the science of astrology (*jyotiḥśāstra*). 6.
Without all of this, the ritual acts prescribed by the Śruti and the Smṛti do not succeed.
Therefore, this was composed by Brahmā in ancient times for the welfare of the world.

Without this, the rituals described in the entirety of the Śrutis and Smṛtis cannot be accomplished; therefore, Brahmā first composed the science of astrology (Jyotiḥśāstra) for the sake of the world's success. (7)
Then, having beheld him, his son Nārada, the best of sages, [acted].
Having first spoken of the two divisions, he [then spoke of] the supreme Saṃhitā division.
Upon seeing her, the sage Nārada, the son of Bālājī, first fashioned a heap of wood. || 8 ||
I shall speak for the purpose of making known the auspicious and inauspicious fruits for those who possess bodies.
For the sake of establishing the practical application of the treatise on the *Horā* section.

Furthermore, for the sake of knowing the auspicious and inauspicious results pertaining to the body and its nourishment, this branch of the *Horā-skandha* is explained for the purpose of establishing practical application. (9)

Having correctly understood all the designations individually as they have been declared, [one should study] the chapter on the introduction to the scriptures, the motion of the planets, and the characteristics of the year. || 10 ||
The lunar day, the weekday, the asterism, and the conjunction known as the combination of the lunar day and the asterism.
The Muhūrta-upagraha of the Sun, as well as its Saṃkrānti and Gocara.

In this [work], distinct designations have been clearly explained: the chapter on the introduction of the treatise (śāstropadeśa), which describes the intent of this scripture; the description of planetary movements (grahacāra); the results of the years (saṃvatsara);
and the conjunctions (yoga) occurring swiftly through the combination of lunar days (tithi), weekdays (vāra), and asterisms (nakṣatra).

The section on the Muhūrta for Inauguration (Inhoṃkā), the section on Planetary Aspects (Upagraha), the results of the Sun’s Transit (Sūryasaṃkrāntiphala), and the Planetary Course (Grahabhāvaphala). ॥ 10 ॥ ॥ 11 ॥
This is the chapter on the strength of the Moon and the stars, known as "The Strength of All Ascendants and Seasons.
It covers conception, the male-impregnation rite (puṃsavana), the parting of the hair (sīmantonnayana), birth, naming, and the first feeding of solid food.
The chapter on observing the strength of the moon and stars; the consideration of all *lagnas*; first, the consideration regarding menstruation;
*ādhāna*, *puṃsavana*, *sīmantonnayana*, *jātakarma*, naming ceremony (*nāmakaraṇa*), and the first feeding of solid food (*annaprāśana*). 12.
The offering of the caulāṅkura and the binding of the mauñjī and the churikā are performed in due order.
The rites of returning home, marriage, consecration, and the characteristics of a dwelling. || 13 ||

The Caulakarma, the offering of auspicious sprouts (maṅgalāṅkurārpaṇa), the Mauñjībaṃdhana, and the Churikābaṃdhana are all described in their proper sequence; furthermore, the Samāvartanaka-rma, the Vivāhaka-rma, the Pratiṣṭhāka-rma, and the characteristics of houses (gṛhalakṣaṇa). || 13 ||
The journey, the entry, the immediate rain, and the characteristics of the tortoise diagram.
The characteristics of sudden outbursts, those mixed with tranquility, and the characteristics of faith. 14.

The chapter on journeys, the auspicious moment for entering [a city], immediate rain, the characteristics of the tortoise, the characteristics of portents, [the section] on pacification rites, the miscellaneous chapter, and the characteristics of ancestral rites (śrāddha). 14.
The Saṃhitā known as the Nāradīya consists of thirty-seven chapters.
He who recites this with devotion is indeed an astrologer, a knower of destiny.

Through these topics, this Nārada Saṃhitā has been composed in thirty-seven chapters; he who reads it with the sentiment of devotion (bhakti-rasa) becomes a knower of the Divine, like a celestial being. || 15 ||

One who knows the three Vedas, is handsome, devoted to the rituals prescribed by the Śruti and Smṛti, free from hypocrisy, truthful, a knower of astrology, and steadfast in his divine destiny. || 16 ||
Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Introduction of the Scripture," in the glorious Nāradīya-saṃhitā. 3.

One who knows the three divisions (skandhas), is worthy of being seen, performs the duties prescribed by the Śruti and Smṛti, is free from hypocrisy, is truthful, and understands destiny— such a person is a steady astrologer (daivajña). || 16 ||
Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Introduction to the Scripture," in the *Śrī Nāradasaṃhitā-bhāṣā*. 1.
In the months beginning with Caitra as well, the transits [of the sun] into Aries and the other signs occur in their respective order.
The lord of the lunar day (tithi) and the weekday beginning with Caitra is the sovereign of that year. || 1 ||

In these months beginning with Caitra, the solar transits (*saṃkrānti*) of Aries and the others occur in their respective order; and whichever day of the week falls on the first lunar day (*pratipadā*) of the bright fortnight of Caitra, that is called the king of the year. (1) The lord of the weekday of the Aries transit shall also be the sovereign of the earth. However, the lord of the weekday of Cancer is the lord of the crops; from that, the results [are determined]. (2) Furthermore, whichever weekday occurs at the time of the Aries transit, he becomes the commander-in-chief (*senāpati*). Whichever weekday occurs at the time of the Cancer transit, he becomes the lord of the harvest (*sasyapati*). (2)

The lord of the weekday on which the Libra transit (tulā-saṃkrānti) occurs is known as the lord of liquids (rasa). Likewise, the weekday of the Capricorn transit (makara-saṃkrānti) is directly the lord of the "dry" (nīrasa), being the master of gold and other minerals, as well as of garments and such, in due order. (3) If the Sun is the lord of the year (abdeśvara), or the commander of the army (camūpa), or the lord of the crops (sasyeśa), then in that year there will be royal wrath, resulting in little grain, high prices, and scanty rain.

4. If the ruler of the year (the king), or the commander-in-chief (the minister), or the lord of the crops (the Sun) is [the planet occupying the ascendant], then in that year there will be anger among kings, little cultivation, high prices for food, and scanty rain. 5. If the lord of the year, or the commander-in-chief, or the lord of the crops (the Moon) is [the planet occupying the ascendant], in that year the earth becomes filled with rice, fruits, and sugarcane.

If the Moon is the lord of the year, the commander-in-chief, or the lord of the crops, then in that year the earth shall be filled with wheat, rice, and other grains, as well as sugarcane and the like. (5) According to the *Nāradasaṃhitā*: "If Mars is the lord of the year, the commander of the army, or the lord of the crops, then in that year he always causes fear from thieves, fire, drought, and hunger. (6)

If the ruler of the year, the ruler of the month, or the lord of the crops is Mars (Maṅgala), there will be fear of thieves and fire in that year; there will be no rain and a famine will occur. (6) If the ruler of the year or the ruler of the month is Mercury (Śaśāṅkaja), or the lord of the crops is Mercury, he causes excessive wind, scanty rain, and conflict among kings. (7) If the ruler of the year, the ruler of the month, or the lord of the crops is Mercury (Budha), there will be extreme winds, little rain, and war among kings. (7)

If the ruler of the year, the commander of the army, or the lord of the harvest is Venus (the son of Bhṛgu), he makes the earth most excellent through sacrifices, grain, wealth, and rain. (8) If the ruler of the year, the commander of the army, or the lord of the harvest is Jupiter, he makes the earth completely full with rice, fruits, and sugarcane. (9)

If the king or the minister, as well as the lord of the crops (Śukra), be Venus, the earth will be filled with rice, grain, sugarcane, and the like. || 9 || If the lord of the year, the commander of the army, or the lord of the crops (Saturn) be Saturn, there will be fear from death, thieves, fire, water, grain, and kings. || 10 || If the king or the minister, as well as the lord of men or the lord of the crops (Śani), be Saturn, there will be famine and fear from thieves, fire, water, grain, and kings. || 10 ||

Having correctly understood the relative strength and weakness [of the planets], one should declare the determination of the results. When the solar disc is seen in the shape of a staff, or pierced like a crow’s beak, or in the form of a stake (11), there is disease, fear, and the loss of wealth and property. When it appears with forms such as umbrellas, banners, flags, or dark masses of smoke (12), there is the destruction of people. By those [spots] which are white, red, yellow, black, or variegated, [the destruction of] the Brahmins and other castes [is foretold] (13).

Having observed all such strengths and weaknesses, one should declare the results for the year. Now, the results of the Sun's transit (sūryacāra) are described: if a piercing (vedha) appears in the form of a staff, a crow, or a stake within the Sun, then affliction, fear, thieves, and the destruction of wealth—these calamities shall occur. Furthermore, if an umbrella, a banner, a flag, or similar objects appear as darkness within the solar disc, or if it appears like a smoke-colored cloud or as if surrounded by flames, then there will be the destruction of men.

If the rays of the sun appear white, red, yellow, black, or mixed together, there will be the destruction of Brahmā and the other [deities] in that respective order. (11, 12, 13) Or, if they appear by twos, threes, or fours, there is the destruction of the king or the common people. If the rays of the sun are copper-colored and directed upwards, that sovereign shall meet his end. (14)

If rays of two, three, or four colors are seen mingled together, there will be the destruction of kings; if other such evil omens occur, there will be the destruction of the subjects. If the rays of the sun spread upwards with a color like that of copper, there will be the destruction of the king. (14) By yellow rays, a prince [is foretold]; by white, the domestic priest; by variegated, the people; by smoky, the king; and by tawny and downward-pointing rays, a cloud [of calamity]. (19)

If it is yellowish-brown (*pīlavarṇa*), there will be the destruction of the king’s son; if it is white, the king’s domestic priest (*purohita*) shall perish; if it is a mixture of many colors, there will be the destruction of the subjects; and if it is smoky (*dhūmra*), [the same result follows]. (Nāradasaṃhitā, Chapter 6, Verse 8) If rays of light from a color or a mass of color are seen directed downward from the clouds, the king shall perish. (Verse 15) At the times of sunrise and sunset, [an auspicious sign is] when they resemble pale-white (*pāṇḍu*). In the cool season (*śiśira*), the sun may appear copper-colored or even tawny (*kāpila*). (Verse 16)

If at the time of rising or setting the sun possesses a whitish-yellow radiance, or if the sun is copper-red or of a tawny hue, it is said to be auspicious during the winter season. || 16 || A saffron-colored or even a tawny sun is praised in the spring; one that is not pale but golden-hued is auspicious in summer, and one of variegated color at the onset of the rains. || 17 ||

In the spring season, a red or tawny color like that of a saffron filament is auspicious; in the summer (heat) season, a red color like gold is auspicious; and in the rainy season, a variegated color is said to be auspicious. || 17 || In autumn, it has the luster of the interior of a lotus; in winter, it has a reddish hue. [A halo] appearing in winter, the rainy season, or summer causes fear of diseases. || 18 ||

In the autumn season, it resembles the center of a lotus; in the winter, a red color is auspicious. If it is red during the rainy season, summer, or winter, disease will arise and there will be no rain. || 18 || If the sun appears yellowish, black, or red in succession, or if it has the form of half a rainbow, it causes opposition between kings. || 19 ||

Furthermore, if a rainbow appears with three colors in this sequence—yellow, black, and then red—or if these colors are seen reflected in the sun, there will be war among kings. (19) [In the Bhāṣāṭīkā, Chapter 2 (9): "If [the sun] resembles a peacock's feather, it does not rain for twelve years; if the sun resembles the blood of a rabbit, a battle will indeed occur before long. (20)

If the sun appears with a color like the wings of a peacock, there will be no rain for twelve years; if it becomes red like the blood of a hare, war will soon occur. (20) Where [the sun] resembles the moon, one should predict another king; if the sun is dark, there is danger from insects; if it has the appearance of ashes, there is danger from weapons. (21)

If the color is like that of the moon, there will be the kingdom of another king; if the color is like a digit [of the moon], there is fear of insects, serpents, and the like among the subjects; if the color is like ashes, there will be the danger of weapons (war). || 21 || When a hole is seen in the solar disc, then there is the destruction of the king; a shape like a water-pot causes fear of famine; a shape like an archway destroys the city. || 22 ||

If a hole is seen in the solar disc, there will be the destruction of kings; if it appears in the shape of a jar, there will be fear of famine; and if it takes the form of an archway (toraṇa), the city (nagara) will be destroyed. || 22 || A shape like an umbrella (chatra) is the destroyer of the country, while a fragmented sun brings about the end of the king. If lightning, meteors, or thunderbolts appear at the rising or setting of the sun, || 23 ||

If the form resembles an umbrella, the country will be ruined; if the sun appears fragmented, the king will perish. If at the time of sunrise or sunset a star falls or lightning strikes, then the death of the king should be known, or else there will be a conflict between kings. If birds circle the sun and moon for half a fortnight, day and night, [the same result follows]. || 23-24 ||

If the king perishes or there is a civil war in the kingdom, the solar and lunar orbs will remain continuously joined day and night for fifteen days or seven days. (24) [10] *Nāradasaṃhitā*: "The two red orbs at sunrise and sunset cause another king to be made; at sunrise and sunset, the sun is severed by weapons resembling blades. Clouds formed like donkeys, camels, and other evil forms bring fear; the sun appearing according to its seasonal nature and possessing a gentle form brings auspiciousness. (28)

26. This movement of the Sun (Ravicāra) must be correctly understood by those who know the truth. 27. Thus ends the "Movement of the Sun" (Sūryacāra) in the Śrī Nāradīya Saṃhitā. If another king's kingdom [is indicated], and at the time of sunrise or sunset the Sun or Moon appears blood-red like the color of raw flesh, then the kingdom will perish. If at the time of sunrise or sunset the Sun and Moon are covered by clouds shaped like weapons, then there will be war and [the appearance of] camels.

If the sky is covered by clouds shaped like camels and the like, there will be fear among the people; however, if the sun possesses a beautiful and clear form according to the season and the time, auspicious results will follow. In this manner, this course of the sun (sūryacara) should be properly understood from learned men. || 25 || 26 || 27 || Thus ends the "Course of the Sun" (Sūryacāra) in the Bhāṣā-Ṭīkā of the Śrī Nāradasaṃhitā. When the moon rises with its southern horn elevated during the signs of Pisces or Aries, it bestows inauspicious results.

The moon's horn is most excellent when gentle and elevated during the rising periods of Pisces and Aries; likewise, it is auspicious if the northern corner of the moon's horn is raised during Gemini and Capricorn. (1) In the [bhāṣāṭīkā], Chapter 7, Section 2: (11) During the rising periods of Cancer and Leo, the horn is even like the number of eyes (two); in Sagittarius and Virgo, it resembles an arrow (five); and in Libra and Virgo, it is thick like a trident (three). (2)

If the moon in Vṛṣabha and Kumbha is shaped like a bow; in both Mithuna and Siṃha, it is like an arrow; in Karkaṭa and Siṃha, it is at the corner; in Vṛścika and Dhanu, its form is thick; and in Tulā and Kanyā, the moon is shaped like a trident (śūla), it bestows auspiciousness. || 2 || A moon that has risen in a contrary manner brings about famine and strife; however, the moon as described above, when not risen [in such a contrary way], produces abundance of food every month. || 3 ||

If the moon rises contrary to this, it causes famine and strife; however, if its rising occurs exactly as described for each respective month, one should know it to be a harbinger of plenty. (3) When the moon moves toward the south during the two Āṣāḍhas, Mūla, and Jyeṣṭhā (Indra), it brings about fire and causes the destruction of aquatic creatures and forest serpents. (9)

If the moon moves toward the south during the asterisms of Pūrvāṣāḍhā, Uttarāṣāḍhā, Jyeṣṭhā, and Mūla, there will be danger from fire, and the destruction of aquatic creatures, forest-dwellers, and serpents. (4) When the moon is situated on the southern side of Viśākhā and Anurādhā, it always causes evil; when it is in the middle of Maghā and in the two auspicious northern asterisms (Punarvasu and Puṣya), it is favorable. (5)

If the Moon, having arrived at Viśākhā or Anurādhā as the foremost among the lunar mansions, moves toward the south, it is always inauspicious. When it is on Maghā, its movement is middling; however, when it reaches Viśākhā, the Moon moving northward is a bestower of auspiciousness. 5. Having traversed six constellations beginning from Revatī, Bhaga, and Ārdrā, the Moon is auspicious. It is middling for twelve constellations, and after passing nine from Dhanisthā (Vāsava), it is favorable. 6. (32) — Nāradasaṃhitā.

When the Moon transits the six asterisms beginning with Revatī, it is auspicious; this is stated in other texts that these six are "future" (anāgata) asterisms. That is to say, the Moon situated in Uttarābhādrapada appears upon the stars of Revatī, and for this reason it is declared auspicious. Furthermore, its transit through the twelve asterisms beginning with Ārdrā is of middling quality and auspicious. || 6 || Among these, the asterisms of Yama (Bharaṇī), Indra (Jyeṣṭhā), Ahi (Āśleṣā), Bhaga (Pūrvaphalgunī), Tvaṣṭṛ (Citrā), Īśa (Mṛgaśīrṣa), Marut (Svātī), and half of the asterism of Tāraka (Punarvasu) [are auspicious]. || 7 || [Note: The provided source text for the final line is incomplete; the translation reflects the standard astrological classification.]

The asterisms Dhruva, Aditi, Divi, and Deva consist of one and a half stars (*adhyardha*), while the others are equal (*sama*). (7) Bharaṇī, Jyeṣṭhā, Āśleṣā, Śatabhiṣā, and Svātī are the asterisms designated as "half" (*ardha*); the asterisms designated as "fixed" (*dhruva*)—Punarvasu and Viśākhā—are those designated as "one and a half" (*adhyardha*); the remaining asterisms are said to be "equal. (7) When the northern horn is elevated, it is excellent; when the southern horn is elevated, it is auspicious. During the bright fortnight, in the month of Piṣpīlikā-kara, there is decrease and increase respectively.

8. A high southern horn is excellent, and a high northern horn is also excellent. In the bright fortnight (śuklapakṣa), the moon that is ant-shaped—meaning thin in the middle—is harmful; however, in the dark fortnight (kṛṣṇapakṣa), it is a bestower of auspiciousness. If the southern horn is thick, there is loss; if the northern horn is more thick, it bestows prosperity. 8. A broad moon brings about abundance of food, while a non-broad moon causes the destruction of wealth.

If the horn [of the moon] or the orb is struck by Mars and the other planets in their respective order, the Moon causes well-being, moderate rain, and the destruction of kings and people respectively. (10) *Commentary in Bhāṣā:* If the horn or the disc of the Moon is struck by Mars and the other planets in due order, the Moon brings about security, moderate rainfall, and the ruin of kings and the populace. (10) *Bhāṣāṭīkā, Chapter 2, Section (1-3).*

Thus ends the "Motion of the Moon" (Candracāra) in the Śrī Nāradīya Saṃhitā. If the horns of the lunar disc are pierced by Mars or other planets, the results are, in order: security, destruction, loss of wealth, cessation of rain, destruction of the king, and destruction of the subjects. (10) Thus ends the "Motion of the Moon" (Candracāra) in the Bhāṣā-Ṭīkā on the Śrī Nārada Saṃhitā. When Mars, having turned retrograde from its own rising point, occupies the seventh, eighth, or ninth asterism, that retrogression is "fiery" (uṣṇa); during that time, there shall be suffering for the subjects arising from fire. (1)

If Mars is retrograde upon the seventh, eighth, or ninth lunar mansion from its own rising mansion, then as long as it remains in that mansion, there shall be suffering among the subjects and an outbreak of fire. (1) If it is retrograde in the tenth, eleventh, or twelfth mansion, there will be little happiness for the people and the destruction of the rains. (2)

2–3. If the planet is retrograde in the thirteenth or fourteenth lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*) from the rising mansion, that retrogression is called *vyāla* (the serpent). In that case, there is an increase in crops, yet there is fear of strife. (14) According to the *Nāradasaṃhitā*: If it is retrograde in the fifteenth or sixteenth mansion, that retrogression is called *rudhirānana* (blood-faced).

If Mars is retrograde in the fifteenth or sixteenth lunar mansion (nakṣatra), it is called Rudhirānana-retrograde; in that case, there will be abundance of food, yet fear and disease shall prevail. (4) Then, when Mars is retrograde in the eighteenth or seventeenth [nakṣatra], it is known as Asimusala-retrograde; in that situation, wealth and grain will be plundered by bandits. (5)

If the eighteenth or seventeenth lunar mansion (nakṣatra) is retrograde, it is named Asimusalana; there, the destruction of wealth occurs due to thieves and the like. || 5 || When Mars rises in Phālguna, moves retrograde in Vaiśvadeva, and sets in the Caturāsya constellation, it causes the destruction of the three worlds. || 6 ||

If Mars rises in the constellations of Pūrvaphālgunī or Uttarāphālgunī, becomes retrograde in Uttaraṣāḍhā, and sets in Rohiṇī, he destroys the three worlds. (6) If Mars rises in Śravaṇā and becomes retrograde in Puṣya, he causes the destruction of kings; from whichever direction Mars rises, he brings fear to the king of that region. (7)

If Mars, having risen in Śravaṇa or Puṣya, becomes retrograde, it causes the ruin of the king; in whichever direction Mars rises, the king of that direction becomes fearful. (7) Mars situated in the middle of Maghā and moving retrograde in that very place brings fear from drought and weapons, and causes the end of the ruler of the Pāṇḍu country. (8)

If Mars rises during the Maghā constellation and subsequently becomes retrograde, there will be no rain; there shall be fear of war among the subjects, and the destruction of the king of the Pāṇḍu country. (8) [From Bhāṣāṭīkā, Chapter 2] (15) If the planet born of the Earth (Mars) causes the junction-stars of the Pitṛ, Dvidaiva, and Dhātṛ constellations to be pierced, it brings about famine, death, and disease. (9)

If Mars transits the stars of Maghā, Viśākhā, or Rohiṇī, piercing their constellations, there will be famine and the great pestilence among the people. (9) When Mars moves through the three Uttaras, Rohiṇī, Svātī, Śravaṇa, or the two [asterisms] of the Moon (Mṛgaśiras and Ārdrā), there is drought; likewise, when it is situated to the south of Rohiṇī. (10)

If Mars transits through the three Uttarās, Rohiṇī, Mūla, Śravaṇa, or Mṛgaśirā, or if it is situated to the south of the star of Rohiṇī, there will be no rain. || 30 || When Mars moves toward the north of all the asterisms, it bestows auspicious results; when it goes toward the south, it yields undesirable fruits, and in the case of its piercing through them, it causes division among men. || 31 ||

If this auspicious planet (Mars) moves toward the north of all the constellations, it should be known as a giver of good fortune; however, if it moves toward the south, it is a giver of inauspiciousness. If it pierces a star, there will be war among the subjects. || 11 || Thus ends the "Motion of Mars" in the Śrī Nāradīya Saṃhitā. Without an omen (portent), the son of the Moon (Mercury) never rises [unfavorably]; yet, he causes drought, fear of fire, misfortune, and conflict with the king. || 1 ||

Thus ends the section on the motion of Mars in the *Śrī-Nāradasaṃhitā-bhāṣāṭīkā*. If Mercury does not rise at its proper time without an eclipse or other portent, there will be no rain, and there shall be fear, calamity, and war among kings. (1) If Mercury, moving through the asterisms of Dhaniṣṭhā, Śravaṇa, Uttarāṣāḍhā, Rohiṇī, and Pūrvāphālgunī, pierces those stars, it causes drought and the fear of disease. (2) (16) — *Nāradasaṃhitā*

If Mercury, while moving through the constellations Dhaniṣṭhā, Śravaṇa, Uttarāṣāḍhā, Mṛgaśirā, and Rohiṇī, should pierce these stars, there will be no rain and disease and fear will arise among the people. (2) If Mercury is seen in the constellations beginning with Ārdrā and ending with Maghā (Pitṛbhā), then it causes an increase in famine, strife, and disease, as well as fear. (3)

If Mercury remains stationed from the asterism Ārdrā up to Maghā and pierces these stars, then there will be famine, strife, and an increase in disease; fear shall prevail among the people. (3) When Mercury moves through the asterisms beginning with Hasta and ending with Aśleṣā, he brings about security, abundance, and health, though there is destruction of livestock. (4) If Mercury is situated over the asterisms from Hasta up to Jyeṣṭhā, there will be well-being, plenty, and health among the people, but there will be the destruction of cattle.

4–5. If Mercury (the son of the Moon) moves through the constellations Āhirbudhnya (Śleṣā), Ārdrā, and Āgneyī (Kṛttikā), he causes the depletion of the seven bodily constituents (dhātus) of living beings; that is, there will be famine. 6. When Mercury moves through the constellations Aśvinī, Vāruṇī (Śatabhiṣaj), and Revatī, he brings about the destruction of physicians, horses, and those who subsist by trade.

When Mercury transits through the constellations Aśvinī, Śatabhiṣā, Mūla, and Revatī while piercing them, he destroys those who practice medicine, those who deal in horses, and those who follow the profession of trade. (6) If Mercury, moving through the three Pūrvās, pierces the junction star (yogatārā), it then brings fear to living beings from famine, weapons, disease, and thieves. (7)

If Mercury, moving forward and backward through the three [asterisms], should devour its own yoga-star, there shall be fear for living beings from famine, royal warfare, disease, and thieves. (7) In the asterisms of Yāmya, Agni, Dhātṛ, and Vāyavya, its motion is considered natural; however, in Īśa, Edus, Sārpa, and Pitrya, its motion should be known as mixed. (8)

If Mercury is situated in Bharaṇī, Kṛttikā, Rohiṇī, or Svātī, its motion is called *prākṛtā* (natural). If it is in Ārdrā, Mṛgaśīrṣa, Āśleṣā, or Maghā, its motion is called *miśrā* (mixed). || 8 || The motion [of Mercury] in the asterisms of Saṃkṣiptā (Punarvasu), Aditi (Puṣya), Bhāgya (Pūrvaphalgunī), Āryama (Uttaraphalgunī), and Ijyā (Hasta) is [called] *saumyā* (gentle). Its motion in Tīkṣṇā (Citrā), Aja (Svātī), Caraṇa (Viśākhā), Hirbudhnya (Anurādhā), Indrā (Jyeṣṭhā), Aśvin (Aśvinī), and Pūṣan (Revatī) is [called] *tīkṣṇā* (sharp/fierce). || 9 || Furthermore, the motion of the Moon’s son (Mercury) when situated in Yogāntikā (Mūla), Ambu (Śatabhiṣaj), Viśva (Dhaniṣṭhā), and Mūla is [called] *ghorā* (terrible). Its motion in Hari (Śravaṇā), Tvāṣṭra (Citrā), Vasu (Dhruva—Dhruva being Śravaṇā here), and Vāruṇa (Śatabhiṣaj) is also [terrible]. || 10 ||

If Mercury is in Punarvasu, Pūrvāphālgunī, Uttarāphālgunī, Puṣya, or Pūrvābhādrapadā, it is called the *saṃkṣiptā* (abbreviated) motion. If it occurs in Uttarābhādrapadā, Jyeṣṭhā, Revatī, or Aśvinī, it is called the *tīkṣṇā* (sharp) motion. If Mercury is in Pūrvāṣāḍhā, Uttarāṣāḍhā, or Mūla, it is called the *yogāntikā* (concluding) motion. If it occurs in Śravaṇa, Citrā, Dhaniṣṭhā, or Śatabhiṣā, it is then called the *ghorā* (terrible) motion.

9–10. (18) *Nāradasaṃhitā*: When [the Sun] is in the asterisms of Indra (Jyeṣṭhā), Agni (Kṛttikā), Mitra (Anurādhā), and Mārtaṇḍa (Puṣya), it is called a "sinful" (*pāpa*) transit. Indeed, whether it has risen or set while in these transits beginning with the Prākṛta, it remains visible for these many days and does not become invisible: forty, thirty, twenty-eight, twenty, and nine respectively. And when [the Sun] is in the asterisms of Viśākhā, Anurādhā, and Hasta, it is likewise declared to be a sinful transit.

When Mercury reaches these states such as Prākṛtā and so forth, whether it rises or sets, the duration for which it remains therein should be known in due order as follows: forty days in the Prākṛtā state, thirty days in the Miśrā, twenty-two in the Saṃkṣiptā, twenty in the Tīkṣṇā, nine days in the Yogāntikā, fifteen in the Śītā, and eleven days in the Śaśin. (11) 1 2. For fifteen and eleven days respectively, the son of the Moon [remains].

In the *prākṛtā* motion, it brings about abundance of crops, well-being, health, and good rain. (Verse 13) In the *ghorā* and *pāpā* motions, Mercury remains either rising or setting for fifteen and eleven days respectively; even when visible during these motions, it remains as if invisible. In the *prākṛtā* motion, there shall be an increase in agriculture, prosperity, health, and auspicious rainfall. (Verse 13) It yields results in the intervals between the *miśrā* and *saṃplikṣā* motions, while in other [motions] it is fruitless. Mercury is auspicious when risen in the months of Vaiśākha, Śrāvaṇa, Pauṣa, and Āṣāḍha. (Verse 14)

It yields the fruit of sin for people in [other] months, while in the others it bestows auspiciousness. In the months of Āśvina and Kārttika, it brings fear of weapons, famine, and fire. When risen, the Moon is excellent when it resembles silver or crystal. Thus ends the "Course of Mercury" (Budhacāra) in the Śrī Nāradīya Saṃhitā. [End of Chapter 2 in the Bhāṣā-Ṭīkā].

(19) Furthermore, auspicious results occur during the *miśrā* and *saṃkṣiptā* motions, while in other motions, inauspicious results occur. If Mercury rises during the months of Vaiśākha, Śrāvaṇa, Pauṣa, or Āṣāḍha, it bestows inauspicious results upon men; however, if it rises in other months, it bestows auspicious results.

If its rising occurs in the months of Āśvina or Kārttika, it produces the results of war, famine, and loss by fire; however, if it rises as clear as silver or crystal, Mercury is said to be auspicious. (Verses 14–15). Thus ends the "Course of Mercury" in the Bhāṣā-Ṭīkā on the Śrī Nārada Saṃhitā. Now begins the "Course of Jupiter": The months beginning with Kārttika (Ūrja) consist of two parts (fortnights), while the last five months consist of three parts each. The year is named after the lunar mansion (nakṣatra) in which Jupiter rises. (Verse 1).

The months beginning with Kārttika consist of two constellations (*nakṣatra*) each, while the fifth, twelfth, and eleventh months consist of three constellations each. The year is named after the constellation upon which Jupiter rises; this is the established rule: the years beginning with Kārttika are determined by pairs of constellations starting from Kṛttikā.

The fifth, eleventh, and twelfth years each consist of three lunar mansions (*nakṣatras*). For example: when Jupiter rises while situated in Kṛttikā or Rohiṇī, that year is called Kārttika; in Mṛgaśiras or Ārdrā, it is Mārgaśīrṣa; in Punarvasu or Puṣya, Pauṣa; in Āśleṣā or Maghā, Māgha; in Pūrvā-phālgunī, Uttarā-phālgunī, or Hasta, Phālguna; in Citrā or Svāti, Caitra; and in Viśākhā or Anurādhā, Vaiśākha.

In the *Jyeṣṭha-nāradasaṃhitā*, it is stated: When Jupiter rises while situated in Jyeṣṭhā, that month is called Āśvina; when in Mūla, Pūrvāṣāḍhā, or Uttarāṣāḍhā, it is Āṣāḍha; when in Śravaṇa, Dhaniṣṭhā, Śatabhiṣā, Pūrvābhādrapadā, or Uttarābhādrapadā, it is Bhādrapada; and when in Revatī, Aśvinī, or Bharaṇī, it is Āśvina. (1) In the year of Kārtika, there shall be suffering for those who subsist by means of chariots, cattle, and fire.

There will be an increase in the affliction caused by hunger and weapons, and for those who live by flowers, safflower, and the like. (2) Thus, if Jupiter rises during the year of Kārtika, there will be suffering for those who subsist on chariots and cattle and other animals, those who live by fire, confectioners and others, and those who live by flowers or safflower; furthermore, there will be famine, war, and the fear of fire. (2) There will be drought in the year of Saumya due to deer, rats, locusts, and birds.

If there is no rain during the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, there will be the destruction of all crops due to diseases, locusts, grasshoppers, parrots, and other such birds; there will be illness among the entire populace and mutual enmity among kings. (3) In the year of Pauṣa, the rulers of the earth will have their enmities ceased and will bring joy to the world; they will all be devoted to rites for prosperity and intent upon the practice of dharma. (4)

In the year known as Pauṣa, there shall be mutual friendship among kings, joy among the subjects, all people shall be happy and intent upon performing sacrifices. (4) In the year of Māgha, everyone will be constantly devoted to the worship of the ancestors; there will be abundance of food, security, health, and rains favorable to the farmers. (8)

In the year of Māgha, may all people remain constantly intent on worshipping their ancestors; may there be abundance of food, security, and health, and may the rains fall according to the wishes of the farmers. (5) In the year named Phālguna, thieves will be powerful, women will suffer misfortune, and kinsmen will be wicked; the rain will fall in some places, crops will grow in others, and prosperity will prevail in yet others. (6)

Women will suffer, there will be wickedness among kinsmen, and though it rains here and there, the harvest will yield little. (6) In the year named Caitra, rainfall will be moderate; excellent grain will be very difficult to obtain, rain and the price of crops will be scanty, yet kings will act for the welfare of their subjects. (7) In the year named Vaiśākha, kings along with their subjects will be intensely devoted to righteousness. (8)

There will be the full ripening of all crops for those whose minds are intent on sacrifice. (8) In the year of Vaiśākha, kings shall remain devoted to righteousness, the growth of dharma among the subjects will be complete, all fields will yield well, and the fear in everyone's heart will cease. (8) In the year of Jyeṣṭha, there will be safety for trees, shrubs, and creepers, yet a destruction of crops; those who know the essence of dharma and the kings themselves will be oppressed by enemies. (9)

In the year of Jyeṣṭha, there will be the destruction of trees, shrubs, creepers, and so forth, as well as the crops; O kings who know the principles of Dharma, you shall be afflicted by enemies. (9) In some places there will be rain, in some places grain, but in other places there will be no grain at all; in the year of Āṣāḍha, the lords of the earth will be desirous of victory over one another. (10)

In the month of Āṣāḍha, kings will desire war among themselves; in some places there will be rain, in some places cultivation, and in some places no cultivation at all. (10) Filled with various crops and abounding in the worship of the gods, the earth—destroying sins and heretics—shines resplendent in the year of Śrāvaṇa. (11) (22) —Nāradasaṃhitā.

In the year named Śrāvaṇa, the earth shall be adorned with various kinds of crops, filled with the worship of the gods, and free from sin and heresy. (11) In the first half [of the month], there will be an abundance of grain, while in the latter half, that which has been produced will perish. There will be moderate rain, excellent crops, and great battles among kings. (12) In the world during the month of Bhādrapada, there will be security in some places and insecurity in others; there will be an abundance of wealth and grain, a period of plenty, yet excessive rains as well. (13)

In the year of Bhādrapada, the first crop (Sāmaṇū) will be good, while the second crop (Sāḍhū) will perish; the middle harvest will be fair, there will be a great war among kings, and there will be well-being in some places and suffering in others. There will be an increase in wealth and grain, and this is the result of excessive rain. || 12 || 13 || In the year of Āśvayuja, there will be good rain, all crops will bear fruit, and all living beings will be satisfied. || 14 ||

In the year named Āśvina, there is beautiful rain, a full harvest of all crops, excellent fruit, and all living beings are happy; such is the result. (14) Moving through the northern quarter of the zodiac signs, the Sun brings about security, health, and abundance; the opposite occurs when it is in the southern quarter, and when it is in the middle, the results are middling. (19)

If Bṛhaspati moves toward the north of his own *yogatārā*, there shall be peace, health, and abundance among the subjects; if he moves toward the south, the result will be the opposite of this; and if he remains in the middle, the result will be middling. (15) The rays [of Jupiter] are, in order, yellow, fire-colored (red), dark, green, and red; at that time, they cause fear for living beings from disease, fire, battle, thieves, and weapons. (16) *Note: This is a commentary on verses 15–16 from Chapter 2 of the Bhāṣāṭīkā.*

(23) If the star of Bṛhaspati is yellow, like fire, dark-blue, green, or red in color, there will respectively be disease among the subjects, fear of fire, war, thieves, and fear of weapons. || 16 || If it resembles smoke, the one worshipped by the gods causes drought; if seen during the day, it portends the death of a king or the destruction of the kingdom. || 17 ||

If the color appears smoke-like, there will be no rain; if it is seen during the day, there will be the destruction of the king or the ruin of the kingdom. (17) Kṛttikā and Rohiṇī are both the body of the year; the two Āṣāḍhās are the navel, Ārdrā is the heart, and Maghā is the flower. (18) The two constellations Kṛttikā and Rohiṇī constitute the body of the year; Pūrvāṣāḍhā and Uttarāṣāḍhā are the navel; Ārdrā is the heart; and Maghā is the flower. (18)

If the body [constellations]—namely Kṛttikā and Rohiṇī—are afflicted by malefic planets, there will be famine, fear of fire, and great destruction. If the navel [constellation] is afflicted by malefic planets, there will be famine; if the flower [constellation] is afflicted, there will be the total loss of roots and fruits. (19)

If the heart [nakṣatra] is afflicted by malefic planets, there will be the destruction of crops; however, if it is afflicted by benefics, it will be auspicious. When Jupiter is situated in the sign of Aries, there will be the destruction of sheep. (20) If the heart nakṣatra is afflicted, there will be the loss of agriculture; likewise, if all these limbs are afflicted by benefic planets, the results will be auspicious. (Nāradasaṃhitā, Chapter 24): If Jupiter is upon the [Aries] sign, there will be fear of locusts and other calamities, as well as the destruction of rams. (30)

When Jupiter is in the sign of Taurus, there is growth of crops, health for the people, and rain agreeable to the farmers. However, there is the destruction of children, women, and cattle; the rainfall is moderate, there is loss of crops, and great war among kings. (21) *The increase of agriculture and well-being for the subjects; rain according to the desire of the farmers.* When Jupiter is in the sign of Taurus, there is the destruction of children, women, and cattle; the rainfall is moderate, there is loss of crops, and great war among kings. (21)

In the third sign [Gemini], there is fear among the people, fear for crops, and a terrible war between kings; there is suffering for Brahmins, moderate rain, and an increase in grain. (22) If Jupiter is in the sign of Gemini, there will be fear for humans and for crops; there will be fear for locusts and the like, a terrible war between kings, suffering for Brahmins, moderate rain, and an increase in grain. (22) Cows will have abundant milk, virtuous men will be happy, and women will be joyful.

When Jupiter is in the sign of Cancer, the earth is filled with the growth of crops; cows yield much milk, noble men find happiness, women become intoxicated with joy, and there is an increase in agriculture upon the earth. (23) When Jupiter has entered the sign of Leo, the earth becomes destitute, O best of gods; there is excessive rain, fear of serpents, and kings meet their end in battle. (24) *Commentary in Bhāṣā:* If Jupiter is in the house of Cancer, the earth is endowed with the abundance of grain. Cows give plenty of milk, excellent people experience happiness, women become intoxicated with joy, and there is an increase in cultivation on the surface of the earth. (23) When Jupiter is situated in the sign of Leo, the earth is impoverished, O most eminent of the gods; there is heavy rainfall, danger from snakes, and kings perish in war. (24) *Bhāṣāṭīkā, Chapter 2.*

(25) If Jupiter is in the sign of Leo, the Brahmins on earth shall be destitute of wealth; there shall be fear of serpents on earth, there shall be excessive rain, and kings shall meet their death in battle. || 24 || When Jupiter has entered Virgo, there is rain, the lords of the earth are joyful, and they remain in good health.

When Jupiter enters the sign of Virgo, all kings shall be pleased, the Brahmins will remain exceedingly joyful, and all people shall be healthy and at ease. (25) When Jupiter reaches Libra, the entire world possesses incomparable wealth from all minerals and roots; nevertheless, the earth remains fully endowed with riches, grain, and excellent rains. (26)

If Jupiter is in the sign of Libra (Tulā), all commodities such as metals and roots will abound in the world; there will be wealth and grain upon the earth, and the rains will be auspicious. (26) When Jupiter is in Cancer (Kīṭaga), there is destruction of the countryside due to war among kings intoxicated with pride; the rains are unsatisfactory, and there is fierce civil unrest (ḍāmara). (27) If Jupiter is in the sign of Scorpio (Vṛścika), there is the ruin of the country in the wars of kings who are maddened by pride; the rains are poor, and there is a terrible conflict. (27)

When Jupiter is in Capricorn, there is fear of living beings, great danger from kings, lack of rain, extreme suffering, and rulers become impoverished. (28) When Jupiter is in Aquarius, people are free from enemies, the earth is filled with crops, and there is abundant rain.

All people will be free from passion and fear when Jupiter is situated in Capricorn, which is honored by the gods. (29) [From the Nāradasaṃhitā]: When Jupiter is in Capricorn, there shall be friendship among all men on earth; for many years, crops will grow in great abundance, and everyone will live in well-being. (29) When Jupiter is in Aquarius, the earth will be filled with people rivaling the gods through rains of fruits, flowers, and wealth, and it will be endowed with freedom from disease. (30)

When Jupiter is in Kumbha (Aquarius), men on earth will equal the gods; there will be abundant rain of fruits and flowers, and peace and health shall prevail upon the earth. (30) When Jupiter is situated in Mīna (Pisces), the price of grain will be low, rain will be plentiful, yet there will be disease in some places and fear in others; all kings will be devoted to the path of justice. (31) Thus ends the "Course of Jupiter" from the Śrī Nāradīya Saṃhitā.

When Jupiter is in Mīna (Pisces), food becomes cheap, there is abundant rain, though there may be disease in some places and fear in others; all kings remain established on the path of justice. 31. Thus ends the movement of Jupiter in the *Śrī Nāradasaṃhitā Bhāṣāṭīkā*. In the northern, middle, and southern paths, there are three lanes each; for Venus, starting from the Aśvinī constellation, the periods consist of three [asterisms] each. 1.

In these three paths—the northern, the middle, and the southern—three rows each have been described; there, one should understand them in their proper order by means of the cycles of Venus (Śukra) upon the three constellations beginning with Aśvinī in each [path]. 1. The nine rows ending in the south are known as Nāga, Airāvata, Vṛṣabha, Go, Jaradgava, Mṛga, Āja, Dahana, and Yāmya. 2.

Namely: 1. Nāga, 2. Gaja, 3. Airāvata, 4. Vṛṣabha, 5. Gau, 6. Jaradrava, 7. Mṛga, 8. Aja, and 9. Dahana; these nine paths extend toward the south. || 2 || Moving through three paths in the northern regions, Bhārgava brings about the fulfillment of grain prices, rainfall, and crops. || 3 || Commentary on Verse 2: Moving through the three paths of the northern course, Śukra [brings about] the abundance of food and crops...

This results in an increase in agricultural produce during the rainy season. (3) If it moves through the three middle paths, it produces a middling result for them; if it moves through the three southern paths, the result for those same things is inferior. (4) Furthermore, when it wanders through the three middle paths, all things yield a middling result; when it wanders through the three southern paths, all things such as grain and the like become expensive. (5)

When Venus is situated in the five asterisms beginning with Maghā, it rises or sets in the eastern direction and brings about a good year; likewise, when it is situated in the three asterisms beginning with Svātī, it rises or sets in the western direction and produces the same auspicious result. (9)

In the opposite case, however, there is drought, accompanied by the death of those who bring rain. When Jupiter is white (Venus) on the eighth day of the dark fortnight, the fourteenth, or the new moon, and undergoes both rising and setting [in conjunction], then the earth becomes filled with water. When Jupiter and Venus are situated in the seventh house from each other, one in the western path and the other in the eastern path, there will be no rain, and they will bring about famine and death. When Mars, Mercury, Jupiter, and Saturn are positioned ahead of Venus, then there will be war, excessive wind, famine, and the destruction of water.

Venus, with a body dark-red in hue, brings about the destruction of the winds. (9) Thus ends the "Motion of Venus" in the Nāradīya-saṃhitā. (28) [From] the Nāradasaṃhitā: If it be otherwise than this, one should know the results to be contrary; when Venus is conjoined with Mercury, then rain falls on the eighth day of the dark fortnight.

If Venus rises or sets on the fourteenth lunar day (caturdaśī) or the new moon day (amāvāsyā), there will be heavy rain upon the earth. Furthermore, if Jupiter and Venus are situated in the seventh sign from each other and positioned in the eastern or western paths (vīthi), there will be no rain; instead, there will be famine and death. If Mars, Mercury, Jupiter, and Saturn are situated ahead of Venus, there will be war, strong winds will blow, and famine will occur.

If Venus does not appear during the rainy season, or if its star is black or red in color, there will be the destruction of the Yavanas (Mlecchas). Thus ends the "Motion of Venus" in the *Śrī Nāradasaṃhitā Bhāṣāṭīkā*. When Saturn moves through the asterisms of Śravaṇā, Svātī, Hasta, Ārdrā, Bharaṇī, and Bhāgya (Pūrvaphalgunī), it brings about abundance of food, health, and crops for mankind. || 1 ||

When Saturn moves through the asterisms of Śravaṇa, Svātī, Hasta, Ārdrā, Bharaṇī, and Pūrvāphālgunī, it is auspicious for humanity and brings about abundance and well-being. (1) In the asterisms of Jaleśa (Śatabhiṣā), Sārpa (Āśleṣā), and Māhendra (Jyeṣṭhā), it causes abundance. In Mūla, Āhirbudhnya (Mūla), and the last two (Pūrvā- and Uttarā-Aṣāḍhā), there is danger from famine, weapons, and drought. (2) [The asterisms are: Śatabhiṣā and Āśleṣā.

If it occurs on Jyeṣṭhā, there will be plenty; if on Mūla, there will be famine, war, and drought—such is the result. If it occurs on Uttarābhādrapadā or Revatī, there will be fear among the people. (2) One [digit] is on the head, three on the mouth, two on the private parts, two on the eyes, five stars on the heart, and four on the left hand. (3) [From the Bhāṣā-Ṭīkā, Chapter 2]

(29) Counting from the birth asterism (*janmanakṣatra*) up to the asterism of Saturn (*śani*), one should then place one asterism on the head, three on the face, two on the anus, two on the eyes, five on the heart, and four on the left hand. || 3 || Three should be placed on the left foot and three on the right; four on the right hand, while the one born under the asterism of *Bhadrapadā* remains [on the head]. || 4 ||

Place three on the left foot, three on the right foot, and four on the right hand; thus, starting from one's birth asterism (janma-nakṣatra) up to Saturn’s asterism, the results are assigned. 4. Illness, gain, loss, profit, happiness, imprisonment, exertion, travel, and the acquisition of wealth—these are the results in successive order. 4.

Its results, in due order, are to be known as: disease, gain, loss, gain, happiness, bondage, suffering, a journey according to one's heart's desire, and the acquisition of wealth. (5) When Saturn is retrograde here, it produces such retrograde results; when moving at an even pace, it produces equanimity; and when moving swiftly, it produces results in reverse order. (6) Thus ends the "Motion of Saturn" (Śanicāra) in the Śrī Nāradīya Saṃhitā. When Saturn is retrograde, its results should be known as inauspicious; when it remains in its mean motion, [the results are neutral].

In that case, one should know the result to be middling; if there is swift motion, one should know the result to be auspicious. ||6|| Thus ends the movement of Saturn in the *Śrī Nāradasaṃhitā-bhāṣāṭīkā*. Because he tasted the nectar, even though his head was severed by Viṣṇu with that discus, he became immortal and attained the status of a planet. ||1|| Due to the tasting of the nectar, although Rāhu’s head was cut off by Lord Viṣṇu with the Sudarśana discus, nevertheless, having drunk the nectar, he became immortal and became a planet. ||1||

(30) *Nāradasaṃhitā*: By the boon of the Creator (Brahmā), Rāhu swallows the Sun and the Moon during every lunar node (*parvan*). Due to the influence of his displacement (*vikṣepa*) and his low lineage (*avanati*), Rāhu remains far removed from them. (2) One should calculate the eclipses of the Sun and Moon by increasing [the interval] by six months.

Likewise, from the beginning of the Kalpa, seven deities are the presiding lords in succession during the six lunar months within which solar and lunar eclipses occur; among these eclipses governed by this rule, the deities are, in order, Brahmā, Indra, Yama, Kubera, Varuṇa, Agni, and Yama. During the Brāhma-parvan (the first month), there is an increase in cattle, crops, and the twice-born. || 4 ||

Brahmā, Indra, Candra, Kubera, Varuṇa, Agni, and Yama—these are the seven. Among them, during a lunar eclipse presided over by Brahmā (brāhma-saṃjñaka), there is prosperity for cattle, agriculture, and Brāhmaṇas. || 4 || The fruit is exactly like that in the case of a lunar eclipse (saumya); however, during an eclipse presided over by Budha (Budha-parvaṇi), there is distress for the planet Mercury. During an eclipse presided over by Indra (aindra), there is conflict among kings and the destruction of crops. || 9 ||

The same results apply during the lunar eclipse known as Candra; however, learned men will suffer affliction. During the eclipse known as Indra, there will be conflict among kings, suffering, and the destruction of crops. (5) In the Artha (Yama) direction, there is loss of wealth for those who seek it; in the Kaubera (Vāyu) direction, there is an increase in grain. In the Vāruṇa (Varuṇa) direction, there is misfortune for kings, but security for others. (6) [This concludes] Bhāṣādī, Chapter 2.

During the lunar station known as Kubera, there will be a loss of wealth for bankers and merchants, yet an increase in grain among the common people. During the station known as Varuṇa, kings will suffer distress while the rest of the populace enjoys happiness. (6) In the lunar station of Agni (Hautāśa), there is abundant rain, an increase in crops, and security. In the station of Yama (Yāmya), there is drought, a loss of crops, and famine. (7)

If rain falls during the period designated as *abhisaṃjñaka*, there will be an abundance of rain, an increase in crops, and well-being for the subjects; however, if it does not rain during the *yāmya* period, there will be loss of crops and famine. (7) If rain falls outside the proper time (*velāhīna*), there is loss of grain and fierce battles among kings; if it falls too early (*ativele*), there is a loss of flowers, fear, and the destruction of crops. (8)

If an eclipse begins before the proper time—that is, before the stated hour—there will be loss of crops and fierce battles among kings. If it occurs after the time or exceeds the duration, there will be loss of flowers, fear, and the destruction of agriculture. (8) When both lunar and solar eclipses occur in the same month, there is conflict among rulers and the destruction of wealth and rain. (9)

If both the moon and the sun undergo eclipses within the same month, there will be enmity among kings, as well as the destruction of wealth and the rains. (9) If both the moon and the sun rise or set while already eclipsed, they cause the destruction of kings and grain. If both the sun and the moon are entirely eclipsed, they bring about the fear of famine, wind, and fire. (10)

If an eclipse occurs at sunrise or sunset, there will be destruction of the king and of grain. If both the sun and the moon are eclipsed in their entirety, there will be fear of famine, wind, and fire. (10) [Nāradasaṃhitā] Rāhu, when eclipsed, destroys the twice-born and others in sequence starting from the direction he is seen in. There are ten varieties of grasping (grāsa), and likewise ten varieties of release (mokṣa). (11)

In the directions starting from the East, whichever direction the eclipse (grāsa) is seen in, it destroys the four castes beginning with the Brāhmaṇa in that respective direction—just as a Brāhmaṇa in the East, a King (Kṣatriya) in the South, and so forth. There are ten varieties of the eclipse, and there are likewise ten varieties of liberation (mokṣa). (11) It cannot be perceived even by the gods, much less by ordinary people. Having brought the planets according to the Siddhāntas, one should contemplate their motion. (12)

All those various divisions are not clearly seen even by the gods; how then could they be seen by ordinary men? One should determine these divisions by calculating the positions of the planets according to the Siddhānta scriptures. (12) Indeed, the movement of the planets is the cause for the occurrence of auspicious and inauspicious times; therefore, it should be investigated by the wise man for the sake of knowing that time. (13) Thus ends the "Movement of Rāhu" in the Śrī Nāradīya Saṃhitā.

The planets are the sole cause for the commencement of inauspicious events during the *samaya* (astrological period). Therefore, a wise person should observe that cause in order to understand the knowledge of time (*kālajñāna*). || 13 || Thus ends the "Motion of Rāhu" in the *Śrī Nāradasaṃhitā Bhāṣāṭīkā*. The risings and settings of comets (*ketu*), which appear as portents (*utpāta*), occur for human beings; they are celestial, atmospheric, and terrestrial, and they bestow both auspicious and inauspicious results. || 1 ||

The rising and setting of comets (*ketu*) are said to be portents for mankind; it is taught that such portents occurring in the heavens, the intermediate space, or on the earth yield auspicious or inauspicious results. (1) Those resembling a sacrificial altar, a banner, a weapon, a temple, a chariot, a tree, or an elephant, as well as those shaped like a pillar or a trident, are proclaimed to be [portents] of the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*). (2)

When signs in the shape of a sacrificial banner, a weapon, a temple, a chariot, a tree, an elephant, a trident, a pillar, or a mace appear to someone in the sky, that is called an atmospheric portent (antarikṣotpāta). || 2 || Whether celestial portents are situated among the stars or terrestrial portents are situated upon the earth, if even one of them appears in an unfavorable form, it indeed brings misfortune to living beings. || 3 ||

Any portent seen occurring among the stars is called a celestial (divya) portent; those portents seen upon the earth are called terrestrial (bhauma) portets. Among these, even a single portent is of the nature of an enemy and should be known as bestowing inauspicious results upon living beings. (3) For as many days as a comet of various forms is seen, for that many months the result should be declared; and by means of months, the years [are likewise determined]. (4)

One should know that the results last for as many months as the Ketu planet (the comet) remains visible; and for as many years as it is seen in months, one should understand the auspicious or inauspicious results. || 4 || These celestial Ketus also constantly yield intense results; those appearing in the atmosphere yield middling results, while those on the earth yield dull results. || 4 ||

Those comets (*ketu*) seen in the sky produce constant and terrible results; those portents (*utpāta*) seen in the sky yield middling results; and portents on the earth yield mild results. (5) A short, glossy, and very bright white comet brings about abundance of food; a long comet produces good rain. (6) (34) *Nāradasaṃhitā*

A comet (*ketu*) that is small, smooth, clear, and white-tailed is a giver of auspiciousness. A long comet that vanishes quickly is also a giver of auspiciousness. (6) A smoke-colored comet (*dhūmaketu*) resembling Indra’s bow (*śakracāpa*), appearing in the form of two, three, or four spikes (*śūla*), brings about the end of the kingdom at that time. (7)

Comets resembling smoke or the colors of a rainbow are inauspicious; if they take the form of two, three, or four tridents, they destroy the kingdom. (7) The sons of the Sun (comets), possessing the luster of jewels, necklaces, and gold, and being radiant, cause the destruction of kings when they appear in the east or the west. (8)

If comets possessing a luster like that of a gem, a pearl necklace, or gold arise, they destroy both preceding and succeeding kings; these are known as the sons of the Sun (Sūryaputra). || 8 || Those comets which resemble the Bandhūka flower, the Bimba fruit, blood, the beak of a parrot, or fire, and which bestow fire, are the sons of Fire (Agnisūnu). || 9 ||

Those resembling the bandhūka flower, the duṣparihārya flower, or red like the color of a parrot, and those with a fire-like hue—these Ketus cause fear of fire; they are called the sons of Agni. (9) Those that bestow disease are the sons of Mṛtyu; those that are crooked are black Ketus. The sons of Bhū are like water or oil, circular in shape, and they bring about the fear of hunger. (10)

The dark-colored Ketus with crooked forms are the sons of Death (Yama); they bestow disease. The round-colored Ketus, possessing a luster like water or oil, are said to be the sons of Earth (Bhūmi); they cause fear of famine. (10) The white Ketus are the sons of Soma (the Moon); they grant security and abundance. The son of the Grandfather (Brahmā), Ketu, possesses three colors and is endowed with three crests. (11)

The white-colored Ketu is said to be the son of the Moon; he brings about security, well-being, and abundance. The son of Brahmā, Ketu, is described as having three colors and three crests. (11) Ketu, who is twice the length of Brahmā’s staff, is always the bringer of the end of living beings. In the northeast, the sons of Bhārgava are white in form and bestow misfortune. (12)

The comet named Baladaṇḍa always causes the destruction of the subjects. Comets with white forms rise in the northeast; they are the sons of Śukra and yield inauspicious results. (12) Those with two crests, called Kanaka, are the sons of Paṅgu and bestow misfortune. Those known as Vikaca are the sons of Guru; even when situated in the south, they are not auspicious. (13) Comets with two crests, possessing a color like gold, are the sons of Śani; they are declared to be inauspicious.

The comet named Vikaca rises in the southern direction; it is the son of Bṛhaspati and is inauspicious. (13) The Sūkṣmas are white, sons of Budha, and terrible; they bring about fear of thieves. The ones called Kuṅkuma are the sons of Kuja; they are red, spike-shaped, and bestow misfortune. (14) The Sūkṣmas are subtle in form, white in color, and are the sons of Budha; they are fierce and cause fear of robbers.

The Ketu named Kuṅkuma, who has the color of bark, is said to be the son of Maṅgala; he bestows inauspicious results. (14) (36) Nāradasaṃhitā: Those known as Viśvarūpa, born of Agni, have the color of fire and grant auspiciousness. Aruṇa is dark-complexioned and, being the sons of Pāpa, they bestow evil. (139) The Ketu named Viśvarūpa is the son of Agni; having a color like fire, he is a giver of auspiciousness.

15. Those comets (ketus) that are red or dark-colored are the sons of Pāpaka; they bestow inauspicious results. 16. Comets resembling Venus or Mercury in appearance are auspicious givers. Those born of Brahmā, known as Kaṅka, are white and resemble bamboo creepers; they are difficult [to endure]. Comets whose forms are similar to the lunar mansions (nakṣatras) and whose brilliance is ordinary are the sons of Śukra and are auspicious givers.

The white-colored comets named Kaṅka arise with shapes resembling bamboo or creepers; they are said to be givers of suffering. (16) Those called Kabandha, the sons of Kāla, are ash-colored and bring about misfortune. However, the white comets that are the sons of Vidhi are not givers of undesirable results. (17)

The son of Kālakā named Kabandha is said to be inauspicious, having a color like that of ashes; and Ketu, who is white in color, is the son of Brahmā, yet he does not bestow auspiciousness. (17) Dhūmaketu, born under the constellation Kṛttikā, brings about the end of living beings; when he appears upon palaces, mountains, or trees, he causes the destruction of kings. (18)

If Ketu rises near the Kṛttikā constellation, it brings about the destruction of the subjects. If Ketu rises above temples, mountains, banyan trees, or similar objects, it causes the ruin of kings. (18) The comet named Kumuda, resembling a white water-lily, brings about an abundance of food. The Ārtaketu is auspicious; it is white and resembles a whirlpool. (19) *Bhāṣīkāsaṃhitā*, Chapter 3.

(37) The comet named Kumuda resembles the flower of the kumudinī; it bestows the fruit of abundance. The white comet known as Āvarta is said to be a giver of auspiciousness. || 19 || The Saṃvarta comet, appearing at twilight with three heads, is terrible and does not grant what is desired. || 20 || Thus ends the second chapter, concerning the movement of comets within the movement of planets, in the Śrī Nāradīya Saṃhitā. || 2 ||

When it rises at the time of twilight with three crests, that is called Saṃvarta Ketu; it is terrible and brings about inauspicious results. || 20 || Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Motion of Planets," within the section on the "Motion of Ketu" in the Bhāṣā-Ṭīkā of the Śrī Nāradasaṃhitā. The measures of Brahma, Daiva, Mānuṣa, Pitrya, Saura, Sāvana, Cāndra, Ārkṣa, and Gaurava—these are indeed the nine measures. || 1 ||

The Brahma, Daiva, Mānuṣa, Pitrya, Saura, Sāvana, Cāndra, Nākṣatra, and Gurumāna—these are the nine kinds of years, months, and other measures of time. (1) Among these nine measures, however, practical application here occurs through five; their respective functions according to usage shall now be described. (2)

The performance of domestic rites (*vāstukarma*), vows (*vrata*), and observances (*niyama*) are reckoned according to the lunar month (*cāndramāsa*); that is, the sequence is taken from the beginning of the bright fortnight of Caitra, which marks the start of the year. Furthermore, the characteristics of the years such as *prabhava* and others are determined by the solar measure (*gurumāna*). || 5 || The movement of the zodiacal circle (*bhacakragati*) constitutes the sidereal (*ārṣa*) month; the civil (*sāvana*) month consists of thirty days; the solar (*saura*) month is declared to be the period of a sun-transit (*saṃkramaṇa*); and the lunar (*cāndra*) month begins with the first day of the lunar phase (*pratipad*). || 6 ||

That which is calculated according to the movement of the constellations is called a *nakṣatra-māsa* (lunar mansion month); that which consists of exactly thirty days is called a *sāvana-māsa* (civil month). That which occurs according to the sequence of the sun’s transits (*saṃkrānti*) is a *saura-māsa* (solar month), while that which follows the sequence of the first lunar day (*pratipad*) and so forth is a *cāndra-māsa* (lunar month).

(77) [From the Bhāṣāṭīkā, Chapter 3, Verse 53]: The six months beginning with Capricorn (Mṛga) are the northern course (saumyāyana) according to the sun's movement; that is the day of the gods (surāṇām). The period beginning with Cancer (Karka) is the southern course (dakṣiṇāyana); that is their night. (78)

As long as the sun remains in the six zodiac signs beginning with Capricorn (makara), that period is called the northern course (uttarāyaṇa), which is the day of the gods; and that which is called the southern course (dakṣiṇāyana) during the six transitions (saṃkrāntis) beginning with Cancer is the night of the gods. || 78 || Auspicious rites such as entering a new house, marriage, consecration, the investiture of the sacred thread (mauñjibandhana), and sacrifices should be performed during the northern course. Inauspicious rites should be performed during the southern course; furthermore, the specific month is also a primary factor. || 79 ||

One should perform auspicious rites such as entering a house, marriage, the investiture of the sacred thread (mauñjībandhana), and sacrifices during the sun’s northern course (uttarāyaṇa); whereas inauspicious rites and those associated with the specific months of the year should be performed during the southern course (dakṣiṇāyana). || 79 || In order, the seasons of Śiśira, Vasanta, and Grīṣma constitute the northern course; while Varṣā, Śarad, and Hemanta constitute the southern course. || 80 ||

During the sun’s northern course (uttarāyaṇa), there occur in succession the three seasons of Śiśira, Vasanta, and Grīṣma; during its southern course (dakṣiṇāyana), there occur the seasons of Varṣā, Śarad, and Hemanta. || 80 || Two months each, beginning with Māgha, constitute the seasons starting with Śiśira. The lunar month ends with the new moon (darśa); the solar month is by transit (saṃkrānti); and the civil (sāvana) month is by days. || 81 || A lunar revolution (bhagaṇa) of the moon in thirty [days] is known as a sidereal (nākṣatra) month. Madhu, Mādhava, Śukra, Śuci, and that called Nabhas; || 82 ||

The two months beginning with Māgha and those beginning with Śiśira are to be understood in their respective order. A lunar month (cāndramāsa) is completed at the new moon (amāvāsyā); a solar month (sauramāsa) is completed upon the occurrence of a transit (saṃkrānti); a civil month (sāvanamāsa) is completed in exactly thirty days; and a sidereal month (nākṣatramāsa) occurs according to the sequence of the lunar mansions (nakṣatra). Madhu 1, Mādhava 2, Śukra 3, Śuci 4, Nabhas 5... [81-82]
