In whichever month the full moon (Paurṇamāsī) is conjoined with a particular lunar mansion (dhiṣṇya), that month is named after that asterism, and the full moon itself is likewise named accordingly. (84)

The month is named after the lunar mansion (nakṣatra) with which the full moon is conjoined in that particular month, and the full moon itself is likewise named accordingly; for example, because of the Citrā nakṣatra, the month is Caitra and the full moon is Caitrī, and because of Viśākhā, the month is Vaiśākha and the full moon is Vaiśākhī, and so forth. || 84 || Its two fortnights are known as the divine (daiva) and the ancestral (paitra), namely the bright (śukla) and the dark (kṛṣṇa); both of these are always considered auspicious for performing virtuous and non-virtuous deeds respectively.

85. Thus ends the third chapter, on the Year (*Saṃvatsara*), in the venerable *Nāradīyasaṃhitā*. There are two fortnights (*pakṣa*) known as *daiva* (divine) and *paitra* (ancestral), corresponding respectively to the bright (*śukla*) and dark (*kṛṣṇa*) halves of the month. They are declared to be auspicious for virtuous and non-virtuous deeds; that is to say, auspicious acts are favorable during the bright fortnight. 85. Thus ends the third chapter, on the Year, in the vernacular commentary (*bhāṣāṭīkā*) on the venerable *Nāradasaṃhitā*. 3. 8-} Vernacular Commentary, Chapter 4.

3. Fire, Brahmā, Gaurī, Gaṇeśa, the Serpent, Viśākha, the Sun, Maheśa, Durgā, Antaka, Viṣṇu, Hari, Smara, Śarva, and the Moon—these are celebrated in the Purāṇas as the lords of the lunar days beginning with the first (pratipadā). Now, the lords of the lunar days beginning with the first (pratipadā) and ending with the full moon (pūrṇimā) are: 1. Agni, 2. Brahmā, 3. Gaurī, 4. Gaṇeśa, 5. Sarpa, 6. Skanda, 7. Sūrya, 8. Śiva, 9. Durgā, 10. Yama, 11. Viśvedevas, 12. Hari, 13. Kāmadeva, 14. Śiva, and 15. Candramas. These are the lords of the lunar days starting from the first day up to the full moon. || 1 ||

The ancestors (Pitṛs) are declared to be the lords of the lunar days (tithis) in sequence. (2) One should know that the Amāvāsyā has the Pitṛs as its presiding deity; thus the lords of the lunar days are to be understood in their proper order. (2) Other designations for the lunar days are now stated in due order. (3) These other names—namely Nandā, Bhadrā, Jayā, Riktā, and Pūrṇā—are to be known as synonyms. In the bright fortnight (śuklapakṣa), they grant results that are undesirable, middling, and desirable respectively. (3)

Even in the dark fortnight (kṛṣṇapakṣa), those [lunar days] situated in the middle, the end, and the beginning of the seat (pīṭha) always yield results in that order: [inferior, middling, and excellent]. (4) One should know that in the bright fortnight (śuklapakṣa), the lunar days from the first (pratipadā) up to the fifth, then up to the tenth, and finally up to the fifteenth, yield results that are inauspicious, middling, and excellent respectively; whereas in the dark fortnight, they should be known to yield results in the order of excellent, middling, and inauspicious. (4) Painting, drawing, wine, fields, oil, beds, seats, and so forth, as well as the felling of trees for the purpose of building a house—these are said to be performed on the first lunar day (pratipad). (5)

Painting, preparing wine, agricultural work, oil massage, making beds, making seats, carving wood, and stonework—these activities performed on the first lunar day (pratipadā) are auspicious. (5) (56) *Nāradasaṃhitā*: Marriage, the sacred thread ceremony, journeys, the installation of deities, ornaments, houses, and all tasks related to flowers are prescribed for the second lunar day. (6)

Marriage, the investiture of the sacred thread (mauñjībandhana), journeys, the installation of deities, ornaments, the commencement of a house, and all rites for complete nourishment—these should all be performed on the second lunar day (dvitīyā). || 6 || The consecration of the sacred thread, the arts and sciences, every auspicious rite, and the decoration of cattle, camels, water-vessels, and vehicles should be done on the third lunar day (tṛtīyā). || 7 ||

The tying of the *mauñjī* (sacred grass girdle), consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*), the science of arts (*śilpavidyā*), all auspicious rites, the purchase of livestock, elephants, and camels, and traveling by water—these activities are auspicious when performed on the third lunar day (*tṛtīyā*). || 7 || The study of the *Atharvaveda*, weaponry, fire-rites, binding, exorcism (*uccāṭana*), and so forth—all such acts, including those for causing death (*māraṇa*) and the like—are prescribed specifically for the *riktā* lunar days. || 8 ||

The Atharva-vidyā—that is, the science of singing as well as the sciences of mantras and so forth, the science of weapons, and rites such as fire-binding, eradication, and killing—should be performed on the empty lunar days (4, 9, and 14). (8) Vehicles, the sacred thread ceremony (upanayana), marriage, pacification of planetary afflictions (śāntika), and nourishing rites (pauṣṭika); all mobile and immobile activities, as well as festive celebrations (maṅgala), should be undertaken on the fifth lunar day. (9)

Traveling by vehicle, the thread ceremony (upanayana), marriage, pacification of the planets (grahaśānti), nourishing rites (pauṣṭika karma), and festivals for moving or stationary deities should be performed on the fifth lunar day (pañcamī). || 9 || Tending to livestock, selecting a site for a house, service, trade, the buying and selling of water, ornamentation, legal proceedings, and other such activities are prescribed for the sixth lunar day. || 19 ||

The work of cattle, the work of building houses, the work of serving desires on the earth, trade, water, buying and selling, and dealings with ornaments—these works should be performed on the sixth lunar day. [From Bhāṣāṭīkā, Chapter 4, Verse 57]: The installation of vehicles, driving them, service to the king and the like, marriage, building houses, ornaments, and the sacred thread ceremony (*upanayana*)—these should be done on the seventh lunar day. (11)

Departing, establishing, carrying, service to a king and similar activities, marriage, building a house, ornaments, and the initiation ceremony (upanayana) should be performed on the seventh lunar day. (11) Agriculture, trade, grain, stone, iron, battle, ornaments, the installation of Śiva, digging, and water-related works are prescribed for the eighth lunar day. (12) Agriculture, commerce, grain, stone, iron, battle, ornaments, the installation of Śiva, the work of digging, and water-related rites should be undertaken on the eighth lunar day. (12)

The installation of a temple, mounting a vehicle, marriage, the tying of the sacred thread (*vratabandhana*), and rites such as the extraction of thorns or the *pṛṣṭhyā* sacrifice are highly commended on the tenth lunar day (*daśamī*). [13] Vows, fasting, trade, agriculture, commerce, ornamentation, craftsmanship, dancing, house-building, and various other activities are excellent when performed on the eleventh lunar day (*ekādaśī*). [14]

Vows, fasting, marriage, agriculture, trade, jewelry-making, artistic crafts, dancing, housework, and various other specialized tasks should be undertaken on the eleventh lunar day (Ekādaśī). || 14 || Except for mobile and stationary activities, all acts of giving, rites for peace, and rites for prosperity, as well as journeys and the receiving of food—everything else is beneficial on the twelfth lunar day (Dvādaśī). || 19 ||

One should perform steady and complete rites, acts of charity, propitiatory (*śānti*) and auspicious (*pauṣṭika*) rites, journeys, and the collection of food; apart from these, other rites performed on the twelfth lunar day (*dvādaśī*) are auspicious. (15) The installation of the sacred fire (*agnyādhāna*), consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*), marriage, the tying of the sacred thread (*vratibandhana*), all auspicious ceremonies, and journeys are recommended on the thirteenth lunar day (*trayodaśī*). (16) (58) *Nāradasaṃhitā*.

The installation of the sacred fire (agnisthāpana), consecration (pratiṣṭhā), marriage (vivāha), the completion of auspicious rites such as the investiture of the sacred thread (yajñopavīta), and journeys (yātrā) are auspicious when performed on the thirteenth lunar day (trayodaśī). || 16 || Binding, kindling the fire, fierce striking, wounding, combat, and activities involving weapons, missiles, and ironwork are prescribed for the fourteenth lunar day (caturdaśī). || 17 || Binding, setting fire, violent blows, battle, weapons, missiles, and all tasks involving iron are auspicious when performed on the fourteenth lunar day. || 17 ||

On the full moon day (pūrṇimā), one should avoid sexual union with an oil-presser’s wife, the use of a tooth-stick, and the ritual of the sacred thread (yajñopavīta) along with shaving; apart from these, all other activities are auspicious. (18) Except for the single rite dedicated to the ancestors (pitṛ-karma) on the new moon day (amāvāsyā), one should never, under any circumstances, perform any auspicious act or similar rite with great care [on that day]. (19)

On the lunar day of the new moon (amāvāsyā), one should never perform any auspicious rite whatsoever, except for those pertaining to the ancestors (pitṛ-karma). || 19 || The eighth, twelfth, sixth, fourth, and fourteenth lunar days are known as *pakṣaraṃdhra*; they are inauspicious and highly censured. || 20 || The eighth, twelfth, sixth, fourth, and fourteenth lunar days—these are called *pakṣaraṃdhra*, meaning "holes in the fortnight"; they are inauspicious and extremely condemned. || 20 ||

The *nāḍikās* known as *anuraṃdhra*, *aṅka*, *tatva*, and *saṃjñā*—namely four, one, fourteen, seven, nine, and five in measure—should always be abandoned during these five inauspicious lunar days (*tithis*). Thereafter, they are not unfavorable. (21) *Bhāṣāṭīkā*, Chapter 4 (59): Having excluded the New Moon (*amāvāsyā*) and the ninth day, which are designated as "odd" (*viṣama*), [the remaining odd days are auspicious].

These lunar days (tithis) are declared auspicious; likewise, the first day (pratipad) is middling. Furthermore, with the exception of the new moon (amāvāsyā) and the ninth day (navamī), these odd-numbered tithis are said to bestow good fortune; the first day (pratipad) is middling. (22) On the new moon, the sixth, the first, the twelfth, on all the parvan days, and on the ninth, one should never perform the cleaning of the teeth. (23)

One should never have one's teeth cleaned on the new moon (amāvasyā), the sixth (ṣaṣṭhī), the first (pratipadā), the twelfth (dvādaśī), or the full moon (pūrṇamāsī). || 23 || In the Kali age, one should avoid oil on the sixth day, meat on the eighth, and shaving on the fourteenth; likewise, one should refrain from sexual intercourse with a woman on the full moon and the new moon days. || 25 || [This means: One should avoid oil on the sixth, meat on the eighth, shaving on the fourteenth, and sexual union with a woman on the full moon or the new moon. || 24 ||

On the *vyatīpāta* yoga, during a solar transit (*saṃkrānti*), on the eleventh lunar day (*ekādaśī*), on the full-moon and new-moon days (*parvan*), on Sundays and Tuesdays, on the sixth lunar day, and during the *vaidhṛti* yoga—one should not perform an oil massage or apply unguents. (29) He who performs a bath with *āmalaka* fruits on the tenth lunar day suffers the loss of his sons; on the thirteenth lunar day, there is a depletion of wealth. (26)

If one performs the bath with *āvalīs* on the tenth day, there will be loss of sons; if one does so on the thirteenth day, there will be loss of wealth. (26) (60) *Nāradasaṃhitā*: "On the second day, there is no doubt that there will be loss of wealth and sons; on the new moon (*amāvāsyā*), the ninth, and the seventh, there is destruction of the lineage. (27)

On the second lunar day, there is the destruction of wealth and sons; if one bathes with *āmalaka* fruits on the new moon (*amāvāsyā*), the ninth, or the seventh, it leads to the ruin of the family. (27) When the full moon (*pūrṇimā*) is accompanied by the moon at night, it is called *anumati*; when it is accompanied by the moon during the day, it is *rākā*. Similarly, the new moon (*amāvāsyā*) is also of two kinds. (28)

That in which the moon is present at night—meaning the full moon (Pūrṇimā) occurs on the fourteenth day—is called Anumati; and that which is endowed with the full digits of the moon during the day is known by the name Rākā, the Pūrṇimā tithi. Likewise, Amāvāsyā is said to be of two kinds: Sinīvālī and Kuhū. Sinīvālī is considered to be Saindhumatī, while Kuhū is Nairṛtamatī. The ninth day of the bright fortnight of Kārtika is the beginning of the Kṛta Yuga. || 28-29 ||

One is Sinīvālī, on which the moon becomes visible; the other is known as Kuhū, on which all the digits (kalās) of the moon have waned. The ninth lunar day (tithi) of the bright fortnight of Kārtika is said to be the beginning of the Satya Yuga. || 29 || The third lunar day of the bright fortnight of Mādhava is designated as Puṇyā, the beginning of the Tretā Yuga. The fifteenth lunar day of the dark fortnight of Māgha is declared to be the beginning of the Dvāpara Yuga. || 30 ||

The third day of the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha is said to be the beginning of the Tretā Yuga and is considered sacred; the new moon of Māgha is said to be the beginning of the Dvāpara Yuga. || 30 || In the dark fortnight of Nabhasya (Śrāvaṇa), the thirteenth day is the beginning of the Kalpa; the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of Ūrja (Kārttika) and the ninth day of the bright fortnight of Āśvayuja (Āśvina). || 31 || [Commentary in Bhāṣā]: The thirteenth day of the dark fortnight of Bhādrapada is said to be the beginning of the Kali Yuga; as well as the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of Kārttika and the ninth day of the bright fortnight of Āśvina. || 31 ||

The third lunar day of the bright fortnight in Caitra and Bhādrapada; the eleventh lunar day of the bright fortnight in Pauṣa; and the tenth lunar day of the bright fortnight in Āṣāḍha. (32) The pure seventh lunar day in Māgha; the eighth lunar day of the dark fortnight in Nabhasya (Śrāvaṇa); the new moon day in the month of Śrāvaṇa; and the full moon day in the month of Phālguna. (33)

The seventh day of the bright half of Māgha, the eighth day of the dark half of Bhādrapada, the new moon of Śrāvaṇa, and the full moon of Phālguna. (33) The full moons of the months of Āṣāḍha, Kārtika, Caitra, and Jyeṣṭha are known as Manvādi days; they bestow infinite merit upon bathing, giving gifts, and performing ancestral rites (śrāddha). (34)

On the thirteenth day of the dark fortnight of Bhādrapada, when the moon is in Maghā and the sun is in Hastā, that is known as Gajacchāyā; it yields the highest fruit for the Śrāddha rite. (38) When three lunar dates fall upon a single solar day due to the omission of a tithi, that is called Kṣayātithi. (39)

If one lunar day (*tithi*) is omitted during three successive weekdays, or if one lunar day is increased during those same three consecutive weekdays, that is declared to be extremely censurable. (36) That lunar day which exists until the setting of the sun on a particular weekday is called "unbroken" (*akhaṇḍā*); if it is deficient [in duration], it is designated as "fragmentary" (*khaṇḍa*). (37)

If the same lunar day (tithi) persists until the setting of the sun at that time, it is called *akhaṇḍā* (unbroken); if it remains incomplete, it is known as *khaṇḍitā* (fragmented). || 37 || The fifteenth part of a lunar day constitutes each successive day beginning with the first (*pratipad*). Among these, two *ghaṭikās* are declared by the wise to be the measure of a *muhūrta*. || 38 || Thus ends the fourth chapter, on the characteristics of lunar days, in the glorious *Nāradīya Saṃhitā*. || 9 ||

The fifteenth part of the moon’s orb—that is, the fifteenth division—is called a *tithi*, such as *pratipadā* and the others; and two *ghaṭīs* constitute one *muhūrta*. 38. Thus ends the fourth chapter, on the characteristics of the lunar days (*tithis*), in the *Bhāṣā-ṭīkā* commentary on the *Śrī Nāradīya Saṃhitā*. Whatever rites for the inauguration of kings, auspicious ceremonies, service, travel, agriculture, medicine, fire-offerings, grains, and so forth are to be performed, they should be undertaken on Sunday. 1.

Royal consecration, auspicious ear-ornaments, service, vehicles, the act of eating, medicine, battle, and activities related to grain should be performed on Sunday. (1) Conch shells, pearls, water, silver, trees, sugarcane, women's ornaments, flowers, songs, sacrifices, milk, and agricultural work should be performed on Monday. (2) *Āṣāḍhī-ṭīkā*, Chapter 5, Verse 63: Conch shells, pearls, silver, trees, sugarcane, women's ornaments, flowers, songs, sacrifices, milk, and farming—these activities should be undertaken on Monday. (2)

Poisoning, fire, imprisonment, theft, treaty-making, and waging war in battle; the working of mines, coral, weapons, and agriculture—these should be performed on Tuesday. (3) Dancing, crafts, arts, singing, writing, the collection of earth, marriage, metallurgy, and acts of war—these should be performed on Wednesday. (4)

Dancing, arts, crafts, singing, writing, the collection of the earth's minerals, marriage, metallurgy, and warfare—these activities should be performed on Wednesday. (4) Sacrificial rites, nourishing ceremonies, auspicious acts, the decoration with gold, clothing, and ornaments, as well as the planting of trees, shrubs, creepers, and the preparation of vehicles—these activities should be performed on Thursday, the day of the preceptor of the gods. (5–6)

Dancing, singing, instrumental music, gold, women, jewels, ornaments, land, shops, festivals, cattle, grain, and activities related to these should be performed on a Friday (the day of Bhārgava). || 6 || Tin, lead, iron, excessive [consumption], poison, sin, liquor, and falsehood, as well as all stable undertakings and the acquisition of property, should be done on a Saturday (the day of Sauri). || 7 ||

Dyeing, lead, iron, stone, weapons, poison, sin, liquor, falsehood, fixed rites (*sthirakarma*), house-entry rites (*vāstukarma*), and accumulation—these activities are auspicious when performed on Saturday. (7) (64) *Nāradasaṃhitā*: The Sun is fixed; the Moon is movable; Mars is cruel; Mercury is all-pervasive; Jupiter is light; Venus is gentle; and Saturn, the son of the Sun, is sharp. (8)

The Sun is stable, the Moon is mobile, Mars is cruel, Mercury is fully auspicious, Jupiter is light (favorable), Venus is soft, and Saturn is said to be sharp. || 8 || A man who applies oil on a Sunday becomes afflicted with distress; under the influence of the Lord of the asterism (Mars), he gains luster; under Mars, there is disease; and under the Moon, there is good fortune. || 9 ||

The person who applies oil and the like on a Sunday becomes miserable; if one applies oil on a Monday, a beautiful complexion increases; if one applies it on Tuesday, illness occurs; and on Wednesday, good fortune is attained. || 9 || On Thursday there is poverty, on Friday loss, and on Saturday all prosperity; from sunrise to sunrise [the result] is excellent—this has been determined previously. || 10 ||

If one applies oil on a Thursday, there will be poverty for Jupiter; on a Friday, loss; and on a Saturday, there will be prosperity in all matters. This is applied every day at sunrise; this has been the established certainty since ancient times. || 10 || From the time of sunrise at Laṅkā, the week-day begins; whether it be after or before that time, another [week-day] occurs by means of the nāḍīs (forty-eight minutes) equal to half the longitudinal distance between two places. || 11 ||

The day on which the sun rises at Laṅkā is the first day of the week; however, due to the longitudinal differences (cara-khaṇḍas) situated above and below Laṅkā, there are discrepancies in the timing of the days. That is to say, the same weekday does not coincide at all times and in all places. The commencement of the weekday is determined according to the methods prescribed in the scriptures. (Bhāṣāṭīkā, Sarga 5, Verse 65). Whatever is performed on the day of a planet that bestows strength becomes successful.

That action which is performed on the day of a weak planet does not succeed even with great effort. (12) The days of Mercury, the Moon, Jupiter, and Venus are granters of success in all undertakings; however, whatever action is stated to be successful on the days of the malefic planets [is indeed so]. (13)

Wednesday, Monday, Thursday, and Friday are auspicious for all undertakings; furthermore, those fierce rites prescribed for the days of the malefic planets are likewise accomplished on them. (13) The Sun is red in color, the Moon is fair-complexioned, Mars is crimson, Mercury has the hue of dūrvā grass, Jupiter is yellow, and Venus is white. (14) The Sun is red in color, the Moon is fair-complexioned, and Mars is crimson.

Budha (Mercury) is green in color; Bṛhaspati (Jupiter) is yellow; Śukra (Venus) is white. (14) Śani (Saturn) is black; on their respective days, activities of their own colors are said to be auspicious. (18) The numbers are: mountains (7), arrows (5), oceans (4), stars (9), mines of water (4), mountains (7); arrows (5), fires (3), eyes (2), Vedas (4), arms (2), and arrows (5). (16)

Now, the *kulika* and other yogas are described: on Sunday, during the 7th, 5th, and 4th watches; on Monday, during the 6th, 4th, and 7th watches; on Tuesday, during the 5th, 3rd, and 2nd watches; and on Wednesday, during the 4th, 2nd, and 5th watches. (16) In the *Nāradasaṃhitā*: "Seven, sixteen, eight, two, seven, three, one, and six—these are the *kulikas* known as *yamaghaṇṭā*, designated as half-watch intervals. (1)

In these [three] watches (prahara) of Bṛhaspati—namely the 3rd, 1st, and 8th—the three yogas known as Kulika, Yamaghaṇṭaka, and Prahārārdha (or Vāravelā) occur respectively in the watches of Śukra—namely the 2nd, 7th, and 3rd—and in the watches of Śani—namely the 1st, 6th, and 6th. (17) These [yogas] should be understood to have a duration of half a watch (praharārdha), starting from Sunday. On whichever day the specific moment (kṣaṇa) is desired, that is the presiding lord of the day. From the first [watch], the sixth; from this [second], the second; from that [third], the sixth; and from the third, the third [is the sequence]. (18)

And for the others, every sixth [counting from each] is remembered as the lord of the *kālahorā*. (19) In whichever weekday the three *praharas* are shown, these yogas remain respectively for half a *prahara* each. For example, on Sunday: in the seventh *prahara*, the *kulika-yoga* lasts for half a *prahara*; then in the fifth *prahara*, the *yamaghaṇṭaka*; then in the fourth *prahara*, the four *ghaṭīs* of the *vāravelā* (half-prahara). Know this to apply to all [the days]. These are censured in auspicious rites.

Whenever a planet's *horā* occurs, at that time it becomes the lord of the day (*vāra-svāmī*). First, there is the current day; then the sixth day from that; then the sixth day from that as well; and again the sixth from that—thus, the *kāla-horā* belongs to each successive sixth day. (18–19) In this manner, by means of two and a half *nāḍīs*, during the day and night respectively, whatever action is prescribed for whichever planet on its day is performed.

The activity of a planet occurs on its day, at that specific moment, and always [during its period]. Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "Characteristics of the Days," in the Śrī Nāradīya Saṃhitā. Commentary in Bhāṣā: Chapter 6 (67). [The influence lasts] for two [periods] in the day and night respectively.

One should know that a *kālahorā* lasts for two and a half *ghaṭīs*. Whatever action is prescribed to be performed on the day of a particular planet, that same action should always be performed during the *horā* of that very planet. For example, if the *horā* of the Moon occurs on Sunday, then the works appropriate for Monday are suitable to be done. Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Characteristics of the Days of the Week," in the *Bhāṣā-ṭīkā* on the *Śrī Nāradasaṃhitā*. The lords of the lunar mansions (*nakṣatras*) in order are: Aśvinī, Yama (Yamā), Agni (Kṛttikā), and Pitāmaha (Rohiṇī).

Candra, Śakra, Aditi, Jīva, Ahi, Pitṛs, and the one named Bhaga [are the first set]. Dastra (the two Aśvinīkumāras), Yama, Vahni, Brahmā, Candramas, Śivajī, Aditi, Bṛhaspati, Sarpa, Pitṛs, and Bhaga. Aryaman, Ārka, Tvaṣṭṛ, Marut, Śakra, Agni, Mitra, Vasu, Nirṛti, Udaka, Viśva, Vidhi, Govinda, Vasu, and Toyapa.

Aryaman (12), Sūrya (13), Tvaṣṭṛ (14), Vāyu (15), Indra-Agni (16), Mitra (17), Indra (18), Nirṛti (19), Jala (20), Viśvedevas (21), Brahmā (22), Viṣṇu (23), Vasu (24), and Varuṇa (25). Then Aja-Ekapāt, Ahirbudhnya, and Pūṣan are likewise proclaimed. Thus, these twenty-seven deities—Aja-Ekapāt (26), Ahirbudhnya (27), and Pūṣan (28)—are said to be the presiding lords of the twenty-seven lunar mansions beginning with Āśvinī. [The rites of] the girdle-tying, the tonsure, and the parting of the hair are performed [under these asterisms]. || 3 || *Note: The numbering provided in the source text appears to be inconsistent; the commentary clarifies that there are twenty-seven deities corresponding to the twenty-seven nakṣatras.*

Now, the actions to be performed under these lunar mansions (*nakṣatras*) are described: [under Aśvinī], the work of making garments, the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*), the parting of the hair (*sīmantonnayana*), and the fashioning of ornaments. (3) || (68) *Nāradasaṃhitā*: Under Aśvinī, one should establish vehicles such as horses, engage in agriculture, the sciences, and so forth; [under Bharaṇī], one should construct ponds, wells, tanks, and the like, as well as administer poisons, employ weapons, and deal with fierce or cruel matters. (4) ||

Establishing foundations, vehicles such as horses and camels, agriculture, learning sciences, and similar activities are auspicious to perform under the Aśvinī asterism; so too is the construction of wells, cisterns, and tanks. However, activities involving poison, weapons, and fierce or terrible deeds [are not]. (4) Entering burrows, calculations, and the depositing of treasures are auspicious under the Bharaṇī asterism. Likewise, the consecration of the sacred fire, the taking up of missiles and weapons, and fierce acts such as treaties or warfare are auspicious. (4)

Entering a cave, learning the science of mathematics (gaṇitavidyā), and depositing a trust—these activities are auspicious when performed under the asterism Bharaṇī. The installation of the sacred fire, the taking up of weapons and missiles, fierce rites, treaties, and violent conflict; battles, medicinal preparations, and musical performances—these are commended under the asterism Kṛttikā (Bāhnibha). The parting of the hair, the investiture of the sacred thread, marriage, clothing, ornaments, and stable undertakings; the laying of elephants, consecration, and installations—these are auspicious under the asterism Rohiṇī (Brahmabha).

Battle, medicine, and trade are auspicious when performed under the Kṛttikā constellation; furthermore, the Sīmantonnayana rite, the investiture of the sacred thread (Yajñopavīta), marriage, wearing new clothes, adorning with ornaments, fixed rites, taking an elephant, building a house, consecration, and installation are auspicious deeds under the Rohiṇī constellation. (6) Installation, adorning with ornaments, marriage, the Sīmantonnayana rite, the investiture of the sacred thread, shaving, building a house, elephants, camels, horses, and journeys are commended under the Mṛgaśiras (Candrabha) constellation. (7)

Consecration, ornamentation, marriage, the *sīmantonnayana* rite, initiation (*upanayana*), shaving, building construction, elephants, camels, and journeys—these are auspicious under the asterism Mṛgaśiras. (7) Raising a banner, constructing an archway, engaging in battle, building a rampart, the manufacture of weapons, treaties, war, sacrificial rites, and the preparation of elixirs—these are auspicious under the asterism Ārdrā (Śiva-bha). (8)

Raising a banner, constructing an archway, engaging in battle, erecting a pillar (or fortress), the manufacture of weapons, making peace, waging war, building a pavilion, and the preparation of medicinal elixirs—these activities are auspicious when performed under the Ārdrā asterism. || 8 || The consecration of deities, the construction of vehicles, the performance of the *sīmantonnayana* rite, the laying of foundations for buildings, the sacred thread ceremony (*upanayana*), the preparation of milk-based offerings, and the crafting of weapons—all these, as well as the acquisition of grain and ornaments, should be undertaken under the Punarvasu asterism. || 9 ||

Installation, travel, the *sīmantonnayana* rite, tailoring, building a house, the sacred thread ceremony (*upanayana*), shaving, archery, grain, and jewelry—these activities are auspicious when performed under the Punarvasu asterism. (9) Travel, installation, the *sīmantonnayana*, the binding of vows (*vratibandha*), and entering a new home—all such rites, except for the taking of a bride’s hand, are auspicious under the Jyeṣṭhā asterism. (10)

Journeying, consecration, the *sīmantonnayana* rite, the investiture of the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*), entering a new home, and likewise all other rites—except for the marriage ceremony—may be commenced under the Puṣya asterism. (10) Deceit, addiction to vice, gambling, anger, fire, poison, burning, disputes, and trade in liquids—these activities are auspicious under the Kṛttikā asterism. (11)

Speed, calamity, gambling, anger, fire, poison, burning, dispute, taste, and trade—these activities are auspicious to perform under the Āśleṣā asterism. (11) Agriculture, trade, cattle, grain, preparations for war, marriage, dancing, singing, and so forth—all such activities are auspicious to perform under the Maghā asterism. (12)

12. (70). *Nāradasaṃhitā*: "Lawsuits, poison, weapons, fire, and the seizing of fierce crocodiles and the like—all such activities, as well as the sale of meat, should be performed during the first three [asterisms]. (33) Lawsuits, poison, enemies, fire, fierce and violent acts, warfare, the selling of meat, and so forth—these activities are auspicious when performed during the three *pūrva* (eastern) asterisms. (13) "Garments, consecration, iron, stone, marriage, the tying of vows, entry, installation, horses, elephants, and building works [are auspicious] during the three *uttara* (northern) asterisms. (14)

Donning clothes, consecration, working with metals and stones, marriage, the investiture of the sacred thread (yajñopavīta), house-entry, consecration rituals, riding horses and elephants, and rites concerning architecture—all these activities are auspicious when performed during the three Uttarā nakṣatras. || 14 || Consecration, marriage, the parting of the hair (sīmanta), traveling, wearing new clothes, the investiture of the sacred thread, shaving, architecture, royal consecration, and the art of ornamentation are all auspicious under the nakṣatra of the Sun (Pūrvaphalgunī). || 15 ||

The installation of deities, marriage, the *sīmantonnayana* ceremony, the acquisition of vehicles, clothing, the initiation (*upanayana*), the rite of shaving (*kṣaura*), house-consecration (*vāstu-karma*), consecration (*abhiṣeka*), and the wearing of ornaments—these rites are auspicious when performed under the *hasta* asterism. (15) Entering a new home, the wearing of clothes, the *sīmantonnayana*, the installation of deities, the tying of the sacred thread, the science of architecture (*vāstu-vidyā*), as well as the rites of shaving and adorning oneself with ornaments—these are [auspicious] under the *tvāṣṭra* (citrā) asterism. (16)

Entering a new home, wearing new clothes, the parting of the hair (sīmantonnayana), consecration (pratiṣṭhā), the sacred thread ceremony (yajñopavīta), house-consecration (vāstuyāga), writing, and the wearing of ornaments—these rites are auspicious when performed under the Citrā constellation. || 16 || Consecration, the sacred thread ceremony, marriage, wearing clothes, the parting of the hair, adorning with jewelry, entering a new home, agriculture, and shaving—these acts are auspicious under the Svāti constellation. || 17 ||

Consecration ceremonies (*pratiṣṭhā*), the sacred thread ceremony (*upanayana*), marriage, clothing, the *sīmantonnayana* rite, ornaments, entering a new home, the purchase of horses and elephants, agriculture, and shaving—these are auspicious to perform under the Svāti asterism. (17) The collection of garments, ornaments, trade goods, grains, and other such items; dancing, singing, the arts, and working with metals, stones, and writing—these are [auspicious] under the Jyeṣṭhā asterism. (18) *Bhāṣā-ṭīkā*, Chapter 6, Verse 73.

The trade of clothing, ornaments, and merchandise, as well as the collection of grain and other goods, dancing, singing, artistic crafts, working with iron and stone, and writing—these activities are auspicious when performed under the Viśākhā nakṣatra. (18) Entering a new home, establishing a residence, marriage, the tying of the sacred thread, the eight auspicious rites, building a house, adorning oneself, wearing clothes, acquiring horses, making peace, and waging war are auspicious under the Anurādhā nakṣatra. (19)

Entering a new home, consecrating a temple, marriage, the investiture of sacred thread, the eight types of auspicious rites (*maṅgala*), construction work, wearing ornaments and garments, tending horses, and matters of peace or war—these activities are auspicious when performed under the asterism Anurādhā. (19) Shaving the head, the use of missiles, the study of scriptures, trade, work involving cattle, buffaloes, and water, as well as singing, instrumental music, the arts, and working with metals, stones, or writing—these are [auspicious] under the asterism Jyeṣṭhā (Indrabha). (20)

Shaving, the use of missiles, the use of weapons, trade, cattle, buffaloes, water-related work, singing, hunting, craftsmanship involving metals, stonework, and writing—these activities performed under the Jyeṣṭhā asterism are auspicious. (20) Marriage, agriculture, commerce, fierce combat, medicine, dancing, craftsmanship, the use of missiles, weapons, working with metals, stonework, and writing—[these are to be done] under the Nairṛta (Mūla) asterism. (21)

Marriage, agriculture, trade, harsh deeds, battle, medicine, dancing, arts, missiles, weapons, ironwork, stonework, and writing—these activities are auspicious when performed under the Mūla Nakṣatra. || 21 || Consecration, shaving, the *sīmanta* ceremony, mounting a vehicle, initiation (*upanayana*), and medicine, as well as the commencement of a house, are declared by the ancients to be suitable under the Viṣṇu Nakṣatra (Śravaṇa). || 22 || (72) According to the Nāradasaṃhitā: consecration, shaving, the *sīmanta* ceremony, vehicles, and initiation;

The Shravana constellation is auspicious for these activities: taking medicine, building a new house, and gathering wealth. The results of the three Purvas and the three Uttarās have already been stated together [in verse 22]. [Verse 23: "Clothing, the investiture ceremony (upanayana), milk, the tying of the sacred girdle (mauñjībandhana), medicine, the construction of a dwelling, the parting of the hair (sīmanta), entry [into a house], and ornaments [are performed under] the Vasu asterism. [Commentary: The rites of the investiture with the staff (vajra-upanayana-karma), shaving (kṣaura), the tying of the sacred girdle (mauñjībandhana), medicine (auṣadha), the construction of a dwelling (vāstu-karma), and the parting of the hair (sīmanta);

Entering a house and wearing ornaments—these activities are auspicious when performed under the asterism Dhaniṣṭhā. (23) Establishing a residence, shaving, the investiture of the sacred thread (mauñjībandhana), medicine, mounting a horse, the *sīmanta* rite, and building work (*vāstukarma*)—these are auspicious when performed under the asterism Śatabhiṣā. (24)

Marriage, the tying of the sacred thread (initiation), consecration, vehicles, ornaments, entry [into a new house], clothing, the *sīmantonnayana* rite, shaving, and medicine—these ten are auspicious when performed under the asterism Revatī. (29) The triad of the eastern [asterisms] (Aśvinī, Bharaṇī, Kṛttikā), Agni (Kṛttikā), Mūla, Ahi (Āśleṣā), Dvidaivatya (Viśākhā), Maghā, and Antaka (Bharaṇī)—this group of nine asterisms is prescribed as "downward-facing" (*adhomukha*). (26)

The three *pūrvas*, Kṛttikā, Mūla, Āśleṣā, Viśākhā, Maghā, and Araṇī—these are the asterisms known as downward-facing (*adhomukha*). (26) Thus ends the section on the downward-facing [asterisms]. This concludes the calculation for entering caves, the determination of spirits, and writing; as well as the work of artisans, [the construction of] wells with creepers, and the depositing or extracting of treasures. (27) *Vernacular Commentary:* Chapter 6.

(73) In these downward-facing constellations, entering a cave, the practice of mathematics, mantras, and yantras, writing, artistic crafts, planting creepers (vela), and retrieving an object fallen into a well are auspicious. || 27 || Mitra, Indu, Tvāṣṭra, Hasta, Ārdrā, Aditi, Bhānti, Aśva, Vāyu, and Bhama—this group of nine constellations is designated as "sideways-facing" (tiryaṅmukha). || 28 || Thus ends the section on the sideways-facing constellations.

Anurādhā, Mṛgaśiras, Citrā, Hasta, Jyeṣṭhā, Punarvasu, Revatī, Aśvinī, and Svātī—these nine lunar mansions (nakṣatras) are designated as "facing sideways" (tiryaṅmukha). || 28 || In these [mansions], it is auspicious to yoke the plough, travel, construct a cart, purchase elephants, camels, goats, and so forth, as well as to purchase horses, and to engage in various activities [related to them]. || 29 ||

Riding donkeys, oxen, chariots, and boats; the work of buffaloes and horses; the operation of carts; likewise, the purchase of camels and the work of other animals—these are auspicious. (30) Thus ends the section on the activities of animals. [The asterisms] Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Maheśa, Ārdrā, Śatabhiṣā, and the three Uttarās...

The group of nine lunar mansions beginning with Ūrdhvāsya is declared and prescribed as follows: || 31 || Thus ends the section on Ūrdhvamukha. Rohiṇī, Śravaṇa, Ārdrā, Puṣya, Śatabhiṣā, Dhaniṣṭhā, and the three Uttarās—these nine nakṣatras are known by the name Ūrdhvamukha. || 31 || (74) Nāradasaṃhitā: The construction of cities, palaces, houses, gardens, elephants, and banners; as well as temples, walls, parks, ramparts, and pavilions. || 32 ||

In these constellations, the construction of cities, palaces, houses, gardens, elephants, banners, and their respective works, as well as temples, pleasure groves, and watchtowers, are auspicious. (32) Thus end the upward-facing constellations. Rohiṇī, the three Uttarās, and Ārdrā are fixed (sthira); Hasta, Citrā, Svātī, and Puṣya are swift (kṣipra); the two deities (Viśākhā and Anurādhā) are common (sādhāraṇa); and Kṛttikā is known as mobile (cara). (33)

Rohiṇī, the three Uttarās, and those known as the fixed (sthira) constellations; Hasta, Aśvinī, and Puṣya are known as the swift (kṣipra); Viśākhā, Bharaṇī, and Kṛttikā are the constellations known as the common (sādhāraṇa). || 33 || Vasubha (Dhaniṣṭhā), Ādityabha (Punarvasu), Vāsubha (Śatabhiṣaj), Svātī, and Viṣṇubha (Śravaṇa) are designated as mild (mṛdu). Citrā, the last one (Revatī), Mitrabha (Anurādhā), and Śaśibha (Mṛgaśīrṣa) are fierce (ugra). Pūrvāphālgunī, Maghā, and Antakabha (Bharaṇī) are sharp (tīkṣṇa). Mūla, Indrabha (Jyeṣṭhā), and Ārdrā are sharp; their results correspond to their own names. || 34 ||

Dhaniṣṭhā, Punarvasu, Śatabhiṣā, Svātī, and Śravaṇa are known as the *cara* (mobile) asterisms; Citrā, Revatī, Anurādhā, and Mṛgaśiras are known as the *mṛdu* (soft) asterisms; and Mūla, Jyeṣṭhā, Āśleṣā, and Ārdrā are the *tīkṣṇa* (sharp) asterisms. These yield results corresponding to their respective names. These designations are utilized when examining auspicious moments (*muhūrta*). [In the asterisms] Citrā, Āditya (Punarvasu), Aśvinī, Viṣṇu (Śravaṇa), Antya (Revatī), Aravi (Śatabhiṣā), Mitra (Anurādhā), Vasu (Dhaniṣṭhā), and Ṛdu (Ārdrā)... [34]

The practice of piercing the ears of young animals is beneficial during the asterisms Mṛgaśiras, Śravaṇa, and Punarvasu (38). Furthermore, all work related to elephants should be performed during the asterisms Darśa, Indu, Svāti, Āśleṣā, and the triad beginning with Kṛttikā, as well as in fixed (sthirabha) signs (39). [Bhāṣāṭīkā, Chapter 6].

(75) Furthermore, the ears of children should be pierced under the asterisms of Citrā, Punarvasu, Aśvinī, Śravaṇa, Revatī, Hasta, Anurādhā, Dhaniṣṭhā, and Mṛgaśiras. The buying and selling of elephants is auspicious under the asterisms of Aśvinī, Mṛgaśiras, Punarvasu, Puṣya, Hasta, Citrā, and Svātī; likewise, lending and borrowing are auspicious under the asterisms designated as "fixed" (sthirasaṃjñaka). || 35 || || 36 || Now, the Muhūrta for horses.

On an auspicious day, during a *cara*, *kṣipra*, *mṛdu*, or *sthira* lunar mansion, all activities concerning horses—especially on Sunday—are recommended. When the weekday is auspicious due to the strength of the Moon and other factors, and the lunar mansions are of the *cara*, *kṣipra*, *mṛdu*, or *sthira* class, then one should undertake all horse-related matters such as selling or purchasing them. [37] Traveling and returning are auspicious under the asterisms of Citrā, Śravaṇa, Viśākhā, Svātī, and the three Uttarās.

On the new moon day, the eighth, and the fourteenth, one should never [slaughter] animals. During the constellations of Citrā, Śravaṇa, Rohiṇī, and the three Uttarās, as well as on the lunar days of Amāvāsyā, Aṣṭamī, and Caturdaśī, one should neither bring cattle such as cows and bulls into the house after purchasing them, nor should one drive them out from the house. (38) Now, the auspicious time for setting the plough: In the Mṛdu, Dhruva, Kṣipra, Cara, Viśākhā, and Pitṛ (Maghā) constellations...

One should first perform the plowing with bulls under the asterism Mūla; this is auspicious for the commencement of agriculture. (39) According to the *Nāradasaṃhitā*, the three asterisms beginning from the one currently occupied by the Sun, as well as Viśākhā and Maghā—known as the soft (*mṛdu*), fixed (*dhruva*), swift (*kṣipra*), and movable (*cara*) classes—are likewise favorable. Plowing with bulls under these asterisms, including Mūla, bestows prosperity. (39) The three asterisms following the one occupied by the Sun lead to the destruction of the bull at the start of plowing; however, the five asterisms preceding it bring wealth, and the group known as Saumya is also auspicious. (40)

Furthermore, at the beginning of the plow and the wheel, there are three constellations starting from the constellation of the Sun (Āśleṣā); they cause the destruction of oxen. Then, there are three constellations at the front part; if one attains fortune (Lakṣmī) therein, it is auspicious. Five constellations in the middle are said to be bestowers of welfare. || 40 || In the three "tridents" (śūla), nine constellations lead to death, while another five lead to prosperity. Three constellations at the tail (puccha) are excellent, and [these] are auspicious in the wheel and the plow. || 41 ||

On the upper part of the trident (triśūla), nine constellations (nakṣatras) bestow death, while the other five bestow fortune (lakṣmī). Furthermore, on the tail (puccha), three constellations are excellent. Thus, having placed the twenty-eight constellations upon the plough and the discus (halacakra), one should consider the auspicious and inauspicious results. || 41 || Sowing seeds in the Mṛdu, Dhruva, Kṣipra, Pitṛ, Vāyu, Vasu, Ṛkṣa, and Samūla constellations yields the most excellent fruit. || 42 ||

Furthermore, sowing seeds under the asterisms known as Mṛdu, Dhruva, and Kṣipra, as well as Maghā, Svāti, Dhaniṣṭhā, and Mūla, is extremely auspicious. || 42 || Three asterisms from the position of Rāhu placed on the head lead to the destruction of grain; three on the neck lead to the loss of collyrium; and twelve in the belly lead to prosperity. || 43 ||

Three constellations on Rāhu’s head cause the destruction of grain; three are on his neck, where there is little rain or the grain is struck by crows; twelve constellations on his belly are givers of prosperity. 43. In the tail, four constellations are said to result in the removal of husks; five are in the navel, which one should consider as being like the sowing of seeds. 44.

On the tail are four constellations; in them, seeds fall unequally. Then there are five constellations on the navel; in them, there is danger from fire. This Rāhu-cakra is also considered when sowing seeds. || 44 || Now, the auspicious time for a sick person's bath: One should not perform a bath after being cured of illness during the fixed (sthira) signs, nor under the constellations Āditi (Punarvasu), Sarpa (Āśleṣā), Pitṛ (Maghā), or Māruta (Svāti), nor on the days of the Moon or Venus. || 45 ||

A person who has recovered from illness should not bathe on the days of the constellations known as Sthira—namely Punarvasu, Āśleṣā, Revatī, Maghā, and Svātī—nor on a Monday or a Friday. || 45 || Now, the auspicious time for dancing: The commencement of dance is recommended during the three Uttarās, Anurādhā, Jyeṣṭhā, Dhaniṣṭhā, Śatabhiṣaj, and the constellations Puṣya, Śravaṇa, and Revatī. || 46 ||

It is auspicious to begin dancing under these asterisms: the three Uttarās, Anurādhā, Jyeṣṭhā, Dhaniṣṭhā, Śatabhiṣā, Puṣya, Hasta, and Revatī. (46) From the asterism of Pūṣan (Revatī), there are six asterisms in the front row; from the asterism of Rudra (Ārdrā), twelve asterisms in the middle row; and nine asterisms in the Indra row (Jyeṣṭhā). (47)

The six lunar mansions beginning with Revatī are called the *pūrvārdha-yuñjā*; then the twelve lunar mansions beginning with Ārdrā are called the *madhyārdha-yuñjā*; and the nine lunar mansions beginning with Jyeṣṭhā are called the *parārdha-yuñjā*. (47) [Nāradasaṃhitā]: "In the *parārdha-yuñjā*, there is mutual affection between the king and his queen in due order. (48). Thus ends the section on *yuñjā*.

Regarding the consideration of the constellations for an excellent bride: if they form a *yuñjā* (pairing), then mutual affection will endure between the man and woman. (48) Thus ends the section on *yuñjā*. Now follows the consideration of moonrise (*caṃdrodayavicāra*): The constellations Āśleṣā, Pūrvaphalgunī, Uttaraphalgunī, Svāti, Anurādhā, Jyeṣṭhā, Mūla, and Śatabhiṣaj are considered inferior; whereas Dhruva (Uttarābhādrapadā), Abhijit, and Rohiṇī are great stars and are equal to the best. (49)

Śatabhiṣā, Ārdrā, Āśleṣā, Svātī, and Revatī are known as the inferior asterisms (jaghanya); the fixed asterisms (dhruva), as well as Punarvasu and Viśākhā, are known as the great asterisms (bṛhat); the others are said to be middling (sama). || 49 || When the moon rises in succession over these, they are respectively worthless, half-value, and middling. [The asterisms] are Aśvinī, Kṛttikā, Mṛgaśiras, Bharaṇī, Āśleṣā, Pūrvaphalgunī, Citrā, and the three Uttarās. || 50 ||

Likewise, in due order: if the Moon rises in the constellations known as *jaghanya*, there will be an abundance of food and other necessities; if it rises in those known as *bṛhat*, the price of goods will be low; and in the *sama* constellations, one should know the prices to be moderate. These are: Aśvinī, Kṛttikā, Mṛgaśiras, Mūla, Pūrvaphālgunī, Citrā, and all three of the Uttarās. (50) Now, the constellations known as *pitṛdvidaivata* are declared to be of the *kula* class for royal expeditions.

Dhātṛ, Jyeṣṭhā, Aditi, Svātī, Pauṣṇa, Ārka, and the asterism of Hari; Ajapāda, Antaka, Bhaujaṅga, and Tārā—these are called the Upakulas. The remaining asterisms are the Kulakulas. Among these, when one proceeds under the Kulakula asterisms, if one is encountered by kings, one suffers defeat. Under the asterisms known as Upakula, the king attains victory. When under the Kulakula asterisms, there is peace or equality between the two parties.

If it falls on a Sunday, Saturday, or Tuesday during the Bhadrā period in an odd-numbered lunar mansion (Viṣamāṅghri), [the following applies]. Maghā and Viśākhā are known as the *Kula* asterisms; Rohiṇī, Jyeṣṭhā, Punarvasu, Svātī, Revatī, Hasta, Śravaṇa, Pūrvābhādrapadā, Bharaṇī, and Āśleṣā are the asterisms known as the *Upakula*. Among these, if kings set out for battle under a *Kula* asterism, they suffer defeat; however, under the *Upakula* asterisms...

Victory is achieved. If one travels during the *kulākula* constellations, two kings will remain like equals and there will be mutual harmony between them. Thus ends the section on Royal Processions (*rājayātrā*). [If travel occurs] under the Sun, Saturn, or Mars, and during odd-footed (*viṣamāṅghri*) constellations... [51, 52, 53, 54]. In the case of *tripuṣkara*, it bestows threefold merit; in the case of a twin-footed constellation (*yamalāṅghribha*), it bestows twofold merit. To destroy that defect, one should give three cows or their equivalent value.

The fruit of the Tripuṣkara yoga is threefold, and that of the Yamalāṅghri yoga is twofold; for the sake of pacifying these defects, one should give the gift of three cows. (55) In the case of Tripuṣkara, one should give two [cows]; there is no fault arising from the mere presence of the asterism. Puṣya is capable of destroying the evil done by another and whatever inauspicious act has been committed. (56) But another is not capable of causing harm even when the Moon is in its eighth house, nor if it is conjoined with a malefic planet, provided that Puṣya is endowed with strength.

97–98. Except for the planet Saturn, it always grants desired results in all auspicious rites. (80) [From] the Nāradasaṃhitā: If a king travels during the Tripuṣkara yoga, he should give away two cows as a gift to pacify that evil influence.

Alternatively, one should pay the "cow-price" (go-mūlya) [as an atonement]; furthermore, a fault cannot arise merely from the asterism in the case of the Tripuṣkara-yoga. Whatever auspicious rites, such as journeys, are performed under the Puṣya asterism, if an unfavorable yoga should occur there, the Puṣya asterism is capable of neutralizing that defect. However, if for some reason the Puṣya asterism itself should be a source of inauspiciousness, no other auspicious yoga can remove it. And as for the Puṣya...

If [the Moon] is endowed with strength, even if it be in the eighth lunar mansion (Aṣṭama-candra) or conjoined with a malefic planet, it destroys all such defects and brings success to all auspicious undertakings. 56–58. Now, the stars of the lunar mansions (nakṣatras): Three, three, six, five, three, one, four, three, five, five; two, two, five, two, one, four, three, and five. 59. Now, the stars of the lunar mansions.

Aśvinī has 3 stars; Kṛttikā has 6; Bharaṇī has 3; Rohiṇī has 5; Mṛgaśira has 3; Ārdrā has 1; Punarvasu has 4; Puṣya has 3; Āśleṣā has 5; Maghā has 5; Pūrvā Phālgunī has 2; Uttarā Phālgunī has 2; Hasta has 5; Citrā has 1; Svātī has 1; Viśākhā has 4; Anurādhā has 3; Jyeṣṭhā has 3; and Mūla has 11 stars. || 59 || [In the Bhāṣāṭīkā, Chapter 6, Verse 81: The numbers are, in order: four Vedas, four Vedas, three fires, three fires, four oceans, one hundred, two, two, and thirty-two teeth.

The number of stars for each of the constellations, beginning with Aśvinī, should be known individually: [60]. That bright star which is seen in the stellar sphere (bhagaṇa) is the junction-star (yogatārakā). [61]. There are four stars in Pūrvāṣāḍhā, four in Uttarāṣāḍhā, three in Abhijit, three in Śravaṇa, four in Dhaniṣṭhā, one hundred in Śatabhiṣā, two in Pūrvābhādrapadā, two in Uttarābhādrapadā, and thirty-two stars in Revatī. Thus, the stars of the constellations beginning with Aśvinī should be understood separately in the sky within the Śiśumāra-cakra. Which... [text ends]

Those stars that appear shining are called *yoga-tārās*. (60–61). Thus ends the enumeration of the stars. From the constellation Aśvinī (*Aśvibhāryā*) comes the bamboo tree (*vṛṣa*); from Purūṣaka [the next asterism] comes the *udumbara* (fig) tree; from Agnidhiṣṇya [Bharaṇī] comes the *drohiṇī* (jāman) tree; and from Rohiṇī comes the jackfruit tree (*jaṃbuka*). (62). The bamboo tree was produced from the Aśvinī constellation; the *phālasā* (a type of tree) from Bharaṇī; the *udumbara* from Kṛttikā; and the *drohiṇī* (jāman) tree was produced from Rohiṇī. (62).

The Khadira tree was born from the lunar mansion Indu; the Kūla tree arose from Raudra. The Vaṃśa tree originated from Diti, and the Pippala tree was produced from Puṣya. (63) In the asterism Mṛgaśiras, the Khaira tree was produced; in Ārdrā, the Baheḍā tree was produced; in Punarvasu, the Bāṃśa tree was produced; and in Puṣya, the Pippala tree was produced. (63) (82) *Nāradasaṃhitā*: From the asterism of the Serpent (Āśleṣā), the Nāga tree arises; the Vaṭa tree is born from Pitṛ (Maghā).

The *pālaśa* tree arises from Bhāgyajāta (Pūrvaphalgunī), and the *plakṣa* tree arises from Caryamasambhava (Uttaraphalgunī). From Āśleṣā, the *nāga* tree (gaṅgerana) is produced; from Maghā, the *vaṭa* (banyan) is produced; from Pūrvaphalgunī, the *ḍhāka* (palāśa); and from Uttaraphalgunī, the *pilakhana* (plakṣa). || 64 || The *ariṣṭa* tree arises from Ravibhā (Hasta), and the *śrīvṛkṣa* (bilva) arises from Āsaṃbhava (Citrā). From the Svātī asterism comes the *arjuna* tree, and from Dvidaiva (Viśākhā), the *pāhika* tree. || 65 ||

From Hasta comes the Riṃṭhaḍā tree; from Citrā, the coconut tree; from Svāti, the Arjuna tree; and from Viśākhā, the Pāha tree. (65) The Bakula tree is born from Anurādhā; Viṣṭi arises from the Puṣya asterism. The Sarja tree comes from Mūla, and the Vañjula from the asterism of Jyeṣṭhā. (66) The Panasa tree is born from Śatabhiṣaj; the Arka tree from Śravaṇa. The Śamī tree is born from Dhaniṣṭhā; the Kadamba from Śatabhiṣaj. (67) The Mango tree comes from Pūrvabhādrapadā; the Picumanda (Neem) from Uttara-bhadrapadā.

One should worship the Madhuvṛkṣa tree at the Pauṣṇa constellation (Revatī) in this manner. One born under the Areei (Aśleṣā) constellation should diligently avoid planting trees. Thus ends the sixth chapter, on the results of the constellations, in the Śrī Nāradīya Saṃhitā.

Under Anurādhā, the Bakula tree was produced; under Jyeṣṭhā, the Devadāru tree was produced; under Mūla, the Rāla tree; under Pūrvāṣāḍhā, the Jalaveta; under Uttarāṣāḍhā, the Phālasā; under Śravaṇa, the Āka; under Dhaniṣṭhā, the Jām̐ṭa; under Śatabhiṣā, the Kadaṃba; under Pūrvābhādrapadā, the Āmra tree; and under Uttarābhādrapadā, the Nīṃva.

Furthermore, for Revatī, the Mahuvā tree has arisen; thus, for the sake of pacifying these constellations, one should worship their respective trees according to the commentary on the *Nakṣatrabhāṣā* (Chapter 7, verse 83). Moreover, one should afflict the tree belonging to whichever constellation has a "hostile" (*śatru*) designation among the animal signs (*yonis*) associated with those constellations. || 66 || 67 || 68 || 69 || Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Chapter on the Results of Constellations," in the *Śrī Nāradasaṃhitā Bhāṣāṭīkā*. || 6 ||

The lords of the yogas are Dharmarāja (Yama), Viṣṇu, the Moon, Brahmā, Bṛhaspati, the Moon, Indra, Water, the Serpent, Fire, the Sun, Earth, Wind, Rudra, and Varuṇa. (1) Gaṇeśa, Rudra, the Ocean, Tvaṣṭṛ, Mitra, and the Six-faced One (Kārttikeya); Sāvitrī, Kamalā, Gaurī, the two Aśvins, the Pitṛs, and Aditi. (2)

Gaṇeśa (16), Rudra (17), Kubera (18), Tvaṣṭṛ (19), Mitra (20), Svāmikārtika (21), Sāvitrī (22), Lakṣmī (23), Gaurī (24), Aśvinīkumāra (25), Pitṛs (26), and Aditi (27)—these are the deities said to preside over the Viṣkambha and other yogas. (2) Both Vyatīpāta and Vaidhṛti are always considered great obstacles (mahāpāta). The first half of Parigha is censured for all undertakings. (3) In Viṣkambha and Vajra there are three [hours of danger]; in Gaṇḍa and Atigaṇḍa, six.

In Vyāghāta there are nine [nāḍīs], but in Śūla, five nāḍīs are condemned. ||4|| Furthermore, both Vaidhṛti and Vyatīpāta are great planetary obstacles (mahāpāta) and must be entirely avoided. The first half of the Parigha yoga is to be avoided; it is censured for all undertakings. Viṣkambha, Vajra... [Nāradasaṃhitā, 84].

Three *ghaṭīs* each at the beginning of these [nakṣatras] are to be avoided, as are six *ghaṭīs* each for *Gaṇḍa* and *Atigaṇḍa*. Nine *ghaṭīs* of *Vyāghāta* and five *ghaṭīs* of *Śūla* are to be avoided. (3–4) Furthermore, Aditi, Indu, Maghā, Āśleṣā, Mūla, Anurādhā, Puṣya, and Citrā are to be known as the *Mūrdhina* nakṣatras, in their respective order. (3) And [the others are]: Punarvasu, Mṛgaśiras, Maghā, Āśleṣā, Mūla, Anurādhā, and Puṣya.

The various asterisms according to their sequence are described as being in the head-poison (mastakapha) and the sequential poison (kramaviṣa). || 5 || One should draw one vertical line and thirteen horizontal lines. Therein, in the Khārjurika diagram, one should place the asterism at the head. || 6 || When the Sun and Moon are situated on the same single line, there is a mutual "single-bar" (ekārgala) aspect; however, this indeed excludes the Abhijit asterism. || 7 ||

There, one vertical line should be drawn and thirteen horizontal lines should be drawn; thus, one should construct there a diagram known as the *Kharjūrikā* (Date-Palm) instrument, which has a shape resembling a date-palm tree. Once all the lunar mansions (*nakṣatras*) have been written there, one should consider: if the moon’s mansion falls upon a single line, the *Ekārgala* aspect-yoga occurs. Here, the *Abhijit* mansion is not to be counted. 6–7.

In the plow-diagram (lāṅgalacakra), the tortoise-diagram (kūrmacakra), the serpent-diagram (phaṇicakracakra), and the three-channel-diagram (trināḍīcakra), the asterism Abhijit is not to be counted; this is especially true in the case of the falling of the wheel (cakrapāta). || 8 || Thus ends the seventh chapter, on Yoga, in the Śrī Nāradīya Saṃhitā. || 7 || In these—the plow-diagram, the tortoise-diagram, the serpent-diagram, and the three-channel-diagram—the asterism Abhijit is not to be included in the calculation, and particularly so in the calculation for the falling of the wheel. || 8 ||

Thus ends the seventh chapter, on the Section of Yoga, in the *Śrī-Nāradasaṃhitā-bhāṣāṭīkā*. [Chapter 73]. Bhāṣāṭīkā, Chapter 8 (85). Now, the results of the lords of the Karaṇas: Indra, Prajāpati, Mitra, Aryaman, Earth, Lakṣmī, Kīnāśa, Kali, Vṛṣabha, Sarpa, and Vāyu—these are said to be the deities of the Karaṇas beginning with Bava, respectively, for each half-tithi. (Verse 1) Indra, Prajāpati, Mitra, Aryamā, Bhūmi, Lakṣmī, Kīnāśa, Kali, Vṛṣabha, Sarpadevatā, and Vāyu are declared to be the presiding deities of the Karaṇas in their respective order.

1–2. The six *karaṇas* beginning with Bava and ending with Vaṇija are auspicious; however, Viṣṭi—whether occurring in its regular or reverse order—is not desired for auspicious rites. [The six *karaṇas*] from Bava up to Vaṇija are auspicious, while Viṣṭi—that is, every moment of Ārdrā—is always impure and should be avoided in auspicious activities. 2. Now, another method regarding Bhadrā: five are said to be in the mouth, one in the throat, and eleven in the chest.

There are four [nāḍīs] at the navel and three at the waist; these are the channels known as the tail (puccha). (3) First, five ghaṭīs of Bhadrākī are to be placed on the face; then one ghaṭī on the neck; then eleven large ones on the chest; four on the navel; three on the waist; and three ghaṭīs on the tail. (3) Failure in one's task occurs when it is on the face, death when on the neck, and poverty when on the chest; rising up occurs when it is on the navel, downfall when on the tail, and victory is certain.

For stable [planets], the middle [ghaṭīs] are preferred; for others, neither the first four nor the last four ghaṭīs are desired. Thus ends the eighth chapter, on the *Karaṇa*, in the venerable *Nāradīya-saṃhitā*. (86) In the *Nārada-saṃhitā*: In the ghaṭīs of the mouth there is loss of work; in the throat, death; in the chest, poverty; in the waist, wandering; in the navel, loss; and in the ghaṭīs of the tail, the accomplishment of one's purpose occurs.

Between these, the Karaṇa known as Sthira is middling, while Nāga and Catuṣpada are both inauspicious. || 4 || Thus ends the eighth chapter, on Karaṇas, in the Bhāṣā-Ṭīkā of the Śrī-Nāradīya-Saṃhitā. || 8 || Now, the auspicious and inauspicious Muhūrtas: During the day, the Muhūrtas are Rudra, Ahi, Mitra, Pitrya, Vasu, Daka, Viśva, Vidhātṛ, Brahmā, Indra, Indrāgni, Nirṛti, and Toya. || 1 ||

1. Rudra (1), Sarpa (2), Mitra (3), Pitṛs (4), Vasus (5), Udaka (6), Viśvedevas (7), Abhijit (8), Brahmā (9), Indra (10), Indrāgnī (11), Rakṣasa (12), and Varuṇa (13). 2. Aryaman and he known as Bhaga are to be known as the fifteen [deities]; likewise Īśa, Ajapāda, Ahirbudhnya, Pūṣan, the two Aśvins, Yama, and Vahni; 3. Dhātṛ, Candra, Aditi, Jyotis, Viṣṇu, Arka, Vāstu, and Vāyu. A fifteenth part of the day is likewise measured by the duration of the night.

The best of astrologers have stated that two *nāḍīs* constitute the measure of one *muhūrta*. Now, the inauspicious *muhūrtas* according to the sequence of the days of the week are as follows: (4) Aryaman (14) and Bhaga (15)—these fifteen *muhūrtas* exist during the day for two *ghaṭīs* each in their respective order; one should know their results to be similar to those of their namesakes, beginning with Rudra. (Śiva 1, Ajapāna 2, Ahirbudhnya 3, Bhādhāṭīkāsa... [End of commentary on Chapter 9].

(87) Pūṣan 4, Aśvinīkumāra 5, Dharmarāja 6, Agni 7, Brahmā 8, Candramas 9, Aditi 10, Bṛhaspati 11, Viṣṇu 12, Sūrya 13, Tvaṣṭṛ 14, and Vāyu 15—these are the fifteen *muhūrtas* of the night. That is to say, just as the day is divided into fifteen parts, one should likewise divide the night into fifteen parts. One *muhūrta* consists of two *ghaṭikās*. If the duration of the day or the duration of the night is less or more than thirty *ghaṭikās*, then from among these [fifteen], one [should be added or subtracted] for each [unit].

One should understand that even a single *muhūrta* is divided into sixty *ghaṭikās*. Now, I shall describe those *muhūrtas* which are inauspicious according to the sequence of the days of the week and so forth. Aryamā, Rākṣasa, Brāhma, Pitrya, Āgneya, and Abhijit; likewise Rākṣasa, Āpa, Brahma, Pitrya, Bhauja, and Īśa—these are the *muhūrtas* associated with the [days] beginning with Sunday. These *muhūrtas* are to be avoided on their respective days for auspicious rites. Furthermore, I shall hereafter describe other *yogas*, both auspicious and inauspicious.

Āryamā is inauspicious during the Muhūrta on Sunday; Rākṣasa and Brahmā are inauspicious on Monday; Pitṛ and Agni are inauspicious on Tuesday; Abhijit Muhūrta is inauspicious on Wednesday; Rākṣasa and Udaka are inauspicious for Jupiter (Thursday); Brahmā and Pitṛ are inauspicious for Venus (Friday); and Sarpa and Śiva are inauspicious Muhūrtas for Saturn (Saturday).

On Sundays and other such days, these *muhūrtas* should be avoided with care for auspicious rites. Now, other auspicious and inauspicious *yogas* are described here: When the lunar asterism (*caṃdrarkṣa*) is at a distance of 12, 4, 7, 6, 10, 13, or 20 [degrees] from the solar asterism (*sūryabhāt*), they are known as *raviyogas*, which destroy the accumulation of defects. Thus ends the ninth chapter, on *Muhūrtas*, in the *Śrī Nāradīya Saṃhitā*. (88) *Nāradasaṃhitā*.

If the lunar mansion (nakṣatra) occupied by the moon—i.e., the current asterism—is at a distance of 4, 9, 6, 10, 13, or 20 [counting] from the asterism occupied by the sun, then Ravi-yogas occur; these destroy multitudes of defects, meaning they should be known as auspicious yogas. || 7 || Thus ends the ninth chapter on Muhūrtas in the Bhāṣā-Ṭīkā of the Śrī Nāradīya Saṃhitā. || 9 || [Furthermore,] Vidyut occurs in the seventh asterism from the sun's position, and Bhṛgu in the fifth. || [8 ||]

In the eighth lunar mansion from Śūla, Saturn [is situated] in the tenth; likewise, Ketu is in the eighteenth. Daṇḍa is in the fifteenth, and Ulkā in the nineteenth. Moha, Nirghāta, and Kampa are in Kulīśa, as is Pariveṣaṇa. These should be known in their respective order starting from the twenty-first asterism. One should not perform auspicious rites when the moon is conjoined with these asterisms.

If the seventh lunar mansion from the Sun’s current mansion occurs, there is the Bhūkampa (earthquake) yoga; if the fifth, Vidyu (lightning); if the eighth, Śalabha (locusts); if the fourteenth, Śani (Saturn); if the eighteenth mansion occurs, it is the yoga known as Ketu; if the fifteenth mansion occurs, it is Daṇḍa; if the nineteenth, Ulkā (meteor); and if the twenty-first, twenty-second, twenty-third, twenty-fourth, or twenty-fifth occur, then in that respective order, the yogas are Moha, Nirghāta, Kampa, Vajra, and Pariveṣaṇa. These are the lunar mansions [that produce these effects].

The moon is observed [by subtracting its position] from the asterism of the sun; that is, one should count the lunar asterism by subtracting it from the solar asterism. (1) (2) (3). Now, the Krakaca Yoga: I shall now describe the Krakaca yoga, which is approved by the scriptures; it is censured in all undertakings, and one should perform auspicious acts only when it is not present. (4) (9A) [From the Bhāṣāṭīkā, Chapter 10].

(89) Now, [the author] describes the yoga named *krakaca*, which is condemned for all undertakings and prescribed in the scriptures; in it, no auspicious rite whatsoever should be performed. || 4 || When the sum of the lunar day (*tithi*) and the weekday (*vāra*) equals thirteen (13), this yoga is called *krakaca*; it is highly censured in all auspicious matters. || 5 || When the addition of the lunar day and the weekday results in the number thirteen (13), then the *krakaca* yoga occurs—for example, on Sunday (1) with [the lunar day] twelve (12). || 5 ||

On Monday the second, Tuesday the tenth, Wednesday the ninth, Thursday the eighth, Friday the seventh, and Saturday the sixth—when these coincide, Krakaca Yoga occurs; it is highly censured for auspicious rites. (5) If Sunday falls on the seventh lunar day and Monday on the first, Saṃvarta Yoga should be known to occur; it causes the destruction of auspicious deeds. (6) Thus ends the Saṃvartaka Yoga in the Śrī Nāradīya Saṃhitā.

When the seventh lunar day (tithi) falls on a Sunday and the first lunar day (pratipadā) falls on a Wednesday, then the Saṃvarddhaka yoga occurs; this yoga destroys auspicious actions. 6. Thus ends the Saṃvartaka Yoga in the *Śrī Nāradīya* [Purāṇa], *Bhāṣā* [Commentary]. Ānanda, Kāladaṇḍa, Dhūmra, Dhātṛ, Sudhākara, Dhvāṅkṣa, Dhvaja, Śrīvatsa, Vajra, Mudgara, Chatraka, Mitra, Mānasa, Padma, Luṃbaka, Utpāta, and Mṛtyu. 7.

Kāṇa, Siddhi, Śubha, Ābhṛta, Musala, Antaka, and Kuñjara—these are known as the Rākṣasa [yoga]. These twenty-eight yogas, which increase in duration from one to eight [ghaṭīs], yield results according to their own names. —(90) Nāradasaṃhitā.

Ānanda (1), Kāladaṇḍa (2), Dhūmra (3), Dhātṛ (4), Candra (5), Dhvāṅkṣa (6), Dhvaja (7), Śrīvatsa (8), Vajra (9), Mudrā (10), Chatra (11), Mitra (12), Mānasa (13), Padma (14), Luṃbaka (15), Utpāta (16), Mṛtyu (17), Kāṇa (18), Siddhi (19), Śubhra (20), Amṛta (21), Musala (22), Roga (23), Mātaṅga (24), Rākṣasa (25), Cara (26), Sthira (27), and Vardhamāna (28)—these are the twenty-eight yogas mentioned in this sequence. These yogas are auspicious or inauspicious according to their respective names.

They grant their fruits [as follows]: 7, 8, 9. On Sunday, starting from the asterism Aśvinī; on Monday, from Śatabhiṣaj; on Tuesday, from Āśleṣā; on Wednesday, from Hastā; on Thursday, from Anurādhā; 10. On Friday, from Jyeṣṭhā; on Saturday, from Śatabhiṣaj. If the Sun is in Hastā on a Sunday, it is called *ubha*; if in Aśvinī on a Tuesday, it is *dasrabha*; 11. If in Anurādhā on a Wednesday, it is *mitra*; if in Puṣya on a Thursday, it is *surācārya*; if in Revatī on a Friday, it is *tiṣya*; and if in Rohiṇī on a Saturday, it is *pauṣṇa*. These are known as the Siddhi-yogas. 12.

Wherever the lunar mansion (nakṣatra) of the moon may be, from that point the sequence of the group beginning with Ānanda is established; this is declared by the wise to be the order of the twenty-eight yogas. Thus ends the section on Siddhi-yogas in the Śrī Nāradīya Saṃhitā.

This is the sequence for observing these yogas: if the Sun’s day (Sunday) falls on the Aśvinī asterism, it is the Ānanda Yoga; if it falls on Bharaṇī, it is the Kāladaṇḍa—such is the sequence to be understood. On Monday, from Mṛgaśirā; on Tuesday, from Āśleṣā; on Wednesday, from Hasta; on Thursday, from Anurādhā; on Friday, from Uttarāṣāḍhā; and on Saturday, from Śatabhiṣā—one should recognize the Ānanda and other yogas. Furthermore, the Hasta asterism occurring on a Sunday [is also significant].

Commentary on the Verses: 0 10, (91). When Mṛgaśirā occurs on Monday, Aśvinī on Tuesday, Anurādhā on Wednesday, Puṣya on Thursday, Revatī on Friday, and Rohiṇī on Saturday, then these Siddha-yogas are formed. Thus, the sequence of Ānanda and other yogas has been described by the learned; one should understand that whichever nakṣatra the Moon occupies at the time, that very one constitutes the Ānanda and other yogas. 10। 31।।

On Sunday and Tuesday, the lunar day (tithi) is named Nandā; on Friday and Monday, it is Bhadrā; on Wednesday, it is Jayā; on Thursday, it is Riktā; and on Saturday, it is Pūrṇā. Nandā on Friday, Bhadrā on Wednesday, Jayā on Tuesday, Riktā on Saturday, and Pūrṇā on Thursday—these are called Siddhi-yogas. (18) If Nandā tithi falls on Friday, Bhadrā on Wednesday, Jayā on Tuesday, Riktā on Saturday, and Pūrṇā tithi on Thursday, these are declared to be Siddhi-yogas. (20) If *Amāvāsyā* falls on *Bhānu*, *Pūrṇimā* on *Candra*, *Pratipadā* on *Maṅgala*, *Tṛtīyā* on *Budha*, *Pañcamī* on *Guru*, *Saptamī* on *Śukra*, and *Navamī* on *Śani*, these are called *Vaidhṛti-yoga*. (20) Now, the *Vyatīpāta-yoga*: * *Amāvāsyā* on *Candra* (Monday), *Pūrṇimā* on *Maṅgala* (Tuesday), *Pratipadā* on *Budha* (Wednesday), *Tṛtīyā* on *Guru* (Thursday), *Pañcamī* on *Śukra* (Friday), *Saptamī* on *Śani* (Saturday), and *Navamī* on *Bhānu* (Sunday)—these are called *Vyatīpāta-yoga*. (21) If *Amāvāsyā* falls on *Candra*, *Pūrṇimā* on *Maṅgala*, *Pratipadā* on *Budha*, *Tṛtīyā* on *Guru*, *Pañcamī* on *Śukra*, *Saptamī* on *Śani*, and *Navamī* on *Bhānu*, these are called *Vyatīpāta-yoga*. (21) Now, the *Viṣkaṃbha-yoga*: * *Dvitīyā* on *Bhānu* (Sunday), *Caturthī* on *Candra* (Monday), *Ṣaṣṭhī* on *Maṅgala* (Tuesday), *Aṣṭamī* on *Budha* (Wednesday), *Daśamī* on *Guru* (Thursday), *Dvādaśī* on *Śukra* (Friday), and *Caturdaśī* on *Śani* (Saturday)—these are called *Viṣkaṃbha-yoga*. (22) If *Dvitīyā* falls on *Bhānu*, *Caturthī* on *Candra*, *Ṣaṣṭhī* on *Maṅgala*, *Aṣṭamī* on *Budha*, *Daśamī* on *Guru*, *Dvādaśī* on *Śukra*, and *Caturdaśī* on *Śani*, these are called *Viṣkaṃbha-yoga*. (22) Now, the *Vajra-yoga*: * *Tṛtīyā* on *Bhānu* (Sunday), *Pañcamī* on *Candra* (Monday), *Saptamī* on *Maṅgala* (Tuesday), *Navamī* on *Budha* (Wednesday), *Ekādaśī* on *Guru* (Thursday), *Trayodaśī* on *Śukra* (Friday), and *Pūrṇimā* on *Śani* (Saturday)—these are called *Vajra-yoga*. (23) If *Tṛtīyā* falls on *Bhānu*, *Pañcamī* on *Candra*, *Saptamī* on *Maṅgala*, *Navamī* on *Budha*, *Ekādaśī* on *Guru*, *Trayodaśī* on *Śukra*, and *Pūrṇimā* on *Śani*, these are called *Vajra-yoga*. (23) Now, the *Atigaṇḍa-yoga*: * *Caturthī* on *Bhānu* (Sunday), *Ṣaṣṭhī* on *Candra* (Monday), *Aṣṭamī* on *Maṅgala* (Tuesday), *Daśamī* on *Budha* (Wednesday), *Dvādaśī* on *Guru* (Thursday), *Caturdaśī* on *Śukra* (Friday), and *Amāvāsyā* on *Śani* (Saturday)—these are called *Atigaṇḍa-yoga*. (24) If *Caturthī* falls on *Bhānu*, *Ṣaṣṭhī* on *Candra*, *Aṣṭamī* on *Maṅgala*, *Daśamī* on *Budha*, *Dvādaśī* on *Guru*, *Caturdaśī* on *Śukra*, and *Amāvāsyā* on *Śani*, these are called *Atigaṇḍa-yoga*. (24) Now, the *Vaidhṛti-yoga* (repeated for emphasis): * *Pañcamī* on *Bhānu* (Sunday), *Saptamī* on *Candra* (Monday), *Navamī* on *Maṅgala* (Tuesday), *Ekādaśī* on *Budha* (Wednesday), *Trayodaśī* on *Guru* (Thursday), *Pūrṇimā* on *Śukra* (Friday), and *Dvitīyā* on *Śani* (Saturday)—these are called *Vaidhṛti-yoga*. (25) If *Pañcamī* falls on *Bhānu*, *Saptamī* on *Candra*, *Navamī* on *Maṅgala*, *Ekādaśī* on *Budha*, *Trayodaśī* on *Guru*, *Pūrṇimā* on *Śukra*, and *Dvitīyā* on *Śani*, these are called *Vaidhṛti-yoga*. (25) Now, the *Parigha-yoga*: * *Ṣaṣṭhī* on *Bhānu* (Sunday), *Aṣṭamī* on *Candra* (Monday), *Daśamī* on *Maṅgala* (Tuesday), *Dvādaśī* on *Budha* (Wednesday), *Caturdaśī* on *Guru* (Thursday), *Amāvāsyā* on *Śukra* (Friday), and *Tṛtīyā* on *Śani* (Saturday)—these are called *Parigha-yoga

If Monday falls on the eleventh lunar day (ekādaśī), Saturday on the twelfth (dvādaśī), Thursday on the sixth (ṣaṣṭhī), and Wednesday on the third (tṛtīyā); || 16 || [If] Friday falls on the eighth (aṣṭamī), Sunday on the ninth (navamī), and Tuesday on the fifth (pañcamī), these are proclaimed as the "burned" (dagdha) yogas. || 17 ||

If the eighth lunar day falls on a Friday, the ninth on a Sunday, or the fifth on a Tuesday, these are called *dagdhayoga* (burnt conjunctions). || 17 || These *dagdhayogas* should be known as the *paṅgu-yogas* (crippled conjunctions): when the moon is in the asterism of Yama (Bharaṇī) on a Sunday; Citrā on a Tuesday; Viśvabha (Uttarāṣāḍhā) on a Wednesday; Dhaniṣṭhā and Aryamabha (Pūrvābhādrapadā) on a Thursday; Jyeṣṭhā on a Friday; and Revatī on a Saturday—these are the *dagdhayogas*. || 18–19 ||

Those which are *dagdhayogas* are also called *paṅgu-yogas*. If Bharaṇī falls on Sunday, Citrā on Monday, Uttarāṣāḍhā on Tuesday, Dhaniṣṭhā on Wednesday, Uttarāphālgunī on Thursday, Jyeṣṭhā on Friday, and Revatī on Saturday, these are declared to be *dagdhayogas*. || 18 || 19 || The four groups beginning with Viśākhā, occurring respectively on Sundays and the other days of the week, are proclaimed as the *siddhiyogas* known as Utpāta, Mṛtyu, and Kāṇa. || 20 ||

Furthermore, among the seven days of the week beginning with Sunday, there are four yogas—namely, *utpāta* (calamity), *mṛtyu* (death), *kāṇa* (blindness), and *siddhi* (success)—occurring in sequence for the four groups of constellations beginning with Viśākhā. For example, if Viśākhā falls on a Sunday, it is *utpāta*; Anurādhā is *mṛtyu*; Jyeṣṭhā is *kāṇa*; and Mūla is *siddhi*. Then, on Monday, Pūrvāṣāḍhā is *utpāta* and Uttarāṣāḍhā is *mṛtyu*; one should understand the sequence in this manner. This same sequence should be applied to all four [groups]. (28)

These four yogas will be perfectly auspicious when occurring on the same lunar day, weekday, and asterism. (20) Yogas arising from the combination of lunar days and weekdays, as well as those arising from weekdays and asterisms, are not desired [in general]. However, they bestow great auspiciousness in regions other than those of the Hūṇas, Vaṅgas, and Khaśas. (21) Thus ends the tenth chapter, titled "The Chapter on Upagrahas," in the *Nāradīya-saṃhitā*. (10)

The yogas produced from the lunar days (*tithi*) and the weekdays (*vāra*) are inauspicious; however, the yogas produced from the weekdays and the asterisms (*nakṣatra*) are auspicious in all countries except for those of the Hūṇas, the Vaṅgas (Bengal), and the Khaśas (Nepal). || 21 || Thus ends the tenth chapter, titled "Upagraha," in the *Śrī Nāradīya Saṃhitā Bhāṣāṭīkā*. Now begins the section on the transits (*saṃkrānti*): Ghorā, Dhvāṃkṣī, Mahodaya, Mandākinī, and Nandā are considered [the names of the transits]. || 1 ||

The mixed *saṃkrānti* is named *Rākṣasikā*; these occur in sequence on Sundays and the other days of the week. [Verse 1] *Ghorā*, *Dhvāṅkṣī*, *Mahodarī*, *Mandākinī*, *Nandā*, *Miśrā*, and *Rākṣasikā*—by these names, one should know the *saṃkrāntis*. For example, if a *saṃkrānti* occurs on a Sunday, it is to be known by the name *Ghorā*. [Verse 1] *Ghorā* and the others are recorded as bestowing happiness upon Śūdras, Vaiśyas, thieves, kings, Brahmins, cattle, and those of low birth; indeed, they are considered to bring happiness to all those not specifically mentioned. [Verse 2]

The Ghorā transit bestows happiness upon Śūdras; Dhvāṅkṣī upon Vaiśyas; Mahodarī upon thieves; Mandākinī upon kings; Nandā upon Brāhmaṇas and learned scholars; Miśrā upon animals; and Rākṣasī bestows happiness upon all low-born castes, such as Cāṇḍālas. (2) It kills kings in the forenoon, Brāhmaṇas at midday, Vaiśyas in the afternoon, Śūdras at sunset, and Piśācas during the evening. (3) [Nāradasaṃhitā, 94]

If the transit (saṅkrānti) of the Sun occurs before the second watch (dupahara), it destroys kings; at midday, it destroys Brāhmaṇas; in the third watch, Vaiśyas; in the evening, Śūdras; and at the time of Pradoṣa, Piśācas. (3) At night, it destroys nocturnal wanderers (rātricaras); in the latter part of the night, food-preparers (nādyakāras); at the twilight (sandhyā), cattle and buffaloes; and if the transit occurs at night, it destroys those who bear sectarian marks (liṅgins). (4)

During the night, it causes affliction to the Rākṣasas, those who dance after midnight, and those who put on spectacles; at the time of twilight, it afflicts the Sun, as well as cows, buffaloes, and the like; and even later, at the very break of dawn, it afflicts the Sun, as well as ascetics (saṃnyāsīs) and others. (4) If the transit of the Sun into Aries (Meṣa-saṃkrānti) occurs during the day, it brings about misfortune and strife; if it occurs at night, there is incomparable abundance of food; and if it occurs at either twilight, there is a destruction of rain. (5)

If the Sun enters Aries during the day, it brings inauspicious results and causes enmity among the subjects; if it occurs at night, there will be extreme abundance of food. If it occurs during both twilights, it destroys the rains. (5) The lion, tiger, boar, donkey, elephant, buffalo, goat, horse, ram, and bull are the mounts of the Karaṇas, serving as their weapons and vehicles. (6)

Whichever Karaṇa is currently in operation—such as Bava and the rest—the mounts (vāhana) corresponding to its sequence are said to be the lion, tiger, boar, donkey, elephant, horse, goat, ram, bull, and cock. Here, in the Bava Karaṇa, the lion is the mount; these eleven Karaṇas should be observed in their proper order. (6) In Khaśa, Bāhlīka, and Vaṅga, the transition (saṃkrānti) has the lunar mansion (dhiṣṇya) as its mount; in other countries, from Bava onwards, it shall have half a lunar day (tithyardha) as its mount. (7) [Commentary on Verse 11] Bāhlīka refers to the country of Balkh. Vaṅga refers to the region of Bengal. "From Bava onwards" means that starting from the Bava Karaṇa, the sequence of mounts is determined by the half-tithis. In this context, the term "mounts" (vāhana) refers to the specific animals associated with each Karaṇa.
