Thus, the lion is the mount for Bava, the tiger for Bālava, the boar for Kaulava, the donkey for Taitila, the elephant for Gara, the horse for Vaṇija, the goat for Viṣṭi, the ram for Śakuni, the bull for Catuṣpāda, and the cock for Nāga. These are the respective mounts for the eleven Karaṇas. (6–7) *Commentary on Verse 11:* The commentary explains that the term *bāhlīka* refers to the land of Balkh (*balhika*). *Vaṅga* refers to the region of Bengal. The phrase "from Bava onwards" indicates that the sequence of mounts begins with the Bava Karaṇa and proceeds through the half-tithis (*tithyardha*). In this context, the word "mounts" (*vāhana*) denotes the specific animals assigned to each Karaṇa. Therefore, the lion is the mount for Bava, the tiger for Bālava, the boar for Kaulava, the donkey for Taitila, the elephant for Gara, the horse for Vaṇija, the goat for Viṣṭi, the ram for Śakuni, the bull for Catuṣpāda, and the cock for Nāga. These constitute the respective mounts for the eleven Karaṇas. (6–7) *Bhāṣā-Ṭīkā-saṃhitā, Chapter 11.*

(95) In the lands of Khaśa, Bāhvika, and Vaṅga (Bengal), one should know the movement of the transits according to the sequence of the lunar mansions; in other countries, however, the movement of the transits occurs according to the sequence of the Karaṇas, such as Vava and the rest. || 7 || The Sun bears in his hands, during the various Karaṇas, the Bhṛśuṇḍī, the discus, the sword, the staff, the bow, the tomara, the spear, the noose, the goad, the weapon, and the arrow. || 8 ||

The Bhṛguṇḍī, Siṃdipāla, Khaḍga, Daṇḍa, Dhanuṣa, Tomara, Jāla, Phāsa, Aṅkuśa, Astra (tegā), and Bāṇa—these weapons are said to belong to the Saṃkrāntis in the sequence of the Karanas beginning with Vava. || 8 || Furthermore, food, milk-rice (pāyasa), alms-food, cakes, milk, curd, variegated rice, molasses, honey, clarified butter, sugar, and sacrificial oblation (havis) are for one born under Vava. || 9 ||

Furthermore, rice, milk-pudding (pāyasa), parched grain (kṣāi), cakes (pūḍaā), milk, curd, variegated rice (citrānna), molasses, honey, ghee, and sugar—these are the foods for the Saṃkrāntis; they should be understood according to the sequence of the Vayas and Karaṇas. || 9 || The Sun is situated above [the earth] during the Niviṣṭī, Vaṇija, Bālava, Gara, Vava, Kaulava, Śakuna, and Kiṃstughna Karaṇas. || 10 ||

Furthermore, when the Sun enters a solar transit (saṃkrānti) during the Karaṇas Viṣṭi, Bālava, Gara, or Vava, it should be known as "seated" (baiṭhī). During Kaulava, Śakuni, or Kiṃstughna, it should be known as "standing" (khaḍī). || 10 || When the transit occurs in Catuṣpāt, Taitila, or Nāga, it is called "sleeping" (supta). At that time, there will be an unfavorable sequence regarding the price of grain and rainfall. || 11 ||

Among these, one should know that when the sun enters a sign during the *catuṣpāda* (quadruped), *taitila*, or *nāga* periods, the transit is "lying down" (*sūtī*). In a "seated" (*baiṭhī*) transit, food is cheap; in a "standing" (*khar̤ī*) transit, there is rain; and in a "lying down" (*sūtī*) transit, one should know the result to be inauspicious. (11) (96) *Nāradasaṃhitā*: Whichever weapon, vehicle, or food belongs to a particular class of people, those people shall suffer destruction if [the sun] sleeps, sits, or stands [in the corresponding period]. (12)

Whatever weapons, vehicles, or food are present at the time of the transit (saṃkrānti), those belonging to the specific class of people corresponding to that birth sign, as well as those who are lying down, sitting, or standing, shall meet their destruction along with their respective objects. || 12 || One should calculate the fourfold asterisms beginning with Rohiṇī in rotation as Andhaka, Mandasaṃjna, Madhyasaṃjna, and Sulocana. || 13 ||

One should know the constellations Rohiṇī and the others in this sequence: Andha, Mandalocana, Madhyasaṃjñaka, and Sulocana. In that regard, one should perform seven revolutions of two constellations each: Rohiṇī is Andha, Mṛgaśiras is Mandalocana, and so forth. (13) When the sun’s transit occurs in fixed signs, it should be known as Viṣṇupadā; when it occurs in dual-natured signs, it should be known as Ṣaḍaśītimukhī. (14)

If the Sun’s transit (saṃkrānti) occurs upon the fixed signs of Taurus, Leo, Scorpio, and Aquarius, it should be known as the Saṃkrānti named Viṣṇupada; and when the Sun is upon the dual-natured signs beginning with Gemini, it should be known as the Ṣaḍaśītimukhī Saṃkrānti. || 14 || The northern and southern solstices (ayana) certainly occur at the transits of the Sun in Capricorn and Cancer respectively; the two equinoxes (viṣuvat) should be known to occur at the transits of the Sun in Libra and Aries. || 14 ||

When the sun enters Capricorn (*makara-saṃkrānti*), the northern transit (*uttarāyaṇa*) begins; when the sun enters Cancer (*karka-saṃkrānti*), the southern transit (*dakṣiṇāyana*) begins on that day; and when the sun enters Libra (*tulā*) and Aries (*meṣa*), it is the equinox (*viṣuvat*), meaning day and night are equal in duration. (15) [Bhāṣāṭīkā, Chapter 11, Verse 97] It is proclaimed that the entire day during the transit is of great merit.

If the Sun’s transit occurs during the night, the rule for all transits is as follows: (16) If the Sun’s transit occurs during the day, it is said that the entire day is highly meritorious; however, if the transit occurs at night, the established rule applies to all transits. (16) If the southern solstice (Yāmyāyana) occurs during the morning twilight of sunrise, then the merit belongs to the day starting from sunrise; if it occurs after the forenoon, [the merit belongs to the following day]. (17)

For example, at the junction of sunrise, if it is the Dakṣiṇāyana—that is, the Saṃkrānti of Karka—the meritorious time (puṇyakāla) should be known to belong to the very day on which the sun rises; and if the Saṃkrānti occurs even before the junction of the time of sunrise, then the meritorious time belongs to the preceding day. This is the rule regarding the Saṃkrānti of Karka. If the Northern Solstice (Saumyāyana) occurs at the time of sunset, then the meritorious time falls on that same day; however, if it occurs after the afternoon [of that day], [the merit belongs to the following day]. (18)

Furthermore, when the sun enters Capricorn (makara-saṃkrānti) at the junction of sunset, one should know that the auspicious time (puṇyakāla) occurs on that very day; if it occurs after the junction during the night, the auspicious time is known to be on the following day. (18) That is to say, the period from sunset is measured as three ghaṭikās [of twilight], and likewise, the period from sunrise (ardhodaya) is measured as three ghaṭikās in the morning. (19)

The evening *saṃdhyā* lasts for three *ghaṭikās* after half the solar disc has set, and the morning *saṃdhyā* is said to last for three *ghaṭikās* before half the disc has risen. 19. (98) *Nāradasaṃhitā*: Before midnight in the forenoon, as previously stated, [the *ṣaḍaśītimukha* occurs] at the feet of Viṣṇu; if it occurs later, it belongs to the following day. 20.

One should know that this period of merit belongs to the transits (saṃkrānti) of Cancer and Capricorn. Regarding the previously mentioned transit named Viṣṇupada and the transit named Ṣaḍaśītimukha: if it occurs before midnight, the period of merit is on the preceding day; if it occurs after midnight, one should know the period of merit is on the following day. || 20 || If the transit occurs in the afternoon, it is the reverse for the Ṣaḍaśīti. The fruit is of the same nature as the lunar mansion (nakṣatra) with which the Sun’s transit coincides. || 21 ||

A person obtains good or evil results according to that sign of the Moon at the time of the transit (saṃkrānti), an eclipse, or during the asterism (nakṣatra); this is the sequence for counting from the previous sign. When the Sun enters a solstitial transit (ayanasaṃkrānti), then the transition into that sign occurs; or during a transit or an eclipse in the asterism, one should count starting from the birth sign. || 22-23 ||

The meritorious period (*puṇyakāla*) of the *saṃkrānti* named *Ṣaḍaśīti* should be understood as being the reverse of these *saṃkrāntis* named *Viṣṇupada*. Just as there is a *saṃkrānti* in the moon, so too is the result; when the *saṃkrānti* occurs on a Sunday, the person for whom the moon is auspicious obtains the best result. On that day of the *saṃkrānti*, the sequence of counting begins from the lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*) of the preceding day.

Whether it be the solstitial transit (*ayana-saṃkrānti*) of the Sun or its transit into another zodiac sign (*rāśi-saṃkrānti*), the calculation is made from the lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*) on that very day up to the birth-mansion. Now, the results of these two are stated: "Three are inauspicious and six are auspicious, rotating again and again; loss, gain, stability, and loss of that [stability] occur in succession from the Sun. (22) *Commentary:* From the sun's position at the time of the transit, one counts three signs as inauspicious and six as auspicious, repeating this cycle. Consequently, there is loss, gain, stability, and the loss of that stability, occurring in order starting from the Sun's position. (22) *Bhāṣā-Ṭīkā*, Chapter 12.

24. First, three constellations are inauspicious; then six are auspicious; thereafter three cause harm; then six bring prosperity; then three cause loss of position; and finally three constellations grant the attainment of position. In this manner, the solar transit (*sūryasaṃkrānti*) is determined by means of the lunar constellations (*candranakṣatra*). 25. Upon a sesame seed, one should draw a trident and a triangle within a circle; having placed gold there, one should offer it for the pacification of that defect.

If the transit (saṃkrānti) is one that bestows inauspiciousness, then for the pacification of that defect, one should draw a wheel upon a sesame seed, and having drawn a triangle and a trident upon it, place gold thereon and give it as a gift. || 25 || The Moon becomes strong by the power of its asterism (tārābala); the Sun is likewise strong by virtue of that; and similarly, a planet gains superior strength from its transit. || 26 || Thus ends the eleventh chapter, on the Characteristics of Transits, in the Śrī Nāradīya Saṃhitā. || 11 ||

By the strength of Tārā (the Moon), the Moon becomes powerful; by the strength of the Moon, the Sun becomes powerful; and that Sun is powerful by obtaining the strength of other planets through the power of the Saṃkrānti. 26. Thus ends the eleventh chapter, on the Characteristics of Saṃkrānti, in the Bhāṣā-Ṭīkā of the Śrī Nāradīya Saṃhitā. 11. Now begins the chapter on Gocara (Transits). The auspicious Sun [is not found] in the third, tenth, first, sixth, or eighth houses from the birth [ascendant].

If the Sun is situated in the 3rd, 11th, 10th, or 6th house from the birth sign (janmarāśi), it is auspicious; however, if it is not in any of the 9th, 5th, 4th, or 12th houses from the birth sign, there is no piercing (vedha). That is to say, the Sun in the 3rd house from the birth sign is auspicious. (Nāradasaṃhitā) [Note: The text specifies that if the Sun is in the 9th, 5th, 4th, or 12th from the birth sign, it does not constitute a piercing.]

However, if any other planet is present in the ninth house, a *vedha* (piercing aspect) occurs; this is auspicious. No planet should be present in the fifth house from the eleventh. If the Sun is in the tenth house, no planet should be present in the fourth house; and if the Sun is in the sixth house, no planet should be present in the twelfth house from the birth sign (*janmarāśi*).

If any planet other than Saturn occupies these positions, there will be a solar piercing (sūryavedha), and consequently, no auspicious results will remain; thus, one should apply this piercing to all these places in their respective order. In the same manner, they speak of the piercing by the Moon and other planets as well. [Verse 2: From birth, if the Moon is pierced by planets situated in the 7th, 1st, 11th, 6th, 10th, 9th, 5th, and 3rd houses, it is inauspicious; however, from birth, it is auspicious if it is pierced by benefic planets situated in the 10th, 8th, 12th, 4th, and 9th houses. [Commentary: From the natal sign (janmarāśi), [the piercing occurs when planets are in] the 7th, 1st, 11th, 6th, 10th, 9th, 5th, and 3rd houses. It is auspicious if the Moon is pierced by benefics situated in the 10th, 8th, 12th, 4th, and 9th houses from birth.

In these positions, the Moon does not cast a *vedha* (piercing aspect), which is therefore auspicious; however, from the birth *rāśi*, no planet other than Mercury should be situated in the 2nd, 5th, 8th, 12th, 4th, or 9th houses. Since Mercury is the son of the Moon, he does not cast a *vedha*. One should examine these piercing positions sequentially against one another. (Verse 2: Mars is excellent when situated in the 3rd, 10th, or 11th house from the birth *rāśi*, as it does not pierce [the Moon].

In the twelfth, second, and seventh houses from birth, Mars is excellent and does not cause *vedha* (piercing); however, no planet should be present in the twelfth, fifth, and ninth houses. One should understand the results of Saturn to be identical to those of this Mars, with the exception that the Sun does not cause *vedha* in the aforementioned houses for Saturn. (3) [Commentary in Bhāṣā-Ṭīkā, Chapter 12]

(101) Mercury is auspicious when not aspected by malefics in the 5th, 8th, and 12th houses from birth; however, it is auspicious from birth if the Moon or other planets—excluding the Sun—are situated in the 9th, 3rd, 1st, 8th, 12th, or 10th houses as manifestors [from birth]. [4] From birth, [Mercury is auspicious] in its own, exaltation, or friendly signs, provided they are not the 12th, 7th, or 4th houses. [5]

Jupiter is most auspicious from the natal ascendant (janmarāśi) provided it is not pierced by other planets. [6] From the natal ascendant, these positions—2, 11, 9, 5, and 7—are excellent; however, no planet should be situated in these positions from the natal ascendant: 12, 8, 11, 4, and 3. [5] Venus is not auspicious from the natal ascendant in the 1st, 2nd, 4th, 3rd, 6th, 8th, 10th, and 11th houses; nor should it occupy the 8th, 7th, 1st, or 10th houses from the natal ascendant, or be situated in the 11th, 6th, or 3rd houses. [6] Furthermore, [from the natal ascendant], the 1st, 2nd, 3rd, 4th, 5th, 8th, 9th, and 12th houses... [are considered].

In these positions, Venus is not pierced (vedhita) and is therefore auspicious; however, no planet should be present in the following houses from the birth chart: 8, 7, 1, 10, 9, 5, 11, 6, and 5. That is to say, one should understand the piercing (vedha) for each position in sequence: for Venus in the first house, [a planet] in the eighth; for [Venus] in the second, in the seventh; for [Venus] in the third, in the first, and so on. (6) When [Venus] is conjoined with a piercing in its own sign (svagṛha), it does not bestow any auspiciousness whatsoever.

Therefore, having considered the piercing (*vedha*), one should then declare its auspicious or inauspicious nature. (7) A planet that is afflicted by a piercing does not yield any auspicious results; therefore, one should consider those various types of piercings and then state the outcome. (8) [Nāradasaṃhitā] (102) By means of the rule of the leftward piercing (*vāmavedha*), even an inauspicious planet becomes auspicious; therefore, having examined those various piercings, one should then declare the result. (8)

Furthermore, even inauspicious planets become auspicious through the method of *vāmavedha* (leftward piercing). That is to say, for example, although twelve solar days are inauspicious, if they are pierced by planets situated in the sixth house from the birth sign (*janmarāśi*), it becomes auspicious. Similarly, when a piercing occurs in the reverse order, it is called *vāmavedha*. Therefore, one should predict the results after considering these various types of piercings. || 8 ||

If an astrologer, without knowing the various types of *vedhas* (piercing aspects), should declare the results, that man, being a speaker of falsehood, will always become an object of ridicule. (9) A planet aspected by a benefic does not yield undesirable results, while one aspected by a malefic bestows auspicious ones.
However, both of those planets become fruitless if they are aspected by their own [planetary] enemy. (10)

Even a planet that bestows inauspicious results produces auspicious results if it is aspected by auspicious planets; likewise, even an auspicious-granting planet becomes fruitless if it is aspected by malefic planets or by its enemy planet. || 10 || A planet situated in its sign of debilitation, or even in the sign of its enemy, or one that is heliacally set, does not yield either auspicious or inauspicious results. || 11 ||

A planet situated in its sign of debilitation, or one that has entered the house of its enemy, or one that is set (astamita), does not yield any fruit whatsoever, whether auspicious or inauspicious. ||11|| When planets are situated in unfavorable positions, one should diligently perform propitiatory rites (śānti). Loss and gain are dependent upon the planets; therefore, the planets are most worthy of worship. ||12|| (Commentary on the Bhāṣāṭīkā, Chapter 1, Verse 3. [103]) If a planet is situated in an unfavorable position—meaning an inauspicious station—one should cause propitiatory rites to be performed for them with great effort.

Since loss and gain are dependent upon the planets, therefore the planets should always be worshipped. (12) The gem called maṇi, the pearl, the one known as coral, that named after Garuḍa (emerald), then topaz, diamond, and those known as sapphire and agate—these should be worn in order for the satisfaction of the Sun and the other planets respectively. (13) Thus ends the twelfth chapter, on the Transit of Planets (*gocara*), in the glorious Nāradīya-saṃhitā. (12)

By wearing these gems in their respective order—ruby, pearl, coral, emerald (*harījāta*), topaz (*puṣparāja*), diamond, sapphire (*nīlamaṇi*), agate (*gomeda*), and cat’s-eye (*vaiḍūrya*)—the planets beginning with the Sun become propitious. (13) Thus ends the twelfth chapter, on the *Gocara*, in the *Bhāṣā-ṭīkā* commentary on the *Śrī Nāradīya Saṃhitā*. On whichever day of the bright fortnight the Moon bestows auspiciousness upon a person, that entire fortnight is auspicious for him; conversely, the dark fortnight is auspicious [on the corresponding days].

1. In whichever fortnight (pakṣa) the Moon resides during the days beginning with the bright fortnight (śuklapakṣa), that fortnight is auspicious for him; whereas in the dark fortnight (kṛṣṇapakṣa), it is otherwise auspicious—that is, it is auspicious to observe the strength of the stars (tārābala) during the dark fortnight. 2. In the bright fortnight, the Moon is auspicious when situated in the second, ninth, or fifth houses, provided it is not located in the sixth, eighth, or fourth houses, and is not pierced by the planets (gaganecara).

In the bright fortnight, the second, ninth, and fifth lunar days are auspicious for the Moon; however, on the sixth, eighth, and fourth, no planet should be present. That is to say, if any planet other than Mercury occupies these positions from the birth asterism (janmarāśi), it results in the piercing (vedha) of the Moon. (104) *Nāradasaṃhitā*: Now, the asterisms (tārās): Birth (janma), Wealth (saṃpat), Misfortune (vipat), Safety (kṣema), Enemy (pratyari), Accomplishment (sādhaka), and Death (vadha).

A friend (mitra), a great friend (paramamitra), and again [the others] from birth (janma) onwards [are the nine stars]. 3. The nine asterisms (tārās) are said to be: Birth (janma) 1, Prosperity (saṃpat) 2, Adversity (vipat) 3, Security (kṣema) 4, Enemy (pratyari) 5, Accomplisher (sādhaka) 6, Slayer (vadha) 7, Friend (mitra) 8, and Great Friend (paramamitra) 9. In that regard, one should count starting from the asterism of birth in due order. If there are more than nine, one should divide by nine. 3. The asterisms known as Birth, Third, and Fifth yield undesirable results. To ward off these undesirable effects, one should give [gifts] to a twice-born (dvijāti). 4.

Likewise, the third, fifth, and seventh lunar days (janmas) are not auspicious; for the pacification of these inauspicious stars, one should give the following gifts to a Brāhmaṇa: vegetables, jaggery, salt, sesame seeds, and gold, in that order. When the star is powerful in the dark fortnight, the moon is powerful in the bright fortnight. 4.

Vegetables, jaggery, salt, sesame seeds, and gold—these are to be given in their respective order. In the dark fortnight (kṛṣṇapakṣa), the star (tārā) is powerful, while in the bright fortnight (śuklapakṣa), the moon is powerful. || 5 || There are twelve states of the moon during the day and night respectively; in marriage and other such rites, the specific designation yields a corresponding result. || 6 ||

The twelve states of the moon during the day and night have been described in their respective order; therein, in matters such as marriage and other rites, the results should be understood to correspond to the specific designation [of each state]. (6) [Commentary in Bhāṣā-Ṭīkā, Chapter 14, Verse 105]: Multiply the lunar asterism by sixty and add the ghaṭīs of the time in question. Divide the result by four hundred and fifteen, and then divide by twelve; these yield the [current] state. (7)

Multiply the asterisms (nakṣatras) beginning with Aśvinī by sixty, then add the ghaṭīs of the current asterism. Multiply that sum by four and divide it by forty-five (45). If the remainder there is greater than twelve, then divide by twelve. || 7 || [The results] correspond to the names: Pravāsa, Naṣṭa, Ākhyamṛta, Jayā, Hāsyā, Rati, Mudā, Supti, Mukti, Jvara, Kampa, and Usthiti. || 8 ||

Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, on the Strength of the Moon, in the Śrī Nāradīya Saṃhitā. (13) Furthermore, one should know that there are twelve states—namely, travel (1), loss (2), death (3), victory (4), laughter (5), passion (6), joy (7), sleep (8), eating (9), fever (10), trembling (11), and stability (12)—which yield results corresponding to their respective names.

In that regard, for one born under the sign of Aries (Meṣarāśi), the designations such as "departure" (pravāsa) and so forth should be understood; for one under Taurus (Vṛṣarāśi), "lost" (naṣṭa) and so forth; and for one under Gemini (Mithunarāśi), "death" (maraṇa) and so forth—thus they should be calculated. 8. Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, on the Strength of the Moon, in the Bhāṣā-Ṭīkā of the Śrī Nārada Saṃhitā. 13. Now, the results of the Ascendant (Lagna): "The tying of a turban, alliance, war, ornaments, metallurgy, mines, battle, and professional work—all these succeed when the Ascendant is Aries. 1. Thus ends the section on the Ascendant of Aries.

The binding of turbans, vehicles, secret alliances (or treaties), war, ornaments, mineral treasuries, and battle—these activities are accomplished in the sign of Aries. 1. Thus ends the sign of Aries. (106) Nāradasaṃhitā: Auspicious rites, permanent structures, the commencement of building work, agriculture, trade, cattle, and so forth, are successfully accomplished in the sign of Taurus. 2. Thus ends the sign of Taurus.

Auspicious rites, the desire for stability, entering a new home, and other such ceremonies, as well as agriculture, trade, and activities concerning livestock, are accomplished under the sign of Taurus (Vṛṣa). (2) Thus ends the section on the Ascendant of Taurus. The attainment of arts and knowledge, the wearing of ornaments, taking up arms, the mounting of elephants, marriage, and royal consecration—these and similar acts should be performed when Gemini (Mithuna) rises. (3) Thus ends the section on the Ascendant of Gemini.

The arts (kalā), knowledge (vijñāna), spiritual accomplishments (siddhi), ornaments (ābhūṣaṇa), combat (yuddha), seeking refuge (āśraya), the buying and selling of elephants, marriage, and consecration (abhiṣeka) and other such rites should be performed in the Gemini (mithuna) ascendant. (3). Thus ends the Gemini ascendant. The construction of ponds, wells, tanks, and the like; the binding and releasing of water; rites for prosperity (pauṣṭika); and writing and engraving should be undertaken when Cancer (karkaṭa) is rising. (4). Thus ends the Cancer ascendant.

Constructing wells, step-wells, ponds, and embankments, laying canals, works for nourishment, writing, and accounting—these activities are auspicious when performed under the Cancer ascendant. (4) Thus ends the Cancer ascendant. Sugarcane, grain, trade, merchandise, agriculture, service, and other stable undertakings, as well as those involving courage and royal wealth, succeed under the Leo ascendant. (5) Thus ends the Leo ascendant. [From the Bhāṣā-Ṭīkā, Chapter 14]

(107) Trade in sugarcane and grain, shops, agriculture, service, and other stable occupations, as well as daring deeds (acts of force), warfare, and royal duties—these activities are auspicious when performed under the sign of Leo. Thus ends the section on Leo. Knowledge, arts, the preparation of medicinal herbs, ornaments, mobile and stationary undertakings—all such matters pertaining to the sign of Virgo are suitable for nourishment and all forms of auspiciousness. Thus ends the section on Virgo.

One should perform rites involving learning, crafts, medicine, ornaments, mobile and stationary objects, as well as nourishing and auspicious ceremonies, under the sign of Virgo (Kanyā-lagna). 6. Thus ends the section on Virgo. Agriculture, commerce, travel, livestock, marriage, vows, and so forth—all such activities, as well as any work related to scales and balances, should be undertaken under Libra (Tulā-lagna). 7. Thus ends the section on Libra.

Agriculture, commerce, vehicles, livestock, marriage, vows and the like, household utensils, and construction work—such activities should be undertaken when the ascendant is Libra (Tulā). (7) Thus ends the section on the Libra Ascendant. All stable undertakings, service to the king, royal consecration, acts of theft, and stable initiatives should be performed when the Scorpion (Vṛścika) ascendant rises. (8) Thus ends the section on the Vṛścika Ascendant.

One should undertake these activities in the Scorpio ascendant: fulfilling desires, stable undertakings, service to the king, consecration, theft, and the commencement of steady works. || 8 || Thus ends the section on the Scorpio Ascendant. Vows, marriage, journeys, as well as the arts and crafts of the limbs, both mobile and stationary matters, and the use of weapons and missiles—these should be performed when the Sagittarius ascendant rises. || 9 || Thus ends the section on the Sagittarius Ascendant. (108) *Nāradasaṃhitā*.

Taking vows and observances, marriage, dying at sacred pilgrimage sites (tīrtha) and the like, the arts of the limbs, crafts, fine arts, stable undertakings, weapons, and missiles—these should be performed during the Aquarius (Dhanu) ascendant. || 9 || Thus ends the Aquarius ascendant. Binding water, releasing it, weapons, agriculture, and work involving camels and the like, as well as setting out on journeys and dealing with livestock, servants, and so forth—these should be undertaken during the Capricorn (Makara) ascendant. || 10 || Thus ends the Capricorn ascendant.

Tying bundles, constructing canals, surgical operations, agriculture, work involving animals such as camels, sexual acts, and the employment of servants—all these should be performed under the ascendant of Capricorn (Makaralagna). || 10 || Thus ends the section on Makaralagna. Agriculture, trade, animal husbandry, water-related works, arts and crafts, sea voyages, and the use of missiles and weapons—all these should be undertaken when the ascendant is Aquarius (Kalaśodaya). || 11 || Thus ends the section on Kumbhalagna.

Agriculture, trade, cattle-rearing, water-based work, craftsmanship, arts and similar skills, traveling by water, and the use of weapons and missiles—all these should be undertaken during the Aquarius (Kumbha) ascendant. || 11 || Thus ends the section on the Aquarius Ascendant. Vows, marriage, consecrations, the installation of water-vessels, settling in a new residence, ornamentation, and the preparation of water-jars—these activities are auspicious during the Pisces (Mīna) ascendant. || 12 || Thus ends the section on the Pisces Ascendant.

Observing vows, marriage, consecration, the installation of water-vessels, the rite of entry, wearing ornaments, and the offering of water-vessels—these rites are auspicious when performed under the sign of Pisces. 12. Thus ends the section on Pisces. The pairs of Taurus, Cancer, Virgo, the last [sign] Scorpio, Libra, and Sagittarius are auspicious; they are favorable when occupied by benefic planets, while the others are considered malefic signs. 13. Commentary in Bhāṣā: [Chapter 14, Verse 109 & 44].

Furthermore, Taurus, Gemini, Cancer, Virgo, Pisces, Libra, and Sagittarius are auspicious ascendants, because these are the stations of benefic planets, whereas other ascendants are the signs of malefic planets. (13) The waning Moon, the Sun, Saturn, and Mars are malefic; Mercury is malefic when conjoined [with them]. The Full Moon, Mercury, Jupiter, and Venus are the benefic planets. (14)

The waning moon, the sun, Saturn, and Mars are malefic planets; Mercury is also inauspicious when associated with them. The full moon, Mercury, Jupiter, and Venus are benefic planets. (14) The nature of the results for these signs arises from their very essence, whether through planetary conjunctions, the influence of benefics or malefics, or by being aspected by celestial bodies. (18)

From the conjunction of three signs, auspicious or inauspicious results arise by their very nature; furthermore, auspicious or inauspicious results also occur through the aspect of auspicious or inauspicious planets. (15) Even a cruel sign is considered auspicious if it is occupied by a benefic planet; conversely, even a benefic sign becomes cruel if it is conjoined with a malefic planet. (16)

If a cruel sign (rāśi) has auspicious planets situated upon it, it should be known as a giver of auspicious results; likewise, if it is conjoined with cruel planets, even an auspicious sign should be known as cruel. || 16 || By means of planetary conjunctions and aspects, the Moon produces results arising from the planets; devoid of these two, it merely resorts to its own nature. || 17 || (3.10) Nāradasaṃhitā.

Through planetary conjunctions (yoga) as well as aspects (dṛṣṭi), the Moon bears the auspicious or inauspicious results of those planets; however, when it is devoid of both, then the Moon produces only its own results. 17. In the beginning, the ascendant (lagna) gives full results; in the middle, it gives middling results; and at the end, it gives insignificant results. Indeed, it is exactly like this in all respects. 18.

The ascendant produces its full fruit at the beginning, moderate fruit in the middle, and very little fruit at the end. (18) In all cases, first [consider] the ascendant, then the strength of the Moon for the doer; in the case of others, when the Moon is strong, other planets also become strong. (19)

In all cases, one should first examine the strength of the *lagna* (ascendant), and then examine the strength of the Moon for the agent (*kartā*). If the Moon is strong in a sign other than that of the bride, one should know him to be endowed with the strength of all the planets. (19) The strength of the Moon is the support (*ādhāra*), and the strength of the other planets is the supported (*ādheya*). By means of the support, the supported is bestowed and rendered stable. (20) The strength of the Moon is the foundation, while the strength of the other planets is what rests upon it. By means of that foundation, the supported is granted and finalized.

That is to say, the Moon is the support; by means of the Moon's strength, the protection of that which is supported [the other planets] is ensured. (20) If that Moon is auspicious, all the planets bestow auspicious results; if it is inauspicious, they bestow inauspicious results—with the exception of the Sun. (21) If the Moon is a giver of auspiciousness, all the planets should be understood as givers of auspicious results; if it is inauspicious, they are likewise inauspicious. However, this rule does not apply to the Sun. (21)

In the Bhāṣā-Ṭīkā, Chapter 15: (11.1) "The planets situated in those ninth-parts (navāṃśas) whose ascendants yield auspicious results bestow results arising from the ascendant; one should calculate in this very manner. (22) One should understand that those planets which yield auspicious results in the ascendants likewise yield auspicious results according to the ascendant when they are situated in the ninth-parts of those ascendants. (22) Indeed, if an ascendant endowed with all virtues is obtained by that [calculation], then...

When a Lagna endowed with all auspicious qualities is obtained, the conjunction of defects remains slight and the virtues (auspicious factors) become extensively prevalent. || 23 || O Grandfather, a time that is indeed corrupted by defects must be avoided; however, if there is an abundance of virtues and a scarcity of defects according to one's capacity, then it is beneficial. || 24 || Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, "On All Lagnas," in the Śrī Nāradīya Saṃhitā. || 11 ||

That time which has become defiled by defects is the greatest of all; therefore, it should be abandoned. Furthermore, if there are many virtues in the *lagna* despite one's best efforts, then other defects remain only slight. || 24 || Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, the Chapter on All *Lagnas*, in the *Bhāṣā-Ṭīkā* commentary on the *Śrī Nāradīya Saṃhitā*. || 14 || Now begins the consideration of the *Rajasvalā* (the period of menstruation). On the new moon, the fourth, eighth, sixth, twelfth, and first lunar days (*tithis*), as well as during the first half of the *Parigha* yoga, and during the *Vyatīpāta* and *Vaidhṛti* yogas; || 1 ||

If the first menses occur during the twilight periods (*saṃdhyā*), during an eclipse, or under the *viṣṭi* yoga, it is inauspicious. (112) [From] the Nāradasaṃhitā: A woman who menstruates on Sunday and the subsequent days, in order, will respectively be: sickly, devoted to her husband, miserable, possessed of sons, an enjoyer of pleasures, dear to her husband, or burdened with affliction. (2)

If a woman first experiences her menses on the new moon (amāvasyā), the *riktā* days, the eighth (*aṣṭamī*), the sixth (*ṣaṣṭhī*), the twelfth (*dvādaśī*), or the first lunar day (*pratipadā*)—or during the first half of the *parigha* yoga, the *vyatīpāta*, the *vaidhṛti*, in the evening, during a "burning of the quarters" (*digdāha*), or the *bhadrā* period—it should be known that the result is inauspicious. Furthermore, the results for the days of the week starting from Sunday, in the order they occur when she first menstruates, are as follows: 1) afflicted by disease, 2) devoted to her husband, 3) sorrowful, 4) possessed of sons, and 5) an enjoyer of pleasures.

One who is beloved by her husband (6), and afflicted by afflictions (7)—such are the fruits to be known from the lords of the asterisms beginning with the Sun. || 1 || 2 || A woman who, during her first menses under the asterism of Aśvinī, is endowed with fortune, blessed, possessed of sons, filled with happiness, stable, dignified, and preeminent in her family; || 3 || If a woman becomes menstruating for the first time under the asterism of Aśvinī, she becomes endowed with wealth, fortunate, possessed of sons, filled with happiness, steadfast, honorable, and highly distinguished within her lineage. || 3 ||

One who is immoral, unchaste, barren, intent on causing abortion, a servant, or a "crow-barren" woman (one who bears only one child)—these are the results for a woman experiencing her first menstruation under the asterism Bharaṇī. Furthermore: One of wicked nature, an adulteress, barren, intent on causing abortion, a prostitute, or one whose children have died—these are the results for a woman experiencing her first menstruation under the asterism Kṛttikā (Vahni).

An unfaithful wife, barren, intent on causing miscarriage, a prostitute, or one whose children die—these are the results to be known for one whose first menses occur under the Kṛttikā constellation. (5) In the Bhāṣāṭīkā, Chapter 15 (113): One who is virtuous, of good progeny, devoted to her husband, firm in her vows, and constantly engaged in the worship of the household deities—such is she whose first menses occur under the Dhātu (Mṛgaśirā) constellation. (6)

One who possesses a beautiful nature, a noble lineage, devotion toward her husband, firm observance of vows, and is always intent upon the worship of the household deities—this fruit is to be known when she first experiences her menses during the Rohiṇī asterism. (6) The woman who is endowed with virtues, devoted to righteousness, patient, chaste, dear to her husband, and blessed with good sons, whose first menses occurs during the Moon asterism (Mṛgaśīrṣa), [attains these fruits]. (7)

Endowed with virtues, devoted to dharma, all-enduring, chaste, loving her husband, and possessing excellent sons—this fruit occurs when a woman first experiences her menses during the Mṛgaśiras nakṣatra. || 7 || An unchaste woman, unfortunate, wicked, one whose sons have died, cruel, dull-witted, and fallen from her vows due to evil conduct—these result if the first menses occur during the Ārdrā (Raudra) nakṣatra. || 8 ||

Inauspicious, unfortunate, wicked, bearing stillborn children, cruel, foolish, of evil conduct, and fallen—these are the results for a woman who experiences her first menses during the Ārdrā nakṣatra. || 8 || Devoted to her husband, possessed of sons, delighting in the offspring of others, skilled in the arts and full of affection—she who experiences her first menses during the Punarvasu nakṣatra. || 9 ||

Devoted to her husband, blessed with sons, bringing joy even to the children of others, endowed with all arts, and abiding in what is dear and beneficial—these are the fruits for a woman experiencing her first menses during the Punarvasu nakṣatra. || 9 || (114) Nāradasaṃhitā: Devoted to her husband, blessed with sons, possessing honor and enjoyment, auspicious, intent on virtuous deeds, and skillful—these are the fruits for a woman experiencing her first menses during the Tiṣya (Puṣya) nakṣatra. || 10 ||

One who loves her husband, is blessed with sons, possesses honor and enjoyment, is auspicious, remains intent upon beautiful deeds, and is clever—these are the results of the first menstruation occurring under the Puṣya constellation. (10) One who is devoted to another husband, a servant, prone to anger, devoid of virtues, lazy, a liar, and one who bears wicked sons—these result from the first menstruation under the Bhujanga (Āśleṣā) constellation. (11)

For a woman whose first menses occur under the asterism Āśleṣā becomes one who dallies with other men, prone to pride and anger, devoid of compassion, lazy, a liar, and possesses wicked offspring. (11) One whose first menses occur under Maghā is free from co-wives and jealousy, yet afflicted by disease; she is always obedient, greedy, devoted to her father’s house, and highly respected. (12)

Free from enmity, yet afflicted by disease, always ignorant, joined with greed, and maintaining delusion in her father’s house—such is the fruit for a woman who first experiences her menses under the Maghā asterism. || 12 || Devoted to the affairs of others, miserable, having wicked sons, possessing meager fortune, filthy, harsh, and angry—such is she who first experiences her menses under the Bhāgya (Pūrva-phalgunī) asterism. || 13 ||

Devoted to the desires of others, wretched, having wicked sons, sharing in suffering, impure, harsh, and prone to anger—this is the fruit of being in one's first menses during Pūrva-phalgunī. || 13 || Having offspring, devoted to dharma, free from enmity, honored by friends, and virtuous—she performs good deeds in the house of her kin when she is in her menses during this asterism (Uttara-phalgunī). || 14 || N1 Bhāṣā-Ṭīkā, Book 15, Chapter 15.

(115) Possessing a lineage, devoted to dharma, free from enmity, honored by kinsmen and friends, faithful to her husband, and attached to the home of one who is beloved and beneficial—these are the fruits of being in one's menses during the first *uttarā-phālgunī*. Free from malice, possessing great wealth, rich in sons, enjoying various pleasures, preeminent, and skilled in giving—these are the fruits of being in one's first menses during the *hasta* nakṣatra. (14)

Free from enmity, possessing great prosperity, having sons, enjoying pleasures, preeminent, and skilled in giving—such a woman experiences her first menses under the asterism of Hasta (15). One who is artistic, sensual, and clever in buying and selling, with unrestrained desires and very refined—she experiences her first menses under the asterism of Citrā (136).

A woman who performs diverse acts of desire, enjoys pleasures, is clever in the business of buying and selling, possesses extensive passion, and is beautiful and skillful, becomes so by having her first menses during the Citrā asterism. || 16 || One who has great wealth, is not skilled in the arts and crafts, yet is virtuous and possesses sons and grandsons, is one whose first menses occurs during the Svāti asterism (Vāyubha). || 17 ||

If a woman experiences her first menses during the Svāti asterism, she will not possess great wealth; however, she will have sons and grandsons skilled in the arts and crafts, and she will be devoted to her husband. (17) If the first menstrual period occurs during the Dvidaiva asterism, she will be intent on base activities, wicked, attached to others, fond of others, childless, unclean, and prone to anger. (18)

One who is engaged in lowly deeds, wicked, attached to another man, fond of others, childless, impure, and prone to anger—such a woman is to be known as born under the Viśākhā asterism. || 18 || In the Nāradasaṃhitā: One who is honored by her husband’s kin, endowed with happiness and virtues, well-adorned, blessed with good sons, auspicious, beloved, and the first wife—she is said to be born under the Mitrarkṣa (Anurādhā) asterism. || 19 ||

One who is honored by her own family, adorned with qualities that bestow happiness, and possesses handsome sons—this should be known as the fruit of the Anurādhā asterism. || 19 || One who is devoted to wicked conduct, causing distress, afflicted, unchaste, lifeless, and possessing a troubled lineage—if the first menses occur under the Jyeṣṭhā asterism, [these results follow]. || 20 ||

A woman who is devoted to wicked conduct, miserable, afflicted by external diseases, unchaste, lacking strength, and having wicked offspring—such a woman becomes so if she experiences her first menses under the constellation Jyeṣṭhā. || 20 || One whose first menses occurs under the Mūla constellation is endowed with other qualities such as progeny and wealth, is a liberator from the distresses of others, and is constantly devoted to her own duties. || 21 ||

One endowed with a lineage, wealth, and virtues, as well as other qualities, who removes the suffering of others and is devoted to her own duties—this should be known as the fruit of the Mūla asterism. || 21 || In the first *ṛtu* (menstrual cycle) under the asterism of Pūrvāṣāḍhā, one bears wicked sons, conceals her sins, is intent on harming living beings, and is constantly addicted to vices. || 22 ||

A woman who commits secret sins, possesses wicked offspring, harms living beings, and is constantly addicted to vices, becomes the first to experience her menses during Pūrvāṣāḍhā. || 22 || One who is skilled in discerning what ought and ought not to be done, always follows the path of dharma, is a repository of virtues, and enjoys pleasures, experiences her first menses during Viśvabhā (Uttarāṣāḍhā). || 23 || [Note: This is a translation of the Sanskrit verses from the Bhāṣāṭīkā-saṃhitā, Chapter 15.]

1. Skilled in discerning what ought to be done and what ought not to be done, ever abiding in righteousness, and a mine of virtues—this is the fruit of Uttarāṣāḍhā. 23. 2. Possessing wealth and grain, endowed with enjoyments, sons, and grandsons, pleasing her family, and highly respected—this is the fruit of Śravaṇa for one afflicted by the first *ārtava*. 24.

Endowed with sons and grandsons, possessing enjoyments, wealth, and grain, devoted to her own duties, and respected—these are the fruits for one whose first menses occur under Dhaniṣṭhā (29). Having many sons, wealthy, devoted to her own duties, virtuous, delighting her family, and respected—these are the fruits for one whose first menses occur under Śatabhiṣaj (Vāruṇa) (26).

Having many sons, wealthy, skilled in her own duties, devoted to her husband, bringing joy to the family, and respected—these are the results for a woman who experiences her first menses during the first Śatabhiṣā nakṣatra. || 26 || A procuress, hateful to her kinsmen, constantly wicked in conduct, malicious, yet skilled in artistic crafts—these are the results for one whose first menses occur during the Ārdrā nakṣatra. || 27 ||

Inauspicious, harboring enmity toward kinsmen, always devoted to wicked people, cruel, yet skilled in the arts—these are the results to be known for Pūrvābhādrapadā. || 27 || Wealthy, possessed of sons, honored, very gracious, dear to her husband, revered by her relatives, and virtuous—these are the results for one whose first menses occur under Āhirbudhnya (Uttarābhādrapadā). || 28 || (118) Nāradasaṃhitā.

Wealthy, having sons, respected, beautiful and pleasant, loving her husband, honored by her kinsmen, and righteous—this is the fruit of Uttarābhādrapadā. || 28 || Firm in her vows, virtuous, endowed with the happiness of sons and wealth, and possessed of the qualities of Viśākhā—such is a woman whose first menses occur under Revatī (Pauṣṇa). || 29 ||

Furthermore, a woman who becomes menstruating during the first lunar mansion of Revatī becomes firm in her vows, virtuous, and endowed with sons, wealth, and happiness; she also possesses the qualities described for Viśākhā. || 29 || The zodiac signs of Cancer, Taurus, Sagittarius, Pisces, Virgo, and Libra are to be known as auspicious for women during their first menses. || 30 ||

For women, when first reaching their menses, the signs of Cancer, Taurus, Libra, Pisces, Gemini, Virgo, and Libra are said to be auspicious as the ascendant (lagna). || 30 || If the lunar day (tithi), asterism (nakṣatra), and day of the week (vāra) are inauspicious, one should not perform the rite of consecration (abhiṣeka). Even so, if the defects are excessive and the merits are few, one should still not perform it. || 31 || If the lunar day, day of the week, and asterism are censured, and if the defects predominate while the merits are scant, then the rite of consecration must not be undertaken. || 33 ||

When the defects are few and the qualities are abundant, one should complete the rite of consecration (*sekakarma*). If flowers are seen on a day characterized by a censurable asterism, lunar date, or weekday, a propitiatory rite (*śānti*) must be performed there with clarified butter, *dūrvā* grass, sesame seeds, and unbroken rice grains. Then, one should offer oblations (*juhuyāt*) one hundred and eight times for each of these items while reciting the *Gāyatrī* mantra. (32–33) And when the defects are few and the qualities are abundant, then the rite of consecration (*abhiṣeka*) should be performed. If there be a censurable asterism, lunar date, or weekday, then a propitiatory rite (*śānti*) must be performed with clarified butter, *dūrvā*, sesame, and unbroken rice; thereafter, one should offer oblations one hundred and eight times for each [substance] while reciting the *Gāyatrī*. (32–33) [Note: *Āṣāṭīkāsa.* refers to the commentary *Āṣāḍhīkā* on the *Sārasaṃgraha*, chapter 16.]

(119) One should perform a fire sacrifice (*homa*) one hundred and eight times with *dūrvā* grass, sesame seeds, and unbroken grains (*akṣata*), reciting the Gāyatrī mantra; furthermore, having first performed the recitation (*japa*), one should effect pacification (*śānti*). || 32 || 33 || To remove all defects, one should give gold, cows, and sesame seeds. Even her husband should avoid approaching her upon seeing [her] menstrual blood. || 34 ||

Thus ends the fifteenth chapter, on the first menstruation, in the Śrī Nāradīya Saṃhitā. (13) By giving gifts of gold, a cow, land, and sesame seeds, all defects are pacified. When a woman has reached her menses, her husband should also practice the renunciation of his wife. (34) Thus ends the fifteenth chapter, on the first menstruation, in the Bhāṣā-Ṭīkā of the Śrī Nāradīya Saṃhitā. (15) Women are untouchable for four days from the appearance of their menses.

Thereafter, this rule regarding purification applies to all castes: after the period of menstruation, a woman remains unfit for touch for four days; she becomes pure thereafter. This is the procedure for all castes. (1) When the Moon is situated in an odd sign or its ninth-part (navāṃśa), and the ascendant is aspected by a masculine planet, on an even lunar day, the husband—wearing the sacred thread—should desire his well-bathed wife. (2) [The Moon] should be located in an odd sign such as Aries, Gemini, and so forth, or in an odd ninth-part.

Now, if the *lagna* is situated in the *navāṃśaka* of an odd sign and is conjoined with or aspected by male planets, then a man, moving clockwise (*savya*), shall approach a woman who has already performed her ritual purification (*śuddhasnāna*) on an even lunar day (*yugmatithi*). (120) *Nāradasaṃhitā*: One desiring a son should avoid the asterisms of Revatī, Mūla, Āśleṣā, and Maghā; [the birth occurs] when the moon is in an even sign and the *lagna* is aspected by a non-female planet. (3)

Furthermore, a woman desiring a son should avoid sexual union with her husband under the asterisms of Revatī, Mūla, Āśleṣā, and Maghā; when the Moon is situated in an even zodiac sign (yugma-rāśi) and the ascendant (lagna) is aspected by female planets, she should likewise abstain. (3) On odd days, a husband seeking a daughter should desire his wife. These [previously mentioned] conjunctions are always fruitless for those who are seedless (impotent). (4)

Furthermore, if one approaches a woman on odd days from the first day of her menses, the birth of a daughter occurs; all these yogas belong to seedless men and are always fruitless—that is, by engaging in sexual union during these times, a female offspring cannot be produced. || 4 || The male planets are the Sun, Mars, and Jupiter; the female planets are the Moon and Venus; the neuter planets are Mercury and Saturn; and Rāhu (the head of the eclipse-demon) is merely the head. || 9 ||

Thus ends the sixteenth chapter, on the Conception of the Embryo (*ādhāna*), in the *Śrī Nāradasaṃhitā*. The Sun, Mars, and Jupiter are male planets; the Moon and Venus are female planets; Mercury and Saturn are neuter; and Rāhu is neuter only in his head. Thus ends the sixteenth chapter, on the Conception of the Embryo (*ādhāna*), in the *Bhāṣāṭīkā* commentary on the *Śrī Nāradīyasaṃhitā*. In a well-known odd-numbered conception, or indeed in the third month...

One should perform the *puṃsavana* rite and likewise the *sīmantonnayana* rite [at the appropriate time]. Thus ends the seventeenth chapter, on the *puṃsavana*, in the Śrī Nāradīya Saṃhitā. (In the Bhāṣā-Ṭīkā, Chapter 138, verse 121: One should perform the *puṃsavana* rite and the *sīmantonnayana* rite during an odd month of pregnancy, or specifically in the third month.

Thus ends the seventeenth chapter, on the *Puṃsavana* rite, in the *Śrī Nāradīya Saṃhitā Bhāṣāṭīkā*. In the fourth, sixth, or eighth month, when the lord of that month is endowed with strength, and the couple possesses the full power of the moon and the stars (lunar and stellar aspects), [then the rite should be performed]. (1) In the fourth month, or else in the sixth month, or in the eighth month, when the planet presiding over that month is possessed of strength, and the husband and wife possess the power of the moon and the stars, [then it should be done]. (3)

On days other than the *rikta* [fourth, ninth, and fourteenth], on Tuesdays, Thursdays, and Sundays, and avoiding those lunar mansions (*nakṣatras*) designated as *tīkṣṇa*, *miśra*, and *ugra*, when the Moon is situated in a male-sign (*pumsaṃjña*) *navāṃśa* [2]; provided that the eighth house from the birth ascendant is pure, and the eighth house from those two [the Moon and the ascendant] is not occupied by the ascendant [3].

If the ascendant and the eighth house are conjoined with or aspected by benefic planets, and not conjoined with or aspected by malefic planets; (3) and if the fourth and eighth houses are aspected by four citron fruits—then, in the first pregnancy of women, the *sīmantonnayana* ceremony is auspicious. (4)

When the eighth month occurs and the Sun is aspected by four planets that fulfill strength and virility, then the *sīmantonnayana* rite during the first pregnancy of women is declared auspicious. (4) [From the] *Nāradasaṃhitā*: When the benefics are situated in the third, ninth, and tenth houses, or in the quadrants (*kendras*), and when malefics are present [but not in the aforementioned positions], provided the Moon is free from the twelfth, eighth, first, and sixth houses. (3)

When benefic planets are situated in the fifth, ninth, or a quadrant (kendrasthāna), and malefic planets are in the sixth, eleventh, or third house, and the Moon is not present in the twelfth, eighth, or the ascendant (lagna), then the Sīmantakarma rite should be performed. || 5 || If even a single cruel planet occupies the sixth, eighth, or twelfth house from the ascendant, it will undoubtedly destroy the healthy fetus of pregnant women, even if that planet is powerful. || 6 ||

Thus ends the eighteenth chapter, on the Sīmantonnayana, in the Śrī Nāradīya Saṃhitā. If even one planet among the cruel planets (malefics) occupies the twelfth, fifth, or eighth house from the ascendant, it destroys the excellent pregnancy of women; that planet is powerful, of this there is no doubt. (6) Thus ends the eighteenth chapter, on the Sīmantonnayana, in the Bhāṣā-Ṭīkā of the Śrī Nāradīya Saṃhitā. Now begins the Jātakarma.

At that very moment of the child’s birth, or even at the end of the period of ritual impurity (sūtaka), the Jātakarman rite must be performed, preceded by the worship of the ancestors. Thus ends the nineteenth chapter, on the Jātakarman, in the Śrī Nāradīya Saṃhitā. When a child is born, one should perform the Jātakarman at that very hour or at the conclusion of the period of impurity, after first performing the worship of the ancestors (specifically, the Nāndīmukha Śrāddha).

Thus ends the nineteenth chapter, on the *Jātakarman* (birth rites), in the *Śrī Nāradīya Saṃhitā Bhāṣā*. Chapter Twenty (123): [The Naming Ceremony]. At the conclusion of the period of impurity (*sūtaka*), the naming ceremony (*nāmakarma*) should be performed according to the custom of one’s own family. A name preceded by auspicious and propitious syllables is said to be excellent. (1) At the end of the period of birth-impurity, the rite of naming should be carried out in accordance with the traditions of one's own lineage; a name that begins with auspicious and fortunate letters is declared to be the best. (1)

If, due to constraints of place, time, or other circumstances, the naming ceremony cannot be performed on the twelfth day at the end of the period of impurity (sūtaka), it should be done during the northern solstice (uttarāyaṇa), provided Jupiter and Venus have not set. (2) On an auspicious weekday, under a movable, fixed, soft, or swift nakṣatra, and on a day endowed with the strength of the moon and the stars, the father of the child [should perform the rite]. (3)

When the asterisms known as Cara, Sthira, Mṛdu, and Kṣipra are present, on an auspicious weekday, and on a day endowed with the strength of the Moon and the stars, then the father of the child [should perform the rite]. || 3 || In an auspicious Lagna and an auspicious Navāṃśa, when the eighth house (Naidhana) is purified; or when the Lagna, the twelfth house (Antya), or the eighth house (Naidhana) is joined with or aspected by a benefic planet. || 4 ||

Thus ends the twentieth chapter, titled "Naming," in the Śrī Nāradīya Saṃhitā. When an auspicious *lagna* (ascendant) contains the *navāṃśaka* (nine-part division) of an auspicious sign, and the eighth house is pure (*śuddha*), and auspicious planets are situated in the first, twelfth, and eighth houses, or there is the aspect of auspicious planets upon them, then it is appropriate to perform the rite of naming (*nāmakaraṇa*). Thus ends the twentieth chapter, titled "Naming," in the Bhāṣā commentary on the Śrī Nāradīya Saṃhitā.

Oṃ. For the purpose of [removing] destruction, Nāradasaṃhitā, K 124): Now, the first feeding of solid food (navānnaprāśana). For males, it should be performed in the sixth or eighth month; for females, however, in the fifth, seventh, or [eighth] month, the auspicious first feeding of solid food should be carried out. (1)

In the sixth or eighth month, one should begin feeding solid food to a male child for the first time; for a girl, the first feeding of food should take place in the fifth or seventh month. || 1 || Excluding the Riktā, Dinakṣaya, Nandā, Dvādaśī, Aṣṭamī, and Amāvāsyā (new moon) lunar days, any other lunar dates are excellent for the first feeding on an auspicious day. || 2 ||

Excluding the empty lunar day (riktātithi), the waning of the lunar day (tithikṣaya), the Nanda lunar days, the twelfth (dvādaśī), the eighth (aṣṭamī), and the new moon (amāvasyā), other lunar days and auspicious weekdays are conducive to the auspiciousness of the first feeding of solid food (annaprāśana). || 2 || In a movable, fixed, soft, or swift nakṣatra, in an auspicious Naidhana yoga, when the tenth house is endowed with purity, and in an auspicious ascendant (lagna) with an auspicious division (aṃśaka), [the rite should be performed]. || 3 ||

When malefic planets are in these houses, and benefic planets are in the angles (kendras), the fifth house, or the ninth house, then [the ceremony is auspicious]. 5. [In the Bhāṣāṭīkā, Chapter 22 (125): The first feeding of food (annaprāśana) is auspicious when the Moon is situated in the twelfth, sixth, or eighth house; or when the waning Moon is situated in the ascendant at the time of the first feeding, or in its sign of debilitation. 9. And [in the] twelfth, sixth, or [eighth]. 12. 6. 8.

In these positions, the Annaprāśana ceremony is auspicious provided that the Moon is not present; furthermore, in those cases, the Moon must not be waning, nor be set (astamita), nor be in its debilitated state. || 5 || If the Moon is in the twelfth, sixth, or eighth house from the ascendant, there will be constant poverty for the eater. || 6 || Thus ends the twenty-first chapter, on Annaprāśana, in the Śrī Nāradīya Saṃhitā. || 21 || [The houses are] 12, 6, 8.

If the annaprāśana ceremony is performed when the Moon is in these [inauspicious] positions at the time of the birth-chart (lagna), the person who eats [the food] will become poor. 6. Thus ends the twenty-first chapter, on Annaprāśana, in the Bhāṣā-Ṭīkā of the Śrī Nāradīya Saṃhitā. 21. Now, the Caulakarma: The Caula rite for children should be performed in the third or fifth year from birth, or according to the custom of one's own family, but certainly within three years. 1.

The *caula-karma* (the tonsure ceremony) for boys is auspicious in the third or fifth year, or according to the family tradition; it should especially be performed before the child reaches three years of age. || 1 || It should be done during the northern solstice (*saumyāyana*), when Jupiter and Venus have not set, on days other than the *parva* and *rikta* lunar dates, and on a Friday, Wednesday, Thursday, or Monday. || 2 || (126) *Nāradasaṃhitā*.

The sun should be in its northern course (uttarāyaṇa), and there should be no setting of Jupiter or Venus; one should avoid the full moon and the *riktā* lunar days (*tithis*). Fridays, Wednesdays, Thursdays, and Mondays are auspicious. || 2 || From the *Dastrā* (Aśvinī) asterism up to the *Tījya* (Puṣya), the *Candra* (Mṛgaśirā), *Indra* (Jyeṣṭhā), and *Pūṣā* (Puṣya) asterisms are auspicious for other rites. For the *caula* ceremony, the three asterisms beginning with *Hasta* and the three beginning from *Viṣṇu* (Śravaṇā) are recommended. || 3 || For the binding of the turban (*paṭṭabandhana*), the tonsure (*caula*), the first feeding of solid food (*annaprāśana*), and the initiation (*upanayana*), the birth asterism (*janmanakṣatra*) brings good fortune; however, it is inauspicious for other types of rites. || 4 ||

The asterisms Aśvinī, Punarvasu, Puṣya, Mṛgaśīrṣa, Jyeṣṭhā, and Revatī are auspicious; furthermore, if the birth asterism falls within three asterisms from Hasta or three asterisms from Śravaṇa, it is beneficial for the Caula-karma (tonsure), Paṭṭabandhana (binding the turban), Annaprāśana (first feeding of solid food), and Upanayana (initiation) rites. In other rites, however, the birth asterism should be understood as inauspicious. || 3 || 4 ||

In the eighth house conjoined with a purification (śuddhi), in an auspicious ascendant and an auspicious ninth-part (navāṃśaka), when the Moon is not in the eighth house, and one should avoid [the sixth, eighth, fifth, and twelfth houses]; nor when the Moon is in the sixth, eighth, or fifth. (5) When benefics are situated in the second, trines, or quadrants, and malefics are in the third, eleventh, or sixth; when it is smeared [with unguents], at the two twilights, at night, for the eater, and not during battle. (6) [Benefic planets... (Note: Verse 6b appears to be a fragmentary continuation of the conditions for auspiciousness regarding planetary positions and specific times.)

If these [planets] are in the houses 9, 5, 1, 4, 7, and 10, and the malefic planets are in the houses 3, 11, and 6, then it is auspicious to perform the rite of shaving after applying an oil massage; however, one should not have a shave during the twilight hours, at the end of an *oja* day, at night, or during battle. (6) [In the] Bhāṣāṭīkā, Chapter 23, Verse 127: For kings, the rite of shaving should not be performed when they are in a state of high excitement, nor when they are adorned with ornaments, nor while traveling, nor on the ninth day, but rather every fifth day. (7)

The shaving ceremony should be performed under a constellation favorable for cutting hair when the visible [sun] has risen. Shaving is auspicious and grants desired results during a king’s command, a sacrifice, at the time of death, upon the release of prisoners, and during marriage, regardless of the day, constellation, or lunar date. Thus ends the twenty-second chapter, on the Tonsure Ceremony (*caula*), in the *Śrī Nāradīya Saṃhitā*. One should not undergo a shave while being extremely agitated, while wearing ornaments, or while seated in a vehicle.

Kings should not have their hair shaved on every ninth day, nor on every fifth day. Shaving should be performed under asterisms suitable for shaving, or during auspicious occasions such as birth celebrations; it may also be done by the command of a king or a Brāhmaṇa. In the case of a sacrifice, death, release from imprisonment, or marriage, one may have shaving performed on any lunar day or weekday without examining specific auspicious moments (muhūrtas). 7–8.

Thus ends the twenty-second chapter, on the Tonsure (Caula), in the Bhāṣā-Ṭīkā on the Śrī-Nāradīya-Saṃhitā. 1. At the commencement of auspicious rites, the offering of auspicious sprouts (aṅkurārpaṇa) should first be performed; this may be done in the ninth month, or the seventh month, or even on the fifth day. [1] It should be performed under a seed-constellation (bīja-nakṣatra), on an auspicious weekday, and during an auspicious rising of the planets. [2]

One should properly decorate the houses with canopies, banners, and arches. (128) [From] the Nāradasaṃhitā: Likewise, on this third day, under the asterism of Garbhādhāna, during an auspicious weekday and an auspicious asterism, and at a favorable *lagna*, one should well-adorn the houses with pavilions, flags, arches, and so forth. (2) The recitation of blessings (*āśiṣo vācanam*) should be performed by virtuous courtesans and others, accompanied by great musical instruments, dances, and the like; having gone toward the north-eastern direction. (3)

Having performed the recitation of auspicious benedictions (*svastivācana*) and having had fortunate women perform auspicious songs in an excellent manner, he should proceed toward the northeast corner, accompanied by the splendor of great musical instruments, dance, and other performances. || 3 || There, having taken fine, smooth sand and returned, he should fill earthen or bamboo vessels with water mixed with various seeds and adorned with flowers. || 4 ||

Thus ends the twenty-third chapter, titled "The Planting of Auspicious Sprouts," in the Śrī Nāradīya Saṃhitā. Then, having brought sand from the Bālūreta river, one should fill earthen vessels or vessels made of bamboo and the like; thereafter, one should sow all kinds of seeds therein, sprinkle water, and beautify it by scattering beautiful flowers. 4.

Thus ends the twenty-third chapter, titled "The Planting of the Auspicious Sprout," in the *Śrīnāradīyasaṃhitā-bhāṣāṭīkā*. For those born of the twice-born (Brāhmaṇas), the tying of the sacred girdle (*mauñjībandhana*) occurs in the eighth year from conception or from birth; for kings (Kṣatriyas) in the eleventh year, and for Vaiśyas in the twelfth. *Note: This is Chapter 24 of the Bhāṣā-Ṭīkā.*

(129) The *upanayana* rite should be performed for Brāhmaṇas in the eighth year from conception or the eighth year from birth; for Kṣatriyas, it should be performed in the eleventh year; and for Vaiśyas, the *yajñopavīta* sacrament should be performed in the twelfth year. 1. Since the glorious one, learned in the Vedas and Śāstras, was initiated in the fifth year from conception, the *upanayana* should be performed there [in that same manner].

2. A Brāhmaṇa who desires proficiency in the Vedas and Śāstras should have the Upanayana sacrament performed in the fifth year from birth; for a twice-born man who undergoes the sacrament in the fifth year becomes illustrious and a reciter of the Vedas. 2. Even if a child is weak, the Jīva-graha bestows strength through propitiatory rites (śānti). The Upanayana should be performed in the year as prescribed; if no specific year has been mentioned, it may be done [in the next available year]. 3.

Even a weak child becomes strong by having the *bṛhaspati-śānti* performed; the sacred thread ceremony (*yajñopavīta*) should be performed during the prescribed year. It must not be performed at an unmentioned time. (3) When Jupiter, Venus, and the Sun are visible, and it is the northern solstice (*uttarāyaṇa*), one should have the initiation performed. Jupiter, Venus, Mars, and Mercury are, respectively, the presiding deities of the Vedas. (4) One should have the initiation performed when Jupiter and Venus are in their period of rising (*udaya*) and the Sun is in the northern course.

Bṛhaspati, Śukra, Maṅgala, and Budha are, respectively, the presiding deities of the Ṛg, Yajur, Sāma, and Atharva Vedas. (4) For the twice-born, the primary [periods] for religious austerity (*tapas*) occur during autumn, summer, and spring; however, the common [periods] for them occur during the five months beginning with Māgha. (8) (330) — *Nāradasaṃhitā*

In the seasons of autumn, summer, and spring, it is appropriate for the twice-born to have the *yajñopavīta* (sacred thread) ceremony performed in that order; these are the primary seasons. However, as a general rule, the *yajñopavīta* ceremony may be performed by all twice-born classes during the five months beginning with Māgha. One who knows the duties and customs of his own lineage [should perform it] in the month of Māgha; one who knows the ritual injunctions and possesses wealth [should do so] in Phālguna; and one who has mastered the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas [should do so] in Caitra. (6)

A man who knows the Dharma, following his own family tradition, performs the *upanayana* ceremony in the month of Māgha. If one who knows the injunctions has the *yajñopavīta* sacrament performed in Phālguna, he becomes wealthy; if in Caitra, he becomes a learned scholar (*paṇḍita*) who knows the Vedas and Vedāṅgas. || 6 || If initiated in Vaiśākha, he becomes wealthy and proficient in the knowledge of the Vedas and Śāstras; if in Jyeṣṭha, he becomes strong and the best among those who know the ritual rules. || 7 ||

In Vaiśākha, he becomes wealthy and a learned scholar versed in the Vedas and Śāstras; in Jyeṣṭha, he becomes strong and one who knows all ritual procedures and performs the investiture of the sacred thread (yajñopavīta). (7) The second, third, fifth, thirteenth, tenth, and seventh lunar days of the bright fortnight are auspicious for the binding of the vow (vratibandhana). (8) The eleventh day is the best, while the sixth and twelfth are middling; the fourth day is to be avoided, as is the middle [day] of the dark fortnight. (9)

The lunar days (tithis) subsequent to the fifth are highly censured; however, the three solar signs beginning with Aries, the last sign (Pisces), the asterisms Jyeṣṭhā, Rudra (Ārdrā), Āditya (Pūrvā-phalgunī), and the Uttarās are excellent. [Commentary in Bhāṣā]: In the bright fortnight, the second, third, fifth, thirteenth, tenth, and seventh lunar days are said to be auspicious for the investiture with the sacred thread (yajñopavīta). Furthermore, the eleventh, sixth, and twelfth lunar days are declared to be middling.

In the dark fortnight, the first *caturthī* (fourth lunar day) is to be avoided, while the days up to the *pañcamī* (fifth) are middling. From the *pañcamī* onwards, other lunar days should be known as extremely censurable. The three asterisms beginning with Hasta, Revatī, Puṣya, Ārdrā, Punarvasu, and all three of the Uttarās [Phalgunī, Āṣāḍhā, and Bhādrapadā] are auspicious for the investiture of the sacred thread (*upanayana*). For the initiation ceremony, the tenth asterism from the birth asterism is the *karma-ṛkṣa* (action asterism), and the sixteenth is the *saṃghātī-ṛkṣa* (conjunction asterism). (8–11)

The three constellations beginning with Śravaṇa—Aśvinī, Anurādhā, and Pūrvābhādrapadā—are declared auspicious for the Upanayana sacrament. The birth constellation, the tenth, and the eleventh are called the *karmasaṃghāta* constellations. (31) The eighteenth is the *sāmudāya*, the twenty-third is the *vināśana*, and the twenty-fifth is the *mānasa*; one should not perform any auspicious rite in these constellations. (12)

The eighteenth lunar mansion is Sāmudāya, the twenty-third is Vināśana, and the twenty-fifth lunar mansion is known as Mānasa; in these lunar mansions, one should not perform even the slightest auspicious rite. (12) The days of the preceptors (Jupiter), Mercury, and Venus are commended, as are those of the Moon and Mars. Those two [days] yield middling results, while the others are censured for a vow. (13)

The days of Jupiter, Mercury, and Venus are auspicious; Monday and Sunday are middling; and the other four days are said to be condemned for the Upanayana sacrament. (13) Dividing the day into three parts, the first portion is for divine rites, the second for human affairs, and the third part is for ancestral rites. (14) *Nāradasaṃhitā* (132)

The day should be divided into three parts; therein, the first part is suitable for rites for the gods (*devakarma*), the second part for human rites (*mānuṣakarma*), and the third part for rites for the ancestors (*pitṛkarma*). If Jupiter, Venus, or the lord of the lunar mansion (*śākheśa*) is in its sign of debilitation, or in its own navāṃśa, or in the sign of an enemy, or in the navāṃśa of an enemy, the initiate will be devoid of noble lineage and good character. (19) If the lord of the lunar mansion, Jupiter, or Venus is situated in its own house or the house of an enemy, or in their respective navāṃśas, the observer of the vow (*vratī*) will become a perpetrator of great violence. (16)

Bṛhaspati, Śukra, and likewise the lords of the branches (śākheśas)—namely Bṛhaspati and the others who are said to be the presiding deities of the four Vedas such as the Ṛgveda—are identified as follows: one should know that for the followers of the Ṛgveda it is Guru (Jupiter), for the Yajurvedins it is Śukra (Venus), for the Sāmavedins it is Maṅgala (Mars), and for the Atharvavedins it is Budha (Mercury). Among these planets, in their respective order, if they are situated in their own sign of debilitation, or in their debilitated degrees, or in the house of an enemy, or in the sign of an enemy...

If [the lord of the ascendant] is situated in its own Navāṃśa, then one should perform the Upanayana saṃskāra; however, if the lord of the Nakṣatra (Śākheśa), as well as Mars or Venus, is situated in the house of one's full enemy or in the Navāṃśa of an enemy sign, and then the Upanayana is performed, the person will become a "Mahāghāta" (one who causes great destruction). But if the lord of the Nakṣatra, Jupiter, or Venus is situated in its exaltation, or in its own Navāṃśa, or in its own sign, or in a Kendra (angle) or a Trikoṇa (trine) house—then [the Upanayana is auspicious]. || 15–17 ||

If the lord of the *śākha* is situated in its own exaltation sign, or in the ninth-part (*navāṃśa*) of its exaltation sign, or in its own sign; and if Jupiter and Venus are likewise situated, or if Jupiter and Venus are in the quadrants or the trines (the 1st, 4th, 7th, 8th, 9th, or 12th houses) from the ascendant—then one should perform the initiation (*upanayana*) sacrament. (17) [From the Bhāṣāṭīkā, Chapter 24, Verse 1.33: "He becomes exceedingly powerful and a master of the Vedas and Vedāṅgas."

If Jupiter is in its sign of exaltation, or in the sign of Libra, or in Virgo, the native is a practitioner of vows, a child, wealthy, and learned in the Vedas and Shastras. If Jupiter is situated in the sign of Gemini, or in its own Navamsha, or in its own sign, [the same results follow]. (18–19)

If an extremely powerful person who has mastered the Vedas and Vedāṅgas—whether it be Bṛhaspati, Śukra, or the Lord of the Branches (Śākheśa)—is situated in the highest exaltation degrees, then the child observing the vow will be wealthy and a reciter of the Vedas. If Jupiter is in the sign of a friend, or in the ninth-part (navāṃśa) of that sign, or in its own sign; || 38 || or if Venus is conjoined with Jupiter, then in that case the child observing the vow [will possess these qualities]. || 39 ||

If Venus and Jupiter are situated in one sign, it is auspicious to perform the Upanayana ceremony. When these planets—Jupiter, Venus, and the lord of the Nakshatra—are situated in their respective houses of friends, or in the exaltation signs of friendly planets, or in the Navamsha of an exaltation sign, if the Upanayana is performed then, the child shall become endowed with learning, wealth, and grain.

20. If Jupiter or Venus is the lord of the *śākha* (branch), [the child] will be endowed with knowledge and wealth. 21. The day of the week of the *śākhādhipati* (lord of the branch), the strength of the *śākhādhipati*, and the ascendant (*lagna*) of the *śākhādhipati*—this triad is difficult to find during the initiation ceremony (*vrata*). The day of the week of the *śākhādhipati* planet, the strength of the *śākhādhipati* for the child, and the ascendant of the *śākhādhipati*'s sign—these three things are rare to encounter during the *upanayana* rite; that is, they are highly auspicious. (134) *Nāradasaṃhitā*.

Therefore, when the Moon is in a benefic Navāṃśa, the observer of vows becomes proficient in learning; however, if a malefic planet is in the eighth house while the Moon is in its own sign or Navāṃśa, he will be poor and perpetually miserable. (22) When the Moon is situated in Cancer within the Śravaṇa and other such asterisms, [the results are as follows].

One who always observes vows becomes prosperous with the Vedas, scriptures, wealth, and grain. (23) If the moon is situated in the Navāṃśaka of Karka or Śaśika during the asterisms of Śravaṇa or Puṣya, then the child undergoing the Upanayana sacrament becomes prosperous with the Vedas, scriptures, wealth, and grain. (23) In an auspicious Lagna and an auspicious Aṃśa, when the eighth house (Naidhana) is endowed with purity; or when the Lagna is not Naidhana, being conjoined with or aspected by benefic planets. (24)

If there is an auspicious ascendant (lagna) with an auspicious sign and a ninth-part (navāṃśaka), and if an auspicious planet is situated in the eighth house or the ascendant, or if there is the aspect of auspicious planets; || 24 || [and] if it is endowed with five powerful planets such as Jupiter, the Sun, and the Moon, or with four [planets] fully possessed of strength through their positions and other factors. || 24 ||

If the five houses beginning with the fifth—namely the fifth, ninth, second, eleventh, and fourth—are aspected by Jupiter, the Sun, the Moon, and others, or if four strong benefic planets are situated in the fifth and other such houses; or if all the signs are conjoined with or aspected by benefic planets and are free from the twenty-one great defects (mahādoṣas), they are considered excellent. || 25-26 ||

Alternatively, if the ascendant (lagna) is aspected by benefic planets, and the twenty-one great defects (*mahādoṣas*)—which are described in other texts as well as later in this very work—are absent, [then the marriage is auspicious]. (Pañcāṅga-śuddhi, Bhāṣā-ṭīkā, Chapter 24).

(135) The absence of [inauspicious] rising and setting (udayāsta-śuddhi), the absence of solar transits (sūrya-saṃkrānti), the malefic six-fold divisions (pāpa-ṣaḍvarga), the junctions (gaṇḍānta), the Kartarī-yoga, and so forth—these should not be present; moreover, a full sign conjoined with or aspected by benefic planets is declared excellent. || 26 || Likewise, auspicious Navāṃśas are to be accepted, as are auspicious signs. Even the Navāṃśa of a malefic planet is acceptable if it is aspected by or conjoined with a benefic. || 27 ||

Furthermore, those signs in which auspicious *navāṃśakas* have arisen are auspicious and fit for selection; likewise, if the *navāṃśaka* of the ascendant occupied by a malefic planet is aspected by or conjoined with an auspicious planet, it is auspicious. (27) Therefore, the signs of Taurus, Gemini, and Pisces, as well as the *navāṃśakas* of Libra and Virgo, are auspicious. When the ascendant is situated in such a *navāṃśaka*, the vow is prescribed. (28)
