Therefore, the ninth-parts (navāṃśas) of Taurus, Gemini, Pisces, Libra, and Virgo are auspicious; it is auspicious to perform the sacred thread ceremony (*yajñopavīta*) when the Moon is situated in such a sign or such a ninth-part. || 28 || When malefic planets are located in the third, sixth, and eleventh houses—avoiding the sixth, eighth, and twelfth—and when benefic planets are not in the sixth, eighth, or twelfth houses, and the Moon is likewise not in the sixth, eighth, or twelfth house... || 29 || [Malefic planets] in the third, sixth, and eleventh houses, and [benefic planets] not in the sixth, eighth, or twelfth houses, and [the Moon] not in the sixth, eighth, or twelfth house... || 6 ||

If the Moon is not present in the ascendant; || 29 || even if the Moon is situated in its exaltation sign, if it occupies the ascendant for one who has taken the vows [of initiation], it makes that child perpetually destitute and afflicted with consumption. || 30 || Even if the Moon is in its exaltation sign, should it occupy the ascendant, it renders the boy—who has undergone the *upanayana* sacrament—constantly poor and suffering from pulmonary consumption. || 30 || (3.36) *Nāradasaṃhitā*: When the Sun is in a quadrant (*kendraka*), it causes the destruction of the lineage of one who has taken the vows. || 31 ||

If Mars is situated in a quadrant (kendram), there occurs the destruction of the disciple and the preceptor. (31) If thundering clouds fall at the time of the Upanayana sacrament while the Sun is in a quadrant, the lineage perishes; and if the cawing of birds occurs at the time of Upanayana in such a Lagna where Mars is in a quadrant, the destruction of the disciple and the preceptor follows. (31) If Saturn (manda) is situated in a quadrant, it causes incomparable diseases and weeping.

If Rāhu is situated in a quadrant from the ascendant (lagna) or in the eighth house, there is the destruction of the mother. If Ketu is situated in a fierce quadrant, there is the destruction of the father and wealth. An ascendant endowed with these five defects is not auspicious for the thread ceremony (upanayana). Furthermore, if Saturn is in a quadrant and at such a time the sound of weeping is heard, then a severe illness will occur.

If Rāhu is in a quadrant from the ascendant, especially in the seventh house, he destroys the mother; if Ketu is in a fierce quadrant, he destroys the father and wealth. A Lagna endowed with these five defects is not auspicious for the Upanayana sacrament. (32–33) One who has been initiated during a time other than the spring season, in the dark fortnight, during the Galagrahas, or during a period of non-study (Anadhyaya), deserves to undergo the sacrament again. (39)

If the initiation (*upanayana*) is performed during the *vasantatuka* period, excluding the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*), or during the *galagraha* conjunctions, then it is fit for re-consecration; that is to say, one should not perform the consecration during these [specific] conjunctions. 34. The four days beginning with the thirteenth, the three days beginning with the seventh, and the fourth—these eight are declared to be *galagraha* [conjunctions]. 35. Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter, on Initiation, in the *Śrī Nāradīya Saṃhitā*.

24. The four lunar days beginning with the thirteenth (trayodaśī), the three days beginning with the seventh (saptamī), and one fourth day (caturthī)—these eight lunar days are designated as *galagraha* yogas. 36. Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter, on the Upanayana, in the Bhāṣā-ṭīkā of the Śrī Nāradīya Saṃhitā. 1. The girding of the sword (*churikābandhana*) for kings should be performed before marriage, during the months prescribed for wedding, in the bright fortnight, when Venus has not set, and when Venus, Jupiter, and Mars possess the strength of the moon and the stars.

On days suitable for the *mauñjī-bandhana* (sacred thread ceremony), excluding Tuesdays. [Verse 2] Now, the auspicious moments (*muhūrta*) for the binding of the *churikā* (knife) are described. Kings should bind their *churikā* prior to marriage; this should be done during the months prescribed for the marriage rites, in the bright fortnight (*śukla-pakṣa*), when Jupiter and Venus are rising, and when Mars is rising, provided there is strength in the Moon and the stars, and the asterisms (*nakṣatra*), lunar days (*tithi*), and weekdays are those specified for the *yajñopavīta* (sacred thread) ceremony.

May they occur on other days, except for Tuesday. (1) At the time of their *lagna-udaya* (the rising of the ascendant), provided it is free from the eighth house from the ascendant and from the eighth house from the *kartṛ-rāśi* (the birth sign of the performer); provided the Moon is pure in the eighth house from the ascendant; and provided the Moon is not situated in the sixth, eighth, or twelfth houses from the ascendant. (3) *Nāradasaṃhitā*: The ascendant should be the sign of three auspicious planets, there should be no planet in the eighth house from the *kartṛ-rāśi*, and there should be no planet in the eighth house from the current ascendant; furthermore, the Moon should not be in the sixth, eighth, or twelfth houses from the ascendant. (3)

When auspicious planets are situated in the second, trines (5th and 9th), or quadrants (1st, 4th, 7th, and 10th), and malefic planets are in the third, eleventh, or sixth houses, one should perform the worship of the gods and the ancestors; in such a Muhūrta, the binding of the sword (churikābandhana) is auspicious. 4.

One should properly worship the dagger in the presence of the deities; thereafter, at an auspicious moment, one should fasten the well-characterized dagger around the waist. (49) I shall describe its characteristics as they were spoken by Brahmā in the past: one should strike [the wood] with a measurement equal to the width of the dagger. (50)

6. Now, we shall describe the characteristics of the sword (khaḍga) as previously stated by Brahmā. One should strike a target equal in length to the sword with that new blade. 6. One should calculate the finger-breadths (aṅguli) divided by the number eight (gaja); one should cut [the wood] according to the measurement of half the length at the tip for its width. 7.

Then, having divided that long mark into eight parts, one should determine the finger-breadths (*aṅgula*), meaning that by measuring with fingers, it should remain at eight or less; taking such a mark, one should subsequently cut that marked object from the tip of a sword-blade whose width is half its length. The fragments resulting from that cutting are as follows: if they fall on the *dhvaja* (banner), there is the destruction of enemies; on the *dhūmra* (smoke), death; on the *siṃha* (lion), victory; and on the *āya* (fortune), freedom from disease. (7)

There is gain of wealth until the bull [sign], but one becomes miserable in the donkey [sign]. (8) Furthermore, the results for each finger-breadth of that broken fragment are stated as follows: if it measures one finger-breadth, the *dhvaja* (flag) sign appears, which destroys the enemy.

If there is a *dhamra* (rhinoceros) at two *aṅgulas*, death occurs; if there is a *siṃha* (lion) at three, victory (*jaya*) is attained; if the fourth is a *dhana* (elephant), there will be health; then, if the fifth is a *vṛṣa* (bull), there is gain of wealth; and if the sixth is a *gardabha* (donkey), one becomes extremely distressed. (8) If there is an *gaja* (elephant), there is extreme joy; if a *dhvākṣa* (crow), there is destruction of wealth. One should calculate the measurement of the sword and the dagger using one's own finger-breadths (*svāṅgula*). (9) In the case of the measurement in finger-breadths (*mānāṅgula*), one should exclude eleven cycles.

And for the remaining fingers, the results shall be in due order: [for the thumb] the gain of a son; [for the index finger] the increase of enemies; [for the middle finger] the gain of a woman; [for the ring finger] an auspicious journey; [for the little finger] loss of wealth; [for the thumb again] the increase of wealth; [for the index finger again] joy; [for the middle finger again] success; [for the ring finger again] victory; and [for the little finger again] praise. Thus ends the twenty-fifth chapter, titled "The Chapter on the Binding of the Knife," in the Śrī Nāradīya Saṃhitā. [Note: The numbering 28 in the source appears to be a scribal error.]

In the eighth house, there is perfect affection for elephants; in the eighth house, there is destruction of wealth in the matter of crows. [Regarding] the measure of the sword and the *charikā*... (140) *Nāradasaṃhitā*.

Measure the length of one’s own forearm with one’s fingers; then, set aside eleven finger-breadths from it—that is, divide it by eleven and retain the remainder. Add together the four finger-breadths of the base (tala) and as many finger-breadths as there were cuts in the middle, and divide that sum by eleven. If one remains, there is the gain of a son; if two remain, an increase of enemies; if three remain, the gain of a wife; if four remain, departure; if five remain, auspicious results; if six...

If it increases, there is loss of wealth; if it increases, there is growth of wealth; if it increases, there is praise; if it increases, there is success; if it increases, there is victory; if it increases, there is praise (fame)—such are the results to be known. 9, 10, 11. Thus ends the twenty-fifth chapter, on the Binding of the Knife, in the Bhāṣā-Ṭīkā of the Śrī Nāradīya Saṃhitā. Now, during the northern solstice (uttarāyaṇa), when Venus and Jupiter are visible, for the twice-born who have returned from the house of their preceptor and are self-restrained: 1.

When the sun is in its northern course (uttarāyaṇa), and during the rising of Jupiter and Venus, twice-born men who observe their vows—that is, those living in celibacy (brahmacarya)—should return from the house of their preceptor. || 1 || On the days of Citrā, Uttarās (Uttaraphalgunī, Uttarāṣāḍhā, Uttarabhādrapadā), Puṣya, Revatī, Śravaṇa, Anurādhā, Mṛgaśīrṣa, Rohiṇī, and Āśleṣā; on the lunar mansions of the Sun, Jupiter, Venus, Mercury, and the Moon; and on the days of the Sun, Jupiter, Venus, Mercury, and the Moon, as well as in favorable ascendants and their corresponding degrees. || 2 || Alternatively, one may also [return] on the day of one's birth-star (janmanakṣatra) and its corresponding weekday and ascendant. One should avoid the first lunar day (pratipad), all the "empty" (riktā) days, the new moon (amāvāsyā), and the three days following the seventh lunar day (saptamī). || 3 ||

3. On another day, having set aside other duties, one should perform the Samāvartana rite and the decoration. Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter, the Chapter on Samāvartana, in the Śrī Nāradīya Saṃhitā. 26.

According to the Bhāṣāṭīkā, Sarga 27, verse 341: One should perform the *samāvartana* ceremony under the asterisms Citrā, the three *uttarās*, Punarvasu, Puṣya, Revatī, Śravaṇa, Anurādhā, and the three beginning with Mṛgaśiras; on the days of the Sun, Moon, Jupiter, Venus, and Mercury; in the *lagna* and *navāṃśas* of these same signs; or under the asterisms, days, *lagnas*, and *navāṃśas* prescribed for journeys. Furthermore, it should not be performed on the first lunar day (*pratipadā*), nor on any of the full or empty lunar days (*riktātithi*).

One should perform the *samāvartana* rite (entering the householder stage of life) avoiding the new moon day (*amāvasyā*), the seventh lunar day (*saptamī*), and the three days following it. || 2 || 3 || 4 || Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter, on *Samāvartana*, in the *Bhāṣā-Ṭīkā* commentary on the *Śrī Nāradīya Saṃhitā*. || 26 || The householder stage of life (*gṛhasthāśrama*) is the most excellent refuge among all stages of life (*āśramas*), because it is established upon a woman who possesses virtuous character. || 1 ||

The householder’s stage of life (gṛhasthāśrama) is said to be the support for all the stages of life; that householder’s stage, in turn, rests upon the support of a wife of excellent character and conduct. (1) Indeed, her attainment of such virtue depends upon an auspicious planetary conjunction (sulagna). Having examined the purity of the conjunction as described by the Grandfather (Brahmā), I shall now explain it. (2)

Furthermore, the attainment of such a woman's character and nature occurs through the power of an auspicious *lagna* (ascendant); therefore, I shall describe the purification of the *lagna* as told by Brahmā. (2) On an auspicious day, having bowed down like unto a deity to an astrologer who is endowed with virtuous marks, seated comfortably, and possessed of a pure mind, one should question him with devotion. (3)

On an auspicious and sacred day, having bowed with devotion to the astrologer who is seated comfortably with a tranquil mind and endowed with beautiful characteristics, and having honored him like a deity, one should question him. || 3 || (142) Nāradasaṃhitā: With palms full of betel, fruits, flowers, and other offerings, standing before him, the performer of the rite should announce the birth-constellation and the zodiacal sign of the couple's birth. || 4 ||

Having filled his hands with betel leaves, fruits, flowers, and other offerings, the querent should announce the birth asterism and the birth sign of the bride and groom before that astrologer. If the Moon in the query is in the ascendant or even in the sixth or eighth house, death of the couple must be predicted, provided it is in the eighth sign from the other [partner's] sign. (3-4) If the Moon of the querent is in the ascendant, or even in the sixth or eighth house, death of the couple should be declared, if [the Moon] is in the eighth sign from the other [partner's] sign. (9)

If, at the time of the query, the Moon is in the sixth or eighth house from the ascendant, or if it is in the eighth lunar mansion from the asterism of the Moon, one should declare that the death of the man and woman (the bridegroom and the brides) will occur. || 5 || If the Moon is situated in the ascendant and Mars is in the seventh house from it, the death of the husband should be known to occur in the eighth year; of this there is no doubt. || 6 ||

If the Moon is in the ascendant at the time of the query and Mars is in the seventh house from that Moon, the death of the husband will certainly occur in the eighth year. (6) If a malefic planet is in the fifth house from the ascendant, aspected by an enemy, and situated in its own sign of debilitation, that girl will have her sons die; she will become unchaste, without a doubt. (7)

If [the Moon] occupies the fifth house and is aspected by malefic or inimical planets, or is situated in its own sign of debilitation, that girl will be one whose children die at birth and she will be unchaste; of this there is no doubt. (7) The Moon, occupying the third, fifth, seventh, ninth, or tenth house from the ascendant and aspected by Jupiter, effects a union between a husband and wife. (8) *Commentary in Bhāṣā:* Chapter 27, Verse 8.

If the Moon is situated in the third, fifth, seventh, eleventh, or tenth house and is aspected by Jupiter, it brings about the union of man and woman. (8) If Venus and the Moon are situated in the ascendant of Libra, Taurus, or Cancer, and are aspected by female planets, then there shall be the acquisition of a maiden for men. (9)

If, at the time of the query, female planets are situated in the ascendant of Libra, Taurus, or Cancer, and Venus is conjoined with or aspected by the Moon, one should certainly predict the acquisition of a daughter for the person. (9) When Venus and the Moon are situated in an even sign and have entered even Navāṃśas, and being strong, aspect the ascendant, then there will be the acquisition of a daughter. (10)

If at the time of the query Venus and the Moon are situated in even signs, or if they are strong and situated in the navāṃśas of even signs while aspecting the ascendant, then one should predict the acquisition of a bride for the groom. || 10 || If both Venus and the Moon are in odd signs, yet these two are strong and aspect the ascendant, then there will be the acquisition of a groom. || 11 ||

If both the Moon and Venus, being strong, aspect the ascendant and are situated in odd signs, it should be declared that the girl will obtain an excellent husband. (11) In this manner, the acquisition of a husband for women occurs when [the ascendant] is aspected by masculine planets. If, during the dark fortnight, the Moon is in an even sign from the query-ascendant and is aspected by malefic planets or situated in the eighth house, then no marriage shall take place. (12) (144) *Nāradasaṃhitā*

Likewise, even if the ascendant is favored by malefic planets, one should predict that the girls will obtain husbands. If, during the dark fortnight, the Moon is situated in an even sign from the query-ascendant (praśnalagna) and is aspected by malefic planets or occupies the seventh house, no union shall take place; that is, the marriage will not occur. (12) Through meritorious omens and auspicious signs at the time of the query, there is welfare for the couple; however, through these inauspicious [signs], misfortune shall prevail on all sides. (13)

Thus ends the twenty-seventh chapter, on the Ascendant for Marriage Enquiries, in the Śrī Nāradīya Saṃhitā. (13) If auspicious omens occur at the time of the enquiry, it should be known as auspicious; if inauspicious omens occur, one should say that inauspicious results will accrue to the bridegroom and the brides. Thus ends the twenty-seventh chapter, on the Ascendant for Marriage Enquiries, in the Bhāṣā-Ṭīkā of the Śrī Nāradīya Saṃhitā. On a day with purity of the five-fold factors (pañcāṅga), endowed with the strength of the Moon and the stars...

The formal selection of the bride (*kanyāvaraṇa*) is desired either at the rising of the marriage asterism (*vivāhabha*) or on a day when the five-fold limbs (*pañcāṅga*) are auspicious, provided that the strength of the moon and stars is present; this should be done during the time of the marriage asterism and its corresponding *lagna*. One should perform the selection with affection in the girl's house, accompanied by ornaments, flowers, betel, fruits, perfumes, unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*), and so forth, as well as white garments, songs, instrumental music, and the benedictory words of Brahmins.

At that time, the father of the girl should joyfully perform the primary rite of betrothal (pradāna). (3) [Bhāṣāṭīkā, Chapter 28, (145): Adorned with ornaments, flowers, betel, fruits, perfumes, unbroken grains (akṣata), and white garments, accompanied by auspicious songs, instrumental music, and the blessings of Brahmins, the father of the girl should celebrate a festival in her home; thereafter, he should, out of affection, formally offer his daughter in marriage.

2 || 3 || And to a bridegroom endowed with noble lineage, character, youth, beauty, wealth, and learning, one should give a daughter who is young in age and possessed of beauty. || 4 || [To a groom] endowed with family, conduct, stage of life, form, riches, and knowledge, one should give a beautiful daughter who is younger than him. || 4 || Having honored and entreated her—the goddess Śacī, the refuge of virtues, the most beautiful woman in the three worlds, divine, and adorned with perfumes, garlands, and garments—|| 6 ||

Having worshipped the goddess Indrāṇī, the very foundation of all virtues, he offered prayers to her—she who is the most beautiful woman in the three worlds, adorned with divine fragrant garlands and wearing exquisite garments; (5) endowed with every auspicious mark, decorated with all ornaments, and illuminating the quarters of the sky with her priceless strings of jewels. (6)

Endowed with all auspicious marks, adorned with every ornament, and illuminating the quarters with garlands of most excellent jewels; (6) being served day and night by thousands of playful women—one should pray to such a maiden at the conclusion of the worship. (7) Having worshipped the goddess Indrāṇī, who is thus attended by thousands of women, one should offer this prayer at the end of the rite. (7)
(346) *Nāradasaṃhitā*: O Goddess Indrāṇī, salutations to you, who speak so dearly to the Lord of the Gods!
Grant me marriage, fortune, health, and the birth of a son. (8)
Thus ends the twenty-eighth chapter, titled "The Selection of a Bride," in the glorious Nāradīya Saṃhitā. 28.

O Goddess! O Indrāṇī! O beloved speaker of Lord Indra! Salutations to you! Grant me the blessings of marriage, conjugal felicity, health, and the birth of a son. (8) Thus ends [the section on] the selection of a bride in the Bhāṣāṭīkā commentary on the Śrī Nāradasaṃhitā.
The twenty-eighth chapter. 28.
Now begins the section on marriage:
For women, the taking of the hand (marriage) in an even year from birth brings about joy.
In the case of men, when this occurs in an odd year, there is a reversal; in that case, it leads to their destruction. || 1 ||
It is auspicious to perform the marriage of a girl in an even year from her birth, while the groom’s age should be an odd (odd-numbered) year; if it be otherwise, their destruction occurs. 1.
The months of Māgha, Phālguna, Vaiśākha, and Jyeṣṭha bestow auspiciousness.
Kārtika and Mārgaśīrṣa are middling; the others are indeed censured.

Kārtika and Mārgaśīrṣa are middling; and other months are inauspicious for marriage.

When Venus or Jupiter has set, or when either of those two is in its state of childhood or old age; likewise, when Jupiter is situated in the sign of Leo, or even when it has entered a Navāṃśa of Leo—on these occasions, one should not perform marriages and other such rites. (4)

When Venus rises in the east or west, it remains in the state of childhood for seven or five days respectively; likewise, at the time of its setting, it attains the state of old age seven or five days prior. The same designation should be understood to apply to Jupiter as well. (5–6)

As long as Hṛṣīkeśa has not awakened, so long there is no auspiciousness; on the day of Vāsudeva’s festival, no other auspicious rite should be performed. (6) One should not perform the marriage ceremony during the month of one's birth, nor under the asterism of one's birth, nor even on the day of one's birth; likewise, it is forbidden for a son born of an illicit womb or for a daughter. (7)

The marriage of the eldest sibling (the senior sibling) should not be performed during the month of birth, the birth asterism (*nakṣatra*), or the birth lunar day (*tithi*). (7) Furthermore, there should be no mutual marriage between an eldest daughter and an eldest son when both belong to the month of Jyeṣṭha; that is, if both are born in the month of Jyeṣṭha, it must not be done, and not otherwise. (8) *Nāradasaṃhitā* (148).

The marriage of an eldest son and the daughter of an eldest sister, as well as the marriage of a bride and groom born in the month of Jyeṣṭha, should not be performed during the month of Jyeṣṭha. (8) After an eclipse caused by an auspicious omen (utpāta), seven days must be avoided; after a total eclipse (akhila-graha), three days; and after a partial eclipse (anakhila), three days. Furthermore, that lunar mansion (nakṣatra) is undesirable for three subsequent seasons. (9)

After an earthquake and other such portents, as well as after every type of solar or lunar eclipse, it is inauspicious to perform marriage and other auspicious rites for seven days. If there is no total eclipse, one should wait three days; likewise, following a portent occurring during the menstrual period, one should not perform pure rites for three days. (9) If the sun or moon sets while eclipsed, the impurity lasts for three days prior [to the setting]; likewise if they rise eclipsed, it lasts for three days after [the rising]. During twilight, if eclipsed, it lasts for three days before and three days after; if the eclipse is total, it lasts for seven days before and seven days after. (10)

In the case of a total eclipse (grasta-grahaṇa), one should avoid three days prior; in the case of a partial eclipse at rising (grastodaya), one should avoid three days after; if an omen occurs during the twilight (saṃdhyā-kāla), avoid three days; and for all other days, know that seven days each are to be avoided. || 10 || At the end of the month, one should abandon five days, as well as the Riktā tithis, the eighth (Aṣṭamī), the sixth (Ṣaṣṭhī), the first half of Parigha, Vyatīpāta, and Vaidhṛti. || 11 ||

The last five days of the month, the *riktā* lunar days, the eighth and sixth lunar days, the first half of the *parigha* yoga, *vaidhṛti*, and *vyatīpāta* in their entirety—these should be avoided for all complete rites such as marriage and the like. (11) The asterisms of Revatī, the three *uttaras*, Anurādhā, Mṛgaśīrṣa, the Moon, the Sun, Maghā, and Mūla, as well as Rohiṇī, are desired for the taking of a woman's hand in marriage. (12) *Bhāṣā-Ṭīkā-saṃhitā*, Chapter 29.

(149) 8. One should perform marriage during the asterisms of Revatī, the three Uttarās, Anurādhā, Svātī, Mṛgaśiras, Hasta, Maghā, Rohiṇī, and Mūla. || 12 || In a marriage, the strength of Jupiter and the Sun for the couple is essential; therefore, their worship must be performed with diligence if those two planets yield unfavorable results. || 13 ||

In a marriage, one must certainly examine the strength of the Sun and Jupiter regarding the bride and groom; furthermore, if these [planets] yield inauspicious results, one must certainly perform their worship with effort. (13) The strengths arising from transits (gocara), from planetary piercing (vedha), and from the nature of the eightfold divisions (aṣṭavarga)—each subsequent one possesses greater strength than the preceding; however, that which arises from the path of transits is considered gross. (14)

The strength of *gocara*, the strength free from piercing (*vedha*), and the strength of the eight groups (*aṣṭavarga*)—all these strengths increase progressively in order; furthermore, the *gocara* path represents the gross strength. (14) Having observed the strength of the moon and the stars, one should consider the strength derived from the planets, the animal omens (*paśu-śakuna*), and the twitching of the limbs. The lunar day (*tithi*) possesses one unit of strength, the day of the week (*vāra*) possesses two units, and the asterism (*bhā*) possesses three units. (19) Thus, the strength of the moon and the stars, the strength of the planets, the strength of animal omens, and the strength of bodily twitching have been described.

The lunar day (tithi) imparts a single unit of strength, the weekday (vāra) a double amount, and the asterism (nakṣatra) a triple amount. (15) The yoga possesses fourfold strength, while that known as the half-tithi (tithyardha, i.e., the karaṇa) has fivefold strength; beyond that, the muhūrta is more powerful, and the ascendant (lagna) is even more endowed with strength. (16) The yoga is four times strong, the half-tithi (karaṇa) is five times strong, the muhūrta is stronger than that, and the ascendant is superior in strength to all of them. (16)

After that, the *horā* is exceedingly strong; after that, the *dreṣkāṇa* is exceedingly strong. After that, the *navāṃśa* is powerful, and after that, the *dvādaśāṃśa* is powerful. (17) The *triṃśāṃśa* is stronger than that; thus, its strength and weakness are observed. All zodiac signs are auspicious for marriage when joined with or aspected by benefic planets. (18) *Nāradasaṃhitā*: The *horā* is stronger than the [sign]; the *dreṣkāṇa* is stronger than the *horā*; the *navāṃśaka* is stronger than the *dreṣkāṇa*; and the *dvādaśāṃśa* is stronger than the *navāṃśaka*. (17) The *triṃśāṃśa* is stronger than that; therefore, its strength and weakness are examined. All signs are recommended for marriage when conjoined with or aspected by benefics. (18)

One should consider strength and weakness by comparing the twelfth-part (dvādaśāṃśa) with the whole-sign (triṃśāṃśa); in marriage, an entire sign becomes auspicious when it is conjoined with or aspected by benefic planets. || 18 || That ascendant is auspicious if five planets—Moon, Sun, Jupiter, and so forth—are favorable to its sign, even if only four of them are endowed with strength. || 19 ||

The ascendant presided over by the lords of the five planets—Candra, Sūrya, Bṛhaspati, and the others—is auspicious; furthermore, if four planets are endowed with strength and are auspicious, that ascendant is also a bestower of good fortune. || 19 || Having examined the twenty-one great defects regarding the purification of the *jāmitra* (seventh house) and the names, forms, and results of those twenty-one defects as spoken by Pitāmaha (Brahmā), I shall describe them here in brief. || 20 ||

The first defect is proclaimed as being devoid of the purity of the five limbs (pañcāṅga-śuddhi). [21] [Now,] the names, forms, fruits, and strengths of the twenty-one major defects (mahādoṣa), which are to be avoided, are stated according to the measure described by Bālājī. The lack of the five-limbed purity is the first [defect]. [22] [From the Bhāṣāṭīkā, Chapter 29, Verse 151: The second [defect] is the solar transit (sūryasaṃkrama) lacking the purity of rising and setting (udyāsta-śuddhi).

The third [house] is the group of six evils; Venus in the sixth, Mars in the eighth; (22) Gaṇḍa, Antaka, Kartarī, Rīḥpha, and the Moon in the sixth or eighth—this is the summary. The eighth house from the ascendant for both husband and wife, a zodiac sign arising from poisonous ghaṭīs, (23) an evil muhūrta, a weekday defect, Khārjurīka, and that born from the same quarter; an eclipse asterism, a portentous asterism, an asterism pierced by malefics, or one conjoined with malefics; (24) a bad Navāṃśa, Mahāpāta, and Vaidhṛti—these are the twenty-one [defects]. The conjunction of the lunar day, weekday, asterism, yoga, and Karaṇa; (25) [these are the defects].

The complete purification of these five limbs is declared to be "Pañcāṅga. A lunar mansion (*lagna*) in which there is a defect in any of these five limbs is useless. This second category of defects consists of: being devoid of purity in both rising and setting; the Sun's transit (*saṃkrānti*); malefic planets occupying the six divisions (*ṣaḍvarga*); Venus being in the sixth house; Mars being in the eighth house; the *gaṇḍānta* junctions; the *kūṭarī* configuration; and the Moon being in the twelfth, sixth, or eighth houses. These constitute the nine defects.

The twenty-one major defects (*mahādoṣas*) are said to be: (1) the eighth house for a woman or man; (10) the *saṃgraha* defect; (11) the *rāśi-doṣa*; (12) the *viṣaghaṭa*; (13) an inauspicious moment (*duṣṭamuhūrta*); (14) the *vāradoṣa*; (15) the *khārjurīka*, which arises from the same foot [of the lunar day], meaning the *ekārgala* defect; (16) the lunar mansion of an eclipse as well as the lunar mansions of portents (*utpāta*); (17) the piercing by malefic planets (*pāpagrahavedha*); (18) being conjoined with malefic planets; (19) an inauspicious *navāṃśaka*; and (20–21) *vaidhṛti* and *vyatīpāta*. Among these, the five components are the lunar day (*tithi*), the weekday (*vāra*), the lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*), the *yoga*, and the *karana*.

To examine the conjunctions of these [planets] and to observe their purity is what is called the *pañcāṅga*. On a day when there is a defect in the *pañcāṅga*, performing the marriage ceremony at that auspicious time (*lagna*) is useless. This is the description of one such *pañcāṅga* defect from the *Nāradasaṃhitā* (verse 152), and the descriptions of the remaining twenty defects are also stated [in the following verses]. 22. 23. 24. 25. 26. If the ascendant (*lagna*) and the degree of the ascendant (*lagnāṃśaka*) are aspected by their respective lords, they are auspicious.

If the death of the groom is not indicated by the mutual fall [of planets] or by a benefic-malefic [configuration], and if the ninth and tenth parts (navāṃśas) from the ascendant are auspicious, there will be no such death for the bride at the time of taking her hand, even if those [malefics] aspect or join them.

If both the ascendant (lagna) and the ninth-part (navāṃśaka) of the ascendant are aspected by or conjoined with their respective lords, it is auspicious; or if they are mutually aspected by or conjoined with each other's lord or with benefic friendly planets, that too is auspicious. Furthermore, if the lords of the ascendant and the seventh house, as well as the lords of the navāṃśakas of these two houses, do not aspect or even cast a glance toward the ascendant and the seventh house, [it is also auspicious].

Likewise, if even their auspicious friends do not aspect [the ascendant], and a marriage is performed in such a lagna, then death occurs for both the bridegroom and the bride. Due to the lack of purity in the lagna, the bridegroom dies; due to the lack of purity in the seventh house, the bride dies. Such is the characteristic of the defect known as being devoid of the purity of the rising and setting signs (udayāsta-śuddhi). ||27||28|| The sun's transit (saṃkrānti) should always be avoided for a period before and after it.

In rites such as marriage and others, sixteen *nāḍīs* [ghaṭikās] before and sixteen *nāḍīs* after the sun's transit (*saṃkrānti*) should be abandoned; these are declared inauspicious for marriage and similar ceremonies. This is the definition of the fault of *saṃkrānti*. (29) [Note: This concludes the commentary on verse 29 from the *Kālanirṇaya*, Chapter 29.]

The ascendant consists of thirty degrees; half of that is called a *horā*. A third part of the ascendant is termed a *dreṣkāṇa*; a ninth part of the ascendant is a *navāṃśaka*. (30) A twelfth part is a *dvādaśāṃśa*; a thirtieth part is a *triṃśāṃśaka*.

The Sun is the lord of Leo, and the Moon is the lord of Cancer. (31) Mars is the lord of Aries and Scorpio; Mercury is the lord of Virgo and Gemini; Venus is the lord of Taurus and Libra; and there is friendship between the two signs of Sagittarius and Pisces. (32) *Note: The term "dvādaśāṃśa" refers to the twelfth-part (1/12th) of a sign, and "triṃśāṃśa" refers to the thirtieth-part (1/30th). The method for observing these will be clearly explained later in the table.*

Mars is the lord of Aries and Scorpio; Mercury is the master of Virgo and Gemini; Jupiter is the lord of Sagittarius and Pisces; Venus is the master of Taurus and Libra; and Saturn is the lord of Capricorn and Aquarius—these are said to be the lords of the zodiac signs. (32) In an odd sign, the Hōrā belongs to the Moon, and in an even sign, it belongs to the Sun. (33) Saturn is the lord of Capricorn and Aquarius; thus these are declared to be the lords of the signs. (33)

In odd signs (*viṣamarāśi*), the Sun’s *horā* lasts for the first fifteen degrees, followed by the Moon’s *horā*; in even signs (*samarāśi*), the Moon’s *horā* comes first, followed by the Sun’s *horā*. When the Moon is in the eighth house from the ascendant, it is the defect named Indvaṣṭama; even if that ascendant is conjoined with a planet in its exaltation or associated with a benefic planet, one should always avoid it. (50) [Bhāṣāṭīkā, Chapter 29, Verse 171]. When Jupiter is in the eighth house from the ascendant, it is the defect named Devaguru-āṣṭama; even if that ascendant is conjoined with a planet in its exaltation or associated with a benefic planet, one should always avoid it. (51) [Bhāṣāṭīkā, Chapter 29, Verse 172]. When Mercury is in the eighth house from the ascendant, it is the defect named Saumya-āṣṭama; even if that ascendant is conjoined with a planet in its exaltation or associated with a benefic planet, one should always avoid it. (52) [Bhāṣāṭīkā, Chapter 29, Verse 173]. When the Sun is in the eighth house from the ascendant, it is the defect named Ādityāṣṭama; even if that ascendant is conjoined with a planet in its exaltation or associated with a benefic planet, one should always avoid it. (53) [Bhāṣāṭīkā, Chapter 29, Verse 174]. When Venus is in the eighth house from the ascendant, it is the defect named Bhṛgu-āṣṭama; even if that ascendant is conjoined with a planet in its exaltation or associated with a benefic planet, one should always avoid it. (54) [Bhāṣāṭīkā, Chapter 29, Verse 175]. When Mars is in the eighth house from the ascendant, it is the defect named Bhauma-āṣṭama; even if that ascendant is conjoined with a planet in its exaltation or associated with a benefic planet, one should always avoid it. (55) [Bhāṣāṭīkā, Chapter 29, Verse 176]. When Saturn is in the eighth house from the ascendant, it is the defect named Śani-āṣṭama; even if that ascendant is conjoined with a planet in its exaltation or associated with a benefic planet, one should always avoid it. (56) [Bhāṣāṭīkā, Chapter 29, Verse 177]. When Rāhu is in the eighth house from the ascendant, it is the defect named Kālāṣṭama; even if that ascendant is conjoined with a planet in its exaltation or associated with a benefic planet, one should always avoid it. (57) [Bhāṣāṭīkā, Chapter 29, Verse 178]. When Ketu is in the eighth house from the ascendant, it is the defect named Śikhī-āṣṭama; even if that ascendant is conjoined with a planet in its exaltation or associated with a benefic planet, one should always avoid it. (58) [Bhāṣāṭīkā, Chapter 29, Verse 179]. When the Moon is in the eighth house from the ascendant, it is the defect named Indvaṣṭama; even if that ascendant is conjoined with a planet in its exaltation or associated with a benefic planet, one should always avoid it. (59) [Bhāṣāṭīkā, Chapter 2

If Mars is situated in the eighth house from the ascendant, that ascendant should be abandoned even if it is conjoined with three auspicious planets and associated with a planet in its exaltation. (37) The junction of the two lunar days known as Pūrṇā and Anandā, lasting for two nāḍīs, is always a Gaṇḍānta that brings death; this applies to birth, journeys, marriages, vows, and other such rites. (38)

The junction (*saṃdhi*) between these *tithis*—namely *Pūrṇā* and *Nandā*—consists of two *ghaṭīs*: one *ghaṭī* at the end of the full moon day (*pūrṇimā*) and one *ghaṭī* at the beginning of the first lunar day (*pratipadā*). This is called *gaṇḍānta*, and it should be known as bestowing death upon birth, journeys, marriages, and other such occasions. One should understand all the *ghaṭīs* of the *tithis* beginning with the fifth (*pañcamī*), which are all *Pūrṇā* and *Nandā*. 39. Between Cancer and Leo, Scorpio and Sagittarius, and Pisces and Aries, there is a *gaṇḍānta* interval of half a *ghaṭī* which brings about death.

Furthermore, the junctions between the ascendants of Cancer, Leo, Scorpio, Sagittarius, Pisces, and Aries are known as *gaṇḍānta*; these too are fatal. || 39 || In the constellations of Āśleṣā, Jyeṣṭhā, and Revatī, the final two *nāḍīs* [forty-eight minutes] are likewise [gaṇḍānta]; and in the constellations following them, the first quarter of each is designated as *gaṇḍānta*. || 40 || 4-(158) Nāradasaṃhitā.

Furthermore, the two final ghaṭīs of Āśleṣā, Jyeṣṭhā, and Revatī, along with the first ghaṭīs of the nakṣatras immediately following them—these four ghaṭīs of the nakṣatras are designated as Gaṇḍānta. (40) The three Ugra periods and the two great Gaṇḍāntas are bestowers of death during birth, travel, marriage, the installation of deities, and other such rites. (41)

Thus, this threefold *gaṇḍānta* is terrible and inauspicious; it is declared to be unfavorable for birth, journeys, and marriages. (41) "When two malefics are situated behind and ahead of the ascendant, moving respectively in direct and retrograde motion, that forms a 'scissors' (*kartarī*). If those same two planets are both in rapid retrograde motion, it is not a *kartarī*; so said the lords of sages. (42)

If there is any malefic planet in the twelfth house from the ascendant and another malefic planet in retrograde motion in the second house, it forms the inauspicious yoga named Karttarī; however, if both those planets are swift-moving as well as retrograde, the Karttarī yoga does not occur—such is the opinion of the sage Vasiṣṭha. || 42 || [When two planets situated on either side of the ascendant are facing toward it...]

That is to be known as *karttarī*; it is the *mṛtikarttarī* (death-knife) for the couple. || 43 || If malefic planets occupy both the positions before and after the ascendant in equal measure, that is the *karttarī* yoga; it brings about the death of the woman and the man. || 43 || Even if [the moon] is joined by benefic planets and endowed with all virtues, if the moon is in the twelfth, eighth, or sixth house, that is designated as the fault of the ascendant (*lagnadoṣa*). || 44 ||

Even if the ascendant is joined by benefic planets and endowed with all auspicious qualities, one should not perform a marriage during a *kartarī* configuration; likewise, it is said that the presence of the Moon in the 12th, 8th, or 6th house constitutes a defect in the ascendant. || 44 || One should carefully avoid such an ascendant even if it is occupied by Jupiter and Venus, whether they are in their exaltation, debilitation, friendly, or enemy signs. || 45 ||

Even if that Lagna is conjoined with Jupiter and Venus, it should still be avoided with great effort; likewise, whether the Moon is in its exaltation or conjoined with a planet in its sign of debilitation, or whether it is in a friendly or inimical sign—regardless of its state—it must be avoided in these positions. (45) Even if endowed with all auspicious qualities, [the Lagna] brings death to the couple when the Moon is conjoined with malefic planets; this defect is known as Saṅgraha. (46)

Even if a lagna is endowed with all auspicious qualities, it brings about the death of both the woman and the man; furthermore, when the Moon is conjoined with malefic planets, that is declared to be the defect known as Saṃgraha.

One should never perform a marriage during that *saṅgraha* defect; if the Moon is conjoined with the Sun, poverty will certainly occur. (47) In the case of *saṅgraha*, death occurs through Mars, disease through Mercury, childlessness through Jupiter, misfortune through [Saturn], and co-wifery through Venus. (78)

If it is conjoined with Mars, there will be death or disease; if with Mercury, there will be no progeny; if with Jupiter, misfortune; and if with Venus, the suffering of enemies. || 48 || (160) Nāradasaṃhitā: If the Moon is conjoined with Saturn, there is renunciation; with Rāhu, constant quarrel; and when conjoined with Ketu, perpetual hardship and poverty. || 49 ||

If it is conjoined with Saturn, the taking of renunciation (saṃnyāsa) occurs; if conjoined with Rāhu, there is strife; and if the Moon is conjoined with Ketu, there will be constant suffering and poverty. || 49 || If the Moon is joined by two malefic planets, the death of the couple will occur. If the Moon is joined by malefic planets, is in its sign of debilitation, or is situated in the sign of Rāhu... || 99 || [If] the Moon is joined by two malefic planets, the death of the bride and groom will occur; [or] if the Moon is joined by malefic planets, is in its sign of debilitation, or is situated in the sign of Rāhu... || 99 ||

50. If the ascendant (lagna) becomes a *doṣāyana*, it brings about the death of both husband and wife. However, if the Moon is situated in its own sign (*svakṣetra*), in its exaltation (*svocca*), or is joined by a friendly planet, [the situation changes]. || 61 || [In that case], the fault of *yuti* (conjunction) does not arise; rather, it leads to the welfare of the couple. || 51 ||

If the sixth house from the ascendant for the couple, or indeed the eighth sign, is situated in the ascendant itself, that too brings about the death of the couple; even if that sign is joined with a benefic, or the ascendant is conjoined with a benefic. (52–53)

The *yuti-doṣa* (conjunction defect) does not occur; it bestows auspiciousness upon both the woman and the man. If the eighth sign from the woman’s or the man’s *lagna* becomes the *lagna*, or if the *lagna* is the eighth sign from the woman’s or the man’s own sign, then the death of the woman or the man occurs. Even if that sign and the *lagna* are conjoined with auspicious planets, it remains inauspicious. (52–53) [Bhāṣāṭīkā, Adhyāya 29, Verse 166]: One should diligently avoid the *lagna*, its *navāṃśas*, and their respective lords.

If the twelfth sign from the couple's [natal] signs is indeed the ascendant (lagna), one should carefully avoid that ascendant; its navāṃśa and its lord are also inauspicious. If the ascendant is the sign of the husband or wife, or if it is the twelfth sign from their birth ascendant, there will be loss of wealth for them both; therefore, one should abandon the lord of that navāṃśa. However, if the ascendant is the sign of the birth [natal] sign or the birth ascendant itself, it is auspicious. (Verses 94–95)

When the auspicious [planets] have entered the ascendant at the place of their accumulation (upacayasthāna), the [periods] are as follows: by the path of the sky (khamārga), they are the Vedas (4), the fortnights of the moon (15), the fires (3), and the oceans (4); the waters (4), the moons (1), the forms (1), the Aśvins (2), the fires (3), the arms of the sky (2), the twice-Aśvins (2), the fires of the sky (3), the zeros (0), the Aśvins (2), the elephants (8), and the earths (1). (96–97)

Because there is a loss of wealth, one should avoid the lords of the navāṃśas of these three ascendants from occupying the ascendant. It is auspicious if there are benefic planets upon the birth sign and the birth ascendant, and if the ascendant is in an upacaya house (the 3rd, 11th, or 5th) from them; this is called the *rāśi-doṣa*. Now, the *viṣaghaṭī* defect is described: there are 50 ghaṭīs in the asterism Aśvinī, 24 in Bharaṇī, 30 in Kṛttikā, and 40 in Rohiṇī.

In Mṛgaśiras, 14; in Ārdrā, 21; in Punarvasu, 30; in Puṣya, 20; in Āśleṣā, 32; in Maghā, 30; in Pūrvaphalgunī, 20; and in Uttaraphalgunī, 18 ghaṭīs. || 55 || 56 || 57 || Rūpa-pakṣa (12), Vyoma-dasra (20), Veda-candra (14), Caturdaśa (14); Śūnya-candra (10), Veda-candra (14), Ṣaṭ-pañca (56), Veda-bāhu (42). || 98 || 11 || (162) Nāradasaṃhitā || Śūnya-dasra (20), Śūnya-candra (10), Śūnya-candra (10), Gaja-indava (18). || 12 || (162) Nāradasaṃhitā ||

Sixty-four, sixty-two, fifty-six, fifty-four, fifty-two, fifty, forty-eight, forty-six, forty-four, forty-two, forty, thirty-eight, thirty-six, thirty-four, and thirty [ghaṭīs] are the durations for the constellations starting from Aśvinī in sequence. (49) In Hasta there are 21; in Citrā, 20; in Svāti, 14; in Viśākhā, 14; in Anurādhā, 10; in Jyeṣṭhā, 14; in Mūla, 56; in Pūrvāṣāḍhā, 24; in Uttarāṣāḍhā, 20; in Śravaṇa, 10; in Dhaniṣṭhā, 10; in Śatabhiṣā, 18; in Pūrvābhādrapadā, 16; in Uttarābhādrapadā, 24; and in Revatī, 30. Thus, these ghaṭīs for the constellations beginning with Aśvinī have been stated. (58–59)

Beyond these, there are four *nāḍikās* known as "poison" (*viṣa*). These poison-*nāḍikās* should be avoided in undertakings such as marriages and other ceremonies. (60) That is to say, the four *ghaṭīs* following these six are designated as "poison. For example, in the case of Revatī, which has thirty *ghaṭīs*, the four *ghaṭīs* from the thirty-first to the thirty-fourth are known as poison-*ghaṭīs*. One should understand this in the same way for all the lunar mansions (*nakṣatras*). These poison-*ghaṭīs* are forbidden for rites such as weddings. (60)

Multiplied by the odd-numbered [period] and adjusted for the beginning and end of the asterism, it is divided by sixty; the quotient obtained should be added to the previous asterism. (63) If the number of ghaṭīs for that asterism does not amount to sixty, one should proceed as follows: multiply the ghaṭīs of the asterism's fixed value (dhruvāṅka) by the ghaṭīs of the asterism’s duration, then divide by sixty. The resulting quotient in ghaṭīs should be understood as the "poisonous ghaṭīs" (viṣaghaṭī) occurring beyond that very amount. (61)

Thus ends the section on the Poisonous Hour (viṣaghaṭī). Those hours declared as censurable for the days beginning with Sunday, as well as those censured for auspicious rites such as marriage, must be avoided even if they are endowed with the favorable qualities of the ascendant (lagna). (62) [Commentary on Verse 62, Chapter 29]. Even if those censured moments are endowed with the qualities of that specific ascendant, they are to be avoided. (63)

Those three days are fit to be avoided during inauspicious moments (duṣṭamuhūrta); even if they are endowed with those [other] qualities, those inauspicious moments are indeed declared to be censurable. 63. Whatever defects exist among the days, starting from Sunday and so forth in order, they must be avoided in all auspicious rites, even if they are possessed of every other excellence. 64.

Furthermore, whatever weekday defects (vāradoṣa) have been described for Sundays and the other days, even if they are endowed with all auspicious qualities, they must be avoided in all rites intended for welfare. 64. If there is an Ekārgala [aspect] with equal feet, one should avoid the lagna at that time. 68.

Furthermore, they speak of the *ekārgala* defect in the *khārjūrika* yoga; it occurs when [the moon] is seen in an even-numbered asterism through its conjunction with the sun or moon. If the *ekārgala* defect arises therein, one should not perform the marriage ceremony under that asterism. (65) Moreover, even if conjoined with Venus and Jupiter, [an asterism] is like milk mixed with poison. An asterism affected by an eclipse or a portentous calamity (*utpāta*) must be avoided in auspicious rites; such an inauspiciousness is threefold. (66)

If Venus is conjoined with Jupiter at that time, even then it becomes as fit to be abandoned as milk mixed with poison; one should likewise avoid the lunar mansion of an eclipse, as well as those three types of asterisms associated with portents such as earthquakes and atmospheric disturbances. (66) As long as the portion of the lunar mansion has been consumed, the remainder is like burnt wood; one should avoid a cruel asterism during auspicious rites, as well as one that is pierced or conjoined with a malefic planet. (67) (164) *Nāradasaṃhitā*

Furthermore, in auspicious rites such as marriage, one should avoid a lunar mansion (nakṣatra) that is pierced by a malefic planet or conjoined with a malefic planet; even if it has been traversed by only a single quarter (pāda), the remainder should be understood to be like wood already scorched by fire. || 67 || An entire mansion is [purified] by the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), and likewise by a drop of liquor; however, a single quarter pierced by benefics is auspicious, whereas the whole mansion is not so. || 68 ||

For the sake of auspiciousness, all constellations (nakṣatras) become abandoned when pierced by even a single quarter (pāda), just as the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) become impure upon contact with a drop of wine; furthermore, the piercing by a malefic planet is inauspicious only when it occurs within a quarter, for the piercing of an entire constellation is not possible. || 68 || A constellation joined with a malefic piercing is entirely [abandoned] from that quarter onwards; likewise, the portions of Libra, Gemini, and Virgo, as well as those conjoined with the portions of Sagittarius, [are to be avoided]. || 69 ||

69–70. These are to be accepted as the *navāṃśas* (ninth-parts); others, however, are *kunavāṃśakas* (inferior ninth-parts). A *lagna* (ascendant) that possesses all auspicious qualities but is a *kunavāṃśaka* should be rejected. When a constellation (*nakṣatra*) is afflicted by a cruel quarter (*caraṇa*), as well as by the conjunction (*yoga*) of a cruel planet, the entire constellation becomes useless. Furthermore, the *navāṃśas* of Libra, Gemini, Virgo, and Sagittarius are declared auspicious; the others are *kunavāṃśakas*.

Even if the ascendant possesses all auspicious qualities, it should be abandoned if it is a *kunavāṃśaka*. (69–70) On that day when there is a *mahāpāta* [conjunction], a wise person should avoid it; for even if it is endowed with all good qualities, it brings death to the couple. (71) On whichever day the *vyatīpāta* yoga occurs, that day should be avoided; even if that day is possessed of virtues, it causes the death of the husband and wife. (71) [Note: This is the Bhāṣā-Ṭīkā commentary on Chapter 29, Verse 71.]

(165) Lightning, mist, rain, the appearance of a second sun in the clouds facing the sun, halos, rainbows, and the thundering of clouds—these and similar phenomena are minor defects even when not explicitly mentioned; their specific application is now established as follows. 72. Lightning striking, the falling of frost and hail, and so forth, are minor defects even if unmentioned; likewise, seeing a second sun within the clouds directly opposite the sun, circular halos, the roaring of clouds, and rainbows. 72. Such being the case, their systematic arrangement is now set forth.

These—lightning, mist, and rain—occur out of season; likewise, if halos around the sun, Indra’s bow (a rainbow), and thick clouds appear during the night, they certainly portend misfortune. However, when they arise at their proper time, they are indeed free from such fault.

[The text] establishes the rules regarding such defects as these: lightning and other portents (*utpāta*), the falling of meteors, the appearance of a second sun or the solar disc, the appearance of a rainbow, and the thundering of clouds—if these occur out of season (*akāla*) rather than during the rainy season, they are certainly defects for auspicious occasions such as marriage; however, if they occur at the proper time, there is no defect whatsoever. (73–74) If Jupiter, Venus, or Mercury is situated in a quadrant (*kendragata*).

Even a single planet, such as Jupiter, Venus, or Mercury, if situated in a quadrant (kendram), destroys many defects and brings about auspicious results. (75) Five lines run horizontally, vertically, and diagonally; two lines each are placed at the corners. One should then place the second Śambhucakra, known as the Agnibhacakra, therein. (76)

(166) In the Nāradasaṃhitā: Draw five horizontal lines and five vertical lines; draw two lines at each corner. Then, place the Kṛttikā nakṣatra where the two lines meet in the northeast (Īśāna) corner, and write all the nakṣatras in their proper sequence. || 76 || On the other hand, with the Abhijit [nakṣatra], there is only one line. A planet pierces the asterism [that falls] in front of it. The Sun and other planets cast a "latta" (kick) upon the asterism located in front of or behind them on the day of the solar revolution. || 77 ||

After writing down the complete list of asterisms (nakṣatras) beginning with Abhijit, if the asterisms of two planets fall upon the same single line, that is a *vedha* (piercing); this is what is called the fault of *vedha*. Furthermore, when the Sun and other planets strike an asterism situated ahead of or behind them, that is the fault of *lattā*; its sequence is stated as follows: || 77 || Mercury, Rāhu, the Full Moon, and Venus [strike] their own asterism at distances measured by seven, nine, five, and five [asterisms] behind them respectively. || 78 ||

Mercury, Rāhu, the Full Moon, and Venus strike their own *nakṣatra*s seven, nine, twenty-two, and five signs behind them respectively; while the Sun, Saturn, Jupiter, and Mars strike the *nakṣatra*s twelve, eight, six, and three signs ahead of them respectively. (78) For example, if Rāhu is in Aśvinī, it will strike Āśleṣā. Similarly, the Sun, Saturn, Jupiter, and Mars strike the *nakṣatra*s located twelve, eight, six, and three signs ahead of them in due order.

They will be struck. Just as when the Sun is in Aśvinī, Saturn will strike the fourth nakṣatra from it, Uttarāphālgunī; on the eighth day, Saturn will strike [the next one]. Know this according to the sequence. (78) One should avoid a nakṣatra that is "latted" (lattita) in the regions of Saurāṣṭra and Śālva. In the regions of Kaliṅga and Vaṅga, a nakṣatra that is "struck down" (pātita) is considered an upagraha. (79) *Āṭīkā-sāra, Chapter 29.*

(167) In Saurāṣṭra and the Śālva country, the defect of *lattā* is absent; in Kaliṅga and the Bengal region, the defects of *pāta* and *upagraha* are absent. || 79 || In Bāhvika and the Kuru country, as well as in whatever other land there may be, no such defect exists; yet there are the lunar days known as *māsa-dagdha*, as well as those *dagdha-lagna*s (burnt ascendants). || 80 || In Bāhvika and the Kuru country, [these are] avoided, for therein lies the defect; likewise, the lunar days called *māsa-dagdha* and the *dagdha-lagna*s [are also to be avoided]. || 80 ||

In the Middle Country (Madhyadeśa), these [defects] are to be avoided, but in other regions they are not considered faults: namely, a lame, blind, or one-eyed ascendant; months that are void; and [inauspicious] zodiac signs. || 81 || In Gauḍa and Mālava, these are to be abandoned, but in other countries they are not censured. However, one that is corrupted by defects should always be diligently avoided at all times. || 82 ||

Those [times] which are to be avoided in the regions of Gauḍa and Mālava are not defective elsewhere; one should always carefully avoid a time that is defiled by defects. (82) Even if there are many virtues, for the sake of another [purpose], the arising of virtue consists in the minimization of defects; having abandoned great defects, one should consider the remaining virtues and defects. (83)

When virtues predominate and defects are few, that entire moment bestows auspiciousness; a single defect cannot prevail amidst a multitude of virtues. (84) Just as a single drop of water falls upon a blazing fire... [Nāradasaṃhitā] (Note: The text provided contains a fragmentary verse regarding the futility of a single drop against a great fire.)

Having reflected thus, one should determine the *lagna* (ascendant) as prescribed in the treatises on calculation (*gaṇita*). Just as even a single drop of water cannot extinguish a great fire, so too should one deliberate upon the strength and weakness of the *lagna* by examining it through the science of calculation. The best of astrologers should provide that *lagna* using a water-clock (*jalayaṃtra*), which should be six finger-breadths in height and twelve finger-breadths in length; he should fashion a copper vessel resembling a skull-cup weighing ten *palas*.

A vessel filled with sixty *jala-palas* of water sinks sixty times in a day. (87) An expert in astrology should determine the *lagna* by constructing a *ghaṭī* (water-clock) using a water-mechanism. One should fashion a vessel out of ten *palas* (40 *tolas*) of copper, shaped like a shallow bowl, six *aṅgulas* high and twelve *aṅgulas* in width; such a vessel, when filled with sixty *palas* (240 *tolas*) of water, will sink sixty times in a full day and night (*ahorātra*) when placed in water. (86–87)

One should create a hole the size of a black gram (māṣa) using a circular gold needle; it should be clearly pierced through the center, and water should be filled up to four finger-breadths (aṅgulas) above it. || 88 || The vessel made of copper for this purpose should weigh six palas more than required; its width at the opening should be twelve [finger-breadths], and its height should be six finger-breadths. || 89 ||

Having fashioned it from a gold *māṣa* and making it four finger-breadths in size, with a tube pierced through its middle part, it is known as a *ghaṭikā*. (90) [From the Bhāṣāṭīkā, Chapter 29, Verse 169(c)]

Furthermore, a copper vessel measuring six *palas* may also be made; its width should be twelve *aṅgulas*, its height six *aṅgulas*, and one should attach a gold *māṣa* in the middle measuring four *aṅgulas*. One should pierce a water-channel in the center; know that to be a *ghaṭikā-yantra*. (89–90) When the copper vessel or an auspicious earthen vessel is filled with water, it should be carefully adorned with perfumes, flowers, and unbroken grains (*akṣatas*). (91)

Having observed that the sun has descended below the mandala, one should place it there—[the vessel] filled with water, joined with gold, covered with a pair of cloths, and containing rice. (92) Then, having worshipped and adorned [the vessel] with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, either in a copper vessel or an earthen vessel filled with water, and having placed rice along with gold and covered it with two cloths, one should release this water-clock (ghaṭī-yantra) into such a water-filled vessel at the time when half of the sunrise has occurred.

[He] saw [it]. (91) (92) By means of this mantra, one should [worship] the excellent yantra possessing the previously mentioned characteristics: "You are the foremost among all yantras, fashioned of old by Brahmā; (93) you are the cause for the accomplishment of the ritual vessels for couples, whether their future is auspicious or inauspicious. It is declared to be twelve finger-breadths in measure, according to the standard of the śaṅku. (94)

One should release that aforementioned yantra with this mantra: "O you who are the foremost among all yantras, tell us first, for the sake of the happiness and suffering of this bride and bridegroom, regarding the cause of the *kala-sādhana*. Furthermore, if this yantra cannot be constructed, one should fashion a twelve-finger-long gnomon (*śaṅku*) and thereby determine the desired time. (93–94) Other applications of yantras for the determination of time are difficult to obtain.

Thus, in such an auspicious moment (*sulagna*), one should properly arrange for the mutual gazing (*īkṣaṇa*) of the bride and groom. (Nāradasaṃhitā 170) In another [text], it is stated that the employment of other [astrological] instruments is difficult to achieve even when seeking desired results; therefore, the marriage of the bride and groom should be performed in such a beautiful *lagna*. (95) [One should construct] a structure four cubits high and four cubits square on all sides, with four smooth pillars, to the left side of one's own house. (96)

There, one should construct a platform four cubits high on the left side of the house, adorned with four beautiful pillars. It should be provided with a maṇḍala on all four sides and be exceedingly beautiful with steps; its commencement should be made with the pillars sloping toward the east and north, and they should be decorated with horse-tails, parrots, and other such ornaments. || 96-97 ||

The four directions should be made beautiful with the enclosures of the mandala; the pavilion should be extended toward the east and north, and its pillars should be adorned with paintings of horses, parrots, and other such figures. (97) It should be decorated with variegated painted pitchers, various archways and sprouts, clusters of flowers and golden water-pots, and colored pigments; it should be made enchanting by the auspicious blessings of Brahmins, virtuous women, and lamps. (98)

Adorned with various pitchers, decorated with diverse types of arches (*toraṇas*), auspicious full jars (*pūrṇakumbhas*), clusters of flowers, and beautiful colors; accompanied by the holy blessings of Brahmins and graced by the songs of fortunate women; enchanting with rows of lamps and delightful to the heart with instrumental music, dance, song, and the like. (99)

One should construct an auspicious altar (*śubhavedī*) for the giving [of the bride]. (98-99) A couple, accompanied by the sacred fire and the Vedas, should ascend such an altar. At the time of marriage, malefic planets should occupy the third, sixth, or eleventh houses, provided the Moon is not in the sixth or eighth house. (100) [Commentary on Āṣāḍha, Chapter 29, Verse 371]: One should perform the marriage rite near such an altar with the fire and the Vedas as witnesses. At the time of marriage, if the malefic planets are situated in the third, sixth, or eleventh houses, and the Moon is not in the sixth or eighth house, [the marriage is auspicious]. (100)

Providing longevity, wealth, and health, they bestow abundance of sons and grandsons; when situated in the trines (tri-koṇa), angles (kendras), or the eleventh house (khāya), the planets produce auspicious results. || 101 || Except for Venus, the Moon in the seventh, the angles, or the eighth house causes one to be endowed with sons and wealth; however, in the sixth, third, fourth, fifth, ninth, and eleventh houses, the Moon [produces] auspicious results. || 102 ||

Furthermore, Venus is auspicious in any house other than the seventh; she makes the daughter endowed with sons, wealth, and married. The Moon is auspicious in the second, third, fourth, fifth, ninth, tenth, and eleventh houses (2, 3, 4, 5, 9, 10, 11). [Verse 102] It makes the married daughter possessed of sons, good fortune, and enjoyments. [Verse 103] [Planets that are] set, in their sign of debilitation, in inimical signs, or defeated [are inauspicious]. [Verse 104] It makes the married daughter possessed of sons, good fortune, and enjoyments.

Furthermore, planets that have set, those situated in a debilitated sign, or those who have entered the sign of an enemy are defeated (parājita). [103] They are unable to bestow their results, just as a gift given to one who is not learned in the Vedas (aśrotriya) yields no fruit. Even a single Jupiter situated in the ascendant destroys the entire accumulation of defects, just as the sun, the teacher of Dharma, destroys darkness. [104] Even a single Venus or Mercury, if situated in the ascendant, [achieves the same]. [109] 9 {172} Nāradasaṃhitā.

They are not capable of yielding fruit in the same way that there is no fruit from giving a gift to a foolish Brāhmaṇa; however, even a single Guru situated in the ascendant destroys all defects just as fire destroys a heap of cotton. Furthermore, a single Venus or Mercury situated in the ascendant [destroys them likewise]. (104-105) He destroys all defects like fire consumes a pile of cotton. (106)

Even a single Guru (Jupiter), Śukra (Venus), or Budha (Mercury) situated in a quadrant destroys such a complete mass of defects, just as fire consumes a heap of cotton. When Jupiter, Mercury, or Venus alone is in a quadrant, it surely destroys the multitude of defects, like a lion destroying a herd of elephants. A powerful Mercury situated in a quadrant destroys a hundred defects; and Venus, having abandoned the seventh house, destroys two hundred thousand [defects], while Bṛhaspati (Jupiter) destroys a hundred thousand.

It destroys the multitude of defects—such as the defects of the ascendant (lagnadoṣa) and those born of the six-fold charts (ṣaḍarga)—just as a lion destroys a herd of elephants. Likewise, Mercury, having attained a strong quadrant (kendram), destroys hundreds of defects; and Venus, if situated in any other quadrant except the seventh house, produces twice the results of Mercury.

Furthermore, Jupiter destroys a hundred thousand defects—namely, those defects of the ascendant as well as those arising from the sixfold divisions (ṣaḍvarga). Jupiter situated in the ascendant destroys them just as the wind disperses a mass of clouds; likewise, if Jupiter, Venus, or Mercury is placed in a quadrant (kendr) or a trine (trikoṇa), [the same result follows]. 109.

Bṛhaspati, having reached the ascendant, destroys all three types of defects just as a gust of wind scatters a mass of clouds. If Jupiter, Venus, or Mercury should be situated in a quadrant, the ninth house, or the fifth house, || 109 || then all defects come to destruction, just as sins vanish upon the remembrance of Hari. A strong Jupiter situated in a trine (trikoṇa) effects the destruction of all defects. || 110 ||

All defects are destroyed in such a manner as sins are destroyed by the remembrance of Viṣṇu. If a powerful Jupiter is situated in the ninth or the fifth house, it destroys all defects. (110) It destroys all sins arising from the Muhūrta, the Ṣaḍvarga, the evil Navāṃśa, and planetary afflictions, just as a prostration destroys [sins] for the wielder of the trident (Śiva). (111)

Just as all sins are destroyed by bowing to Lord Śiva, so too these defects—such as the fault of an inauspicious hour (muhūrta-doṣa), the sixfold group of sins (pāpa-ṣaḍvarga), and the defects arising from malefic Navāṃśakas—are surely destroyed [by this], just as the moon in the eleventh house destroys all defects, where the sun in the eleventh house likewise destroys them all. || 112 ||

Just as the moon situated in the eleventh house quickly removes all defects, or even the sun situated in the eleventh house destroys all defects; ||| 112 || just as all sins are swiftly destroyed by bathing with devotion in the Gaṅgā, so too all defects arising from wind, fire, the sun, breath, and thunderclouds go to their destruction when Jupiter is situated in a quadrant (kendrasthāna). ||| 113 ||

Whatever defects arise from the month, the lunar day (*tithi*), or the ascendant (*lagna*)—such as the *vaidhṛti*, *vyatīpāta*, *pratisūrya*, smoke, dust, clouds, thunder, and so forth—are destroyed when Jupiter is situated in a quadrant (*kendrasthāna*), just as sins are quickly destroyed by bathing in the Gaṅgā with devotion. Whatever defects there may be, such as those of the "burnt month" (*māsadagdha*), the "burnt lunar day" (*tithidagdha*), or the "burnt ascendant" (*lagnadagdha*), [they are likewise destroyed]. (113–114) *Nāradasaṃhitā* 7.174.

All those [calamities] go to dissolution when Jupiter is situated in a quadrant (kendrasthāne). Jupiter, being strong and occupying a quadrant, destroys the defects arising from solar halos and other such portents. || 114 || [When Jupiter is] fully established in a quadrant position, [the defects] are destroyed; moreover, Jupiter reaching a quadrant destroys the defects of portents such as the solar halo. || 115 || Or, Venus, being strong and aspected by benefics while situated in the eleventh house, [destroys these defects]. || 116 ||

Jupiter situated in a quadrant destroys the defects arising from the three kinds of portents (116). Just as the wielder of the Pināka bow [Śiva], endowed with the full strength of his station and other attributes, destroyed Tripura, so too does the powerful Jupiter, occupying a quadrant, destroy the defects produced by the ascendant and its navāṃśa (117).

Fulfilled by the strength of its position and other factors, the powerful Jupiter, having reached a quadrant (kendram), destroys the defects arising from the ascendant and its navāṃśa just as Śiva reduced Tripura to ashes. (117) It reduces those defects to ashes like fire consumes fuel; whatever defects arise from the year, the solstice, the season, the month, or are produced by the ascendant, they all go to destruction when Jupiter is situated in a quadrant. (118)

Bhāṣāṭīkā-saṃgraha, Chapter 29. (175) Furthermore, if Jupiter is situated in a quadrant (kendrasthāna), the defects arising from the year, solstice, season, month, and the ascendant are destroyed just as fire reduces fuel to ashes. || 118 || The powerful Jupiter, or even Venus, situated in a quadrant, destroys those defects—both those mentioned and those not mentioned—just as Garuḍa destroys a serpent. || 119 ||

The powerful Jupiter or Venus situated in the ascendant destroys all major and minor faults—whether explicitly mentioned or unmentioned—just as Garuḍa destroys a serpent. (119) When the ascendant is in its Vargottama state, all defects go to their destruction, just as actions [perish] upon the realization of the Supreme Imperishable; of this there is no doubt. (120)

If the ascendant attains the Vargottama state, all defects are destroyed just as the latent impressions of karma (karmavāsanā) are destroyed through the knowledge of strength. || 220 || All those evils produced by malefic planets situated in the houses of misfortune go to their dissolution when Jupiter is placed in a quadrant (kendrasthāna). || 221 ||

The defects caused by planets situated in malefic positions, as well as all the evils produced by malefic planets, are destroyed when Jupiter is stationed in a quadrant (kendrasthāna). || 121 || Even a single Jupiter, situated in its exaltation and occupying the ascendant, destroys a multitude of defects, just as the vow of fasting on a holy day (Haridina) destroys all sins. || 122 ||

If Jupiter alone, situated in the sign of his exaltation, occupies the ascendant, he utterly destroys the multitude of defects, just as sins are destroyed by observing the vow of Ekādaśī. || 122 || (176) Nāradasaṃhitā: The eightfold Rāśikūṭa consists of the signs of the woman, her distance, the number, the signs, the lords of the signs, their birth-animals, and their castes; if these are pure, they bestow sons and grandsons. || 123 ||

If the eight factors—the *rāśikūṭa*, the three distances (*tridūra*), the *gaṇarāśi*, the *rāśisvāmī*, the *yoni*, and the *varṇa*—are pure, they are said to bestow sons and grandsons. (123) The joining of hands (marriage) between a husband and wife who are in the same zodiac sign (*rāśi*) but different asterisms (*dhiṣṇya*) is excellent; that between those in different signs but the same asterism is middling. (124)

If they belong to the same zodiac sign (*rāśi*) but have different asterisms (*nakṣatra*), the marriage of the girl and the groom is excellent; however, if they have different signs but the same asterism, it should be known as mediocre. (124) But if they are in the same asterism and the same sign, the marriage brings about the loss of life. Within the first nine asterisms from one's own natal asterism, marriage with a woman is extremely censured and leads to great distance [from her]. (126)

Furthermore, if both belong to the same lunar mansion (nakṣatra) and the same zodiac sign (rāśi), there is loss of life in marriage. If a man’s nakṣatra falls within nine nakṣatras from a woman’s nakṣatra, that woman is far removed and exceedingly censurable. [125] In the second [group of nine], it is middling; in the third group of nine, it is excellent. The three stars beginning with Pūrvā, the Uttarās, Dhātṛ (Rohiṇī), Yāmya (Bharaṇī), and Māheśa (Ārdrā)—[these constitute the first group]. [126]

Furthermore, among the nine constellations that follow, if the Puruṣaka constellation occurs within the second group of nine, its fruit should be known as middling. If it occurs within the nine constellations following that, its fruit should be known as exceedingly auspicious. The three Pūrvās, the three Uttarās, Rohiṇī, and Bharaṇī—these constitute the group of mortals (martyagaṇa); the other group is that of the immortals (amartyagaṇa). [The immortals' group consists of: Aśvinī, Āditya (Punarvasu), Arka (Puṣya), Vāyu (Svātī), Vijya (Anurādhā), Mitra (Anurādhā), Indu (Mṛgaśīrṣa), Viṣṇu (Śravaṇa), and the last asterism (Revatī). 126–127. (From Bhāṣāṭīkā, Chapter 29).

(377) The groups of humans are those [associated with the following asterisms], while Aśvinī, Punarvasu, Hasta, Svātī, Puṣya, Anurādhā, Mṛgaśiras, Śravaṇa, and Revatī are the groups of deities. || 127 || The Rakṣasa group consists of Maghā, Citrā, Viśākhā, Jyeṣṭhā, Dhaniṣṭhā, Śatabhiṣā, Mūla, Āśleṣā, and Kṛttikā; these are the Rakṣasa groups. || 128 ||

Venus, Saturn, Jupiter, the Moon, and Mars are the enemies, friends, and neutrals of the Sun respectively. Aquarius and Virgo, Aquarius and Pisces, Virgo and Taurus, Gemini and Scorpio, Aquarius and Cancer, and Leo and Capricorn—these sign combinations for a bride and groom are extremely censured. Now, the Yonis: Horses, elephants, rams, serpents, and snakes; rams, goats, and mice.

There is enmity between the mongoose and the snake, and between the ram and the monkey; there is enmity between the lion and the elephant, between the cow and the tiger, and between the rat, the cat, the buffalo, and the horse. The Śūdra [belongs to] Gemini, Libra, and Aquarius; the Vaiśya [belongs to] Virgo, Taurus, and Capricorn. (110) [In the *Nāradasaṃhitā*: Pisces, Scorpio, and Cancer belong to the Brāhmaṇa caste; Aries, Leo, and Sagittarius belong to the Kṣatriya caste; Gemini, Libra, and Aquarius belong to the Śūdra caste; and Virgo, Taurus, and Capricorn belong to the Vaiśya caste. (140) [One should never marry] a girl of a higher caste if the groom is of a lower caste. Indeed, the first, middle, last, and final-middle [nakṣatras] are the daughters of Aśvinī.

One should calculate by number that death occurs if the marriage is performed within a single *nāḍī*, but not if it is across two sides. The *prājāpatya*, *brāhma*, *daiva*, and *ārṣa* forms of marriage are auspicious when joined with a girl of a higher caste and a groom of a lower caste. In the case of the constellations beginning with Aśvinī, the *nāḍīs* are respectively: first-middle-last, last-middle-first, first-middle-last; if one performs the marriage within a single *nāḍī* there, death shall occur.

There is no fault in living separately; furthermore, the Prājāpatya, Bala, Daiva, and Ārṣa forms of marriage are declared to be the best. (141) These four, when performed at the prescribed time, yield their respective fruits; whereas the Āsura form arises from the giving of wealth, and the Paiśāca from the abduction of the maiden. (142)

If these four types of marriage are performed at the prescribed time (during an auspicious moment), excellent results are obtained. That in which the father of the girl gives her away for wealth is the Āsura marriage. That in which the groom carries off the girl by deception is the Paiśāca marriage. (142) The Rākṣasa is from abduction through combat, and the Gāndharva is from mutual agreement. However, those known as Gāndharva, Āsura, Paiśāca, and Rākṣasa are not considered the best. (143)

Taking a maiden away after conquering her in battle is the Rākṣasa marriage; when the bridegroom and the bride perform the marriage ceremony after having informed each other, that is the Gāndharva marriage. These marriages—Gāndharva, Āsura, Paiśāca, and Rākṣasa—are not as excellent as the preceding ones. (343) [Bhāṣāṭīkā, Chapter 29, Verse 181]. The fourth asterism from the ascendant at sunrise and the seventh from the asterism at sunset constitute the two types of Godhūlika; both are conducive to the attainment of sons and grandsons in marriage. (164)

The fourth ascendant from the sunrise ascendant is known as Abhijit, and the seventh ascendant is known as Godhūlika; both of these ascendants bestow sons and grandsons in marriage. (144) For the people of Prācya and Kaliṅga, Godhūlika is considered the primary [time]; Abhijit is the primary [time] in all regions and is the destroyer of defects. (144)

For those residing in the eastern regions as well as the inhabitants of Kaliṅga, the Godhūlika lagna is said to be auspicious; however, among all those countries, Abhijit is the foremost, as it destroys all defects. (145) When the sun has reached the meridian, the Muhūrta named Abhijit destroys all defects, just as the wielder of the Pināka bow destroyed Tripura. (146)

At the time of midday, the Muhūrta named Abhijit arrives; it destroys all defects just as Mahādeva burnt Tripura. (146) When the sun has reached the meridian, Abhijit renders the entire accumulation of defects useless, just as fire consumes a heap of cotton. (147)

The *abhijit* [muhūrta] occurring at the time of midday destroys all defects just as fire consumes a heap of cotton.
