(147) Even a single great defect here destroys a hundred thousand virtues, just as the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) purify a full jar [of wine] in a temple of the gods. (148) *Nāradasaṃhitā* (182)

Furthermore, if even a single great fault exists, it destroys millions of virtues, just as a drop of wine defiles a vessel of pure *pañcagavya*. (148) After the son’s marriage, the daughter’s marriage should not take place within three menstrual periods (*ṛtu*). For those two, there is no other auspicious rite (*maṅgala*) than their own marriage. (149)

After the marriage of a son, for six months one should not perform the marriage of a daughter; after the marriages of three sons and daughters, for six months no vow or other auspicious rite should be performed. (149) If the marriage of siblings born of the same parents takes place within six months, undoubtedly, within three years, one of them will become a widow. (140)

If the marriages of sisters with a single womb take place within six months, then within three years one of them shall become a widow. (150) A reciprocal marriage (pratyudvāha) should not be performed; two daughters should not be given to one man, nor should two daughters born of the same birth be given to two men born of the same birth. (193)

One should not perform a second marriage after the first; two daughters should not be married simultaneously for the sake of one groom; nor should two sisters from the same womb be married to two brothers from the same womb. (151) In this manner, a marriage should never take place [if these conditions exist], nor should there be two hair-shavings (tonsure ceremonies) at the same time. One born during the day [causes] harm to the father, while one born at night likewise harms the mother. At the two twilights (saṃdhyā), it harms oneself; however, in the case of Gaṇḍa [births], the reverse is true. (152)

A son or a daughter born under the *mūlā* nakṣatra certainly kills the father-in-law. (193) [Bhāṣāṭīkā, Chapter 29, Verse 183]. Now, the consideration regarding birth during the *gaṇḍānta* periods is being stated: one should not perform two marriages at once, nor should one have two tonsure ceremonies performed simultaneously. (Note: The provided text contains a fragmentary commentary on the verse regarding the *mūlā* nakṣatra, followed by a transition to the topic of *gaṇḍānta*.)

If birth occurs during the day, it destroys the father; if birth occurs at night, it destroys the mother; if birth occurs during the junctions (saṃdhyās), it destroys oneself. There is no other such reversal in the case of the Gaṇḍānta asterisms. A daughter or son born under the Mūla asterism destroys one's own father-in-law. (152–153) However, one born in the last quarter of that [Mūla] does not do so, nor does one born in the first quarter of Āśleṣā.

One born in the last quarter of Jyeṣṭhā destroys the elder brother, but a girl does not. (191) There is no fault if one is born in the last quarter of the Mūla asterism, nor is there any fault in the first quarter of Āśleṣā. A son born in the last quarter of the Jyeṣṭhā asterism destroys his elder brother, but if a girl is born, this fault does not apply. A girl born in the Mūla asterism [destroys] her mother and likewise her father.

A girl born under the asterism Aindrī (Jyeṣṭhā) destroys her husband; one born under Dvidaivaja (Viśākhā) destroys her brother-in-law. (194) If a girl is born under the Mūla asterism, she brings ruin to her mother and father; if born under Jyeṣṭhā, she destroys her elder brother; and if born under Viśākhā, she destroys her brother-in-law. (195) Thus it is said: "The thirty-second part of the time during which the eye of a healthy man sitting at ease blinks is proclaimed as 'tatpara'."

The time known as *pala* is that which passes before the eyes of a person sitting comfortably; its thirtieth part is called *tatpara*. (156) A hundredth part of a *tatpara* is designated as a *truṭi*; a thousandth part of a *truṭi* is said to be the duration of a *lagna*. (197)

Even a god does not know that, much less an ordinary person. Whether it be that [specific] time or another time, it occurs by the power of past karma. (198) A thousandth part of a *saumām̐hī* is a *truṭi*, and a thousandth part of a *truṭi* is said to be the time of the *lagna*. Even the gods do not know that; how then could an ordinary man know it? That lost time or another time arrives of its own accord through the power of past karma. (157–158)

The astrologer considers the omen alone; auspicious or inauspicious results do not arise from its power. A pure, auspicious sacrificial peg (śaṅku) should be made from the wood of the Nyagrodha, Khadira, Aśvattha, or red sandalwood trees, or from Śrīkhaṇḍa (sandalwood) or the tusk of an elephant. It should be twelve finger-breadths in height and six finger-breadths in circumference. || 169-170 ||

In that regard, the astrologer is merely an instrumental cause; no auspicious or inauspicious result occurs by his power alone. There, one should fashion an auspicious and pure *śaṅku* (peg) made of *bada*, *khaira*, *pīpala*, red sandalwood, coconut, *agaru*, or ivory, twelve *aṅgulas* in height and six *aṅgulas* in thickness. (159-160) One should prepare such a [peg] endowed with these characteristics for the calculation of time, beginning from the day of the wedding on either the sixth or the eighth day.

161. One should have a gnomon (*śaṅku*) endowed with such characteristics constructed for the purpose of determining the time, on the sixth or eighth day from the wedding day. Commentary on Āṣāḍha, Chapter 30: (185) The bride's entry (*vadhūpraveśa*) should be performed for the sake of prosperity on the tenth or an even day. Having avoided the two solstices (*ayanadvaya*), the birth month, and the days [of birth], as well as retrograde Venus (*pratiśukra*), the bridal journey (*vaivāhikī yātrā*) is auspicious. 162. Thus ends the twenty-ninth chapter, the "Chapter on Marriage" (*vivāhādhyāya*), in the *Śrī Nāradīya Saṃhitā*.

The entry of the bride (vadhūpraveśa) is auspicious on the tenth day or an even-numbered day; it is declared auspicious to bring the bride home after performing the marriage while avoiding both solstices (ayana), the month and day of the groom’s or bride’s birth, and when Venus is unfavorable (sanmukha). || 162 || Thus ends the twenty-ninth chapter, on Marriage, in the Bhāṣā-Ṭīkā of the Śrī Nāradīya Saṃhitā. [Chapter 29] The installation of all the deities, which bestows prosperity, should be performed during the northern solstice (uttarāyaṇa).

While the preceptor of the gods (Bṛhaspati) and the former preceptor of the gods (Śukra) are visible, it is auspicious to install the complete pantheon during the sun’s northern course (uttarāyaṇa). The rising of Jupiter and Venus is also auspicious. (1) Likewise, it is traditionally taught that [the installation] should take place during the five months beginning with Māgha when the moon is in the Viśākhā constellation, as well as during the first five lunar days of both the bright and dark fortnights. (2)

It is auspicious to perform the installation of a deity during the five months beginning with Māgha following Caitra; it is auspicious to perform the installation of a deity during the bright fortnight (*śuklapakṣa*) or up to the fifth lunar day (*pañcamī*) of the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*). On whichever lunar day (*tithi*) a particular deity is worshipped, on that day the installation of that deity is performed. For two [deities], starting from the second lunar day, and for three, starting from the fifth lunar day, in due order. (Nāradasaṃhitā, 186)

The installation is also auspicious on the specific lunar day (tithi) belonging to whichever deity it concerns; furthermore, the two lunar days beginning with the second (dvitīyā) and the three lunar days beginning with the fifth (pañcamī) are auspicious in that order. || 3 || The four lunar days beginning with the tenth (daśamī), especially the full moon (paurṇamāsī), as well as the three constellations following Uttarā, the three constellations ending with Hasta, and Jupiter and Venus [are also auspicious]. || 4 || The four lunar days beginning with the tenth, and especially the full moon, are auspicious. The three [constellations] following Uttarā, the three ending with Hasta, and Jupiter and Venus [are likewise auspicious]. || 4 ||

In the constellations of Uttarā, Punarvasu, Revatī, Hasta, and the three Puṣyas; likewise in Aśvinī, Rohiṇī, Śatabhiṣā, Śravaṇa, Anurādhā, and Dhaniṣṭhā—on days other than Tuesday when the Sun bestows strength upon the performer, provided that the aforementioned auspicious day is endowed with the strength of the Moon and the stars.

On an auspicious day during the third watch of the day, endowed with the strength of the moon and the stars, when there is an auspicious *lagna* (ascendant), an auspicious *navāṃśa*, and the eighth house and eighth sign (*aṣṭamabhāva*) of the performer are pure; [all signs are excellent when] joined with or aspected by benefic planets, and when the *lagna* is joined with or aspected by benefic planets. (6–7) All signs are declared auspicious when they are aspected by benefic planets.

The ascendant should be conjoined with a benefic planet. (7) A sign, setting aside its own inherent nature, adopts the influence produced by the planets occupying it; yet even that [sign] which yields undesirable results becomes a giver of excellent results when occupied by the Moon. (8) [The Moon] should be aspected by Jupiter, who is in a friendly or exalted sign, or by a benefic planet; and the auspicious ascendant should possess the five-fold excellence (*pañceṣṭika*), be free from the *naidhana* yoga, and be endowed with purity. (9) *Bhāṣā-Ṭīkā-saṃhitā*, Chapter 3, Verse 7 (187).

Setting aside the results naturally arising from the nature of the ascendant sign, one considers the effects produced by the planets; even an inauspicious Moon is auspicious if it is situated in the house of Venus and is aspected by a friend or Jupiter. Furthermore, it is auspicious to perform a consecration (pratiṣṭhā) when the Lagna is endowed with purity in all five limbs (pañcāṅga-śuddhi) and the eighth house is pure. 8–9.

The Sun, Moon, Rāhu, Ketu, and Saturn situated in the ascendant bring death to the performer; the other planets bestow wealth, grain, and happiness. (10) Malefic planets in the second house are undesirable, whereas the benefics and the Moon grant wealth. In the third house, all the planets bestow happiness through sons and grandsons. (11)

In the second house, malefic planets are not auspicious, whereas benefic planets and the Moon are givers of wealth. In the third house, all planets bestow the happiness of sons and grandsons. || 11 || In the fourth house, gentle planets are givers of happiness, while cruel planets and the Moon cause suffering. In the fifth house, cruel planets bring loss, whereas gentle planets grant the joy of children. || 12 ||

In the fourth house, gentle planets (saumyagraha) are auspicious givers; malefic planets and the Moon cause suffering. In the fifth house, malefic planets cause loss, while auspicious planets grant the happiness of sons. || 12 || If the Moon is full or waning there, the son will bring about the destruction of other sons. In the sixth house, auspicious planets cause enemies, while malefic planets bring about the destruction of enemies. || 13 || 188) Nāradasaṃhitā.

If the moon is full, it bestows sons; if waning, it destroys sons. In the sixth house, auspicious planets produce enemies, while malefic planets destroy enemies. (13) Whether full or even waning, the moon in the sixth house quickly brings about the destruction of all enemies for the doer, and bestows longevity, sons, and wealth. (16)

In the sixth house, the Moon destroys the enemies of the one who performs the installation very quickly and bestows longevity, sons, and wealth. (14) Malefic planets in the seventh house cause disease, while benefic planets grant auspicious results. All planets situated in the eighth house bring death to the performer. (19)

In the seventh house, malefic planets bestow disease, while benefic planets bestow auspicious results. All planets situated in the eighth house from the Pratiṣṭhā Lagna cause the death of the performer. (15) Malefic planets in the ninth house destroy [virtue], while benefics grant auspicious results; the Moon likewise grants auspicious results. Malefics in the tenth house cause failure, whereas benefics and the Moon bestow fame. (16)

In the ninth house, malefic planets are inauspicious, while benefic planets and the Moon are givers of auspicious results. In the tenth house, malefic planets and the Moon are inauspicious, whereas benefic planets bestow fame. (16) All planets situated in the eleventh house (house of gain) grant abundant profit; those situated in the twelfth house (house of loss) constantly cause great expenditure. (17)

Whatever is obtained in the house of gain (the eleventh) is all highly beneficial; however, in the twelfth house, all planets constantly cause great expenditure. (17) If the ascendant possesses an abundance of virtues and is relatively free from defects, the installation of deities therein grants the fulfillment of the performer's desired aims. (18)

In that lagna where virtues predominate and defects are few, the desires of the person who installs the deity are fulfilled. (18) One deficient in wealth destroys the patron; one deficient in mantras destroys the officiating priest; and one deficient in auspicious marks destroys prosperity. There is no enemy equal to a faulty installation. (19) Thus ends the thirtieth chapter, on the Installation of Deities, in the Śrī Nāradīya Saṃhitā. (30)

A consecration performed without the requisite materials ruins the patron; one performed without the mantras ruins the preceptor; and one performed without the proper characteristics ruins prosperity. Therefore, there is no enemy equal to a deficient consecration. (19) Thus ends the thirtieth chapter, on the Consecration of Deities, in the *Bhāṣā-Ṭīkā* commentary on the *Śrī-Nāradīya-Saṃhitā*. Now begins the section on Vāstu (Architectural Site Planning).

In the construction of cities, villages, houses, and so forth, one should first briefly examine the site through its smell, color, taste, and moisture. (1) [One should examine] the smells of honey, flowers, sourness, and meat, in the order of the castes beginning with the Brāhmaṇas. (2)

The earth is auspicious when it possesses a fragrance like honey for Brāhmaṇas, like flowers for Kṣatriyas, like sour gruel (kāñjī) for Vaiśyas, and like meat for Śūdras; furthermore, the colors of the earth—white, red, green, and black—are auspicious for Brāhmaṇas and the other castes respectively. (2) [Note: The phrase "nāradasahitā" appears to be an editorial marker or a reference to a specific commentary.]

Sweet, pungent, bitter, and astringent—these tastes, in their respective order, are auspicious for Brahmins and the other castes according to the quarters starting from the northeast. Furthermore, ground that slopes toward the northeast, the east, or the north is known to grant great prosperity to all social classes. (3)

If the float drifts toward other directions, it portends constant and extreme misfortune for all those castes. Regarding another test of the earth: the performer should dig a pit measuring one cubit (hasta) and then fill that excavation with the very same soil. 4.

If [the ground] is higher, there is excessive growth; if lower, decay; if level, it remains the same. Having thus leveled the site with water at night, one should fill it with water in the morning. If the water moves, there will be growth; if it remains still, it is level; if it sinks into mud or a depression, there is loss. When the site is thus endowed with these characteristics and properly leveled— (5–6)

If the soil increases, there will be great prosperity for the builder of the house; if the soil remains deficient—that is, if the pit is not filled—it portends loss. If the soil remains level, one should know the result to be middling. Furthermore, having dug a pit one cubit deep, one should fill it with water at night and observe it in the morning; if that pit is then slightly higher than the water level, [it is auspicious]. (Bhāṣāṭīkā-saṃhitā, Chapter 31)

(191) If it appears elevated, one should know it to be increasing; if it remains level, one should know the result to be equal; if one sees a hole in the mud, one should know the ground to be destructive. Having thus observed the site with these characteristics, one should make the ground level. 5 || 6 || Then, for the purpose of determining the directions, one should draw a circle on that level ground. Thereafter, one should place [the instrument] in its center, endowed with the previously mentioned characteristics. 7.

Then, for the purpose of performing the *dik-sādhana* (directional determination), one should draw a mandala in the center of that ground, dividing it into equal parts. There, at the previously mentioned auspicious moment (*lagna*), one should install the yantra. || 7 || Subsequently, wherever the shadow touches the circle during the forenoon and afternoon, two points should be made there on the circle according to the method for determining the east and west. || 8 ||

Then, where the shadow falls before midday and after midday, one should mark two points in the east and west to identify the shadow's path. (8) A line or a thread should be established as the north; in the middle of that, a clear line should be drawn from the tip of the shadow to the other tip, forming an east-west line. (9) Having drawn the lines in this manner, one should determine the northern direction.

Having established the northern direction, one should draw a line through its center, slanting like a fish, toward the east and west. (9) Then, by means of the "fish" figures at the intermediate points, the cardinal directions are determined; from those needle-pointed marks, lines should be drawn outward from the center to delineate a square. (10)

Then, having drawn a fine line in the middle shaped like a fish with a needle-pointed tip, one should determine the intermediate directions (the corners). Using the threads extending from the center, one should construct a square, four-peaked area on the outside. Nāradasaṃhitā: When the field has been made square and purified by the six divisions, a very beautiful enclosure wall should be constructed along the path of the lines. (11)

Then, having purified the square area according to the rules of the *ṣaḍvarga*, one should draw a single circular line on all four sides within the path of the lines. || 11 || Even though there are [lines] in the four directions starting from the east, there shall be eight doors in each direction in due order. || 12 || And their results, proceeding in a clockwise manner, are as follows: loss, poverty, acquisition of wealth, honor from the king, and great wealth. || 13 ||
Within that extent, one should demarcate the divisions of the four directions; then, in the directions starting with the east, eight squares each should be constructed in their proper sequence.

In the eastern direction, eight doors are situated in clockwise order; their results are described as follows: (in the first part of the east, near Īśāna, there is loss; in the second, poverty; then in the third, acquisition of wealth; in the fourth, gain from royalty; and in the fifth, the attainment of very great wealth. || 12 || 13 || In the direction of the Lord of Śacī (Indra), there is excessive thievery, extreme anger, and fear. [In the subsequent directions: death, imprisonment, fear, acquisition of wealth, and the increase of wealth. || 14 ||

Furthermore, in the six divisions there is excessive theft; in the seventh, excessive anger; and in the eighth, fear—these are the results of the eight doors in the eastern direction. And in the southern direction, according to their respective order, they are: death (1), bondage (2), fear (3), acquisition of wealth (4), and increase of wealth (5). || 14 || In the southern direction, there is freedom from affliction, fear of disease, and lack of strength. [The results for the other quarters are: loss of sons, increase of enemies, attainment of fortune, and arrival of wealth. || 15 || *Commentary on the Bhāṣā-Ṭīkā, Chapter 31.*

(193) Health (6), fear of disease (7), and poverty (8)—these are the results for the eight gates of the southern direction. Furthermore: loss of sons (1), increase of enemies (2), attainment of fortune (3), and arrival of wealth (4). || 15 || Good fortune, extreme misfortune, suffering, and grief [occur] in the west. Loss of children (1), lack of vigor (2), loss [of status] (3), [loss of] grain (4), and arrival of wealth (5). || 16 ||

Good fortune (5), extreme misfortune (6), suffering (7), and grief (8)—these are the results for the eight doors in the western direction. Furthermore, loss of wife (1), poverty (2), loss (3), grain (4), and arrival of wealth (5) || 16 || prosperity (6), great fear (7), and disease (8) [are the results] in the direction of the Moon (the north). Thus, in houses and other structures, the door should be twice as high as its width. || 17 ||

The fruits resulting from performing [the rite] eight times in the northern direction are: prosperity (6), great fear (7), and disease (8). One should construct the doors in houses and other such structures in this manner; it is auspicious to make the height twice the width of the door. Thus, the clockwise placement of the door and its results starting from the northeast corner have been declared for the main entrance; one should not deviate from this elsewhere. || 17-18 ||

Thus have been described the results for all directions, starting from the northeast and proceeding clockwise to the farthest points. This result pertains to the *mūladvāra*—that is, the main entrance—and not to the results of windows and the like. || 18 || One should place the door-panels in the west, the south, or the east. One should make the ground into a rampart so that it forms eighty-one squares. || 19 || 13 (194) Nāradasaṃhitā.

If the door is placed toward the west or the south of the house, there is a *vāstu* consisting of eighty-one squares; that is to say, it is taught that eighty-one deities reside within that *vāstu*. (19) In the center, the nine-square area is the station of Brahmā, which is highly censured [for a doorway].
There are thirty-two parts for the enclosures on all sides, with equal adjacent sections. (20)

In that case, know that the place called the Brahma-sthāna, which is said to be in the middle nine-pada (nine-square) area, is censurable; and having divided the four sides like a stake, there are thirty-two parts (sections). || 20 || The Piśāca-śās (Piśāca portions) at the commencement of a house bring about misery, grief, and fear; the remaining portions, however, when the house is constructed, bestow sons, grandsons, and wealth. || 21 ||

In those [sections] where the Piśācas have their portions at the commencement of a house, if one begins the construction of the house there first, there will be suffering, grief, and fear; however, if the construction of the house is begun from some other location, there will be the attainment of sons, grandsons, and wealth. || 21 || The lines located in the western part of the head, arising from the cardinal and intermediate directions, belong to the portion of Brahmā and the Piśācas, where there is a gathering of children. || 22 ||

The line proceeding through the center reaches the cardinal directions and the corners; there, from the head of the Vāstupuruṣa toward the northeast (īśāna), lies the region of Brahmā and the location of the assembly of children belonging to the Piśāca portion. One should recognize the vital points and joints of those residing in each of those respective places. || 22 ||
The vital points (marmas) and the joints are not desired for placement in those very locations. || 23 ||

If one stays there for two nights, one should understand the vital points (*marma*) and joints (*sandhi*) of the site; staying there for the first time is inauspicious. 23. [Bhāṣāṭīkā, Chapter 33, Verse 195] The months of Mārgaśīrṣa, Phālguna, Vaiśākha, Māgha, Śrāvaṇa, and Kārtika are suitable for the construction of a house, as they bestow sons, health, and wealth. 25.

If one begins the construction of a house during the months of Mārgaśīrṣa, Phālguna, Vaiśākha, Māgha, Śrāvaṇa, or Kārttika, there will be the attainment of sons, health, and wealth. || 24 || In the consonants beginning with 'ka' (the *kavarga*) and so forth, corresponding respectively to the directions starting from the East, the lords of the birds (the *kavarga*), the lords of the directions are known as Hari (the *tavarga*), Īśa (the *pavarga*), the Serpent (the *yavarga*), the Mouse (the *savarga*), the Elephant (the *tavarga*), and the Boar (the *śavarga*). || 26 || These should be understood as the lords of the classes (*varga*) in sequence; the fifth letter from one's own class is the enemy. The best of astrologers declare that the highest affection exists between those belonging to the same class. || 26 ||

In the directions starting from the East, respectively within the vowel groups (akārādi) and so forth, there are eight groups: 1. Garuḍa, 2. Cat, 3. Lion, 4. Dog, 5. Snake, 6. Mouse, 7. Elephant, and 8. Boar. Astrologers have stated that one should know these as belonging to the East and other directions; therein, the fifth group from one's own group is to be known as the enemy. 25–26. Now, another method: Having doubled one's own group, one should add it to the other group.

"Divide by eight; whoever has a remainder is the debtor. (He. 27). Furthermore, there is this second method: double one's own square and add it to the other's square, then divide by eight; whatever number remains there, know that to be the result. In the same way, double the other's square and add it to one's own square, then divide by eight; observe whatever numbers remain. Among these remaining numbers, whichever number remains as the larger is [the indicator].

One should know that person to be a debtor; here, it is correct for the house-number to be a debtor. 27. [The number] is 7 (196). *Nāradasaṃhitā*, Chapter 9, Section on Area (*Kṣetraphala*): "The length multiplied by the width shall be the area of the house-plot. That, divided separately by eight, leaves a remainder which is the income, beginning with the 'flag' (*dhvaja*) and so forth. 28.

Multiply the width of the house by its length; that is the area (kṣetraphala). Then, divide by eight. The remainder is to be known as the *āya* (income/profit), beginning with *dhvaja* and so forth. *Dhvaja*, *dhūma*, *siṃha*, *śvā*, *saurabheya*, *khara*, *gaja*, and *dhvāṅkṣa*—these eight are declared to be the *āyas* in this sequence. (29) 1. *Dhvaja* (flag), 2. *Dhūma* (smoke), 3. *Siṃha* (lion), 4. *Śvāna* (dog), 5. *Saurabheya* (bull), 6. *Khara* (donkey), 7. *Gaja* (elephant), 8.
*Dhvāṅkṣa* (crow)—thus these eight *āyas* have been described in order. (29)

The banner of a Brāhmaṇa is to be known as the elephant; that of a Kṣatriya is indeed the lion; and that of a Vaiśya is the bull, though for all [castes], the elephant is traditionally prescribed. (30) Fame, grief, victory, enmity, wealth, poverty, happiness, and disease—these are the results, in order, of the commencement of building with the elephant and the other banners. (31)

Furthermore, if the first banner (dhvaja) arrives, there is fame; then if the second is smoke (dhūma), there is sorrow; then 3 victory, 4 enmity, 5 wealth, 6 poverty, 7 happiness, and 8 disease—one should know these to be the results of these eight banners and so forth. || 31 || Now, the results of the zodiac signs (rāśiphala): The second and twelfth [houses] lead to poverty, the trine (trikoṇa) to quarrel, and the sixth and eighth to death; the other signs are givers of auspiciousness. || 32 || *Bhāṣāṭīkā-saṃhitā*, Chapter 33.

(1977) If the sign of Carakī (Saturn) and the sign of the lord [of the year] are mutually in the twelfth house from each other, one should predict the result of poverty; if they are in the ninth or fifth houses, predict quarrels; if they are in the sixth or eighth houses, predict death; in any other signs, they should be known as bestowers of auspiciousness. ||32|| The day and divisional portions (vārāṃśa) of the Sun and Mars grant fear of fire; the day and divisional portions of the other planets lead to the fulfillment of all desires and purposes. ||33||

If one begins constructing a house during the Navāṃśaka of the Sun or Mars, there will be fear of fire; however, if it is done during the Navāṃśakas of other planets, all desires shall be fulfilled. (33) In the three months beginning with Nabhasya (Bhādrapada), and likewise in the subsequent triads of months in due order, a man should face the same direction when building his house as he faces when laying its foundation. (34)

During the three-month periods beginning with Bhādrapada, the face of the Vāstu deity faces the cardinal directions starting from the East; it is auspicious to construct the door of the house in whichever direction the face of the Vāstu deity is turned. (34) A house with its entrance facing the opposite direction brings disease, grief, and fear; however, this defect does not exist for houses whose entrances face all directions. (35)

If one installs the door in a manner contrary to these three, disease, grief, and fear will arise; however, this defect does not occur in those houses where a verandah (caukhaṭa) is constructed on all four sides. || 35 || One should place a clay box, filled with gold, gems, grain, and moss, for the purpose of consecration (nyāsa), into a pit in the center of the house measuring one cubit. || 36 || The navel is half the length of the site-plan (vāstu); from that point, three finger-breadths [outward] is the belly. One should plant a ritual peg (śaṅku) there, which increases sons and grandsons.

37. || (198) Nāradasaṃhitā || One should collect earth, a wooden box, gold, gems, grain, and moss; having dug a pit one cubit deep in the center of the house, one should draw lines within it. In half the extent of the Vāstu site is the navel; from that navel, one should know the *kukṣi* (flank) to be seven *aṅgulas*. If one plants a peg (*śaṅku*) there, there shall be the attainment of sons, grandsons, and wealth. || 36 || 37 || [With] twenty-four, twenty-three, sixteen, or twelve *aṅgulas*... || 37 || 38 || [The text continues: ...with twenty-four, twenty-three, sixteen, or twelve *aṅgulas*.

The measurement for the *śaṅku* (gnomon) of the Brāhmaṇas and other castes should be made respectively as twenty-four, twenty-three, sixteen, and twelve *aṅgulas*. The *śaṅku* should be adorned with gold, cloth, and other ornaments. (38) It should be made from *khadira*, *arjuna*, or *śāla* wood, or from the *pūga* (betel) tree; or it may be produced from red sandalwood, *pālāśa*, red *śāla*, or *viśāla* wood. (39)

The *khaira*, *arjuna* tree, *śāla*, *supārī* tree, *tejapāta* tree, red sandalwood, *ḍhāka*, and beautiful *lāka-śāla* trees; || 39 || as well as the *nīpa*, *kuṭaja*, *vaiṣāva*, and trees born from the *bilva*—from these one should fashion the *śaṅku*. Then, having divided the *śaṅku* into three parts, it should thereafter be made four-cornered. || 40 || One should fashion the *śaṅku* from the *kaṭaja* tree, the *kadaṃba* tree, bamboo, or the *bilva* tree. Having divided the *śaṅku* into three parts, one should then make it four-cornered. || 40 ||

Having fashioned a gnomon (śaṅku) endowed with such characteristics—either having eight parts, or three parts, or being smooth-sided and without blemishes—on an auspicious day, one should perform the desired calculations and commence the construction of the house. A- Bhāṣāṭīkā, Chapter 3, Verse 399: On days other than Sunday, in the Lagna (ascendant) of Capricorn, excluding the eighth house.

In the Naidhana fire-pit, conjoined with purification, at an auspicious *lagna* and an auspicious *navāṃśa*—that is, when the Sun and Mars do not occupy the *lagna*, when Sagittarius (*dhanu*) is not in the eighth house, when no planet is situated in the eighth house, and when there is an auspicious *lagna* and the *navāṃśa* of an auspicious sign—at that time, one should plant the sacrificial post (*śaṅku*). This should be done while reciting the *puṇyāha* mantras, accompanied by musical instruments and auspicious women. || 42-43 ||

One should install the conch in such a lagna that it is aspected by benefic planets and joined with benefic planets; one should then cause auspicious rites to be performed with the recitation of *puṇyāhavācana*, instrumental music, songs, and auspicious songs sung by women. (43) When the other [planets] are situated in their own quadrants (*kendras*), in their trines (*trikoṇas*), or in the third, eleventh, or twelfth houses from the lagna, and when the Moon is in the sixth or eleventh house from the lagna, [the rite should be performed] preceded by the worship of the astrologer. (49)

If auspicious planets are situated in the second house, the quadrants (kendras), or the ninth and fifth houses, while malefic planets are in the third, eleventh, and sixth houses, and the Moon is in the sixth or eleventh house—then, after performing the worship of the astrologer, one may begin the construction of a house in such a Lagna. || 44 || Houses are known to have one, two, three, four, or seven wings (śālas). Furthermore, these wings are of six types, and each of those is again of ten kinds. || 46 ||

There are houses provided with one hall, two halls, three, four, or seven halls; these also have six varieties, making sixteen types of houses in total. Their names are: Dhruva, Dhānya, Jaya, Nanda, Khara, Kānta, Manorama, Sumukha, Durmukha, Krūra, Śatru, Svarṇaprada, and Kṣaya. [45-46] [From the Nāradasaṃhitā: Ākranda, Vipula, and Vijaya; thus the house is of sixteen kinds. [A-(200)]

There are exactly ninety-six types of houses according to their various arrangements (prastāra-bheda). These sixteen kinds of houses are: Dhruva (1), Dhānya (2), Jaya (3), Nanda (4), Khara (5), Kānta (6), Manorama (7), Sumukha (8), Durmukha (9), Krūra (10), Śatraprada (11), Svarṇaprada (12), Kṣayaprada (13), Ākranda (14), Vipula (15), and Vijaya (16). Thus, these are the sixteen varieties.
Oṃ, there are these [varieties]; their *prastāra* has ninety-six varieties. 46. 47. A short [syllable] should be placed below a long one; one should arrange it as before, above.
Thereafter, one who has mastered all the prescribed rites should worship the gurus according to the ritual injunctions. 48.
One should place a short (laghu) syllable below a long (guru) position; then, write [the sequence] above it in descending order. Next, differentiate between the large and small positions.
In this way, since there are six variations for each house, there will be ninety-six variations in total. || 48 ||
In the directions starting from the east, two elephants have been placed upon the firm ground of the hall.

The sum of the *dhruvāṅka* (fixed numbers) of the halls, increased by one, constitutes the house-number starting from the *dhruvāṅka*. (19) Now, the divisions of these houses, which possess sixteen names, are described. The *dhruvāṅka* for a house with an eastern door is 1; for a house with a southern door, it is 2; for a house with a western door, it is 8; and for a house with a northern door, it is 8. By adding 3 to this *dhruvāṅka*, whatever number results, that is the *dhruva* for grain and other such items.

One should understand the designations of houses as follows: for example, if there is a house with two doors, one in the east and one in the west, the fixed number (dhruvāṅka) for the east is 1 and for the west is 4; adding these gives 5, and adding 1 results in 6. This should be known as the place named Kānta.
|| 49 || [From Bhāṣāṭīkā, Chapter 31, verse 201]

One should construct the bathhouse in the eastern direction, the kitchen in the southeast; the bedchamber in the south, and the armory in the southwest. (90) Thus one should arrange these locations: the milk-hall, the butter-hall, and the rice-hall; as well as the places for the bed, the thread, the weapons, their respective sciences, food, and auspicious objects. (91)

In the northeast (Īśāna) corner should be the places for milk, drinking water, and ghee; in the southeast (Agni) corner, the places for the bed, urine, weapons, and food. || 51 || Grain, women, enjoyment, wealth, and the abodes of adornment—by proceeding from the northeast, the construction of these houses is auspicious. || 62 ||

Grains, female companions, and wealth—these locations are in the southwest (Nairṛta); the places for amorous arts and the like are in the northwest (Vāyavya) corner; such locations are also said to exist in the corners beginning with the northeast (Īśāna). || 52 || These are auspicious in their own respective locations, as well as in their own respective directions. [The trees] known as Plakṣa, Udumbara, and Āmra, as well as Nimba, Snuhī, and Vibhītaka, || 43 ||

Those trees are auspicious when situated in their respective corners according to the expansion of their specific functions; for example, it is auspicious for the fire-place to be located in the southeast corner. Furthermore, the following trees are praised: the *pīlū*, *galūra*, mango, *nimba*, *thohara*, and *baheḍā* (53). However, these thorny and burnt trees are censured: the *vadara*, *aśvattha*, *kapittha*, *agastya*, *śigru*, *tāla*, and the *tiṃtiṇī* (49). (Nāradasaṃhitā, 20.2)

Those trees that are thorny, burnt trees, banyan, pipal, wood-apple, agasti, sahojanā, palmyra, and emblic myrobalan—these trees are said to be extremely censurable and should not be brought in front of the house. (54) The house should be like a father for its eldest brother; [trees] in the west and south are auspicious. The household pillars should be symmetrical; they are praised when equal, and not when unequal. (55)

Likewise, the house for the father and the elder brother should be constructed from one's own house toward the west and south directions; the foundations and pillars of the houses should be level and not uneven. (55) The height of the walls should not be too high nor too low, but according to one's preference; one should consider the same for all houses, including those situated above other houses. (56)

The height of the walls should be neither too high nor too low; they should be made beautiful. On top of the house, one should not construct walls of that same height, nor place doors and such in those very locations. (56) Regarding houses and other structures, various proportions for the flow [of light or space] within the home are prescribed in sequence: the Pañcāla, Vaideha, Kaurava, and Kanyaka measurements. (47)

It is auspicious to perform the various methods of pouring water into houses and other structures; furthermore, the measurements for the regions of Pañcāla, Vaideha, Kuru, and Kānyakubja, such as the *hasta* and so forth, are correctly stated. || 57 || The sequence for Māgadha, Śūrasena, and Vaṅga is thus remembered; one should purify that [area] which has a width of four parts, and that is what is being described. || 58 ||

For the Magadhas, Śūrasenas, and Vaṅgālas, the measurement of their own [Madhyadeśa] human expansion is auspicious when multiplied by four. (58) The measurement of Pañcāla is incomparable; it should be determined by increasing successively from the measurements of other regions. The remaining measurements, such as those of Videha and others, should be taken in their proper order. (59) The measurement of the Pañcāla country (Punjab) should be calculated by correctly increasing the measurements of other countries in successive stages. (59)

Beyond this, the measurement of Pañcāla is common to all. The measurement of Avantī is auspicious for Brāhmaṇas, and that of Gāndhāra for Kṣatriyas. (60) The measurement of Kaujaṇya is for Vaiśyas; for Brāhmaṇas and the others, it should be applied progressively as described, with water-channels provided for houses of two or three stories.

61. A Vaiśya should adopt the measurement system of the Kaujaṇya country. Brāhmaṇas and the others should take their measurements according to the progressive increase [of one unit] respectively. In a house that has two or three halls (śālās), one should appropriately provide a place for water to fall [into a well or pond]. 62. For the stables of camels and elephants, a banner-marked (dhvajāya) [pillar] or [the image of] an elephant [is auspicious]; for the stables of cattle and horses, a banner-marked pillar or [the image of] a bull [is auspicious]. At the door, beds, seats, mantras, and banners marked with a lion or a bull are auspicious.

Thus ends the thirty-first chapter, on the rules for building sites (*vāstuvidhāna*), in the venerable *Nāradīyasaṃhitā*. It is auspicious for the *dhvaja* (flag) or *gaja* (elephant) *āya* to reside in the stables of camels, elephants, and the like; likewise for the stables of cattle and other such animals. (204) *Nāradasaṃhitā*.

In a stable for horses, a banner or a bull is auspicious; at the door of a hall for beds, seats, or mantras, a banner, a lion, or a bull is said to be auspicious. (62) Thus ends the thirty-first chapter, on the rules for architecture, in the *Bhāṣā* commentary on the *Śrī Nāradīya Saṃhitā*. I shall now describe the worship of Vāstu upon entering a new house: one should draw lines measuring one cubit each, ten toward the east and ten toward the north. (1)

Now, at the time of entering a new house, the Vāstupūjā is described. On a platform measuring one cubit (hasta), one should draw ten lines toward the east and ten lines toward the north. || 1 || In the center of the house, upon rice, there should be eighty-one squares; or one may place forty-five squares as will be described hereafter. || 2 ||

Then, having placed rice in three compartments, one should construct eighty-one squares (*koṣṭaka*). Therein, forty-nine deities—five and forty-four *athīvas*—are situated separately in the interior. (2) Thirty-two are to be worshipped on the exterior, while thirteen remain within; I shall now describe their locations and names in due order. (3)

Furthermore, thirty-two deities are to be worshipped externally; distinct from them are the thirteen deities within. Now, we shall state their names in order. (3) These thirty-two (32) external-designated deities are located in the northeast corner: Kṛpīṭayoni, Parjanya, Jayanta, and Pākaśāsana. (4) *Commentary on the Bhāṣā-Ṭīkā, Chapter 32.*

(205) Sūrya, Satya, Bhṛśa, Ākāśavāyu, Pūṣan, Nairṛta, Gṛharkṣata, Daṇḍadhara, Gāndharva, Mṛgarājaka, Mṛgapitṛgaṇādhīśa, then the one named Dauvārika, Sugrīva, Puṣpadanta, Jalādhīśa, and likewise Asura. || 6 ||

Mṛga, Pitaragaṇādhīśa, Dauvārika, Sugrīva, Puṣpadantaka, Jalādhīśa, and Asura; Śeṣa, Pāparoga, Bhogī, Mukhya, Niśākara, Soma, Sūrya, Aditi, and Diti—these are the thirty-two deities. (6–7) Śeṣa, Pāparoga, Bhogī, Mukhya, Niśākara, Soma, Sūrya, Aditi, and Diti—these are the thirty-two deities. (7) Now, there are four situated in the corners starting from the northeast (Īśāna), located near them.

Āpa, Savitṛ, Jaya, and Rudra—these are the four deities situated in order in the intermediate directions (corners) beginning with Īśāna. || 8 || In the center is Brahmā occupying nine squares; his eight [attendants] are situated near him, separated by one square each, starting from the east and extending all around Brahmā. || 9 ||

It is constructed within nine central squares, and near it are eight others situated one space apart in the directions starting from the east, surrounding Brahmā on all four sides. (206) Nāradasaṃhitā: Aryamā, Savitā, Vivasvān, Vibudhādhipa, Mitra, Rājayakṣmā, and the one named Pṛthvīdhara. || 10 ||

Including Āpavatsa as the eighth, these are the forty-nine deities. Āpa, Āpavatsa, Parjanya, Agni, and Diti follow in sequence. This is the group of one-footed deities (padikās) in all the corners without exception. In their center are twenty, and among them, the two-footed ones (dvipadās) are always present. Thus, including the eight Āpavatsas, all together amount to forty-nine.

Āpa, Āpavatsa, Parjanya, Agni, and Diti reside in the four corners; this is known as the group of the *padikas*. Among them, twenty deities are external; these are always called *dvipadas*. (11-12) Aryaman, Vivasvat, Mitra, and the one named Pṛthvidhara—these four gods are recorded as being around Brahmā in the cardinal directions. (13)

Āryamā, Vivasvān, Mitra, and Pṛthvīdhara—these four Brahmās are said to be designated as occupying three quarters (tripada) each. || 13 || One who knows the ritual of Vāstu should likewise worship the deities with one, two, or three quarters using the Vāstu-mantra, along with dūrvā grass, curd, unbroken rice (akṣata), and other offerings. || 14 ||

There, the twice-born who knows the ritual should worship Brahmā, as well as Ekapadika, Dvipadika, Tripadika, and the deities Oṃ; then, with the Vāstu-mantra, he should perform the worship of Vāstu using dūrvā grass, unbroken rice, curd, and other offerings. || 14 || Having caused a pair of white garments to be offered with the Brahma-mantra, and then having given betel-leaf, he should pray to the Vāstupuruṣa. || 15 || (207) Commentary in Bhāṣā: Chapter 32. With the Brahma-mantra, one should cause a pair of white garments to be presented; then, after giving betel-leaf, one should pray to the Vāstupuruṣa. || 15 ||

One should offer two white garments with mantras dedicated to Brahmā, and after offering betel-leaf (tāmbūla), one should pray to Vāstupuruṣa. (15) One should perform all the services, beginning with the invocation (āvāhana), in their proper sequence; and having offered the food offering (naivedya) consisting of various kinds of cooked food, one should present it accompanied by musical instruments and the like. (16) All the services, starting with the invocation, should be performed in order; and after presenting the food offering of many varieties of meals, one should make the final offering while playing various kinds of musical instruments.

16–17. "O Vāstupuruṣa, obeisance to you, O Lord who delights in resting upon the earth! May you always make my house prosperous with wealth, grain, and other riches. (17) Having thus prayed, one should give a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to the worshipper according to one's ability, and before him, one should provide food for the Brahmins according to one's means. (18)

Having made such a prayer, one should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the Brāhmaṇa who has performed the sacrifice according to his ability; then, having seated those deities before him, he should feed the Brāhmaṇas with faith according to his means. (18) He who performs the worship of Vāstu properly according to this rite shall obtain health, the birth of sons, wealth, and grain. (19)
The person who performs the Vāstupūjā well according to this procedure attains health, sons, wealth, and grain. (19)

(208) Nāradasaṃhitā: One should never enter a house that lacks door-panels and bolts, that is left uncovered, or where the ritual offering (*bali*) and the feeding of Brahmins have not been performed; for such a place is indeed a mine of calamities. Thus ends the thirty-second chapter, on the characteristics of architecture (*vāstulakṣaṇa*), in the venerable Nāradīya Saṃhitā. One should not enter a place that is without door-leaves and bolts, that is unsheltered, and where the sacrificial offering and the meal for the Brahmins have not been provided.

It should be avoided, for it is a treasury of calamities. (20) Thus ends the thirty-second chapter, on the Characteristics of the Site, in the Bhāṣā-Ṭīkā of the Śrī-Nāradīya-Saṃhitā. Now begins the section on Departure (Yātrā). I shall now duly describe how the departure of those whose birth has been correctly ascertained may lead to the attainment of their desired fruits. (1)

Just as a journey yields the desired fruit for men, so too shall I explain it well for the sake of the wise twice-born. (1) For those men whose births are unknown, the attainment of results is like the markings of a wood-boring insect; yet for those who rely on the rising of questions and omens, there is likewise the emergence of results. (2)

Furthermore, even for those ignorant and foolish people whose births are unknown, the attainment of happiness occurs by the maxim of the "worm-eaten letter" (*ghuṇākṣaranyāya*). (The *ghuṇākṣaranyāya* is as follows: just as a wood-boring insect eats through wood and leaves a mark, sometimes by the turn of fate, letters such as "Rāma" are inscribed; this is the *ghuṇākṣaranyāya*). [From the Bhāṣāṭīkā, Chapter 33].

Even for the foolish, the arising of results occurs solely through the influence of questions, planetary transits, and other such factors. (2) On the sixth, eighth, twelfth, the *riktā* tithis, the new moon (*amāvāsyā*), and the full moon (*pūrṇimā*), as well as on the first day of the bright fortnight (*śukla-pratipadā*), undertaking a journey leads to death or to poverty. (3) Journeying on the sixth, eighth, twelfth, the *riktā* lunar days, the new moon, the full moon, and the first day of the bright fortnight is undertaken for the sake of death or for the sake of destitution. (3)

A journey undertaken during the asterisms of Revatī, Hasta, Mṛgaśiras, Aśvinī, Anurādhā, Kṛttikā, Śravaṇa, Puṣya, and Dhaniṣṭhā, and when the Moon is in the ninth, fifth, seventh, or eleventh house, bestows the desired fruit. (9) One should not travel toward the east on a Saturday, nor toward the south on a Thursday. (4)

On Monday and Sunday, one should not travel toward the west or the north; on Saturday, one should not go toward the east; on Thursday, one should not travel toward the south; on Friday and Sunday, one should not go toward the west; and on Wednesday and Tuesday, one should not travel toward the north. Indra, Japa, Caturāsya, Aryaman, and the asterisms [beginning with] Kṛttikā are situated in the east.

The *śūla* (piercing) asterisms for all directions are Maitra (Anurādhā), Ārka (Hasta), Ījya (Puṣya), and Aśvinī. (Nāradasaṃhitā 4A.14, v. 6). Jyeṣṭhā, Pūrvāṣāḍhā, Rohiṇī, and Uttarāphālgunī are the asterisms that constitute the *śūla* in the cardinal directions starting from the East in order; whereas Anurādhā, Hasta, Puṣya, and Aśvinī are auspicious in all directions. (Nāradasaṃhitā 4A.14, v. 6). The asterisms of the directions and gates follow the sequence of seven, seven, and three constellations respectively.

One should not cross the staff-line (daṇḍa) or the bar-line (parigha) situated in the directions of the wind (northwest) and fire (southeast). Furthermore, the seven constellations beginning with Kṛttikā are declared to be the directional gate-constellations (digdvāra-nakṣatra) for the east and other directions in their respective order; and there is a line-staff (rekhā-daṇḍa) in the northwest and southeast corners.

That is to say, one should travel northward from the lunar mansions at the eastern gate, and while merging the south and west, one must not cross this line of the Vāyavya (northwest) and Agni (southeast) corners; one should not proceed within this Parigha. 7. Likewise, the intermediate directions are determined by the lunar mansions of the southeast and the east; furthermore, the zodiacal signs of the directions follow in sequence, beginning with Aries and repeating again and again. 8.

If movement is to be made toward the intermediate corners (koṇas), the following arrangement applies: when the asterisms (nakṣatras) belong to the eastern direction, one should proceed to the southeast (agnikoṇa); then, following this same sequence, when the asterisms belong to the southern direction, one should proceed to the southwest (nairṛta); and when the asterisms belong to the northwest (vāyavya), one should proceed to the western asterisms. Furthermore, the zodiac signs beginning with Aries (meṣa) remain in the directions starting from the east after completing three cycles, as follows: 1, 5, and 9 are in the East; 2... [and so on].

6. 1. 0 South 0. 3; 7. 11 West 0. 4; 8. 12 North. Among these, this is the abode of the Moon. || 8 || Now, the lords of the directions and the *lalāṭīyoga*: The lords of the directions are the Sun, Venus, Mars, Rāhu, Saturn, the Moon, and Mercury. When the lord of the direction is situated on the forehead (*lalāṭastha*) [of the ascendant], there is no return for the traveler. || 9 || *Commentary in Bhāṣā:* Chapter 33, Section (21.3). The Sun (1), Venus (2), Mars (3), Rāhu (4), Saturn (5), the Moon (6), Mercury (7), and Jupiter (8) are the lords of the directions starting from the East.

O Lord of the Quarters, when this *lalāṭa* occurs on the forehead of those traveling, there shall be no return for them. (9) When the Sun is situated in the ascendant (*lagna*) and located on the forehead of one traveling toward the eastern direction; and when Venus is in the twelfth or eleventh house and located on the forehead in the south-eastern direction (*āgneyī*). (10) For example, when the Sun is in the ascendant, there is a *lalāṭa-yoga* for one going toward the east; and when Venus is in the twelfth or eleventh house, there is a *lalāṭa-yoga* in the south-east. (10)

If Mars is situated in the tenth house from the ascendant, it is a *lalāṭaga* (forehead-mark) yoga in the southern direction; if Rāhu is in the ninth or eighth house, it is a *lalāṭaga* yoga in the southwest (*nairṛtyāṃ*) direction. (11) If Saturn is in the seventh house from the ascendant, it is a *lalāṭaga* yoga in the western direction; and if the Moon is in the sixth or fifth house, it is a *lalāṭaga* yoga in the northwest (*vāyvyāṃ*) direction. (12)

If Saturn is in the seventh house from the ascendant, there is a *lalāṭaga* (forehead-touching) configuration in the western direction; if the Moon is in the sixth or fifth house, it is *lalāṭaga* in the north-western corner. || 12 || If Mercury is situated in the fourth house, there is a *lalāṭaga* configuration in the northern direction; if Jupiter occupies the second or third house, it is *lalāṭaga* in the north-eastern direction. || 13 || If Mercury is in the fourth house from the ascendant, there is a *lalāṭaga* yoga in the northern direction. If [Jupiter] is in the second or third house from the ascendant, it is *lalāṭaga* in the north-east. || 13 ||

If there are three *bṛhaspatis*, then the Lord of the Direction (*digīśvara*) is upon the head of one traveling toward the northeast (*īśāna-kona*). (33) [Nāradasaṃhitā] || 212 || A man desiring life should avoid that which touches the forehead. If a planet moving in retrograde (*viloma-ga*) has entered the ascendant at the time of departure (*yātrā-lagna*), [he should likewise avoid it]. || 14 ||

A person desiring to live should avoid departing during this *lalāṭaga* yoga. If a planet that is unfavorable to the king in his birth chart occupies the ascendant at the time of travel, then in that ascendant—[verse 14]—that planet, as well as its sign and its *navāṃśa*, will cause the ruin of the king. However, the journey of the Sun and the Moon is favorable and bestows auspiciousness. [Verse 34] If the king sets out, his desires are frustrated, and the sign and *navāṃśa* of that [malefic] planet are also inauspicious.

Furthermore, it is auspicious for the sun and moon to move in accordance with their respective solstices (ayanas): if the sun is in the northern solstice (uttarāyaṇa) and the moon is also in the northern solstice, then one should travel toward the northeast; if the sun and moon are both in the southern solstice (dakṣiṇāyana), then one should travel toward the southwest. (15) In the absence of such [favorable conditions], traveling by day or night results in the death of the traveler; otherwise, there is destruction. When Venus is retrograde (mūḍha), there is loss of the undertaking; when Venus is in opposition (pratiśukra), there is defeat. (16)

Furthermore, if the Sun and Moon are in different *ayanas*, one should travel during the day when the Sun is in its *ayana*, and during the night when the Moon is in its *ayana*. Traveling contrary to this results in death. If one travels when Venus is eclipsed (*astamita*), there will be loss of the undertaking; if one travels facing Venus, there will be defeat. However, Venus does not destroy the fault caused by [traveling against] other planets. (16)

Vasiṣṭha, Kāśyapeya, Atri, Bharadvāja, and Gautama—(17). [Commentary: Only Śukra can remove the fault of Śukra entering one's mouth; no other planet can. Furthermore, for these five lineages (gotras), there is no prohibition against Śukra (Pratiśukra) occurring during a marriage within the same village, or during times of famine or royal upheaval. (18)

For these five types of people, there is no fault in proceeding toward Venus (Pratiśukra). Furthermore, in the case of a single village, a marriage, a famine, or the collapse of a kingdom; || 18 || during a disturbance among the twice-born or a revolt by the king, Pratiśukra does not exist [as a defect]. Even if Venus is in its sign of debilitation, situated in an enemy’s house, retrograde, or defeated; || 19 || due to the curse of a Brahmin or the wrath of a king—in these matters, there is no fault in proceeding toward Venus.

Venus situated in a debilitated sign, in the house of an enemy, retrograde, or afflicted by malefic planets [19] bestows misfortune upon the traveler; however, if Venus is situated in its own Navamsha, it bestows victory, even if it is in its own desired Ascendant, in the eighth house from the Ascendant, or in the sixth house from the enemy's sign [20]. Such a Venus destroys the desires of the one setting out on a journey, whereas if it is situated in its own sign's Navamsha, it brings victory. [In the case of] its own desired Ascendant or from the Ascendant...

If Venus is situated in the eighth house from the natal sign (rāśi) or the sixth house from the sign of an enemy [of the ascendant lord], [the traveler will die]. || 20 || Or if it is in the sign of the lord of those [two], there is no doubt that death will come to the traveler. If the lord of the birth [ascendant] and the lord of the eighth house from the birth ascendant are situated in a mutual state of friendship, || 21 || or if the signs of enemies are in the house of the lord of the [natal] ascendant, then the death of the one setting out on a journey occurs; provided that both the lord of the birth ascendant and the lord of the eighth house from the birth ascendant are mutually friendly. || 21 ||

21. || 4A (234) In the Nāradasaṃhitā, it is said that defects [arising] from the eighth lunar mansion from the birth asterism are destroyed by one's own nature. Even a dual-natured [sign] causes destruction if it is conjoined with or aspected by a malefic planet. 22. If [malefics] are situated in the birth ascendant as well as in the eighth house, all defects are destroyed by their very nature; furthermore, a malefic planet, when conjoined with or aspected by another malefic planet, brings about the failure of the undertaking. 22.

If a planet is aspected by benefics in a vehicle, or is itself conjoined with or aspected by benefics, it is auspicious for the collection of grass and wood within five asterisms beginning from Svāti and Revatī. However, one should not undertake travel toward the southern direction, nor the making of a bed, nor the protection of a house [during such times]. || 23 ||

At the time of departure, if that malefic planet is not aspected by benefic planets, it is inauspicious; however, if it is conjoined with or aspected by benefic planets, it should be known as auspicious. Furthermore, the five constellations beginning from the latter half of Dhaniṣṭhā up to Revatī are known as the *pañcaka*.

One should not collect grass, wood, and the like in the hut, nor should one travel toward the southern direction; one should not cultivate a garden, nor should one thatch the house. (23) If the Moon is in the ascendant at birth, or if it is in the eastern ascendant (dig-lagna), or even if it is in the [eastern] ascendant while the Sun is in any of the four auspicious angles (kendras), there shall be the destruction of enemies. (24)

If the birth ascendant is joined by benefic planets, or if one travels during that ascendant or during the "directional" ascendant (*diglagna*), or when benefics occupy all four *kendras*, the destruction of enemies occurs for the traveler. (24) [Note: *Śīrṣodaya* refers to those signs where the head rises first, namely the 5th, 6th, 7th, and 8th houses.]

25. If the ascendant (lagna) is one that rises by its head (śīrṣodaya), or if it is the ascendant of a cardinal direction (digdvāra), or if the ascendant is the sign of a benefic planet, then the traveler obtains auspicious results. 26. Likewise, if the ascendant is a head-rising sign (śīrṣodaya) and is conjoined with a benefic, and the traveler is situated in the sign occupied by either of those two [planets], there shall be the destruction of his enemies.

If the ascendant at the time of departure is the same as the ascendant at birth, or if the natal ascendant is occupied by or conjoined with auspicious planets, and one travels when that very sign is the ascendant, then the enemy shall be destroyed. (26) If the ascendant at the time of departure is the ascendant at birth, or if the sign of death (the eighth house from birth) is the ascendant, then in whichever sign these two coincide, if one travels in that sign, the destruction of the enemy will occur. (27)

If one travels when the ascendant is the eighth sign from the enemy's birth-ascendant (janmalagna) or birth-sign (janmarāśi), the enemy of the traveler shall be destroyed. (27) Traveling in a retrograde planet, in Pisces as the ascendant, or even in a Pisces navāṃśa, is censurable in all journeys; likewise, Aquarius as the ascendant and Aquarius as the navāṃśa [are censurable]. (28) Traveling in Pisces as the ascendant, as well as in a Pisces navāṃśa, is inauspicious.

Furthermore, undertaking a journey in any direction while Aquarius is the ascendant or in the Aquarius Navāṃśa is inauspicious. || 28 || When the rising sign is a water-sign, or when it is in a water-navāṃśa, [the following] bring about auspiciousness: the first house (mūrti), the treasury (kośa), the archer (dhānuṣka), the vehicle (vāhana), that which is called mantras (mantrasaṃjñaka), || 29 || the path of enemies (śatrumārga), as well as longevity (āyu), fortune (bhāgya), and that designated as business (vyāpāra); gain (prāpti) and loss (aprāpti)—these indeed are the twelve houses from the ascendant (udaya). || 30 || (236) Nāradasaṃhitā.

55. Undertaking activities related to aquatic creatures when the ascendant (lagna) and the navāṃśaka are of the watery sign (jalacara) is auspicious. Now, the designations of the houses (sthānasaṃjñā) are stated: Body (mūrti) 1, Treasure (kośa) 2, Archer (dhānuṣka) 3, Vehicle (vāhana) 4, Mantra (mantra) 5, Enemy (śatru) 6, Path (mārga) 7, Longevity (āyu) 8, Fortune (bhāgya) 9, Business (vyāpāra) 10, Gain (prāpti) 11, and Expenditure (vyaya) 12; these are the names of the twelve houses beginning with the first. || 29 || 30 || The Sun and Mars destroy everything from a house except for the house of longevity (āyu). || [31] ||

Malefic planets do not destroy houses other than the eighth; O gentle ones, they cause destruction only for the enemy [the eighth house]. (33) Malefic planets in the eleventh house destroy houses other than their own, while the Sun and Mars are not inauspicious in the sixth house, and auspicious planets are benefic in all houses except the sixth. (31) Even when Venus is in its setting or is full, and even when the Moon is in its sign of death (Mūrti), traveling toward the southern direction on a Riktā tithi is unfavorable for those traveling in any direction. (32)

Venus in the seventh house is inauspicious, and the Moon, even when powerful, is inauspicious in the ascendant and the eighth house; it is especially inauspicious in the southern direction, while the Riktā tithis are forbidden in all directions. || 32 || This Abhijit-kṣaṇa yoga bestows the attainment of desired results; it grants its fruit even on a day devoid of purity in the five limbs (pañcāṅga). || 33 ||

In such a Muhūrta, the Abhijit Kṣaṇayoga occurs; by traveling during that time, one's desires are fulfilled. Even on a day lacking the purity of the five limbs (pañcāṅga-śuddhi), this yoga bestows complete auspiciousness. || 33 || I shall now describe various other yogas for journeys from here and there. For a king, the attainment of results comes from the yoga and the ascendant (lagna); for a Brāhmaṇa, it comes from the lunar mansion (dhiṣṇya). || 34 || Bhāṣāṭīkā-saṃhitā, Chapter 33.

(217) Since a journey undertaken when there is an auspicious planetary conjunction (*grahayoga*) yields various kinds of results, those conjunctions are now described. For kings, success is achieved through the *yoga-lagna*; for Brahmins, success is achieved by traveling under an auspicious lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*). || 34 || For others, it is determined from the physical form (*mūrti*); for thieves, from their power (*śakti*) and omens (*śakuna*). A conjunction with Venus (*śukra*) or Jupiter (*sūri*) occurring in any one of the angles (*kendras*) or trines (*trikoṇas*) [is favorable]. || 35 ||

With two [planets] there is *atiyoga*, and with three there is *adhikayoga*. For those desiring to travel, success comes through *yoga*; victory comes through *atiyoga*. (36) Furthermore, for others such as Vaiśyas and so forth, [success] is achieved from the ascendant (*lagna*) as well as from an auspicious moment (*muhūrta*). When a thief departs, success occurs only when there is an auspicious omen (*śakuna*).

If Venus alone or Jupiter alone is situated in a quadrant (kendram) or a trine (trikoṇa), it constitutes an excellent yoga; if both are present, it is an *atiyoga*; and if there is an excellent yoga involving three planets, it is an *adhiyoga*. If one sets out during an excellent yoga, one remains safe and well; in an *atiyoga*, victory is achieved. || 35 || 36 || In an *atiyoga* and an *adhiyoga*, there is safety, victory, and prosperity. || 37 ||

If one proceeds on a military expedition (adhiyoga), there will be security, victory, and prosperity. (37) When the Moon, Saturn, and the Sun are situated in the tenth, sixth, or eighth house from the ascendant, the royal fortune of victory is assured for the king who has gone to battle. (38) That is to say, if the Moon, Saturn, and the Sun occupy the tenth, sixth, or eighth house from the ascendant at the time of departure, the king who has entered the fray attains the goddess of victory. (38)

(238) Nāradasaṃhitā 1. Now, he describes another yoga called Citrapadā: "If Mercury is in the second house, the Sun is in the third house, and Venus is in the ascendant, then all [the enemies] shall perish like locusts before the king who sets out on his expedition. (39) Now, he explains another yoga in the Citrapadā meter: If Mercury is situated in the house of wealth (the second house), the Sun is in the third house, and Venus is in the ascendant, then all [the enemy forces] will be destroyed like locusts in the presence of the king who is about to march forth. (39)

When Jupiter is situated in the ascendant and other planets are in the second or eleventh houses, the enemy army of the departing king is sent to the abode of Yama (the Lord of Death). When Venus is in the ascendant, the Sun is in the eleventh house, and the Moon is in the third house, [the same result follows].

If the benefic planets occupy the trines and angles while the malefic planets are situated in the third, sixth, and eleventh houses, the king who sets out on his journey destroys the enemy's army just as Lord Keśava destroyed Pūtanā. (41) If the benefics are placed in the trines and angles and the malefics are in the third, sixth, and eleventh houses...

When Jupiter, the Sun, the Moon, and the Ascendant occupy the fifth, ninth, and eighth houses respectively, the fortune of the enemy of the king who sets out on his journey perishes like an unfaithful woman. (42) If Jupiter, the Sun, the Moon, and the Ascendant should go to the fifth, ninth, and eighth houses [respectively] when one departs... (219)

In his presence, even a small measure of friendship is not stable against the army of enemies. (43) O Bṛhaspati, when Jupiter, the Sun, and the Moon are situated respectively in the sixth and seventh houses from the ascendant, the army of the departing king is destroyed in such a manner that even a slight friendship quickly perishes. (43) If Jupiter is in its exaltation in the ascendant and the Moon is in the eleventh house...

If Saturn and Mars are strong and auspicious in the third, sixth, or eleventh houses, the enemy's land shall fall into the hands of that king during his expedition. (44) When Jupiter is situated in its exaltation sign and the Moon is in the eleventh house, and Saturn and Mars are in the third, sixth, or eleventh houses, and the benefic planets are powerful, then the departing king seizes the territory of his enemy. (44)

If Jupiter is in its exaltation in the ascendant and the Moon is in the eleventh house, the king who has gone forth destroys his enemies just as the wielder of the Pināka bow destroyed Tripura. (45) When Venus is in the ascendant at its maximum altitude and Jupiter is situated in the eleventh house from the ascendant, the king who has gone forth destroys his enemies just as Kumāra destroyed Tāraka.

46. When Venus is situated in the ascendant at 5°, 6°, 7°, 8°, or 11° and Jupiter occupies the eleventh house, the departing king destroys his enemy in such a manner as Svāmikārtika destroyed Tārakāsura. 46. 47. When Jupiter is in the ascendant and Venus is in a quadrant (kendram) or a trine (trikoṇam), the king who has set out conquers his enemies, just as one [heals] a wound with black ointment (*kṛṣṇavatī*). 47.

If Jupiter is in the ascendant and Venus is in a quadrant or a trine (the ninth or fifth house), the king who goes forth shall destroy his enemy just as a wound is destroyed in the Kṛṣṇavatī river. 47. When Mercury is in the ascendant and a benefic is in a quadrant or in an Upakula asterism, kings plunder their enemies like the rays of the sun scorching [the earth] in summer. 48.

If Mercury is in the ascendant, other benefic planets are in the quadrants, and Jupiter is in the fourth house, then the king who goes forth destroys his enemies just as the rays of the sun destroy the lotus ponds. 48. When a benefic planet is situated in a trine or a quadrant, and the Moon or the Sun is in the eleventh house, the king who has gone forth destroys his enemies just as the sun destroys the darkness. 49.

If there are auspicious planets in the ninth, fifth, or a quadrant house, and the Moon or the Sun is in the eleventh house, then the departing king destroys his enemies just as the sun destroys darkness. (49) When the Moon is in its own sign, is a benefic, and is situated in a trine or the eleventh house, the king who has gone forth destroys his enemies like fire consumes a heap of cotton. (60)

When the benefic planets are in their own signs and the Moon is in a trine or the eleventh house, the king who goes forth destroys his enemies just as fire consumes a heap of cotton. (50) [Commentary in Bhāṣā-Ṭīkā, Chapter 33, Verse 221]

When the Moon is in the tenth house, Jupiter is in a quadrant, and Venus has gone to the seventh house, the king who sets out destroys all his enemies, just as the five-syllabled mantra (Pañcākṣarī) destroys all sins. || 51 || When Venus is in its Vargottama division and is situated alone in the ascendant...

Just as a king who has gone forth destroys his enemies, so too does one destroy their foes when Venus is in the eleventh house in the ascendant; just as sins are destroyed by the remembrance of Hari. (92) When the Moon is situated in a quadrant or a trine, and has entered its *vargottama* division, one destroys enemies of the same lineage, just as Indra (the breaker of mountains) destroys the mountains. (63)

If a benefic planet is situated in a quadrant (kendram) or a trine (trikoṇam), and the Moon is in its exaltation, then the king who sets out destroys his enemies along with their families, just as Indra destroyed the mountains. || 53 || When Jupiter is in a friendly sign and situated in a quadrant or a trine, the king who goes forth slays his enemies, just as Garuḍa slays a serpent. || 54 ||

When Jupiter has entered the house of a friend and is situated in a quadrant (*kendram*), or when Venus is in a trine (*trikoṇam*), the king who goes forth shall destroy his enemies just as Garuda destroys the serpents. || 54 || When a benefic planet is situated in a quadrant or a trine and is in its *vargottama* division, the king who goes forth destroys his enemies just as the Bhagirathi destroys the wicked. || 44 || [From] the Anāradasaṃhitā. || 222 ||

When a benefic planet is situated in a quadrant (kendram), a trine (trikoṇam), or in its exaltation sign, the king who goes forth shall destroy his enemies just as the Gaṅgā destroys sins. || 55 || These kings go forth to conquer their foes; in that state, there are two auspicious planetary configurations (yogas) for the king. The fire of his wrath is extinguished by the teardrops from the eyes of his enemies' wives. || 66 ||

These two lunar mansions (nakṣatras) are named after kings; for those who travel under them, the fire of the king's wrath is extinguished by the falling tears of the wives of his enemies. || 56 || The moon wanes when its power is diminished, yet it becomes full through that very loss of luster. For those traveling under these [mansions], there is victory; in all matters, diplomacy is superior to valor. || 47 ||

The full moon is strength-giving, while the waning moon is destructive. In those [lunar] days when the moon is strong, for a king who travels, there is victory, success in meetings, and an increase in all forms of prowess. (57) It is traditionally held that the primary source of success arises from omens, auspicious signs, and the like; therefore, the mental disposition is the cause of the fruit, which results in birth and longevity. (98)

The rising of fortune through astrological signs (nimita), auspicious moments (muhūrta), omens (śakuna), and so forth, is not the primary factor; rather, the cause of success in all auspicious undertakings such as journeys is the state of mental cheerfulness. || 58 || A wise mortal should never undertake a journey during festivals, the sacred thread ceremony (upanayana), a wedding, the impurity caused by a corpse, or during an eclipse. || 49 ||

During festivals, the thread-ceremony (*upanayana*), weddings, the birth of a child (*sūtaka*), or during an eclipse, a wise person should not undertake a journey. (59) [In the commentary on verse 59: During a fight between a buffalo and a ram, during a domestic quarrel, when clothing or other items have fallen, in a fit of anger, upon hearing harsh words, or while sneezing, one should not go out. (60)

One should not travel at times when there is a battle between dogs and donkeys, during a conflict among women, when clothes and such items fall off, when anger arises, when harsh words are spoken, or when one sneezes. || 60 || Having eaten ghee-rice, sesame-cake, fish, and ghee-porridge in the order starting from the east, the king proceeds toward the city of victory. || 61 ||

If one consumes these four items—clarified butter with rice, sesame paste, fish with rice, and milk pudding—with clarified butter—in sequence while departing for a royal expedition toward the eastern and other directions, one shall destroy the enemies. || 61 || Having consumed scum of boiled rice, parched rice flour, sour gruel, milk, curd, hair-shaving water, and sesame-rice, on Sundays and the other days respectively, || 62 ||

62. It is auspicious to travel after consuming, in order according to the days of the week starting with Sunday, these items: *śikharaṇī* (1), milk (2), fermented rice-water (*kāñjī*) (3), boiled milk (4), curd (5), raw milk (6), and sesame-rice (*tilaudana*) (7). 63. Kulmāṣa (half-cooked grain), sesame-rice, curd, honey, ghee, milk, venison, its essence (venison broth), milk-porridge (*pāyasa*), *āṣaka* (a type of bird), and venison; 64. Rabbit meat, sixty-day rice (*ṣaṣṭikya*), millet (*priyaṅgu*), and unleavened cakes (*apūpa*).

The Citrāṇḍaja fruit, tortoise, Sārī bird, iguana, and porcupine; sacrificial food (haviṣya), rice mixed with sesame (kṛsarānna), mung-bean rice (mudgānna), barley flour, fish, variegated rice, and rice with curd—these are the offerings for the Dastras in successive order. (224) *Nāradasaṃhitā* and *Aurabālī*: 1. Sesame paste, 2. sesame paste, 3. curd, 4. honey, 5. ghee, 6. milk, 7. deer meat, 8. deer blood, 9. milk pudding (*khīra*).

9. Meat of the *papaiyā* bird; 10. Deer; 11. Meat of the boar; 12. *Sāṃṭhī* rice; 13. *Mālakāṅganī*; 14. *Pūḍe*; 15. Meat of birds produced from various grains; 16. Fruits; 17. Meat of the tortoise; 18. Meat of the *sārika* bird; 19. Meat of the *gohaka*; 20. Meat of the *sehaka*; 21. *Haviṣyānna*; 22. *Khicḍī*; 23. Mung beans; 24. Flour of barley; 25. Fish-dish; 26. Variegated food (*vicitrānna*); 27. Curd-rice (*dadhibhāta*). Having consumed these items, [one attains] Aśvinī and the others...

It is auspicious to undertake a journey during the twenty-eight lunar mansions (nakṣatras) in their respective order. || 63 || 64 || 65 || Having eaten, a king who desires victory should conquer his enemies; he should worship the fire with sesame seeds and honor the Lord of the Quarter (Dikpāla). || 66 ||

In this manner, a king who desires victory and sets out on a journey after consuming these items under the asterisms of Aśvinī and the others conquers his enemies. At the time of departure, having offered oblations of sesame seeds into the fire, he should worship the presiding deity of the direction toward which he intends to travel. (66) Having bowed to the gods and the Brahmins, the king should address them with blessings; then, having performed the "Dāruṇa" oblation according to its mantra, he should set forth. (67)

Having thus offered salutations to the deities and received their blessings as prescribed by the Brāhmaṇas, and having performed the Homa sacrifice excellently with the mantras of the Lords of the Directions (Digeśvaras), one should depart. || 67 || In this manner, with devotion, one should worship the Lord of the Direction (Digeśvara) using garments, colors, perfumes, and other offerings. [One should meditate on] Indra, resplendent together with Śacī, mounted upon his elephant Airāvata. || 68 || *Bhāṣāṭīkā*, Chapter 33.

(225) One should offer garments of the colors of the lords of the directions with devotion, and perform worship using perfumes and other offerings. One should worship Indra, who is seated upon the elephant Airāvata and accompanied by Indrāṇī. || 68 || [One should worship him] as the wielder of the thunderbolt, golden-hued, adorned with divine ornaments, possessing seven hands, seven tongues, six eyes, and having a ram for his vehicle. || 69 ||
