One should meditate upon Indra, who holds a vajra in his hand, possesses a complexion like gold, and is adorned with divine ornaments; he has seven hands, seven tongues, six eyes, and rides upon a ram. (69) One should worship Agni, who is dear to Svāhā, red in color, and who bears the sacrificial ladles *sruk* and *sruva* as weapons. (70) [He is] one who makes Svāhā beloved, red-hued, and the bearer of the *sruk* and *sruva* weapons. (70)

Yama, who has a staff as his weapon, red eyes, and a buffalo for his vehicle; Śyāmalā, who is accompanied by him, is red in color and faces upward; and the auspicious Nīla Nirṛti, who holds a sword and shield and has a human for his vehicle. (73)

One should meditate upon Dharmarāja in the southern direction as having a staff and weapons, red eyes, riding a buffalo, accompanied by his dark-complexioned messenger, facing upward, and auspicious; [and one should meditate upon Varuṇa] as blue-colored, holding a sword and a shield, and riding a human being. || 71 || [And one should meditate upon Kubera] as having upward-pointing hair, odd eyes, possessing a long neck, all-pervading, holding a noose of serpents, yellow-colored, and riding a crocodile. || 72 ||

15 (226) Nāradasaṃhitā: One should worship the powerful Nairṛta (Rākṣasa), who has a withered child held aloft, with distorted eyes and a long neck; he wears a garland of snakes, is yellow in color, and has a crocodile for his vehicle. // 72 // One should worship Varuṇa and Kālinātha, adorned with jewel ornaments, the very form of the life-breath of all living beings, possessing two arms and holding a staff in his hand. // 73 //

One should meditate upon Varuṇadeva, adorned with ornaments of jewels, O Kālinātha; he is the life-force of all living beings, two-armed, and holds a staff in his hand. (73) One should worship Vāyu, the lord of Añjanā, seated upon a black antelope, possessing two arms, holding a spear in his hand, and resembling gold in complexion. (74) One should worship Vāyu, the husband of Añjanā, mounted upon a black deer.

He was mounted upon a horse, holding a rosary and weapons in his hands, possessing two arms, and endowed with a luster like gold. (74) One should worship Kubera, the lord of Citralekhā, the leader of the Yakṣas and Gandharvas; likewise, the wielder of the Pināka bow, mounted upon a bull, the supreme husband of Gaurī. (75)

One should meditate upon Mahādeva as white-complexioned, bearing the moon upon his crest, and wearing a serpent as a sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*); likewise, worship should be performed when there is no journey, according to one's own requirements. (76) [This is the worship of the Lord of the Īśāna corner.]

It is indeed proper to perform worship at the time of departure; even if one does not intend to travel anywhere, one should nevertheless worship these guardians of the directions (dikpālas) in this manner according to the requirements of the task. || 76 || The departure for the mission should be made with an umbrella, a banner, horses, and unbroken grains (akṣata), proceeding from one's own place to the destination at a distance of two hundred bows (dhanus). || 77 ||

One should set out equipped with banners, umbrellas, horses, and unchanging vehicles; it is proper to depart from one's own home at a distance of two hundred *dhanus*, that is, eight hundred *hasta*s. (77) Having departed from his own home, a king or any other person should not stay in one place for forty, twelve, or seven days. (78)

Alternatively, setting out at a distance of forty bow-lengths or twelve bow-lengths, or setting out from one's own house to another house—this indeed constitutes "going. Having gone, the king should not stay in another house in one place for more than seven days; as for other people, [they should stay] for five nights, and beyond that, they should proceed to another auspicious moment (lagna). 78.

In the event of untimely lightning, thunder, or rain, the king [should not set out]. (79) One should not depart for seven nights during the three types of portents; however, on the journey, the cries of the owl, the crow, and the pigeon are auspicious. (89) (228) Nāradasaṃhitā.

Thus, when such portents as earthquakes and other threefold calamities occur, the king should not undertake a journey for three days. Furthermore, at the time of departure, the cries of the female jackal, the crow, and the female dove are auspicious. (80) The female cuckoo, the female owl, the female parrot, the female pig, and the *ralā* bird on the left side are auspicious; likewise, the monkey, the crow, the bear, the dog, and the *bhāsa* bird on the right side are auspicious. (81)

If the cuckoo, the chameleon, the *potakī* (the Durgā-bird), the sow, and the *khātī* bird come from the left side, they are auspicious. Furthermore, the monkey, the crow, the bear, the dog, and the *bhāsa* bird (*paṭabījanā*) are auspicious on the right side. (81) Quadrupeds other than the black antelope are auspicious when moving to the left; however, if one proceeds having avoided the black antelope, the lizard should not be observed [as a sign of danger]. (82)

If four-footed animals or birds move toward the left without a black cake (pūpa), it is auspicious; if they move toward the left without a black cake, it is auspicious. Seeing the thorn of any other kind [of bird] except for the black one is not auspicious. (82) The mention of a boar, a rabbit, a lizard, or snakes is auspicious; however, upon merely seeing them during a journey, all such omens are reversed in the case of entering [a city]. (83)

The utterance of these—*sūkara*, *śaśā*, *goha*, and *sāṃpa*—is auspicious; this is an omen for departure (*yātrā*). At the time of entry (*praveśa*), the omen should be understood as the opposite: the sight of these snakes and others is good, but their utterance is not. || 83 || Success in the journey occurs when a corpse is seen that is free from weeping; at the time of entry, the sight of a corpse accompanied by weeping shall be auspicious. || 84 || *Bhāṣāṭīkā-saṃhitā*, Chapter 33.

(129) If one sees a corpse that is free from weeping, there is success in the journey; however, seeing a corpse accompanied by weeping at the time of departure brings happiness upon entering [the destination]. || 84 || One should avoid [auspicious sights] such as those fallen, eunuchs, those with matted hair, the insane, those vomiting, those smeared with medicinal ointments and the like, wood, bones, charcoal, and fires of chaff. || 84 ||

Now, one who has fallen from his caste, one who is dull-witted, one who wears matted hair, one who is mute, while walking; the application of medicinal herbs, *māṅliśa* oil, and so forth; wood, bone, leather, charcoal, husks, and smoke [are inauspicious]. (85) With jaggery, cotton, salt, fat, oil, grass, and a snake; a barren woman, a diseased man, one who is one-eyed, one with disheveled hair, and one who is hungry. (86)

86. If an unfavorable *lagna* (ascendant) is seen at the time of departure, success does not arise. [However, the following are auspicious: a blazing fire, auspicious words, flowers, sugarcane, and groups of liquor; 87. all these, if they appear during the *lagna* at the time of going, do not result in the accomplishment of the task. Furthermore: a blazing fire, auspicious speech, flowers, sugarcane, wine, 87. fragrant flowers, unbroken rice (*akṣata*), an umbrella, a fly-whisk (*cāmara*), a palanquin, kings, edible auspicious fruits, an elephant, a horse, and a bull on the right side in battle; 88. [these are favorable].

Sandalwood paste, flowers, unbroken grains (akṣata), an umbrella, a palanquin, a *pinnasa* [a type of vessel], a royal insignia, edible foods, auspicious fruits, elephants, horses, a mirror, and a bull that has arrived; || 88 || Well-washed fish and meat, a garment, a white bull, a banner, a virtuous woman, a full water-jar, jewels, an ornamented cow, and a twice-born (brāhmaṇa); || 89 || (23) Nāradasaṃhitā.

Fish-meat, a washed garment, a white bull, a banner, a fortunate woman, a water-pitcher, jewels, ornaments, a cow, and a Brāhmaṇa (89). The sounds of the *bherī*, *mṛdaṅga*, *paṭṭaha*, conch, melodies, songs, and the auspicious chanting of the Vedas bring success to those who travel. (90) The sounds of the *bherī*, *mṛdaṅga*, *ḍhola*, conch, musical modes, songs, and the auspicious resonance of the Vedas—all these omens grant success to those setting out on a journey. (90)

If a traveler sees an inauspicious omen at the outset, he should remember his chosen deity and proceed; if a second inauspicious omen appears, he should perform worship of the Brahmins and return, and only then set out again. (91) Sneezing in all directions is not desired; a cow’s sneeze brings about death.

A sneeze made by a child, an elderly person, one who is ill, or one suffering from a cold is fruitless; likewise, a sneeze feigned as a pretense carries no fault. (92) Thus ends the thirty-third chapter, the Chapter on Travel (*Yātrādhyāya*), in the *Śrī Nāradīya Saṃhitā*. Sneezing in all directions is inauspicious, and a cow’s sneeze bestows death. However, there is no defect in the sneezing of children, the elderly, the sick, those with colds, or a sneeze taken under false pretenses. (92) Thus ends the thirty-third chapter, the Chapter on Travel, in the *Śrī Nāradīya Saṃhitā Bhāṣāṭīkā*.

At the outset, during the northern course of the sun (uttarāyaṇa), the entry into a new house should be performed; likewise, when a king returns from a military expedition, or at the entrance of the bride and groom [into the home], it should be done at such a time. (1) [Commentary in Bhāṣā]: When the sun is in its northern course, one should enter a new house; when a king returns from his journey and enters his residence, or at the entry of the bride and groom, that too should take place at an auspicious moment (muhūrta). (1)

Having performed the worship of Vāstu and the offering of oblations on the preceding day, it is auspicious to enter [the house] during the months of Māgha, Phālguna, Vaiśākha, or Jyeṣṭha. (2) The entry should be known as mediocre during the months of Caitra and Kārttika, provided it occurs under the following constellations: Dhaniṣṭhā, Puṣya, Revatī, Aśvinī, Śatabhiṣaj, Citrā, Anurādhā, and the fixed asterisms. (3)

Furthermore, entering [the house] during the months of Mārgaśīrṣa and Pauṣa is middling. One should enter under the asterisms of Dhaniṣṭhā, Puṣya, Revatī, Mṛgaśiras, Śatabhiṣaj, Citrā, Anurādhā, and under those known as the fixed (sthira) asterisms. (3) The entry is auspicious when Jupiter and Venus are visible, on days excluding Sunday and Saturday, and on lunar dates (tithis) excluding the Riktās and the new moon. (4)

It is auspicious to enter [the city] during the rising of Jupiter and Venus, excluding Tuesdays and Saturdays, and on days other than the Riktās and the new moon; such entry on other days is said to bestow welfare. || 4 || Whether by day or by night, entry is a source of well-being if it occurs when the Moon and stars possess strength, provided the previously mentioned [inauspicious] times are avoided. || 5 ||

Entering [the house] during the day or even at night is auspicious; however, one should avoid the previously mentioned inauspicious lunar days (*tithi*) and so forth, and instead observe the strength of the moon and the stars. || 5 || (232) *Nāradasaṃhitā*: When the ascendant is fixed (*sthiralagna*), in a fixed degree (*sthirāṃśa*), and when the eighth house (*naidhana*) is pure and conjoined with auspiciousness; when the benefic planets occupy the trines (*trikoṇa*), angles (*kendrakhatri*), or the eleventh house (*ekhyāya*), while the malefic planets are situated in the sixth house (*ari*). || 6 ||

If the ascendant is a fixed sign and the navāṃśa is also a fixed sign; if there are no planets in the eighth house; if the fifth and ninth houses, as well as the kendras, are occupied by auspicious planets; and if malefic planets are situated in the third, eleventh, and sixth houses—[then it is a favorable yoga]. || 6 || If the Moon is free from occupation by a planet in the sixth or eighth house from the ascendant; and if the natal star of the querent (or the querent himself) is in the ascendant, or in an upacaya house from either of those two [the ascendant or the Moon]—[then it is a favorable yoga]. || 7 ||

If the Moon is not situated in the sixth or eighth house from the ascendant (lagna), or if it is the natal ascendant of the performer, and the ascendant is at 3, 4, 10, or 11 signs from the natal ascendant, then one should enter. (7) Having placed the Sun to his left and being adorned with ornaments, the wise man should enter. (8) Thus ends the thirty-fourth chapter on Entry in the Śrī Nāradīya Saṃhitā. The wise man, having seen the Sun to his left and being joined with auspicious adornments, should enter the house. (8)
Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter, on the commencement [of planetary periods], in the *Śrīnāradīyasaṃhitā-bhāṣāṭīkā*. 34.

Now, the inquiry regarding rain. In an inquiry concerning rain, if the full moon is situated in a watery sign, or if the Moon is in the ascendant, or if the Moon is in a quadrant during the bright fortnight (śuklapakṣa) and aspected by benefic planets, there will be excessive rain. (1) In an inquiry regarding rain, if the full moon is in a watery sign, or if the Moon is in the ascendant, or if the Moon is in a quadrant during the bright fortnight and aspected by benefic planets, there will be excessive rain. (1) [Commentary in Bhāṣā-Ṭīkā, Chapter 35]

(233) O one of sinful vision, if the Moon is aspected by malefic planets during the rainy season, there will be little rain after a long time. When the Moon is endowed with all such qualities [of being aspected by benefics], the same applies to Venus; thus, one should declare all results, whether auspicious or inauspicious, in this manner. || 2 || If, during the rainy season, the Moon is situated seven signs away from Venus and is aspected by benefics, or if it is located in the seventh, a trine, or the seventh house from Saturn, it will produce rain. || 3 ||

During the rainy season, if Venus is in the seventh house from the Moon and is aspected by benefics, or if the Moon is in the ninth, fifth, or seventh house from Venus, there will be rain. (3) When Venus is near Mercury, it brings immediate rain; however, when the Sun is situated between those two, there is a destruction of rain. (4)

If Venus is near Mercury, it brings rain quickly; however, if the Sun enters between them, it destroys the rain. (4) When Venus is situated in the five asterisms beginning with Maghā, and subsequently in the three beginning with Svātī, it causes heavy rainfall; in the opposite case, it does not rain. (4)

If Venus is situated in the five constellations beginning with Maghā—the three *Pūrvās* (Pūrvaphalgunī, Pūrvāṣāḍhā, and Pūrvabhādrapadā)—or in the three constellations beginning with Svātī, it brings rain; if the opposite occurs, it does not rain. (5) If the planets are positioned near the Sun either in front of it or behind it, they then produce rain; however, this is not the case when they move in retrograde (*pratiloma*). (6) Venus produces rain when it follows its northern course (*saumya-mārga*), but not when it follows its southern course (*yāmya-ga*). Rain occurs at the times of its rising and setting, as well as when the Sun enters the constellation Ārdrā. (7)

(234) *Nāradasaṃhitā*: If the Moon, as the first among the planets, is near the Sun either behind or ahead of it, it brings rain; however, if it becomes retrograde and moves away from the Sun, it does not bring rain. If Venus is in northern motion (*uttaracārī*), it rains; if it is in southern motion (*dakṣiṇacārī*), it does not rain. Rain falls at the time of Venus's rising or setting. Now, the results for the day when the Sun enters the constellation Ārdrā are described.

6–8. If the entry into Ārdrā occurs during the day, there will be calamity and loss of crops; if it occurs at either of the two twilights (saṃdhyā), there will be an increase in crops; and if it occurs at night, all people will attain complete prosperity. If the entry into Ārdrā occurs during the day, there will be little rain and high prices for grain; however, if there is rain, there will be abundance of crops.

If there is rain during the rising of Ārdrā, there will undoubtedly be a great drought. (9) If there is even a little rain at the time of the moon’s entry into Ārdrā, food and other grains will become expensive; if there is no rain, there will be an increase in agriculture; and if the wind blows, there will be an infestation of locusts and the like. (9) If the Moon, Jupiter, Mercury, or Venus is in a quadrant (kendram), the drought perishes. When the Sun has entered the month of Āṣāḍha, it is surrounded by halos (pariveṣa) caused by clouds. (10)

If, at the time of the commencement of Ārdrā and the moment of the ascendant, the Moon, Jupiter, Mercury, and Venus are situated in the angles (kendras), then disturbances such as locusts and the like shall be destroyed. When the Sun enters the constellation Pūrvāṣāḍhā (during the Dhanu Saṃkrānti), if the Sun remains shrouded by clouds, [then rain falls]. || 10 || [From Bhāṣāṭīkā-saṃhitā, Adhyāya 35 (235): "Rain falls daily and visibly from the beginning of Ārdrā until the end of Mūla; likewise, there is rain in the constellation Revatī (Pauṣṇa). Therefore, it does not rain during the other constellations. || 11 ||

As long as the sun remains from the asterism Ārdrā up to Mūla, there is beautiful rain according to the season; however, if it rains while the sun is in Revatī, then from Revatī through the next ten asterisms, the sun does not cause rain. (11) If the lion [sign] has been pierced, how can there be rain? If the crab [sign] has not been pierced, how can there be rain? If the maiden [sign] has been pierced at its rising, then there will certainly be excellent rain. (12)

If there are clouds on the day of the Siṃha-saṃkrānti but no rain on the day of the Karka-saṃkrānti, the rainy season will not be favorable for the year. (12) Ahirbudhnya [Kṛttikā] brings abundance of the first crop, Revatī brings abundance of the subsequent crop, Bharaṇī brings abundance of all crops, and Aśvinī leads to the destruction of everything. (13)

If the sun is in Uttarābhādrapadā and the clouds remain pregnant [with rain], then there will be no harvest of early crops; if the pregnancy occurs in Revatī, it is called *parasasya*, meaning there will be no harvest of late crops. If the sun is in Aśvinī or Bharaṇī and the clouds nevertheless rain, then all the crops will be destroyed. (13) When Venus is visible while situated in the seventh house from Jupiter, there will be excessive and abundant rainfall during the monsoon season, provided Jupiter is devoid of strength. (16)

If Venus is situated in the seventh house from Jupiter, then even after it has rained during the rainy season, there will be excellent rainfall. (14) When a halo surrounds the nearby sun and moon, when lightning flashes, and when frogs are full of sound, then there will be drought. (15)
(236) Nāradasaṃhitā:

If a halo appears to the north near the sun or the moon, or if lightning flashes and crickets chirp in the northern direction, there will be no rain. ||15|| When frogs, situated upon their own dwellings, leap toward the west or fall from the south, then there will soon be no rain. ||16||

If a mongoose, sitting in its own place in either the western or southern direction, begins to leap about, one should know that rain will fall soon. (16) Cats scratching with their claws while remaining free from greed, and children intent on building dams, are indeed immediate causes for rain. (17)

Furthermore, if cats dig up the earth with their claws and remain there without greed, or if children build bridges and play upon them, one should know that rain will fall. (17) Ants with severed heads, copulation between two snakes, snakes climbing trees, and a reflection of the moon in water are indicators of rain. (18)

If an ant climbs upon another ant, or if an ant walks away carrying an egg; if a male snake and a female snake are seen staying in one place, or if a snake is seen climbing a tree; or if a second moon is seen facing the moon amidst the clouds—all these are to be known as signs that rain will fall. (18) If at the time of sunrise or sunset the sun or the moon appears discolored, or if there is an excessively strong wind with the color of honey, then there will be excessive rain. (19)

Thus ends the thirty-fifth chapter, on the signs of immediate rain, in the Śrī Nāradīya Saṃhitā. [Chapter 36 in the Bhāṣā-Ṭīkā]. (237) If, at the time of rising or setting, the color of the sun or moon appears foul (dull), or if it appears like the color of honey, or if there is an exceedingly strong wind, then there will be abundant rainfall. 19.

Thus ends the thirty-fifth chapter, on the signs of immediate rain, in the *Śrī-Nāradīya-saṃhitā-bhāṣā-ṭīkā*. One should divide this earth into nine parts within the nine limbs of the tortoise facing east, arranging the regional circles (*khaṇḍamaṇḍala*) in a clockwise direction. Antarvedī and Pāñcāla constitute its navel region. (1)

One should divide this earth into nine parts upon the nine limbs of the tortoise whose face is turned toward the east; that is, having constructed a tortoise-diagram facing east and divided it into nine sections, one should fashion the mandala in a clockwise direction. The navel-mandala of that tortoise—the central region—is the Antarvedi, meaning the middle ground between the Gaṅgā and Yamunā, as well as the Pāñcāla and Pañjāba regions; these constitute the navel-mandala of the tortoise-diagram. || 1 ||

The eastern regions, such as Māgadha, Lāṭa, and others, constitute his face; the regions known as Strīkaleya and Kirāta constitute the region of his arms. (2) The regions of Avanti, Draviḍa, and Bhilla constitute the region of his sides; the Gauḍas, Koṅkaṇas, Śālvas, Iṣṭas, and Puṇḍras likewise constitute the region of his sides. (3)

Avantī, the region of Ujjain, Drāviḍa, and the Bhilladeśa are its side-maṇḍalas (238); according to the Nāradasaṃhitā, [these] are the Pāṃśu-maṇḍalas. Gauḍa, Koṅkaṇa, Śālva-deśa, and Puṇḍra-deśa are also its side-maṇḍalas. || 3 || Sindhuka, Kāśī, Mahārāṣṭra, and Saurāṣṭra constitute the tail-maṇḍala; Pulinda, Bhīṣma, Yavana, and Gurjara constitute the foot-maṇḍala. || 4 ||

The regions of Sindhudeśa, Kāśī, Mahārāṣṭra, and Saurāṣṭra constitute its tail-region (puccha-maṇḍala). The regions of Pulinda, Bhīṣma, Yavana, and Gurjara constitute its foot-region (pāda-maṇḍala). || 4 || Kuru, Kaśmīra, Mādreyaka, and Matsya constitute its side-region (pārśva-maṇḍala). Khaśa, Aṅga, Vaṅga, Bāhlika, and Kāmboja constitute its hand-region (pāṇi-maṇḍala). || 9 ||

Kuru, Kāśmīra, Mātreya, Matsyadeśa, Ye-tisaka, Pārśvamaṇḍala, Khaśa, Aṅga, Yaṅgavāhīka, and Koja—these regions should be understood as the locations of his hands. One should place the asterisms beginning with Kṛttikā, three by three, in order upon the nine limbs starting from the navel; [the positions] are inauspicious when afflicted by malefic planets and auspicious when joined by benefics. Thus ends the thirty-sixth chapter, titled "The Division of the Kūrma," in the Śrī Nāradīya Saṃhitā.

In this manner, having divided that tortoise into nine sections, one should place three constellations each, beginning with Kṛttikā, in their respective order. First, placing three constellations upon the navel-maṇḍala in the center, one should then place them sequentially upon these nine limbs for regions such as Magadha, Lāṭa, and so forth. Furthermore, in whichever region the constellations of a particular limb have malefic planets, there will be inauspicious results for that region; whereas in whichever region the constellations have benefic planets remaining, [there will be auspicious results].

Know that such [planetary positions] bring auspicious results for that country. 6. Thus ends the thirty-sixth chapter, titled "The Division of the Land" (Kūrmavibhāga), in the Bhāṣā-Ṭīkā on the Śrī Nāradīya Saṃhitā. Chapter 37 (239): Now begins the chapter on Portents (Utpātādhyāya). Where the deities dance, fall, and blaze; where they suddenly weep, sing, perspire, and laugh; 1.

Where the deities dance, fall down, or their images rise up in water; where they weep, sometimes sing, or sweat from their forms; where they laugh; || 1 || where they vomit fire, smoke, oil, blood, milk, or water; where they stand with faces turned downward, or move from place to place. || 2 ||

From the mouths of the images, fire, incense, oil and other unguents, blood, milk, and water emerge; or the mouth turns downward, or the image is perceived in one place and then in another. 2. Indeed, such transformations are seen in the images, as well as the appearance of a city of Gandharvas by day and the sight of stars during the daytime. 3.

Such portents as these appear in the images of the deities; and in the sky, the appearance of a city of Gandharvas (celestial mansions), and the sight of stars during the day. || 3 || The falling of great meteors, the raining down of wood, grass, and blood, the appearance of Gandharva-cities, smoke in the quarters, and earthquakes by day and night. || 9 ||

The breaking of boats, rainfalls of wood, grass, and blood, the appearance of smoke in the sky and in all directions, and other such portents, as well as earthquakes occurring during the day and at night. (240) Nāradasaṃhitā: Sparks without fire, and blazing without fuel; a rainbow at night, frogs on the mountain peaks, and white crows. 4.

Fire blazed up without fuel, sparks flew from within the fire, rainbows appeared at night, and mongooses, white peaks, and crows were seen. (5) Sparks are seen issuing from the bodies of cows, elephants, horses, and camels; and creatures with two or three heads are born, or beings are produced from improper wombs. (6)

If fire is seen emerging from the bodies of cows, elephants, horses, or camels; or if a child with two or three heads is born, or if a child of one species is born from another—(6). If four suns appear simultaneously in the four directions, or if there is a gathering of jackals in the village, or if comets are observed—(7).

If a second sun is seen facing the [actual] sun, if rainbows appear simultaneously in all four directions, if many jackals gather near a village, or if stars with tails (comets) are seen—such portents as these are observed. || 7 || If crows are agitated at night and pigeons during the day, or if trees are seen flowering and bearing fruit out of season, then those [trees] should be cut down; thereafter, pacification rites should be performed by the wise. || 8 ||

Such great portents as these, occurring in abundance, bring about the destruction of one's dwelling. (9) Furthermore, if one hears the cries of crows at night, or hears the calls of pigeons during the day, or if flowers and fruits appear on trees out of season, one must not cut down such trees; for wise men have prescribed propitiatory rites (*śānti*) to ward off these calamities. (Bhāṣāṭīkā-saṃhitā, Chapter 37).

(241) One should perform [the rites], etc.; thus many great calamities that destroy [the results] have been described. 8. 9. Some bring about death, some cause fear from enemies; there is danger from the middle [of the animal], death from the eyes, ill-repute at the end, and [experiences of] pleasure and pain. 10.

Some portents bestow death; some portents cause fear from enemies or fear from indifferent persons; they indicate the death of livestock, decline, loss of fame, and sorrow amidst happiness. (10) Now, the fire-oblation (homa): One should predict the loss of sovereignty, the loss of food, and the fear of portents. [The rite should be performed] in a temple or in one's own home, in the northeast or even in the east. (11) These include the destruction of prosperity, the loss of food, and so forth—all such fears arising from portents should be understood.

In a temple of the deity or in one's own home, in the northeast corner or the east, one should prepare a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) endowed with the proper characteristics and provided with a girdle (mekhalā). Having established the fire there according to the procedure prescribed in the Gṛhya-sūtras, [one should proceed]. 11–12.

One should construct a most excellent fire-pit (*agni-kuṇḍa*) and fashion a girdle (*mekhalā*) around the pit. Then, according to the tradition of one's own lineage, one should perform the installation of the sacred fire (*agni-sthāpana*) through the auspicious rites prescribed for marriage and other ceremonies. (12) At the conclusion of the offering of clarified butter (*ājya-bhāga*), one should offer oblations separately one hundred and eight times with the mantras beginning with "yata indra bhayāmahe" and "svasti-dā ghora. (13) Likewise, one should offer sacrificial fuel sticks (*samidh*), clarified butter, cooked rice (*caru*), grains, and sesame seeds while reciting the *Vyāhṛtis*. One may perform a *koṭi-homa* (ten million oblations), half of that, or even a *lakṣa-homa* (one hundred thousand oblations). (14) 16 (242) Nārada-saṃhitā.

621. One should offer one hundred and eight oblations (*āhutis*) with the mantras known as *ghṛtasā* and *ājyabhāga*. Then, one should offer oblations with the mantras "yata indra bhayāmahe" and "svastidā," as well as the *aghora* mantra. One should offer oblations of fuel-sticks (*samidh*), clarified butter (*ghṛta*), sacrificial porridge (*caru*), rice, and sesame seeds using the *vyāhṛti* mantras. One may perform ten million (*koṭi*) oblations, or half of that, or one hundred thousand (*lakṣa*) oblations. (13–14) — 4. According to one's wealth, the calculation [of the number] may be less or more than that.

One should perform the fire-sacrifice (homa) for twenty-one nights, or for half a fortnight (fifteen days), or even for half a lunar month, according to one's own means. (14) One should perform the rite of homa for five nights or three nights; then one should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the preceptor who maintains a family. (16)

Those who perform the fire-sacrifice (homa) for five nights or three nights are fit; then, one should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) for the sake of the preceptor who has a family. 16. For the propitiation of Gaṇeśa, Kṣetrapāla, Arka, Durgā, Kṣoṇī, and the auxiliary deities, recitation (japa) should be performed; the remainder should be carried out as previously described. 17.

For the propitiation of Gaṇeśa, Kṣetrapāla, Sūrya, Durgā, the sixty-four Yoginīs, and the deities of the limbs (Aṅgadevatās), one should have the recitation of these mantras performed; other rites such as the Homa sacrifice should be carried out according to the previously mentioned procedure. || 17 || One should give sacrificial fees (Dakṣiṇā) to sixteen officiating priests (Ṛtviks) according to one's own capacity. || 18 || Thus ends the thirty-seventh chapter, titled "The Chapter on Portents," in the Śrī Nāradīya Saṃhitā. [In the Bhāṣā-Ṭīkā, Chapter 38].

(243) One should give sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) to the sixteen officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) according to one's own capacity. 18. Thus ends the thirty-seventh chapter, titled "Portents," in the Bhāṣā-ṭīkā commentary on the Śrī Nāradīya Saṃhitā. 37. "Portents in the world are of three kinds: celestial, terrestrial, and atmospheric. I shall correctly describe their names and the propitiatory rites (*śānti*) for each of them individually. 1.

In this world of *saṃsāra*, there are three types of portents (*utpāta*): those occurring in the three realms of heaven, earth, and sky. Their names and their pacification (*śānti*) are described separately. (1) If a man should see the mating of crows either by day or by night, that man meets with death or the destruction of his dwelling. (2)

If a man sees the mating of crows either by day or by night, that man’s death shall occur, or his position shall be destroyed. (2) He should then observe the vow known as Kākaghāta for one year, along with daily salutations with devotion to the ancestors, the gods, and the twice-born. (3) That person must perform the vow called Kākaghāta for as many days as there are days in a year, and he must offer obeisance every single day with devotion to the ancestors, the deities, and the brahmins. (3)

One who has conquered the senses, whose mind is pure, and who is devoted to truth and righteousness, should perform a rite of pacification (*śāntikarma*) in this manner to quell that defect. (4) (244) *Nāradasaṃhitā*: One should prepare a place for the fire-oblation (*homa*) in the northeast corner of the house; there, having established the sacrificial fire according to the procedure prescribed in one's own *Gṛhya-sūtra*, [the rite should be performed]. (4)

In the chosen spot, having prepared the fire-pit toward the northeast corner, one should establish the fire there according to the ritual prescribed in one's own Gṛhya-sūtra. (5) At the conclusion of the recitation of the mantras, one should perform a hundred and eight oblations (*homa*) with fuel-sticks (*samidh*) and clarified butter (*ājya*), using either the *Tryambaka* mantra or the *Mṛtyuñjaya* mantra for each individual mantra. (6) One should arrange the rite beginning and ending with the *japa* of rice and sesame seeds accompanied by the *Vyāhṛtis*. Then, the performer, being pure and adorned, should offer the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*). (7)

Then, with sacrificial fuel (samidh), clarified butter (ghṛta), sesame seeds (tila), and other grains, one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) according to the number of recitations (japa) using either the mantra "Tryambakaṃ yajāmahe" or the Mahāmṛtyuñjaya mantra—that is, the Tryambaka mantra together with the Vyāhṛtis beginning with "Bhūḥ Bhuvaḥ Svaḥ"—using rice and sesame seeds. At the conclusion of the oblation, the performer, the patron (yajamāna), adorned with sacred threads (pavitra), should offer the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti). || 6 || 7 ||

One should give a black, milch cow adorned with golden horns and silver hooves, decorated with garments and ornaments, and accompanied by twelve *niṣkas* [of gold] (equivalent to forty-eight *tolas*). Or else, one may give half of that, or half of that again.

One should determine the amount—whether less or more—according to one's wealth. (9) Alternatively, half of three [parts], or even a quarter of three, or even an eighth of three, whether gold or silver, should be given according to one's means. (9) [Commentary on Verse 10] One should give a cow to the preceptor who is learned in the Vedas and maintains a family; and one should give a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to distinguished Brāhmaṇas according to one's capacity. (10)

The reciter of the Vedas should give this cow as a gift for the sake of the family preceptor (ācārya), and he should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) according to his capacity to the most excellent Brāhmaṇas. Afterwards, he should feed the Brāhmaṇas preceded by the recitation of auspicious prayers (svastivācana). He who performs this correctly is liberated from that sin. Thus ends the thirty-eighth chapter, titled "The Characteristics of the Copulation of Crows," in the Śrī Nārīya Saṃhitā. 38.

Furthermore, one who properly performs the feeding of a Brāhmaṇa preceded by the recitation of auspicious verses (*svastivācana*) is freed from that fault—the fault of crow-mating and the like. || 11 || Thus ends the thirty-eighth chapter, titled "The Characteristics of Crow-Mating," in the commentary on the *Śrī Nāradīya Saṃhitā*. || 38 || Regarding the falling of crows, the preceding auspicious and inauspicious results have been stated: [If it falls] on the head, there is sovereignty; on the crest, the attainment of fortune; and on the crown, the increase of power. || 1 ||

The ancient teachers have described the results of a chameleon falling upon the body: if it falls on the head, there is the attainment of sovereignty and fortune; if it falls on the crown of the head, there is an increase in prosperity. (1) One should discern the auspiciousness or inauspiciousness resulting from the falling of a lizard or its emergence [from its hole], specifically according to each respective location. (2)

One should specifically understand the auspicious and inauspicious results for each respective location regarding clinging to the body, falling down, or climbing upon thorns. 2. (246) *Nāradasaṃhitā*: Victory is declared when [the lizard] is on the left arm, while great fear occurs on the right arm (*apasavya*). Likewise, there is gain of wealth on the right side of the belly. 3.

If [the bird] alights upon the right arm, there is the attainment of victory; on the left arm, great fear arises; and on the right side of the belly, there is the gain of wealth. (3) But on the left side of the belly, death has been declared by the ancient sages. On the right hand, there is the acquisition of friends; on the left hand, however, there is poverty. (4) On the left side of the belly, death; on the right hand, the gain of friends; and on the left hand, poverty—thus it was said by the scholars of old. (4)

If it falls on the left side of the abdomen, the acquisition of a virtuous son is said to occur; on the left [side of the body], a great disease; on the right hip, great fame. (5) The sages who perceive the truth have declared that if it falls on the left hip, there is death. One should know it to be likewise for the knees; on the right foot, it brings auspiciousness. (6)

The sages who perceive the truth have declared death to occur upon the left hip; one should likewise know death to occur upon both knees, while auspicious results are to be known for the right foot. (6) The great seers have stated that movement [to another place] occurs upon the left foot; however, for women, the lizard itself [indicates this], and one should declare the results as being reversed. (7)

The great sages have stated that if it falls upon the left foot, there will be a journey; the fruit of the *kirila-kaṇṭaka* should be understood in this same manner. For women, however, this result is the reverse—that is, on whichever limb of a man an auspicious result has been declared, for a woman it becomes inauspicious in that very place. (7) Furthermore, the result [is determined] by the falling of the lizard (*saraṭa*) and its movement.

One should discern the auspiciousness in all the limbs and perform pacification (śānti) according to one's capacity wherever [the mark] appears. (8) Wherever it ascends upon the limbs, one should consider the fruit of that specific place; if it be an inauspicious fruit, one should cause pacification to be performed according to one's power. (8) In an auspicious location, there is the attainment of good fortune; in an inauspicious one, for the sake of pacifying defects. Its form should likewise be fashioned from gold in the likeness of Rudra. (9)

If it ascends to an auspicious position, there will be the attainment of auspicious results; however, if it ascends to an inauspicious position, one should perform a propitiatory rite (śānti). Having fashioned a golden image of the *tisra-kiraḷa-kaṇṭaka* and recognizing it as the form of Rudra, one should worship it. || 9 || One should then worship it with the *Mṛtyuñjaya* mantra using garments and other offerings. Having established the sacred fire there, one should offer oblations of sesame seeds and milk-porridge (*pāyasa*). || 10 ||

Having offered garments and other articles while reciting the Mṛtyuñjaya mantra, one should perform worship; having established the sacred fire, one should perform oblations (homa) with sesame seeds and milk-rice. || 10 || There, the preceptor should perform the consecration (abhiṣecana) with hymns dedicated to Varuṇa; having performed the inspection of the clarified butter (ājya), he should feed the Brāhmaṇas according to his capacity. || 11 ||

The preceptor shall perform the consecration there with mantras dedicated to the deity Varuṇa; the patron, having looked at his reflection in clarified butter (offering his shadow), shall feed the Brāhmaṇas according to his capacity. (11) (248) Nāradasaṃhitā: For the propitiation of Gaṇeśa, Kṣetrapāla, Arka, Durgā, the Earth, and the limb-deities, the recitation [of their mantras] should be performed; the remainder should be carried out as previously described. (12)

For the sake of pleasing Gaṇeśa, Kṣetrapāla, Sūrya, Durgā, the sixty-four Yoginīs, and the deities of the limbs (Aṅgadevatās), one should perform the recitation (japa) of their respective mantras; all other rites should be performed as previously described. || 12 || One should give sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) to sixteen officiating priests (ṛtvij) according to one's own capacity. || 13 || Thus ends the thirty-ninth chapter, titled "The Rite for Peace in Auspicious Places such as Pallīsaras," in the Śrī Nāradīya Saṃhitā. || 39 ||

One should give sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) to the sixteen officiating priests according to one's capacity. 13. Thus ends the thirty-ninth chapter, titled "The Rite for Averting Evil from the Pallī and Sarṭā," in the Bhāṣā-Ṭīkā on the Śrī Nāradīya Saṃhitā. If a pigeon alights upon someone’s house or enters it, that person will suffer loss of position or a succession of misfortunes. 1.

If a pigeon (the bird of prey) enters a house or perches upon it, there will be loss of that place or some form of suffering. (1) In the house of the wealthy, this is for ill omen, whereas for the poor, it is auspicious. Its pacification should be performed through the rites of recitation (japa) and fire-oblation (homa). (2)

Entering the houses of wealthy men yields inauspicious results, whereas entering the houses of poor men or empty houses should be known to yield auspicious results; its pacification should be performed through the rites of *japa* and *homa*.
2. *Bhāṣāṭīkā-saṃhitā*, Chapter 40. (249)

There, one should select sixteen, twelve, or eight Brāhmaṇas who are devoted to the performance of Śrauta and Smārta rites, preceded by the recitation of the Svasti-vācana. (3) The recitation of the five Ṛgvedic verses beginning with "devāḥ kapota" should be performed. Having carefully prepared the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) according to the procedure prescribed in one's own Gṛhya-sūtra, (4)

One should perform the recitation (*japa*) using the five verses beginning with "devāḥ kapota," and have a fire-pit (*agnikuṇḍa*) constructed according to the specific branch (*śākhā*) of one's own Veda. (4) One should establish the fire in the northeast corner and offer one hundred and eight oblations (*āhuti*) into the mouth of the fire at the conclusion of each [verse], using sacrificial wood (*samidh*), clarified butter (*ājya*), and cooked rice (*anna*), preceded by the syllable *Oṃ*. (5)

One should offer sesame seeds with the three *tryambaka* mantras beginning with "yata indra bhayāmahe," as well as with the *vyāhṛtis*. (6) Then, the performer himself should devoutly perform the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*). He should give sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) to the Brahmins and then recite prayers for the pacification of faults. (7)

Then the sacrificer himself should perform the *pūrṇāhuti* with devotion and give the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to the Brāhmaṇa; by doing so, the pacification of that fault occurs. (7) Afterwards, he should feed the Brāhmaṇas and then eat himself along with his kinsmen. He who performs this with devotion is liberated from that fault. (8) 1 1 6 (250) Nāradasaṃhitā.

Furthermore, after feeding the Brāhmaṇas, you yourself should eat along with your kinsmen; he who does this with devotion is liberated from those three defects. (8) The same [rites for pacifying] should be performed for the cries of the Piṅgalā (the woodpecker), as well as for the Madhu and Vālmīka birds. In a house full of auspiciousness there is loss, while in an empty house there is auspiciousness. (9) In the case of the Piṅgalā’s (the woodpecker’s) calling, as well as in the calling of the Madhu and Vālmīka birds, one should likewise perform the rites for pacification.

If its recitation occurs in a place already full of auspiciousness, there will be harm; however, if it is uttered in an empty space, the result is auspicious. (9) In the case of ramparts, city gates, temples, and the like, as well as in streets, the fruit belongs to the village headman; and at the boundary, it belongs to the lord of the boundary. (10)

If [the bird] cries upon a threshing floor, a city wall, a gate, a temple, a royal palace, or a street, that result accrues to the lord of the village; if it cries upon a boundary, the result accrues to the owner of that boundary. (10) All rites for pacification should be performed according to the sequence previously described. (11) Thus ends the fortieth chapter, titled "The Pacification of Doves, Pigeons, and the Like," in the Śrī Nāradīya Saṃhitā. (40)

In accordance with the previously mentioned sequence, one should perform the complete rites for pacification (*śānti*) regarding the utterances of these woodpeckers and other such birds. 11. Thus ends the fortieth chapter, titled "The Pacification of Woodpeckers, Piṅgalas, and Others," in the Bhāṣā Commentary on the Śrī Nāradīya Saṃhitā. 40.

Indeed, all portents that indicate auspiciousness are inaccessible to ordinary people; nevertheless, a great portent that causes immediate results and produces sudden looseness [of structure] is significant. (1) Commentary on the Bhāṣā-Ṭīkā, Chapter 4, Verse 1 (251): Complete portents indicating auspiciousness are difficult for humans to encounter. However, a portent such as "śithilījanana"—meaning the sudden loosening and subsequent falling or flying up of an object—produces great results immediately. (1)

If this aforementioned portent occurs in a village, on a bridge, or in a temple, its fruit belongs to the village headman; if it occurs on a boundary, it belongs to the lord of that boundary. (2) In the case of a loosening [of the earth], there is loss in all places and in all directions.

To pacify those defects, one should perform a propitiatory rite (śāntikarma). || 3 || In every location and in all directions, wherever there is the portent of "loosening" (the sudden deformation or slackening of the form of any object), harm occurs; to neutralize that defect, a śānti should be performed. || 3 || Having fashioned an image of Death out of gold according to one's means, [depicting him] as red-colored, holding a skin and a staff, and mounted upon a buffalo. || 4 ||

One should have an image of Death fashioned out of gold according to one’s means; it should be red in color, holding a staff and an *ala* [lotus], and mounted upon a buffalo—such an image should be made. (4) Having wrapped it in new cloth, one should worship it upon rice with its specific *liṅga-mantra*, offering oblations (*naivedya*) according to the prescribed rite. (9) [Nāradasaṃhitā, 252]

Having wrapped the image of Tisra Mūrtika in a new cloth and placed it upon rice, one should perform its worship; reciting the mantra of that Dharmarāja, one should offer the *naivedya* according to the prescribed ritual. (5) To the northeast of that [image], one should offer water from a full pitcher wrapped in a red cloth and provided with the five barks and sprouts, while reciting the mantras. (6)

Having placed a water-filled pitcher in the northeast corner, one should cover it with a red cloth. Adorned with the five sprouts (*pañcapallava*), the five barks (*pañcavalkala*), mango wood, and so forth, one should pour water into that pitcher while reciting mantras. (6) One should establish the fire in the east according to the procedure prescribed in one's own *Gṛhya-sūtra*. One should perform one hundred and eight oblations for each [deity] using the *Aghora* mantra alone. (7)

According to the tradition of one's own lineage, one should establish the fire in the eastern direction and perform one hundred and eight (108) oblations with the Aghora mantra. (7) With the mantra, one should offer sacrificial fuel, clarified butter, and cooked rice; the remainder of the ritual should be performed as previously described. To ward off all defects, one should give the image to a brahmin. (8)

One should perform the *homa* with sacrificial fuel (*samidh*), clarified butter (*ghṛta*), sesame seeds (*tila*), and other such foods; all other rites should be performed as previously described. To ensure that all defects are completely eradicated, one should give that golden image to a Brāhmaṇa. (8) Having sprinkled that place with water from a sacred ford (*tīrtha*) while reciting the water-mantra (*jalamantreṇa*), he who performs this correctly is liberated from the defect. (9)

Thus ends the forty-first chapter, titled "The Pacification of the Birth of a Lame Child," in the Śrī Nāradīya Saṃhitā. **Chapter 42 (253): The Varuṇa Mantra** Having recited the Varuṇa mantra, one should sprinkle that place where the portentous event occurred with water from holy sites such as the Gaṅgā and others. The person who performs this act in this manner is liberated from the defect caused by the portent. 9.

Thus ends the forty-first chapter, titled "The Propitiatory Rite for the Birth of a Child with a Limp Limb," in the Śrī Nāradīya Saṃhitā Māṣāṭīkā. [The results of the planets] beginning from the East are: prosperity, loss of kinsmen, loss of wealth, great fame, gain of relatives, loss of sons, anxiety regarding one's wife, and a severe illness. [If these afflict] Indra-lupta (Alopecia) on the head, [one should perform the rite]. By means of five types of leaves, the five nectars (pañcāmṛta), and the water of fruits, and by anointing with mantras consecrated by sacred formulas, one is released from the defect caused by bathing.

In the same way, even when there is a fire, or when the head is defiled by something in its center; when there is a fracture of a tooth, or when bitten by a crow, or even when a lizard falls upon it—one should, after having caused the Brahmins to recite benedictions, feed them while remaining pure.

If *indralupta* (alopecia) occurs on someone’s head—that is, if hair falls out from any spot on the head—one should assign the directions starting with the East and understand the following results for those directions: 1. acquisition of wealth, 2. loss of fire (or digestion), 3. destruction of kinsmen, 4. loss of property, 5. great fame, 6. gain of relatives, 7. loss of sons, 8. anxiety regarding women, and 9. a severe illness. These are the results for the directions beginning with the East; the ninth result should be understood as pertaining to the central part of the head. In that regard, this...

In rites for pacification (*śāntika*), one should have the image bathed with the five barks (*pañcavalkala*), the five sprouts (*pañcapallava*), the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*), and fruit-water, while reciting the consecration mantras (*abhiṣeka-mantra*); then purification occurs. In the same manner, [purification] from fire-burning and other such causes occurs by means of [mantras] starting from the center of the head—(254)—Nāradasaṃhitā.

If [the ear] becomes infected, or if the teeth and so forth become jagged, or if it is struck by a crow's beak, or if a thorn from a *krirela* plant becomes lodged there, one should consider the auspicious or inauspicious results for that specific location, have a *svastivācana* (recitation for well-being) performed, feed the Brahmins, and remain pure. 1. 2. 3. 4. The throbbing of the right [ear] brings gain for women, while throbbing on the left brings the opposite; the throbbing on the left brings loss, and the throbbing on the right brings the opposite. 9.

Thus ends the forty-second chapter, on the Propitiation of Omens, in the Śrī Nāradīya Saṃhitā. Those omens which are beneficial for men should be known as inauspicious, contrary, and destructive of wealth for women. For a man, the throbbing of the right limb is auspicious; the throbbing of the left limb is inauspicious. (5) Thus ends the forty-second chapter, on the Propitiation of Omens, in the Bhāṣāṭīkā commentary on the Śrī Nāradīya Saṃhitā.

The forms that meteors take upon falling from heaven to earth are indeed as follows: they are known to be of five kinds—*dhiṣṇya*, *ulkā*, lightning (*vidyut*), thunderbolt (*aśani*), and stars (*tārā*). (3) The characteristics and results of these five types shall now be explained in detail.

Those known as *dhiṣṇya*, *ulkā*, and *aśani* ripen [their effects] in three fortnights. (2) [Now] the rule, characteristics, and results of the five types of meteors are stated in their clear form: the meteor named *vidyut* produces its result in six days; the *tārā* likewise yields its fruit. The *tārā* brings about the ripening of the result, while the one called *dhiṣṇya* yields its fruit after half a month. (3) *Bhāṣāṭīkā-saṃhitā*, Chapter 43, (255) The meteor named *vidyut* produces its result in six days; the *tārā* likewise yields its fruit. The *tārā* brings about the ripening of the result, while the one called *dhiṣṇya* yields its fruit after half a month. (3)

Lightning yields its fruit within six days, and the fall of a star (tārāpāta) also yields its fruit within six days; indeed, the fall of a star produces the full result, whereas a lunar mansion (dhiṣṇya) produces half the result. || 3 || Meteors, lightning, and thunderbolts—known by these names—bestow their full results upon men respectively upon horses, elephants, camels, cattle, trees, and the earth. || 4 || The thunderbolt (śani), having fallen, tears everything apart with a great roar, while lightning clearly produces terror in the sky like a mother [terrifying her child]. || 5 ||

The meteor (*ulkā*), the thunderbolt (*aśani*), and the lightning (*vidyut*) bestow full results upon men. They fall respectively upon horses, elephants, camels, cattle, humans, and rows of trees, shattering and destroying them while emitting a most formidable crackling sound; this is the characteristic of the thunderbolt (*aśani*). Furthermore, when lightning flashes intensely in the sky and displays great terror, this is the characteristic of the lightning (*vidyut*). (4–5)

The *cakrā* is large, wheel-shaped, and blazing; it falls over great distances among the rows of forests. The *dhiṣṇyā* is known to have the shape of a tail at its end; it falls blazing like glowing embers. (6) When viewed from nearby, it appears to be two cubits (*hasta*) in measure. It is white like the body of a star-lotus, and its long lotus-like tail is reddish. (7)

That star should be known as one that appears nearby, measuring two cubits in size, white like the moon; and another that is one cubit long, red like a lotus. || 7 || [K (256) Nāradasaṃhitā] Whether upwards, or sideways, or downwards within the expanse of the sky, a large meteor with a head-like tip increases in bulk as it falls. || 8 ||

One should recognize such a meteor as having a broad head, falling either upwards, downwards, or horizontally through the sky, and increasing in its lateral extent. (8) It possesses a long tail, and there are many varieties of it; moreover, they cause affliction through camels, snakes, jackals, donkeys, diseases, and fanged beasts. (9) That meteor has a long tail, and its characteristics are manifold.

Resembling a camel, a serpent, a jackal, a donkey, a cow, an elephant, or a scorpion, their forms are hollow and they cause suffering to all these beings. || 9 || Resembling a monkey, a lizard, or smoke, they are of various kinds and bring evil to men; others are like a horse, an elephant, the moon, silver, a bull, a swan, or a banner. || 10 ||

If there are many forms resembling a monkey, a hyena, or smoke, they bring inauspicious results for men; likewise, those resembling a horse, an elephant, the moon, silver, a bull, a swan, or a banner [are auspicious]. || 10 || Those having the form of a diamond, a conch, a pearl-oyster, or a lotus bestow auspiciousness and happiness. However, if these sounds fall into the fire, they lead to the destruction of the king and the kingdom. || 11 ||

Alternatively, if meteors fall resembling a diamond, a conch, a pearl-oyster, or a lotus, they bring auspiciousness and happiness, O Mother. If a meteor falls into fire, there shall be the destruction of the king and the country. (11) If it falls in the sky, there is great confusion for the world; if it touches the sun or the moon, there is an upheaval of the king. (12) A - A Bhāṣāṭīkā-saṃgraha, Chapter 43. (257)
Furthermore, if it remains only in the sky, it causes great exhaustion to people; if it touches the sun and moon, there shall be trembling among kings. || 12 ||

There is fear for people from the arrival of enemy armies, as well as fear of famine and water. If a meteor falls to the right of the sun and moon, it brings destruction to those living outside the city in insignificant outlying villages. When the sun and moon rise or set, a meteor appearing on the opposite side bestows auspiciousness.

A meteor that is white and red, or yellow and white, is not desired by the twice-born. When it rises white on both sides, with its tail pointing toward the cardinal and intermediate directions, such phenomena as falling meteors and the like are inauspicious for the Brahmins and other castes.

If a meteor falls during the twilight following the rising or setting of the sun and moon, it should be known as auspicious. However, if white, red, or yellowish-white meteors fall, it is not favorable for the twice-born (dvijātis). When both [the head and tail] are of equal whiteness, and the tail portion of the meteor remains in the cardinal directions or in the intermediate directions such as the southeast (agnikoṇa) and so forth, and then falls upon the earth—such broken stars are inauspicious for the Brāhmaṇas and other castes. Regarding them...

It is said: 14–15. A star that resembles the *kunda* flower, white and glossy, brings auspiciousness to kings; however, one that is blue, dark, reddish, or the color of fire brings inauspiciousness. 16. [From the *Nāradasaṃhitā*]: A star resembling the *kunda* flower—white and glossy—if it breaks apart, bestows auspiciousness upon kings; but if a star that is blue, dark, red, or the color of fire breaks apart, it should be known to bring inauspiciousness. 16. At twilight, there is affliction by fire, and if [the star] is split, it causes the destruction of kings. 17. (258). [From the *Nāradasaṃhitā*].

When a star or planet is eclipsed, it brings misfortune to those belonging to its respective color. (17) If a star should break during the time of twilight, it causes suffering from fire; if a star is seen fragmented, it destroys the king. Furthermore, one should know that for those whose lunar mansion has a deity of the Gaṇas, there will be inauspicious results for men. (17) Falling upon fixed mansions (*sthiradhiṣṇya*), it is said to bring fear to women; upon swift-moving mansions (*kṣiprabha*), it causes affliction to the common people (*viś*); and upon movable mansions (*cara*), it afflicts kings. (18)

If it falls upon the constellations known as *sthira* (fixed), one should know it brings ill fortune to women; if it falls upon the *kṣipra* (swift) constellations, that star causes affliction to the Vaiśyas; and if it falls upon the *cara* (movable) constellations, it causes affliction to kings. || 18 || In the *mṛdu* (soft) constellations, it is harmful to the twice-born (*dvijāti*); in the *dāruṇa* (terrible) ones, it is likewise; in the *ugra* (fierce) constellations, it affects the Śūdras; and in the *miśra* (mixed) constellations, it affects others. || 19 ||

If it falls upon the constellations designated as "mild" (mṛdu), it causes suffering to Brāhmaṇas; if it falls upon the "fierce" (dāruṇa) and "sharp" (tīkṣṇa) constellations, it causes suffering to fierce and wicked men; if it falls upon the constellations designated as "terrible" (ugra), it causes suffering to Śūdras; and if it falls upon the "twins" (mithuna) constellations, it causes suffering to those of low birth. It leads to the destruction of kings, kingdoms, and their own wealth, as well as to temples and idols; it brings suffering to the masters within their homes, and to kings upon the mountains.

Bhāṣāṭīkā-saṃgraha, Chapter 43 (259): If lightning strikes the king’s palace or the images of the deities, it destroys the kingdom; if it falls upon the house, it causes suffering to the master of the house; if it falls upon mountains, it brings affliction to the kings. (20) [If it strikes] the consecrated, the lords of the directions, the fields of farmers, the ramparts, the moats, the gates, or the center of the city, [it brings misfortune]. (21)

If it falls on dry land, those who have been initiated (such as celibate students), the lords of the directions, and farmers will suffer; likewise, there will be affliction for forts, walls, moats, city gates, and the city center. (21) There will be fear of the arrival of enemy armies, loss of the kingdom, and the destruction of the citizens; there will be suffering for the owners of cattle in the cow-pens, and for artisans in the waters. (22)

If it falls into this [house], there is fear of another kingdom arriving and the destruction of the city's inhabitants; if it falls into the cowshed, there will be suffering for the owners of the cattle; if it falls into the water, there will be suffering for the artisans (śilpīs). 22. One resembling a royal swan, or like a thread, or like the moon-bannered [flag], if moving against the current, indicates the queen; if moving crosswise, the commander of the army. 23.

If it falls with a form resembling a thread, it destroys the king; if it falls like a rainbow, it also destroys the king; if it falls inverted, it destroys the king’s queen; and if it falls sideways, it destroys the commander-in-chief. (23) If it faces downward, it destroys the king; likewise, if it points upward, it destroys the brahmins. Resembling a tree or a tail, it causes agitation among the people. (29)

An *ulkā* with its face downward destroys the king; one with its face upward destroys the Brahmins; and those shaped like a tree or a tail cause terror among men. (24) In the *Nāradasaṃhitā*: "An *ulkā* that creeps along like a serpent brings misfortune to the [royal] hosts. A circular *ulkā* destroys the city, and one shaped like an umbrella destroys the domestic priest. [An *ulkā*] spreading toward a serpent falls.

For servants, any [such omen] is inauspicious. If a globular meteor falls, it destroys the city; if it falls in the shape of an umbrella, it destroys the king's priest. (25) One shaped like a bamboo, a shrub, or a creeper causes the ruin of the kingdom; likewise, one resembling a skull or a serpent, as well as one in the form of a fragment, bestows evil. (26)

If it falls with a shape resembling bamboo, shrubs, or creepers, it destroys the kingdom; and if the meteor falls with the form of a boar, a serpent, or in a fragmented shape, it bestows sin (is inauspicious). || 26 || One resembling a rainbow brings about the kingdom, while one that is motionless destroys the clouds. || 27 || Thus ends the forty-third chapter, on the Characteristics of Meteors, in the Śrī Nāradīya Saṃhitā. || 43 ||

If a meteor falls with a shape resembling a rainbow, it destroys the kingdom; and if a "mūrchitā" (faint) meteor—that is, one devoid of luster—falls, it causes suffering to those who depend on water for their livelihood. 27. Thus ends the forty-third chapter, titled "Characteristics of Meteors," in the *Śrī Nāradīya Saṃhitā Bhāṣāṭīkā*. Rays of light, struck by the wind, rising up and forming circles, appearing in various colors and shapes, are known as *pariveṣas* (halos) surrounding the moon and the sun. 1.

Bhāṣā-Ṭīkā-saṃgraha, Chapter 44. (261) When the rays of the sun and moon are struck by the wind and turn upward, they form circular halos (*maṇḍala*). These possess many colors and many shapes, and they are called the *pariveṣas* (halos) of the sun and moon. || 1 || Those that are red, blue, pale-white, pigeon-colored, cloud-like, tawny, yellow, and white in color, appearing in the directions starting from the East, bring rain. || 2 ||

They dissolve again and again and do not yield their full fruit. However, auspicious *kapila* [spots] are glossy and resemble milk, oil, or water. They possess colors such as reddish-brown (*lāla*), blue, pale-white, pink, pigeon-grey, cloud-like, tawny, yellow, and green. If these colors appear in the directions starting from the East in successive order, there will be rain; likewise, if the colors of the *maṇḍala* repeatedly...

If they vanish after appearing, they do not yield their full fruit. Those that are tawny-colored, glossy, and possess a luster like milk, oil, or water [are auspicious]. (2–3) A halo having the appearance of a bow, a shrṛṅgāṭaka, a chariot, or blood-red is auspicious; however, halos with the colors of various trees bring about the end of kings. (4)

Earrings shaped like a bow, a shield, or a chariot, and those as red as blood, are said to bestow auspiciousness; however, earrings resembling various trees and green in color destroy kings. (4) When the Moon, the Sun, or Varuṇa are eclipsed day and night, they cause the death of a king; likewise, when [the planet] is red, it does so. (4)

If, by day and night, a rule is established such that the red-colored disks of the sun and the moon remain visible—meaning the sun’s disk by day and the moon’s by night—the death of the king occurs. (5) (262) Nāradasaṃhitā: When Saturn is surrounded by two disks, it destroys the commander of the army; when by three disks, it kills the king; and when situated within a halo, it causes the destruction of minor grains. (6)

If there be two maṇḍalas, they destroy the commander-in-chief; if there be three maṇḍalas, they destroy the king; and if Saturn reaches the center of the maṇḍala, there shall be the destruction of inferior grains. (6) Mars causes war, while Jupiter bestows fearlessness upon all. Mercury brings about the loss of crops, and Venus brings famine and strife. (7)

If it enters the orb of Mars, it causes war; if it is Jupiter, it grants fearlessness to all; if it is Mercury, it brings about the destruction of agriculture; and if it reaches the orb of Venus, it causes famine and strife. (7) Ketu, when situated within a halo, bestows famine and quarrels; Rāhu causes suffering, the death of kings, and the miscarriage of fetuses. (8)

If Ketu enters the solar disc, it causes famine and strife; if it enters the lunar disc, it brings affliction, the death of the king, and the destruction of embryos—such are its effects. (8) When two planets are situated within a halo (pariveṣa), they bring about conflict among kings. When three planets have entered the halo, they cause quarrels and poverty. (9)

If two planets should enter the halo (pariveṣa), there will be war among kings; if three planets should enter, it causes strife and makes the price of grain very high. (9) If four planets are situated in the halo, they bring about the death of the king; if five planets have entered the halo, those planets bestow great strength. (10) [Commentary in Bhāṣā-Ṭīkā, Section 1, Chapter 44]

(263) If four planets should be in retrograde motion, they cause the death of the king; if five planets should be in the lunar disc, they should be known as bestowers of strength (bestowers of auspicious results). || 10 || In this same manner, one should understand the results of two or four retrograde planets; if Mars and the other planets individually enter the lunar disc, there is loss for the king. || 11 ||

13. || Likewise, the halo around the constellations yields results for two or three [days]; however, a halo around the twice-born (the moon) on the first lunar day and others is not desired. || 12 || In this same manner, one should understand the results if there are two or three stars within the solar or lunar disc; furthermore, if it occurs in the solar or lunar disc during the four lunar days beginning with the first (pratipadā), it should be known as inauspicious for a Brāhmaṇa. || 12 || Indeed, during the three [days] beginning with the fifth, it is likewise inauspicious for the king. || 13 ||

On the eighth day, even an eclipse of the moon brings desired results to the crown prince. (13) If a halo occurs on the first three lunar days beginning with the fifth, it should be known as inauspicious for the king; however, if it occurs on the eighth day, it should be known as bringing auspiciousness to the crown prince. (13) Furthermore, on those [first] three lunar days, it bestows misfortune upon kings; on the twelfth day, it leads to the destruction of the royal priest. (14) On the thirteenth day, there will be an agitation of the army or perhaps an obstruction by the king.

An atmospheric halo on the fourteenth day portends disease for the king’s wives. (264) *Nāradasaṃhitā*: One should know that kings face inauspiciousness during the three lunar days beginning with the ninth. If a halo occurs on the twelfth day, there will be the destruction of the king and his priest; if it occurs on the thirteenth day, there will be an uprising in the army or the confinement of the king; if it occurs on the fourteenth day, there will be illness among the queens. (14–15) A halo on the fifteenth day brings misfortune to the lords of the earth.

If a line should appear in the middle or on the outside of the halo: for stationary objects it is situated in the center and is not desired; for moving objects it is situated at the side. Furthermore, a halo during the rainy season and autumn brings rain.

If there is a full orb (*maṇḍala*), it is inauspicious for kings. If a line occurs in the middle of the orb or on its outer edge, it should be known as mediocre for stationary kings (those remaining within their own fortresses). If a line occurs among equal [parts], it should be known as inauspicious for traveling kings. If there is a full orb during the rainy season (*prāvṛṭ*) or the autumn season (*śarad*), it will cause rain. (16–17)

Generally, in other seasons, they yield the results as previously described. (18) Thus ends the forty-fourth chapter, titled "Characteristics of Halos," in the Śrī Nāradīya Saṃhitā. (44) And specifically, if halos around the sun or moon occur during other seasons, one should understand the results to be exactly as stated before. (38) Thus ends the forty-fourth chapter, titled "Characteristics of Halos," in the Bhāṣā commentary on the Śrī Nāradīya Saṃhitā. Commentary in Vernacular, Chapter 47. (265)

The rays of the sun, struck by clouds and wind, assume various colors and take the form of a bow in the sky; that which is thus seen is called the bow of Indra (Indradhanus). Or else, it arises from the long sighs of the lord of serpents, Śeṣa; appearing in the intermediate directions or the cardinal directions, it portends the destruction of the sovereign of that quarter.

Alternatively, from the heavy breathing of Śeṣanāga, the king of serpents, Indra’s bow (the rainbow) appears; it destroys the king who is the lord of the direction or the corner in which it occurs. (2) A rainbow made of yellow, white, or blue [clouds] causes fear of fire, weapons, and missiles. One born of trees brings disease, while one born of the earth brings the destruction of crops. (3) One arising from water causes drought, and one appearing over an anthill brings fear of war. It grants rain during a drought, but causes drought in a region where rain is already plentiful. (4)

If a rainbow appears in yellow, pale-red, blue, or the color of a *pāṭala* flower, it portends fear of fire and war. If the brilliance of rays falls upon a tree and the rainbow is seen in the shape of a bow, there will be disease among the people; if it is seen upon the ground, it destroys the crops. If the rainbow is seen reflected in water, there will be no rain.

If the curvature of a rainbow falls upon a mountain or a burrow, there will be fear of war among the subjects. If a rainbow appears in the eastern direction when there is no rain, rain will begin; however, if a rainbow is seen in the eastern direction while it is already raining, the rain will cease. || 3 || 4 || A rainbow always bestows rain in the western direction, and likewise in the other [southern] direction. If a rainbow appears in the east during the night, there will be the loss of the king. || 5 || (266) Nāradasaṃhitā.

If a rainbow is seen in the western direction, it always brings rain; if it appears in other directions (namely the north or south), it also causes rain. If a rainbow is seen in the eastern direction at night, it causes the ruin of the king. (5) In the southern direction it kills the commander-in-chief, in the west the supreme leader, in the northern quarter the minister, and one appearing from a corner [causes harm to] the counselor. (6)

If seen in the southern direction, it destroys the commander-in-chief; if in the west, it destroys a great governor or general; and if seen in the north or the corners such as the northeast, it destroys the king’s minister. (6) A rainbow appearing in the kingdom, rich in white color, clearly destroys the preeminent king presiding over the direction in which it arises, beginning with the Brahmins. (7)

If a white-colored rainbow is seen in the eastern direction at night, it destroys the Brāhmaṇas; and whichever direction a distinct rainbow appears in, the king of that very direction perishes. (7) Two rainbows that are deeply embedded in the earth, severed, and contrary to one another cause the end of the king; however, if they are favorable, that is not auspicious. (8) Thus ends the forty-fifth chapter, titled "The Characteristics of the Rainbow," in the Śrī Nāradīya Saṃhitā. (45)

A rainbow without a halo produces auspicious results on the earth; two rainbows produce inauspicious results, destroying the king and failing to bring favorable or auspicious fruits. ||8|| Thus ends the forty-fifth chapter, titled "Characteristics of the Rainbow," in the Bhāṣā-Ṭīkā commentary on the Śrī Nāradīya Saṃhitā. Bhāṣā-Ṭīkā, Chapter 46 (267): A city of Gandharvas seen in various directions brings misfortune in succession.

The appearance of a city of Gandharvas in the various directions portends inauspicious results for kings, army commanders, ministers, and priests respectively. A white, red, yellow, or black city of Gandharvas appearing at night brings misfortune to Brahmins and the other castes, while it signifies the destruction of the sovereign if it appears during the day.

Furthermore, these colors—white, red, yellow, and black—are inauspicious for the Brāhmaṇas and the other classes respectively when they appear [in dreams]. If a city of Gandharvas (an illusory city) is seen at night, it portends the destruction of the king. A rainbow, smoke-colored like fire, or anything of variegated color and form, appearing as a rampart, a banner, or an archway, brings misfortune to everyone. || 32-33 ||

If a city of Gandharvas (a mirage) is seen resembling a rainbow, fire, or smoke, it brings inauspicious results to everyone. If it appears with variegated colors, diverse forms, the shape of a skull, or like a banner or an archway, a great battle between rival kings will be witnessed. Thus ends the forty-sixth chapter, titled "The Observation of the City of Gandharvas," in the Śrī Nāradīya Saṃhitā.

If their appearance is seen, a great war will break out among kings. || 4 || Thus ends the forty-sixth chapter, titled "The Vision of the City of Gandharvas," in the Bhāṣā-Ṭīkā on the Śrī-Nāradīya-Saṃhitā. (268) Nāradasaṃhitā: A sun resembling a second sun, yet glossy, appearing at the side [of the actual sun], bestows auspiciousness; one that is as clear as lapis lazuli or white brings about an abundance of food. || 3 ||

In the clouds, a second sun appears due to the brilliance of the [real] sun; if it appears glossy-colored and symmetrical, it is auspicious. If it appears as clear and white as a lapis lazuli gem, it brings about plenty. (1) If it has a yellowish hue, it causes disease; if black, it brings death and fierce warfare. If there is a garland of such secondary suns, it constantly bestows fear of thieves. (2)

If a mock sun (*pratisūrya*) of yellowish-white color is seen, there will be disease among the subjects; if it is black in color, it brings death and a terrible war occurs. If a garland of mock suns is seen within the clouds, there will be constant fear of thieves. (2) A mock sun of the sun situated in the west brings rain; one situated in both directions bestows water on both sides. One above the king brings harm to the king, while one below destroys the people. (3)

If a mock sun (pratisūrya) is seen in the northern direction, there will be rain; if seen in the southern direction, the wind will blow; if seen equally on both sides, it stops the rain; if a mock sun is seen above the sun, it destroys the king; if a mock sun is seen below the sun, it destroys the subjects. (3) Mock suns appearing all around the sun of sharp rays (the sun) bring about the defeat [of the ruler], and likewise, those around the moon bring about the destruction of the world.

4. Thus ends the forty-seventh chapter, titled "The Characteristics of the Counter-Sun" (Pratisūryalakṣaṇādhyāya), in the glorious Nāradīya-saṃhitā. [Bhāṣā-Ṭīkā, Chapter 48, Verse 269]: If a counter-sun appears on all four sides of the sun and directly eclipses the sun's own declination (krānti), it portends the destruction of the world; the same result should be understood for the moon as well. 4. Thus ends the forty-seventh chapter, titled "The Characteristics of the Counter-Sun," in the glorious Nāradīya-saṃhitā, with its Bhāṣā commentary.

Now, the characteristics of *nirghāta* (a thunderous atmospheric phenomenon): When wind, impelled by [another] wind, falls from the sky to the earth and becomes ignited by its own weight, that *nirghāta* causes extreme harm. This should be understood as the characteristic of a lightning strike. A *nirghāta* occurring at sunrise is undesirable; it brings about the destruction of kings.

If a thunderclap occurs at sunrise, it brings misfortune to kings and causes destruction; if it occurs before the first watch of the day, it brings loss to the Śūdras residing in the city. (2) At midday, it is not auspicious for Brāhmaṇas or those who live off the king; in the third watch, it brings ill fortune to Vaiśyas and aquatic creatures. (3) In the fourth watch, it leads to the loss of wealth, and at twilight, it portends the mixing of castes. (4)

In the first watch [of the day], there is loss of crops; in the second, however, [it portends ill for] the Piśācas. (Nāradasaṃhitā, 4.270) If a thunderclap occurs at midday, it is inauspicious for Brāhmaṇas as well as for those who reside as servants at the royal court. If it occurs in the third watch, it is inauspicious for Vaiśyas and aquatic creatures. In the fourth watch of the day, it causes the destruction of wealth. In the evening, it is inauspicious for the low-born castes. In the first [watch] of the night...

In the first watch, there is loss of crops; in the second watch, it destroys the Piśācas. (3-4) At midnight, it kills horses; in the third watch, artisans and scribes. When a thunderbolt falls during the fourth watch, it then slays the people. (5)
