A thunderclap occurring at dawn destroys horses; in the third watch of the night, it destroys artisans and scribes; and in the fourth watch of the night, a fallen thunderbolt destroys all people. A thunderous roar that is harsh and broken [destroys] the lord of each respective direction. Thus ends the forty-eighth chapter, titled "The Characteristics of Thunderbolts," in the Śrī Nāradīya Saṃhitā.

If a thunderclap—that is, a stroke of lightning—should strike with a terrifying, crashing sound, it destroys the king of the very direction in which it falls. (6) Thus ends the forty-eighth chapter, titled "The Characteristics of Thunderclaps," in the Bhāṣā-ṭīkā on the Śrī Nāradīya Saṃhitā. A fire-colored or yellowish glow in the sky portends fear for kings; a glow the color of fire or reddish-brown portends the destruction of the country and brings forth wind. (1)

If the color is yellow, it causes fear among kings; if it is fire-like in color, it brings about the destruction of the country; if it is red, it sets the wind in motion—thus ends the section on *digdāha* (the blazing of the quarters) at the time of sunrise or sunset, when colors such as red appear across the directions. Smoke [in the sky] portends the destruction of crops, and black smoke brings the fear of weapons. A preternatural glow in the eastern direction (*prāgdāha*) is inauspicious for Kṣatriyas and sovereigns.

If it is smoke-colored, it destroys agriculture; if it is black, there will be a depletion of weapons. If a preternatural glow (digdāha) is seen in the eastern direction, it brings inauspicious results for Kṣatriyas and kings. || 2 || In the southeast, it brings misfortune to the crown prince and artisans; in the south, the mute, Vaiśyas, and the lowest of men suffer affliction. || 3 ||

If it is in the southeast (Agnikoṇa), it brings inauspicious results for the crown prince and artisans; if it is in the southern direction, there will be suffering for fools, Vaiśyas, and low-born people. || 3 || In the southwest (Nairṛtyā) direction, there will be thieves, and among men, widows and women of the king; in the west (Pratīcī), there will be affliction for farmers, and in the northwest (Vāyavyā), for species of livestock. || 4 ||

If it occurs in the southwest (Nairṛta) corner, there will be suffering for thieves, those who arrange second marriages, and women; if it occurs in the western direction, farmers will suffer; and if it occurs in the northwest (Vāyu) corner, the animal species will perish. || 4 || If it occurs in the north (Saumya), Brahmins and others [will suffer], and in the northeast (Aiśānī), all the Vaiśyas and artisans [will suffer]. A fire in the sky with a golden hue brings auspiciousness to the people. Thus ends the forty-ninth chapter, titled "Characteristics of the Sky-Fire," in the Śrī Nāradīya Saṃhitā. || 49 ||

(272) *Nāradasaṃhitā*. If [the fire] occurs in the north, there is suffering for Brāhmaṇas and others; if it occurs in the northeast (*īśānakoṇa*), there is suffering for Vaiśyas as well as all people. If the flaming glow of the horizon is like the color of gold, it brings auspiciousness to all people. || 5 || Thus ends the forty-ninth chapter, on the Characteristics of the Flaming Horizon, in the *Bhāṣāṭīkā* commentary on the *Śrīnāradīyasaṃhitā*. Now begins the chapter on the Characteristics of Dust (*rajas*).

When the quarters, villages, forests, and mountains are covered by white dust, in such a manner the lords of the earth meet their end at the conclusion. (13) If the directions, villages, forests, and mountains are shrouded by white dust—that is, if a blinding white haze rises into the sky—then kings shall attain death. Destruction occurs in whichever direction the dust arises.

In each such direction, it causes harm to living beings through the wrath of weapons. (2) Furthermore, dust that rises and spreads toward a particular direction brings destruction to the living beings in that very direction by means of the fury of arms. (2) Dark dust portends disease for ministers and the people of the realm; it expands at sunrise and veils the sky. (3) Dust that persists for two or three days brings about most terrible fear. Dust that remains for a single night destroys the king without fail. (4)

If dust of the color of a corpse (dust that causes blindness) rises at the time of sunrise and covers the sky, it brings ruin to the king’s ministers and the country. (Bhāṣā-Ṭīkā, Adhyāya 50, Verse 273).

Furthermore, if extremely fierce winds blow for three days and dust continues to rise incessantly for one night, they destroy the king. (3–4). If this occurs continuously for three nights, there will be no arrival of a foreign army; likewise, if it continues for three nights, there will be a wasting disease and a pestilence. (4).

If dust continues to rise for two nights, there will be no invasion by a foreign army; however, if the dust remains for three nights, there will be fear among the subjects from wicked dacoits and the outbreak of disease. (5) If it continues for four nights, there will be incomparable famine; if for five consecutive nights, it portends the destruction of the great king. (6)

If [the blood] remains for four nights, there will be constant fear of locusts and other pests, as well as famine; if it lasts for five nights, it destroys the great king. (6) Except during the winter season, the menstrual flow yields its full fruit at other times. (7) Thus ends the fiftieth chapter, titled "The Characteristics of Menstrual Blood," in the Śrī Nāradīya Saṃhitā. (60)

In the winter season (*śiśira-ṛtu*), the movement of dust (*rajas*) other than that of the season yields full results; that is to say, there is no fault whatsoever in the movement of dust during the winter. || 7 || Thus ends the fiftieth chapter, on the characteristics of dust, in the *Bhāṣā-Ṭīkā* on the *Śrī-Nāradīya-Saṃhitā*. An earthquake arising from the long sighs of the lordly serpents, distressed by the burden of the earth, will then bring misfortune to the worlds. || 1 ||

18 (274) Nāradasaṃhitā: An earthquake occurs from the heavy breathing of Śeṣanāga, who is distressed by the burden of the earth; it brings inauspicious results to the world. 1. An earthquake occurring during the watches of the day (yāma-krama) is harmful to the twice-born (dvijātis); likewise, one occurring at either of the two twilights (saṃdhyā) is harmful to the lords of the earth (kṣitīśas). 2.

An earthquake occurring in successive watches (praharas) yields inauspicious results for the twice-born: in the first watch of the day, it is inauspicious for Brāhmaṇas; in the second, for Kṣatriyas; in the third, for Vaiśyas; and in the fourth watch, one should know it is inauspicious for Śūdras. Furthermore, if an earthquake occurs during both twilights (saṃdhyās), it is inauspicious for kings. || 2 || [The asterisms] beginning with Aryamā are four; then those of the Aśvins, Indu, and Aditi.

This is the Vāyavya-maṇḍala; if an earthquake occurs within this [region]—namely, during the four asterisms beginning with Uttarā-phalgunī, and the asterisms Aśvinī, Mṛgaśiras, and Punarvasu—it brings about the destruction of kings, crops, merchants, courtesans, artisans, and rain. [4] [An earthquake occurring] during Puṣya, Viśākhā, Bharaṇī, Maghā, Pūrvā-phalgunī, Kṛttikā, and Pūrvā-bhādrapadā [brings similar results]. [4]

If this fiery mandala occurs during the months of Kṛpa (Kārtika), it leads to the destruction of agriculture, kings, Vaiśyas, courtesans, artisans, and rain; likewise for the asterisms Puṣya, Viśākhā, Bharaṇī, Maghā, Pūrvaphālgunī, Kṛttikā, and Pūrvābhādrapada. Thus ends the Śāṃbara-ṭaṅkaṇa [section]. || 4-5 ||

This is called the *abhimaṇḍala* of these constellations. If an earthquake occurs during this period, there will be the destruction of the king; there will be no rain, and prices will remain high. Substances such as *śāmbharanamaka* (rock salt), borax, and the like will become expensive. (5) [Bhāṣāṭīkā-saṃhitā, Adhyāya 51] (275). The *vāsava-maṇḍala* consists of the constellations Abhijit, Dhātṛ, Vaiśva, Aindra, Vasu, Vaiṣṇava, Maitra, and Bhram. If an earthquake should occur during this time, (6) [Bhāṣāṭīkā-saṃhitā, Adhyāya 51] (276).

Abhijit, Rohiṇī, Uttarāṣāḍhā, Jyeṣṭhā, Dhaniṣṭhā, Śravaṇa, and Anurādhā are known as the Vāsava-maṇḍala; if an earthquake occurs during these, it leads to the destruction of kings and to strife, while it destroys the regions of Māheya and Dardura. (6–7) Mūla, Āhirbudhnya (Śatabhiṣaj), Varuṇa (Śatabhiṣaj), Pauṣṇa (Revatī), Ārdrā, and Ahibhāni (Āśleṣā)—if an earthquake occurs during these, it results in the destruction of the king and mutual enmity among kings; furthermore, the destruction of the regions of Māheya and Dardura occurs. (7)

Mūla, Uttarābhādrapadā, Śatabhiṣā, Pūrvāṣāḍhā, Revatī, Ārdrā, and Āśleṣā. (7) This is the Vāruṇa Maṇḍala; if an earthquake should occur within it, O King, it causes the destruction of kings and destroys the Pauṇḍras, Cīnas, and Pulindas. (8) Generally, all such portents bring misfortune to rulers.

An earthquake yields its fruit within six months, while a fiery portent (digdāha) bestows its results within two months. Specifically, all such portents are said to be inauspicious for kings; the result of an earthquake occurs in six months, and the result of a fiery portent occurs in two months. Dust that has not been previously mentioned yields its fruit at that time within five months. Thus ends the fifty-first chapter, titled "The Characteristics of Earthquakes," in the Śrī Nāradīya Saṃhitā. (276) Nāradasaṃhitā.

Furthermore, dust, blindness, walking unsteadily, and disturbances caused by other objects produce results during the five months [of the rainy season]. || 10 || Thus ends the fifty-first chapter, titled "Characteristics of Earthquakes," in the Bhāṣā-Ṭīkā on the Śrī-Nāradīya-Saṃhitā. Now begins the "Fruits of Birth under the Asterisms": A man born under Aśvinī is handsome, fortunate, robust, intelligent, fond of ornaments, beloved by women, and brave. || 1 ||

A person born under the asterism Aśvinī is handsome, possessed of great prosperity, fair-complexioned, intelligent, fond of ornaments, beloved by women, and a heroic warrior. (1) One born under Bharaṇī is skilled in the arts of love, truthful, firm in his vows, free from disease, fortunate, light-eating, and pleasant-faced. (2)

One born in Bharaṇī becomes skilled in the science of erotics (kāmaśāstra), truthful in speech, firm in his observances, free from disease, endowed with beautiful sovereignty, moderate in eating, and happy. (2) One born in Kṛttikā (Agnikṣatra) is radiant, intelligent, charitable, a great eater, beloved by women, profound, skillful, wise, and pure. (3)

A person born under the Kṛttikā nakṣatra is radiant, intelligent, charitable, a great eater, fond of women, profound, clever, and proud. (3) One born under the Rohiṇī nakṣatra is handsome, steady-minded, honorable, an enjoyer of pleasures, fond of sexual dalliance, sweet-spoken, clever, capable, radiant, and devoted to the Brahman. (4)

A man born under Rohiṇī is handsome, steady-minded, proud, wealthy, fond of sexual pleasure, skilled in pleasant speech, adept in all desired pursuits, and radiant in luster. (4) One born under the lunar mansion of Mṛgaśirā is always energetic, fickle, timid, wealthy, fond of conciliation, pure, learned in the scriptures, authoritative, and wise. (9)

Furthermore, a person born under Mṛgaśiras is fickle, energetic, timid, wealthy, fond of conciliation, pure, a knower of the Vedic branches, powerful, and learned. || 5 || One born under Śiva’s asterism (Ārdrā) is devoid of reflection, cruel, skilled in buying and selling, violent toward cattle, fierce-tempered, and ungrateful. || 6 ||

A person born under the Ārdrā constellation is lacking in discernment; he is skilled in the business of buying and selling cruel goods, is violent, possesses fierce anger, and is ungrateful. (6) One born under the Punarvasu asterism is either dull-witted or handsome, is expert in matters concerning the wives of others, is patient, yet remains excessively dissatisfied. (7)

One born under Punarvasu is of poor intellect from birth, yet handsome; he is skillful in the affairs of others' wives, patient, devoid of contentment, and swift in movement. || 7 || One born under Puṣya is wise, fortunate, brave, compassionate, righteous, wealthy, skilled in the arts, truthful, lustful, and light [in nature]. || 8 || (278) Nāradasaṃhitā.

Furthermore, if birth occurs under the Puṣya nakṣatra, the person becomes a scholar, handsome, wealthy, heroic, compassionate, righteous, affluent, skilled in the arts, truthful, and straightforward. (8) A man born under the Āśleṣā nakṣatra is excellent, cunning, cruel, brave, devoted to the wives of others, deceitful, straightforward, addicted to vices, yet self-controlled. (9)

A person born under the asterism Āśleṣā is excellent, cunning, cruel, heroic, an adulterer, foolish, free from crookedness, addicted to vices, yet self-controlled. (9) One born under the asterism Maghā is brave, has a thick jaw and a large belly, is prone to anger, eloquent, and a lord; he is devoted to the worship of elders and deities and is full of splendor. (10)

A person born under the Maghā constellation is heroic, possesses great physical strength, has stout hips, speaks words of anger, is intolerant, capable, devoted to the worship of elders and deities, and is radiant. (10) One born under the Bhāgya (Pūrvaphalgunī) constellation is brilliant, a traveler, a donor, an expert in royal policy and the scriptures, a knower of what ought and ought not to be done, and is clever. (11)

A person born under the Pūrvaphālgunī asterism is a wanderer, a donor, skilled in royal science, adept in discerning between what ought and ought not to be done, and clever. (11) One born under the Aryaman asterism (Uttaraphālgunī) is a conqueror of enemies, happy, an enjoyer of pleasures, a poet, proficient in the arts, devoted to truth, and pure. (12)

One born under Uttarāphālgunī conquers his enemies; he is happy, a possessor of enjoyments, skilled in sporting with women, knowledgeable in the arts, devoted to truth, and pure. 12. [Bhāṣāṭīkā, Chapter 52, Verse 279] One born in the mansion of the Sun (Aśleṣā) is intelligent, incites thieves, is intent on the affairs of others, a warrior, stays in foreign lands, is brave, and gains women. 13.

A man born under the Hasta nakṣatra is intelligent, enthusiastic about theft, devoted to the affairs of others, heroic, a resident of foreign lands, valorous, and gains profit through women. (13) One born under the Citrā nakṣatra wears wonderful garlands and garments, is an expert in the science of love, radiant, wealthy, an enjoyer of pleasures, and learned. (14)

One born under the Citrā constellation wears variegated garlands and beautiful, diverse garments; he is skilled in the science of love (Kāmaśāstra), radiant, wealthy, a man of enjoyment, and wise. || 14 || One born under the Svātī constellation is righteous, pleasant of speech, brave, expert in buying and selling, lustful, possessed of many sons, self-controlled, and learned. || 14 ||

A person born under the Svāti constellation is righteous, pleasant-spoken, heroic, skilled in the business of buying and selling, lustful, possessed of many sons, self-controlled, and learned. || 15 || One born under the Viśākhā constellation is free from injustice, gentle, clever in deceit, lacking in effort, self-controlled, eloquent, and greedy for wealth. || 16 ||

A person born under the Viśākhā nakṣatra is intent on injustice, clever, skilled in the fabrication of illusions, devoid of industry, yet self-controlled, wealthy, and greedy. (16) One born under the Anurādhā nakṣatra is devoted to the king’s service, brave, the husband of a woman residing in a foreign land, handsome, a hidden sinner, and tawny-complexioned. (17) (280) Nāradasaṃhitā.

A man born under the Anurādhā nakṣatra is intent on the affairs of a good king, a heroic warrior, a resident of foreign lands, a master of women, handsome in form, a secret sinner, and tawny in complexion. || 17 || One born under the Indradhiṣṇya (Jyeṣṭhā) nakṣatra is inclined toward great expenditure, endures hardship, is lustful, difficult to overcome, cruel in conduct, a speaker of falsehoods, and wealthy. || 18 ||

A person born under the Jyeṣṭhā nakṣatra is one who spends much, endures hardship, is lustful, attains his goals with great difficulty, acts with cruelty, speaks falsely, and is wealthy. (18) One born under the Nairṛta (Mūla) mansion is violent, proud, a seeker of enjoyments, one who reveals the affairs of others, deceitful in conduct, addicted to women, and gentle. (19)

One born under the Mūla constellation is violent, arrogant, a seeker of pleasures, one who reveals the desires of others, a practitioner of deceitful conduct, fickle toward women, and clever. (19) One born under the Jala (Pūrvāṣāḍhā) constellation possesses a good wife, acts according to his own will, is skillful, firm in friendship, shares in hardships, is vigorous, and is proud. (20)

A person born under Pūrvāṣāḍhā possesses beautiful women, is lustful, clever, firm in affection, capable of enduring hardships, strong, and proud. || 20 || One born under Uttarāṣāḍhā is knowledgeable in ethics, righteous, brave, has many friends, is humble, possesses a good wife, and is enriched with excellent sons. || 21 ||

One born under Uttarāṣāḍhā is a knower of the science of ethics (nītiśāstra), righteous, heroic, possessed of many friends, a scholar of political philosophy, and endowed with a beautiful wife and handsome sons. (21) One born under the Śravaṇa asterism has a firm belly, is illustrious, eloquent, wealthy, skilled in the amorous arts described in poetry, and virtuous. (22) *Commentary in Vernacular (Bhāṣāṭīkā), Book 52, Verse 281.*

A person born under Śravaṇa is firm-bellied, prosperous, talkative, wealthy, knowledgeable in poetic ornaments, and righteous. || 22 || One born in Vasudhiṣṇya (Dhaniṣṭhā) is righteous, addicted to vices, greedy, fond of dance, song, and women, capable of being won over by conciliation alone, radiant, and heroic. || 23 ||

A person born under the Dhaniṣṭhā constellation is righteous, addicted to vices, greedy, fond of dancing, singing, and women, one who accomplishes his tasks through persuasion, radiant, and powerful. || 23 || One born under the Śatatārā (Śatabhiṣaj) constellation has a foul odor, is addicted to vices, cruel, subject to decline and growth, deceitful, devoted to the wives of others, and brave. || 23 ||

If birth occurs under the Śatabhiṣā asterism, the man becomes foul-smelling, addicted to vices, cruel, afflicted by the diseases of consumption and swelling, foolish, devoted to another's wife, yet a heroic warrior. (24) One born under the Ajavīthī asterism is anxious, dominated by women, gentle, intent on censuring others, hypocritical, unbearable, and brave. (29)

If birth occurs in Pūrvābhādrapadā, one becomes anxious-minded, dominated by women, gentle, a slanderer of others, heretical, difficult to endure, and a hero. || 25 || One born in the Vāhirbudhnya asterism (Uttarābhādrapadā) is prolific, righteous, eloquent, a conqueror of enemies, happy, powerful, firm in his vows, yet always lustful. || 26 ||

One born under Uttarābhādrapadā possesses progeny, is righteous, eloquent, a conqueror of enemies, happy, capable, firm in his observances, and is always lustful. (26) [From the *Nāradasaṃhitā*: One born under Revatī (Pauṣṇa) is handsome, wealthy, an enjoyer of pleasures, learned, one who consumes water and grain, lustful, ill-behaved, brave, and a traveler to foreign lands. (27) Thus ends the fifty-second chapter, titled "The Qualities of the Lunar Mansions," in the venerable *Nāradīyasaṃhitā*. (42)

A person born under the Revatī asterism is handsome, wealthy, an enjoyer of pleasures, learned, one who earns wealth through dealings with water, lustful, of wicked conduct, heroic, and a resident of foreign lands. (27) Thus ends the fifty-second chapter, titled "The Qualities of the Asterisms," in the *Bhāṣāṭīkā* commentary on the *Śrī Nāradīya Saṃhitā*. Now begins the section on Miscellaneous Matters (*Miśraprakaraṇa*). The periods of no solar transit (*asaṃkrānti*) and two solar transits (*dvisaṃkrānti*) are equal to the *saṃsarpa* and *āhastika* periods respectively.

Two months are indeed lunar (*cāndra*), while the *adhimāsa* (intercalary month) and the *kṣayamāsa* (lapsed month) are further [distinctions]. || 1 || Those two months that lack a solar transit (*saṃkrānti*) as well as those that possess two transits are called, respectively, *saṃsarpa* and *āṣāḍha*. Furthermore, there are the *adhimāsa* and *kṣayamāsa*; all these varieties are to be understood as belonging to the lunar month. || 1 || Between the two divisions of the Himālaya mountains lies the earth honored by the gods; between the Godāvarī and Kṛṣṇaveṇī rivers lies the earth of the poet (Kāvya). || 2 ||

Know that the land between the Himalayas and the Gaṅgā belongs to Bṛhaspati; know that the land between the Godāvarī and Kṛṣṇaveṇī rivers belongs to Śukra. (2) The land between the Vindhya mountains and the Godāvarī belongs to the son of the Sun (Saturn); and the land between the Vindhya mountain and the Gaṅgā belongs to Budha. (3) *Commentary on the Bhāṣā, Chapter 53.*

(283) Know the land between the Vindhya mountain and the Godāvarī to belong to Śani; the land that lies between the Vindhya mountain and the Gaṅgā is known to belong to Budha. 3. The earth between the Yamunā and the Gaṅgā belongs to the son of the Earth (Mangala). The Sun and the Moon are the lords of the two regions situated on either side of the confluence. 4.

One should know that the land between the river Veṇī and Laṅkā is the region of Maṅgala, and the lords of the land near the ocean are said to be the Sun and the Moon. (4) On the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Āśvina, or on the new moon day when the moon wanes, occurring at the beginning of Kārttika and conjoined with the Svāti asterism, then the Dīpāvalī festival takes place. (5) [This refers to] the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of Āśvina or the new moon, as well as the fourteenth day of Kārttika and the Dīpamālikā. (5)

On the day of Dīpāvalī, Lakṣmī resides in oil and Gaṅgā resides in water; therefore, for the purpose of warding off misfortune (Alakṣmī), one should perform an oil-bath. (6) During a lunar eclipse, at the transit of the sun (Saṃkrānti), on a Sunday, during an eclipse of the moon, or on the day of the end of a fortnight—on these occasions, an oil-bath causes no fault, and when performed in the morning, it removes sin. (7)

If one performs an oil-bath at dawn on the new moon day, on the day of a solar transit (saṃkrānti), on the day of Vyatīpāta, or on the day of a lunar day's omission (tithi-kṣaya), all sins shall be removed. 7. (284) Nāradasaṃhitā: In the month of Bhādrapada, during the dark fortnight, the eighth lunar day conjoined with the Rohiṇī asterism is known as Jayantī; it was on that night that Janārdana was born. 8.

The eighth lunar day of the dark fortnight of Bhādrapada, when it coincides with the Rohiṇī asterism, is that famous Jayantī Aṣṭamī; on that day, the birth of Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa took place. (8) He who observes a fast and performs a vigil on the eighth day joined with midnight shall obtain the fruit of a horse sacrifice. (9)

He who performs the vigil on the eighth lunar day (Aṣṭamī) joined with midnight, marked by the birth-signs of the day of his own birth and observing the vow, attains the fruit of the Aśvamedha sacrifice. || 9 || On the eighth lunar day conjoined with Rohiṇī, or in the month of Śrāvaṇa, or during those two [months], one should perform it when Rohiṇī is conjoined with those two. || 10 || If the eighth lunar day conjoined with Rohiṇī occurs during the month of Śrāvaṇa, then due to that conjunction with Rohiṇī, that too should be known as Jayantī Aṣṭamī; the vow should be observed on that very day. || 10 ||

In the month of Bhādrapada, during the bright fortnight, when it is conjoined with the Jyeṣṭhā asterism, one should perform the worship of Jyeṣṭhā on that day at night. (11) If the eighth lunar day of the bright fortnight of Bhādrapada is joined with the Jyeṣṭhā asterism, then one should perform the worship of the Jyeṣṭhā asterism either on that night or during that day. (11) Where the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of Māgha is joined with midnight, there the vow of Śivarātri should be observed; one shall obtain the fruit of a horse-sacrifice. (12)

Furthermore, when the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of Māgha coincides with midnight, that day is for the Śivarātri vow; it bestows the fruit of the Aśvamedha sacrifice. (12) [In the] vernacular commentary, Chapter 53: (28) For vows observed at night (*naktavrata*), the lunar day (*tithi*) that extends into the evening twilight (*pradoṣa*) should be taken. For all vows involving worship (*pūjāvrata*), it is traditionally taught that the one extending into midday (*madhyāhna*) is to be observed. (13)

In the case of vows observed at night, that lunar day (tithi) which extends through the *pradoṣa* period is accepted; however, for all complete worship-vows (*vrata*), it is said to be that which extends through midday. (13) In the case of eating once a day (*ekabhukta*) or fasting (*upavāsa*), [the tithi] should consist of twenty *ghaṭikās*; likewise, in the consumption of flour-based foods (*piṣṭānna*), it should be free from salt and sourness. (14)

In the vows of eating once (eka-bhukta) or fasting (upavāsa), the lunar day (tithi) that lasts for twenty ghaṭīs is to be accepted. Even in the case of consuming flour-based foods (pīṭhī-padārtha) or when renouncing salt and sourness, the lunar day lasting for the desired twenty ghaṭīs is to be taken. 14. On the fifth day of the bright fortnight of Āṣāḍha, having fasted and not consumed food, one should worship the six-faced god (Kārttikeya) for liberation from debt and disease. 19.

On the fifth day of the bright fortnight of Āṣāḍha, one should not eat; by observing a fast and performing the worship of Lord Kārttikeya (Ṣaṇmukha), debts and diseases are dispelled. (15) Likewise, on the fifth day of the bright fortnight of Śrāvaṇa, there is the worship of the Nāgas; the offering of milk to the serpents leads to liberation from fear and disease. (16) Similarly, on that day—the fifth of the bright fortnight of Śrāvaṇa—there is the worship of the Nāgas. [Disease...]

One should give milk to snakes in order to drive them far away. || 16 || On the fourth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Bhādrapada, one should worship Gaṇanāyaka with offerings of modakas (sweetmeats) for the pacification of all obstacles. || 17 || (286) Nāradasaṃhitā: On the fourth day of the bright fortnight of Bhādrapada, one should perform the worship of Lord Gaṇeśa; by worshipping him with modakas and eating modakas oneself, all obstacles are pacified. || 17 ||

And on the seventh day of the bright fortnight of Māgha, the man who worships the Sun-god and partakes of ghee and milk-rice attains health and prosperity. (18) He who offers side-dishes, sandals, an umbrella, curd, and a vessel of food to the foremost of Brahmins in the month of Vaiśākha does so out of devotion to Dharma. (19)

By giving golden sandals, a pair of shoes, an umbrella, a chowrie, golden ornaments, along with divine food and drink, to excellent Brahmins for the sake of Dharma during the month of Vaiśākha, a person attains heaven. (20) Furthermore, that man who gives these gifts—golden sandals, shoes, an umbrella, curd, food, and a platter—to the best of Brahmins, and who also bestows gold, palanquins, umbrellas, chowries, golden ornaments, and divine food and drink, reaches the celestial realm.

19–20. On the ninth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Āśvayuja, one should worship Lakṣmī, Sarasvatī, and weapons with devotion; such a person shall become victorious and wealthy. 21. By worshipping Lakṣmī, Sarasvatī, and weapons with devotion on the ninth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Āśvina, a man becomes victorious and wealthy. 22. Furthermore, having fasted on the full moon day of either Kārttika or Vaiśākha, a man endowed with devotion who releases a bull for the pleasure of Śiva shall partake in heaven. 22.

Bhāṣā-Ṭīkā-saṃgraha, Chapter 53. (287) On the full moon day of the bright fortnight of Kārttika or Vaiśākha, having observed the vow of fasting, one should release a bull (or set free a plow). A person who acts in this manner with devotion for the pleasure of Lord Śiva attains heaven. || 22 || The signs of the zodiac beginning from Aries—namely, Aquarius, Taurus, Gemini, Virgo, Scorpio, Libra, Sagittarius, Cancer, Capricorn, and Leo—are the "empty" signs starting from Caitra. || 23 ||

Furthermore, Aquarius, Pisces, Taurus, Gemini, Virgo, Scorpio, Libra, Sagittarius, Cancer, Capricorn, and Leo—these signs should be known as void (*śūnya*) in the months of Caitra and the others respectively; for example, Aquarius in Caitra, Pisces in Vaiśākha, and so forth. (23) Now, the void ascendants (*lagna-śūnya*) for the lunar days (*tithi*): On the first lunar day (*pratipad*), Libra and Scorpio are void; on the third, Leo and Scorpio; on the fifth, Gemini and Virgo; and on the seventh, Sagittarius and Cancer. (24)

On the first lunar day (pratipadā), the signs of Libra and Capricorn are devoid of the rising sign (lagna); on the third, Leo and Capricorn; on the fifth, Gemini and Virgo; and on the seventh, Sagittarius and Cancer are devoid of the rising sign. || 24 || On the ninth, Leo and Scorpio; on the eleventh, both are in the house of Jupiter; and on the thirteenth, Pisces and Taurus—these are the signs burnt by the day (dinadagdharāśis). || 25 ||

The ninth lunar day is said to be "poisoned" for Leo and Scorpio; the eleventh is "poisoned" for Sagittarius and Pisces; and the thirteenth is "poisoned" for Pisces and Taurus, as well as for the ascendant (lagna). (25) One should avoid those signs known as "month-poisoned" (māsa-dagdha) and those that are "day-poisoned" (dinadagdha). (26) Thus, one should exclude the month-poisoned signs and the day-poisoned signs. (288) *Nāradasaṃhitā*: Now, the lunar days that are "void" (śūnya) by month: The eighth and ninth lunar days of both fortnights in the month of Caitra [are void].

The twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī) in both fortnights of Vaiśākha is void (śūnyā). (27) One should know that the eighth and ninth lunar days (tithis) in both fortnights of Caitra are void, and the twelfth lunar day in both fortnights of Vaiśākha is void. (27) The thirteenth lunar day of the bright fortnight (śukla) in Jyeṣṭha, the fourteenth in the dark fortnight (kṛṣṇa), the sixth in the dark fortnight of Āṣāḍha, and then the seventh on a Friday (śukre)—(28)

In the month of Jyeṣṭha, the thirteenth day of the bright fortnight and the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight; and in Āṣāḍha, the sixth day of the dark fortnight and the seventh day of the bright fortnight—these should be known as the "void" (śūnya) lunar days. || 28 || Likewise, in Śrāvaṇa, the second day of both fortnights; and in Prauṣṭhapada (Bhādrapada), the second day of the bright fortnight and the first day of the dark fortnight. || 29 ||

In the month of Śrāvaṇa, both the second and third lunar days (tithis) of both fortnights should be known as void; likewise, in the bright or dark fortnight of Bhādrapada, the first and second lunar days are to be known as void. || 29 || In the month of Āśvina, the tenth and eleventh lunar days of both the bright and dark fortnights are void; and in the month of Kārtika, the fourteenth lunar day of the bright fortnight and the fifth (śara) of the dark fortnight are void. || 30 ||

In the month of Āśvina, the tenth and eleventh lunar days (tithis) of both fortnights should be known as "void" (śūnya). In Kārtika, the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight and the fifth day of the dark fortnight should be known as void. || 30 || In Mārgaśīrṣa, which is designated by the numbers seven and eight, the same applies to both fortnights; likewise, in Pauṣa, the fourth and fifth days of both fortnights are void. || 31 ||

In Mārgaśīrṣa, both the seventh and eighth lunar days of both fortnights should be known as void; in Pauṣa, both the fourth and fifth lunar days of both fortnights should be known as void. (31) [Bhāṣāṭīkāsaṃgraha, Chapter 53, Verse 289]. In Māgha, the fifth and sixth [lunar days] of the bright and dark fortnights respectively; and in Phālguna, the third and fourth [lunar days] of both the bright and dark fortnights. (32)

In the month of Māgha, the fifth lunar day (pañcamī) of the bright fortnight and the sixth (ṣaṣṭhī) of the dark fortnight are to be known as void days (śūnyatithi). In the month of Phālguna, the third (tṛtīyā) of the bright fortnight and the fourth (caturthī) of the dark fortnight are to be known as void days. Thus end the void lunar days. Now follows the consideration of the Gaṇḍāntas: Whether it be a son or a daughter born under the unenjoyed portion of Mūla (abhuktamūla), one should abandon them; or else, the father should not look upon their face for eight years. (33)

If a son or daughter born under Mūla is abandoned, or even if they are an eight-year-old child, the father shall not look upon their face until that time. (33) One born in the first quarter of Mūla kills the father; one born in the second quarter kills the mother; one born in the third quarter destroys wealth; and one born in the fourth quarter destroys all possessions. (34)

If a boy is born during the first watch of the Mūla nakṣatra, he destroys the father; if born in the second quarter, he destroys the mother; in the third, he destroys wealth; and in the fourth quarter, he destroys all possessions. (34) One born by day destroys the father, while one born at night likewise destroys the mother; one born during the two twilights destroys oneself. However, there is no Gaṇḍa [doṣa] when it is free from affliction. (35)

If a child is born during the day, it destroys the father; if born at night, it destroys the mother (Nāradasaṃhitā 290); and if born during the two junctions (saṃdhyā), it destroys one's own self. A child born under such a Gaṇḍānta asterism is not free from fault. || 35 || A child born within the interval between Jyeṣṭhā and Mūla is said to be born under "unconsumed" (abhukta) Mūla; the same applies to one born between Āśleṣā (Sārpam) and Maghā. || 36 ||

A child who is born during the watches between the constellations Jyeṣṭhā and Mūla, or one who is born during the watch between Āśleṣā and Maghā, is called an *abhukta-mūlaja*. (36) In that case, a propitiatory rite (*śāntika*) must be performed to remove the defect of the *gaṇḍa* junction; through the performance of such auspicious rites, the danger (*ariṣṭa*) is shattered into a hundred pieces. (37)

In that case, one should perform the pacification (śānti) rite for birth under a Gaṇḍānta asterism; by performing the auspicious rite of pacification, affliction (ariṣṭa) is removed in hundreds of ways. (37) Therefore, one should diligently perform the pacification according to the prescribed rules. [Otherwise,] after one year it destroys the father, but after three years it destroys the mother. (38)

Therefore, one should diligently perform the pacification rites according to the prescribed rules; for if such pacification is not performed, the Gaṇḍānta asterism destroys the father within one year and the mother within three years. (38) It likewise destroys wealth within two years, the father-in-law within nine years, the newborn child within one year, and the elder brother within five years. (39)

In two years it destroys wealth; in nine years it destroys the father-in-law; in one year it destroys that born son; and in five years it destroys the elder brother of the son. 39. It destroys the brother-in-law in eight years; and it destroys those not mentioned [here] in seven years. 40. Thus ends the fifty-third chapter, titled "The Chapter on Various Characteristics such as the Intercalary Month," in the Śrī Nāradīya Saṃhitā. 93.

The *sālāka* (the horse-omen) destroys [the life] within eight years; thus has been stated the duration for one to whom it is inauspicious. Furthermore, even without being explicitly mentioned, it destroys the members of the family within seven years. Thus ends the fifty-third chapter, titled "Various Characteristics such as the Intercalary Month," in the *Bhāṣāṭīkā* commentary on the *Śrī Nāradīya Saṃhitā*. Now begins the Horse-Auspicious Rite (*Aśvaśānti*). I shall proclaim the Horse-Auspicious Rite for the removal of their defects, on Sundays, at the transit of the sun (*saṃkrānti*), during the solstices (*ayana*), and at both the equinoxes (*viṣuvat*). || 1 ||

Now, for the purpose of removing the defects of horses, I shall describe the Horse-Propitiatory Rite (Aśvaśānti). It should be performed on a Sunday, during a solar transit (saṃkrānti), at the time of the northern or southern solstice, or on a day when day and night are equal. || 1 || It may also be performed on the new moon day (dinakṣaya), during the Vyatīpāta yoga, on the twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī), or under the Aśvinī asterism; especially so when the Sun is conjoined with the Svāti asterism. || 2 ||

On the day of a lunar day (tithi) loss, or on the day of Vyatīpāta yoga, or on the twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī) under the asterism Aśvinī, or on a Sunday conjoined with the asterism Svātī. (2) (292) Nāradasaṃhitā: One should construct a pavilion (maṇḍapa) to the northeast, measuring eight or four cubits, adorned with four doors, canopies, arches, and other ornaments. (3)

In the northeast corner (īśāna-kona), one should construct a pavilion (maṇḍapa) measuring eight cubits or four cubits; it should be adorned with four doors, arches (bandanavāla), garlands, gateways (toraṇa), and so forth. (3) In its center, there should be an altar (vedikā) measuring twenty-five [units]; outside the pavilion, to the east, there should be a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) measuring one cubit. (4)

In the middle of the twenty-fifth part (section) of the triple pavilion, one should construct an altar; and outside the pavilion, toward the east, one should construct a sacrificial fire-pit (agni-kuṇḍa) measuring one cubit. || 4 || One should choose Vedic scholars (śrotriya) as Brahmins, preceded by the recitation of auspicious benedictions (svastivācana); [one should worship] the son of the Sun, mounted upon a horse, five-faced, and three-eyed. || 5 ||

Then, after performing the recitation of auspicious verses (*svastivācana*), one should select the Vedic-reciting Brahmins and meditate upon the son of the Sun, mounted upon a horse, five-faced and three-eyed, clad in white garments, bearing a sword, possessing two arms, and known as Raivata. "O son of the Sun, salutations to you! Salutations to you, O five-faced one! (5–6)

One should remember the god Raivanta, who has two arms and holds a shield and a sword, and is white in complexion. "O son of the Sun! O five-faced god, salutations to you! (6). [In the vernacular commentary: (293) With this mantra—"Salutations to the Gandharva god, salutations again and again to Raivanta"—one should worship Raivanta according to the prescribed rites in the center of the altar upon rice-grains, using garments, perfumes, unbroken grains (*akṣata*), and other offerings. (7).

"O Gandharva deity Raivataka, obeisance to you! With this mantra, one should worship Raivataka on that altar according to the prescribed rites, having established him upon rice grains with offerings such as cloth, scents, and unbroken rice (akṣata). || 7 || There, five groups (gaṇas) should be arranged all around Raivataka: the Raudras, the Śākras, the Vaiṣṇavas, along with the Gāṇapatyas and the Sauras. || 8 ||

There, one should establish five types of Gaṇas: the Raudra-gaṇa, the Indra-gaṇa, the Vaiṣṇava-gaṇa, the Gaṇeśa-gaṇa, and the Sūrya-gaṇa; these should be established on all four sides of Raivata. (8) One should worship the four Vedas, beginning with the Ṛgveda, at the eastern and other doors. (9) [One should place] full jars of red color, adorned with cloth, perfumes, and so forth.

Having filled [the vessels] with the five barks (*pañcavalkala*), the five sprouts (*pañcapallava*), and the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*), and having adorned the full pitchers (*pūrṇakalaśa*) of red color with garments, perfumes, and other offerings, one should place them at the doors and worship the Brahmins with the mantras of those [deities]. Thus, the preceptor (*ācārya*), having performed the worship according to the rules of the *Gṛhya-sūtras*, [should proceed]. (Nāradasaṃhitā 11)

Having established [the deities] at the four doors, he should perform the individual worship of four Brāhmaṇas there with the mantras of each respective Veda; thus the Ācārya performs the worship according to the family tradition. (11) Then, with the Vyāhṛtis, he should establish the sacrificial fire in that pit; thereafter, at the conclusion of the portion of clarified butter (ājyabhāga), he should, being vigilant, offer the principal oblation. (12) Then, with the Vyāhṛtis, he should establish the fire in that pit.

Then, becoming very attentive, one should offer the *ājyabhāga* oblations and then present the principal oblations. (12) Having first carefully offered to Agni with clarified butter, saying "Svāhā to Agni," one should likewise offer the first oblation with the *pūjā-mantra* and with the *praṇava*. (13) One should offer one hundred and eight oblations of *palāśa* wood, clarified butter, and cooked rice; thereafter, one should devotedly offer sesame seeds individually with the *vyāhṛtis*. (14)

First, one should diligently perform the *homa* with clarified butter using the mantra "Agnaye Svāhā. Reciting the syllable *Oṃ* at the beginning and end of such worship-mantras, one should offer one hundred and eight (*aṣṭottaraśatam*) oblations of *palāśa* wood, clarified butter, sesame seeds, and rice. Then, prefixing each mantra with the *vyāhṛtis* "Bhūr Bhuvaḥ" and so forth, one should perform the *homa* with sesame seeds. [1.3.14] This may be done for one night, three nights, or even nine nights.

One who has conquered the senses should perform this according to the prescribed method and to the best of one's ability—whether for one night, three nights, or nine nights. Having performed the recitation (*japa*) and other preliminaries, the performer should properly offer the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*). Then, amidst auspicious sounds, one should present the food offering (*naivedya*). (Bhāṣāṭīkā, Section 54, Verse 295)

The patron (yajamāna), preceded by the recitation of mantras (japa) and other rites—meaning having offered oblations (āhuti) equal to one-tenth of all the recitations—should then perform the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti). Next, he should offer the food-offering (naivedya) accompanied by auspicious words. Then, O twice-born ones, those brahmins, proceeding clockwise with the remnants of the oblations and with water from the ritual jars, should circumambulate the horse Jayanta, the most excellent sacrificial offering (bali). || 17 ||

Then those four Brahmins, having released the streams from the four jars while moving to the right of the horses, should offer the excellent Jayaṃta bali with the remnants of the oblation. (17) One should scatter [the offerings] in the four directions while reciting the Anuvāka beginning with "jīmūtasya. Then one should give five gold coins as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the preceptor (ācārya). (18)

Furthermore, one should offer oblations in the four directions using the mantra words from the section beginning with "jīmūtasya. Then, one should give five palas (twenty suvarṇas) of gold to the preceptor; or half of that, or half of that again, according to one's capacity. One should also give sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) to the officiating priests, such as a cow, clothing, wealth, and so forth.

One should give a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) of three hundred, or even half of that, according to one's capacity; and cows, clothing, and wealth should be given as the fee for the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*). (19) Afterwards, one should feed the Brahmins, preceded by the recitation of the *Śāntivācana*. He who thus properly performs this unsurpassed propitiation of the horse (*aśvaśānti*)—(20)

Furthermore, having first performed the recitation of auspicious verses (svastivācana), he should feed the Brahmins; that man who thus properly performs the excellent Aśva-śānti [attains his goal]. || 20 || He obtains prosperity for his horses and the fortune of a hero, without a doubt. By means of this sacrifice, Dhātṛ, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara are fully satisfied. || 21 ||

He attains an abundance of horses and the fortune of heroic warriors; of this there is no doubt. Furthermore, through this sacrifice, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Mahādeva become pleased. (21) All the planets beginning with Āditya, the ancestors, and the hosts [of deities] become gratified; the world-protectors, the Piśācas, and the hosts of Ḍākinīs are also satisfied. (22)

Furthermore, the Sun and all other planets, the hosts of ancestors (Pitṛs), the world-protectors (Lokapālas), the Piśācas, and the Gaṇas of Ḍākinīs—all these become propitiated. (22) The Bhūtas, Pretas, Gandharvas, Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, and Pannagas—(23) all these also become propitiated. (23) Thus ends the fifty-fourth chapter, the Miśrakādhyāya, in the Śrī Nāradīya Saṃhitā. [Thus concludes the Aśvaśānti.]

Thus ends the fifty-fourth chapter, the Chapter on Miscellaneous Matters, in the Bhāṣā-Ṭīkā on the Śrī-Nāradīya-Saṃhitā. Now begins the Chapter on the Characteristics of Śrāddha: The fourteenth lunar day, the Nandā and Bhadrā tithis, Fridays, the setting of Venus and Jupiter, a double-footed asterism, and an odd-footed asterism [are inauspicious]. (1)

On the fourteenth lunar day (caturdaśī), the Nandā and Bhadrā tithis, on Tuesdays, Fridays, and Saturdays; during the setting of Jupiter or Venus; under a nakṣatra with two feet (dvicaraṇa) or an odd-footed nakṣatra (viṣamāṅghri)—such as Kṛttikā, which has one foot in Aries and is thus odd-footed, or Mṛgaśiras, which has half a foot in Taurus and is thus two-footed—one should know this to apply everywhere. || 1 || Having abandoned the bright fortnight (śuklapakṣa), one should again perform the excellent cremation (dahana). || 1 ||

In the five constellations from the latter half of Dhaniṣṭhā, during the three births [of the moon], the second marriage (paunarbhava) performed under the constellations of Revatī and Rohiṇī leads to the destruction of the family. This should be done during the latter half of the day, when the performer is endowed with the strength of the moon and the stars. || 2-3 ||

Furthermore, it is best to perform the cremation of a *preta* by means of the *puttalavidhāna* (effigy rite) and other methods after abandoning the bright fortnight (*śuklapakṣa*). However, if the rites of the *puttalavidhāna* and cremation are performed during the latter half of Dhaniṣṭhā and the other five *pañcakas*, or during the *tripuṣkara* yoga, or under the asterisms of Revatī and Rohiṇī, the destruction of the family occurs; yet this applies except on the day following midday and for one who performs the rite on a day when the moon and stars are favorable. || 2 || 3 ||

When a malefic planet is endowed with strength and Venus is not present in the ascendant or its navāṃśa, that cremation is said to be auspicious; now the time for the Śrāddha rite is described. (4) Thus, it is auspicious to perform the cremation rite at a moment when a malefic planet is strong and Venus is not in the ascendant. Now the times for the Śrāddha are stated: (298) Nāradasaṃhitā: The Sapindīkaraṇa rite should be performed after one year, or after a year and a half, or after three months, or after three fortnights, or monthly, or on the twelfth day. (9)

The Sapiṇḍīkaraṇa rite should be performed on the anniversary of the death, or within six months; it is auspicious to perform the Sapiṇḍīkaraṇa after three months, or one and a half months, or on the twelfth day following the cremation rite. || 5 || On these very occasions, these sixteen Ekoddiṣṭa rites are performed; [they are also forbidden] under Kṛttikā, on a Nandā tithi, on a Saturday, or during the three birth-asterisms (trijanma). || 6 ||

At this very time, one should perform the sixteen Ekoddiṣṭa Śrāddhas during the Kṛttikā nakṣatra, the Nandā tithis, Friday, and the Tripuṣkara yoga. (6) The offering of Piṇḍas should not be performed [on these occasions], as it causes the destruction of the lineage; likewise on the three births, the three-quartered asterisms, the Nandā tithis, and on Friday. (7)

One should not perform the offering of funeral cakes (*piṇḍadāna*), for by performing it, the lineage of the performer is destroyed. [This applies during] the *triṣūṣkara-yoga*—that is, a constellation consisting of three quarters, such as Punarvasu (which has three quarters, while Mithuna has four)—and on Friday. || 7 || The Śrāddha should not be performed under the asterisms of Rohiṇī (*dhātṛ*) and Revatī (*pauṣṇa*), because of the destruction of the family; nor on the *Nandā* tithis, on Friday (*bhṛgurvāra*), under Kṛttikā, or during the three birth-asterisms (*trijanmasu*). || 8 ||

(299) One should not perform the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* and other *śrāddhas* under the asterisms of Tripuṣkara, Rohiṇī, or Maghā; however, one should certainly perform the *mahālaya śrāddha*—that is, the *pārvaṇa śrāddha* for the ancestors—during the dark fortnight (*kanāgata*) of the month of Bhādrapada, as well as all other complete or incomplete *śrāddhas*. 8–9. Indeed, one should contemplate all of this regarding the deceased when the month of Bhādrapada has arrived and its dark fortnight has set in. 10.

In the case of Śrāddhas performed with common desires, this aforementioned consideration of the Muhūrta should be observed during the dark fortnight of the month of Bhādrapada. (10) If one is unable to perform the Śrāddha every day, one should perform it once on a distinguished day, endowed with the strength of the moon and the stars. (11)

One should perform the Śrāddha even for a destitute person just once; however, for one who performs it on other auspicious moments, the Śrāddha should be performed when the Moon and the stars are in their full strength. (11) The Nandā lunar days are censured [for this purpose], while for those killed by weapons, the fourteenth day (Bhūtā) is recommended. The second lunar day is to be known as mediocre, and the third lunar day conjoined with the Bharaṇī constellation is likewise [to be avoided]. (12)

One should avoid the Nanda-tithis (the first, sixth, and eleventh lunar days) and perform the Śrāddha for those who died by the stroke of a weapon on the fourteenth day (Caturdaśī). The second lunar day is a middling tithi, while the third is joined with the Bharaṇī asterism. || 12 || If the fourth lunar day is also worshipful, it bestows prosperity in rites for the ancestors; furthermore, the Ānanda-yoga occurs on the fifth day when the moon is situated in the Yāmya (Bharaṇī) asterism. || 13 ||

Alternatively, the fourth lunar day is the best for rites for the ancestors (*pitṛkarma*), as it bestows prosperity (*lakṣmī*). If the fifth lunar day falls on Monday under the *Bharaṇī* nakṣatra, one should recognize it as the "Yoga of Bliss" (*ānandayoga*) for ancestral rites. (30.0) Nāradasaṃhitā: He who feeds the ancestors on that [fifth] day shall obtain sons, grandsons, and wealth. The seventh lunar day brings fame, while the eighth bestows enjoyment (*bhoga*). 14.

The son who feeds the ancestors there obtains progeny and wealth; the seventh lunar day (saptamī) brings fame in the performance of śrāddha rites, and the eighth (aṣṭamī) bestows enjoyment. The ninth (navamī) grants all desired fruits to the performer of the śrāddha. When the sun has entered Virgo (kanyā) and the moon is situated in the Raudra asterism (Ārdrā), || 15 ||

Furthermore, for one performing a Śrāddha on the ninth lunar day (navamī), all desires are fulfilled when the Sun is in the sign of Virgo (Kanyārāśi) and the Moon enters the Ārdrā constellation on that very day. On the seventh, eighth, and likewise on the ninth lunar day, this conjunction brings welfare to the ancestors; on such an occasion, one should worship the Pitṛs.

If the seventh, eighth, or ninth lunar day (tithi) occurs, this is called the yoga named Pitṛkalyāṇa; in this yoga, one should perform the worship of the ancestors. By doing so, one attains prosperity in this world and subsequently reaches heaven. On the tenth lunar day, when the Puṣya asterism is present, there is an excellent yoga known as Amṛta. || 16-17 ||

A person who worships the ancestors during the aforementioned conjunction attains prosperity in this world and reaches heaven in the next. If the Puṣya asterism occurs on the tenth lunar day, it forms the beautiful conjunction known as Amṛta. (17) [Bhāṣāṭīkā, Chapter 55, Verse 301]: Those ancestors who are worshipped there shall remain eternally satisfied with him.

The twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī) is the most excellent for the performer [of the rite], bestowing all prosperity. In this conjunction, the ancestors of one who performs the worship remain eternally satisfied; and for the performer, the patron, it is said that the twelfth lunar day is supreme, granting every kind of wealth. (18) On the thirteenth and fourteenth lunar days, there is loss of wealth and wife. However, the thirteenth lunar day known as Gajacchāyā bestows the fruit of infinite merit. (19)

If one performs a *śrāddha* on the thirteenth or fourteenth lunar day, there will be loss of wealth and wife; however, the thirteenth day joined with the *gajacchāyā* yoga bestows infinite meritorious fruit. (19) In the rite of *śrāddha*, the new moon (*amāvāsyā*) bestows the fruit of the fortnightly *śrāddha*; that is, performing the *śrāddha* for fifteen days yields its full merit. (20)

One who bestows *śrāddha* under the two *Pauṣṇa* stars, the four beginning with *Puṣya*, the three beginning with *Hasta*, the four beginning with *Maitra*, the two beginning with *Saumya*, and the three beginning with *Śravaṇa* shall possess many sons. Thus ends the fifty-sixth chapter, titled "The Characteristics of Śrāddha," in the *Śrī Nāradīya Saṃhitā*. [The asterisms are: Revatī, Aśvinī, the four beginning with Puṣya, the three beginning with Hasta, the four beginning with Anurādhā, and the two beginning with Mṛgaśiras. (302) *Nāradasaṃhitā*.

A person who performs a *śrāddha* during these three asterisms—Śravaṇa and the others—becomes possessed of many sons; that is, performing a *śrāddha* on the days of these asterisms is excellent. (21) Thus ends the fifty-fifth chapter, titled "The Characteristics of Śrāddha," in the *Bhāṣā-Ṭīkā* on the *Śrī-Nāradīya-Saṃhitā*. (55)

Thus ends the *Nāradasaṃhitā*, together with its commentary named *Saralā*, composed by Rāma, son of the twice-born Śāligrāma, a resident of the city of Vātaverī in the region of Indraprastha. May there be auspiciousness! May prosperity attend! Verse 1: In the year marked by the Vedas (4), the arrows (5), and the digits (9) [i.e., 1494], during the bright fortnight of the month of Taiṣa, on the full moon day under the constellation Kavi (Śukra), this commentary reached completion. This work is finished.
Place for obtaining the book: Khemarāja Śrīkṛṣṇadāsa, “Śrīveṅkaṭeśvara” Press, Bombay. Books for sale (Jyotiṣa texts)—Price: Rs. 1.00.

A-5: *Sūryasiddhānta* with the Sanskrit commentary *Gūḍhārthadīpikā* and the Hindi translation by Baladevaprasāda Miśra. This work contains: the divisions of time; the causes of planetary motion; the determination of the prime meridian (east-west lines) and other directions; the true positions of the Moon, Sun, and other planets; the knowledge of shadows (*chāyājñāna*); lunar parallax (*candra-lambana*); solar eclipses; the calculation of the *pāta* (node); the observation of stars; the determination of the times of heliacal rising and setting; the rising of the moon; the chapter on eclipses (*pātādhikāra*); spiritual science (*adhyātmavidyā*); and celestial instruments (*golayantra*).

There are many subjects such as the determination of the *kola* (time-unit) and others. (2) *Siddhāntadaivajñavinoda*, composed by Paṇḍita Maṇirāma, accompanied by a Sanskrit commentary and a Hindi translation (*Āṣāṭīkā*). This work contains: the determination of auspicious moments (*muhūrta-nirṇaya*), the investigation into the formless body (*amūrta-kāya-mīmāṃsā*), descriptions of terrestrial geography (*bhūgola*) and celestial spheres (*khagola*), the calculation of the number of days since creation (*sṛṣṭi-ahargaṇa*), the method for calculating mean planetary positions (*madhyama-graha-anayana-vidhiḥ*), the calculation of the apogees (*mandocca*) of the planets, the calculation of the nodes (*pāta*) of Mars and other planets, the sequential computation of the true positions (*sphuṭīkaraṇa*) of the planets, and the method for calculating the true positions of Mars and the other planets.

The methods for calculating lunar and solar eclipses, examples of planetary conjunctions (graha-yuddha), the numerous yogas of the lunar mansions (nakṣatras), the rules for heliacal rising and setting, the method for determining the strength of the five-fold calendar (pañcāṅga), the annual almanac (upakaraṇa-sāriṇī), the method for calculating the movement of planets through the nakṣatras and zodiac signs, the Vyāmuhuja and Āgākṣara tables, the birth chart (janmapatrī) of Rasaja, the procedure for writing the pañcāṅga, and the determination of religious vows (vrata) and other matters have been demonstrated here; these are fit to be acquired by astrologers. ... 2) Notice. 3 4 3 6 p.

Q: The mathematical section of *Paramasiddhāntajyotiṣa* composed by Premacaṇḍabhaṭṭa covers the following subjects: knowledge of the celestial sphere (*gola-jñāna*), mean motion (*madhyama-adhikāra*), true motion (*spaṣṭa-adhikāra*), calculation of the ascensional difference (*carārdha*), determination of rising and setting (*udayāsta-adhikāra*), calculation of the three parallax corrections (*triprakṣepa*), calculation of the altitude of the zenith distance (*gonnaya*), the chapter on eclipses (*grahaṇa-adhikāra*), the chapter on lunar nodes (*pāta-yaṃtra-adhikāra*), the chapter on instruments (*yantra-adhikāra*), and the determination of location (*deśajñāna*) and other related topics.

2) *Grahalāghava*: The original text composed by Gaṇeśa Daivajña, along with the *Anvaya* commentary and examples composed by Paṇḍita Rāmasvarūpa; this work on calculation (*gaṇita*) is considered unprecedented, and all inhabitants of India hold it in high esteem. 1U *Līlāvatī*: The original text composed by Bhāskarācārya, together with the Hindi commentary composed by Rāmasvarūpa; it is unprecedented in the field of algebraic calculation (*vyakta-gaṇita*), and by means of it, one can perform all types of calculations. Furthermore... 1U? And...

*Rapha* ... ... ... ... ... 1U *Karṇakutūhala* with commentary and examples—a mathematical treatise belonging to the Balapa school. *Siddhāntaśiromaṇi* (namely, the *Golādhyāya* with its vernacular commentary). In this work, the exposition of the *Golādhyāya* begins with the "Praise of the Sphere" (*Golapraśaṃsā*).

The following subjects have been clearly elucidated: questions regarding the nature of the celestial sphere (gola-svarūpa), the terrestrial globe (bhuvana-kośa), the astronomical rationale for mean motion (madhya-gati-vāsanā), the rationale for true motion (sphuṭa-gati-vāsanā), the rationale for constructing the celestial sphere and the three problems thereof (golabandha-triprabhā-vāsanā), the rationale for eclipses (grahaṇa-vāsanā), the correction for rising and setting (udayāsta-dṛkkarma), the rationale for the non-eclipsed portion and the altitude of the lunar horns (śṛṅgonati-vāsanā), the chapter on instruments (yantra-adhyāya), descriptions of various instruments, inquiry into questions (praśna-vicāra), the origin of the Jyotiṣa (jyotpatti), and the detailed exposition of the origin of the Jyotiṣa (jyotpatti-vivaraṇa). Khemarāja Śrīkṛṣṇadāsa, "Śrī Veṅkaṭeśvara" Steam Press, Bombay.
